en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Root Commentary on the Five Treatises in the Abhidhamma Piṭaka.
Commentary on the Introduction to the *Dhātukathāpakaraṇa-mūlaṭīkā*:
In order to show the time at which the Blessed One taught the *Dhātukathāpakaraṇa*, [the author] indicates that it was immediately after the *Vibhaṅga*.
Or, in order to show that the treatise being taught has the nature of a *dhātukathā* (discourse on elements), he says, "eighteenfold," and so forth.

In this context, because the Māra of the son of a god (*devaputtamāra*) was shattered at the foot of the Bodhi tree by means of overcoming the domain of his assault with power; because the Māras of the defilements (*kilesamāra*) and volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhāramāra*) were shattered by means of making them no longer arise;

and because the Māra of the aggregates (*khandhamāra*) and the Māra of death (*maccumāra*) were shattered by means of the full understanding (*pariññā*) that abandons their origin; [the eighteenfold nature is established].
Because that crushing [of Māra] was unsurpassed and devoid of dependence on others, the Blessed One alone is praised as "the Crusher of Māra" (Mārabhañjana).
In this context, he is called "the Crusher of Māra" because he crushed Māra, or because crushing Māra belongs to him, and not because he crushed other kings and so forth.
He is a "Great Hero" (Mahāvīra) because he is greatly expansive and possesses great energy.

The phenomena beginning with the aggregates and ending with the bases of conflict (*araṇa*) are called "elements" (*dhātu*) in the sense of their intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), or they are so called in the sense of being the foundation for discourse on the Abhidhamma;
because this treatise discusses them, its designation is *Dhātukathā* (Discourse on Elements).

Although those intrinsic natures have been discussed in other treatises as well, here, however, all of them are treated in relation to the fourteen topics such as inclusion (*saṅgaha*) and non-inclusion (*asaṅgaha*).
Because it is taught with particular excellence within each of the methods (*nayā*), this very work bears this name. For elsewhere, only partial explanations were given.

Alternatively, since the methods concerning the inclusion and non-inclusion of the aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth—up to the bases without conflict (*araṇa*)—are stated by way of the aggregates, bases, and elements, herein the discussion is by way of the elements because they have a wide scope; thus it is called the *Dhātukathā*.

It should be understood that its name has been stated. Because it "proclaimed the analysis of elements in two ways, three ways, six ways, eighteen ways—in many ways," it is called the *Dhātubhedappakāsana* (The Exposition of the Analysis of Elements).
Its meaning (*tassattha*) is the meaning of that *Dhātukathā*. One should understand that the letter *a* is the elision of the vowel *ā*.
Alternatively, the word *pakaraṇa* (treatise) is to be supplied here [in the compound] as "the *Dhātukathā* treatise" (*yaṃ dhātukathaṃ*). It refers to the seven...
Because the commentary proceeds according to the sequence of the treatises (*pakaraṇa*), one forms the connection by saying "the meaning of that treatise" (*tassattha*);

alternatively, there is the elision of the vowel *a* [in the compound], resulting in "its meaning" (*tassattha*). "Listen to that exposition" (*taṃ dīpanaṃ suṇātha*)—or rather, "attend to that meaning through hearing the words that expound it"—is the sense.
"Composed" (*samāhitā*) means those whose minds are not distracted by various duties, or whose minds are placed within their own hearts.
The commentary on the commencement of the book is finished.
1. Commentary on the Matrix (Mātikā). 1.
Commentary on the Matrix of Methods (Nayamātikā).
1. What, then, is the division (*pariccheda*) of this treatise? It need not be stated here, as the division of the treatise has already been explained in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*;
thus, showing this, he said: "It is stated to be analyzed in fourteen ways.

These are called "guides" (*naya*) because by means of them the teaching on the aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth is led (*nīyati*) or set in motion, or because by these modes the aggregates and so forth themselves are led—that is, made known.
The *nayamātikā* is the enumeration of the matrices (*mātikā*) of the methods (*naya*), or the methods themselves are the matrix; thus it is called the "matrix of methods.

It is called the "root matrix" because it serves as the root for these fourteen terms—such as inclusion and non-inclusion—which ought to be called so by virtue of being the foundation for this treatise that analyzes phenomena such as the aggregates.
The meaning is that it serves as the basis for the analysis of these phenomena.
2. Explanation of the Internal Matrix (Abbhantaramātikāvaṇṇanā) 2.
By the words "the five aggregates" (*pañcakkhandhā*) and so forth, the terms for the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*) and the others are shown;

and by the expression "dependent origination" (*paṭiccasamuppāda*), there are twelve [terms] whose meanings correspond to those twelve factors (*aṅga*) in which the term "dependent origination" applies individually.

Regarding the phrase "the terms have been shown," he says "by means of one hundred and twenty-five terms" with reference to those terms— such as contact (phassa) and so forth— which were shown in their specific forms,
and which were shown in that manner. In this context, because karma, rebirth, sensual existence (kāmabhava), and so forth, which are analyzed here,

are not undesirable in the same way that sorrow (soka) and so forth are undesirable in relation to existence (bhava), nor is aging-and-death (jarāmaraṇa) [undesirable] in relation to becoming (bhava) through the state of being a process of becoming (bhāvanabhavana).

Furthermore, because they exist as suffering caused by that [craving] and because they are included within aging and death, the dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) should be understood as having twelve factors. And here,
it should be understood that by taking up even the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) and so forth—
which were not explicitly separated in the text— by separating them, he demonstrates that they too ought to be explained separately.
The matrices beginning with the *Nayamātikā* and ending with the *Lakkhaṇamātikā* are called the "matrix of the *Dhātukathā*" because they are not shared with other treatises (*pakaraṇa*).
Within that [matrix], the enumeration of those things to be analyzed is called the "internal matrix. Explaining this point, he said, "For this...
and so forth. Therein, "without saying thus" refers to how [the text] says, "All... [etc. ...the matrix."
The meaning is: "not stated outside of the *Dhātukathā-mātikā*";
and "within the *Dhātukathā* itself" should be understood as "within the *Dhātukathā-mātikā* itself.
For when something is placed within the *āveṇika-mātikā*, it is said to be placed within that very [matrix]. Alternatively, "not stated thus" means, for example: "all... [and so forth].

By this statement, “the matrix (mātikā),” it is meant that the matrix—beginning with the wholesome and ending with the non-conflicting—which is not included within the *Dhātukathā* and belongs to another treatise, has been mentioned;
the sense is that it was not stated [there]. And by the phrase “within the *Dhātukathā* itself,” the meaning is that it was established by being shown in its own form within this very treatise.
This is because [that matrix] is not included in the matrix of the entire Abhidhamma.
The state of being "scattered" (pakiṇṇaka) should be understood by way of their being dispersed.
3. Commentary on the Matrix of the Gateways of Methods (Nayamukha-mātikā):

The phenomena that constitute the doors for the occurrence of the methods—namely, those that are included or not included, and those that are dissociated or associated—are the "gateways of methods" (nayamukha). Of these...

The enumeration (uddesa) is the matrix of the methods (nayamukha-mātikā). For indeed, even the fourteen compendia proceed by way of the mixture of inclusion, non-inclusion, conjunction, and disjunction;
those factors by which these four [compendia] exist are the "gates" (mukhāni) of all fourteen methods.
In that regard, although inclusion and non-inclusion may occur, as far as possible, through the Truths and so forth, within the categories of the included and the non-included, etc.:
However, that [statement] was spoken by those [categories] acting as the *saṅgāhaka* (the encompassers), not by those acting as the *saṅgaha* (the encompassed).

Furthermore, even in the extraction of the phenomena to be questioned and answered—beginning with "Those phenomena which are included under the aggregate-inclusion by means of the eye-base, but are not included under the base-inclusion"—it was stated there too by defining them specifically through the inclusions of aggregates and so forth.
Therefore, it is said: "Inclusion by three; non-inclusion by three."

It has been stated. Furthermore, in the extraction of the phenomena to be asked about and answered, as well as in the questions and answers themselves, since the aggregates beginning with the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) and ending with the unconditioned (araṇa) have, as applicable, association and dissociation only with the four aggregates, it is said:
"association with four, dissociation with four."
But surely there is dissociation from both material form (*rūpa*) and Nibbāna as well; why then is it said, "dissociation from four"?

Because even for one who exists with material form and Nibbāna, [dissociation] occurs only from four [aggregates]. For material form is not dissociated from material form or from Nibbāna, nor is Nibbāna dissociated from material form;
rather, it occurs only from the four aggregates. Thus, [the term refers to] dissociation from the four aggregates, excluding material form and Nibbāna.
Dissociation, too, is determined by the four aggregates that are dissociated from it, because there is no dissociation apart from them.
Furthermore, this dissociation does not occur for that which is without an object (anārammaṇa) with those that are without an object, nor for that which is mixed with those without an object;

however, it occurs for that which is without an object with that which has an object (sārammaṇa), and for that which has an object with both that which has an object and that which is without an object.
And it should be understood that [it] exists by way of combination.
4. Commentary on the Summary of Characteristics:

"Combination" (saṅgaha) is itself the method of combination. Regarding the terms "homogeneous" (sabhāga) and "heterogeneous" (visabhāga), [it is said]: "By three [factors] there is combination; by three [factors] there is non-combination."
By this, the connection should also be made separately with the statement: "Conjunction with four, disjunction with four. By that, the following meaning is understood:
that which is both inclusive and non-inclusive is both homogeneous and heterogeneous; likewise for conjunction and disjunction.
Or else, that phenomenon (dhamma) which possesses both inclusion and non-inclusion is both homogeneous and heterogeneous; likewise...
That which has both association and dissociation is likewise both similar and dissimilar.

In this context, that common nature—beginning with "being affected" (ruppana) and so forth—by which the aggregates such as matter (*rūpakkhandha*) up to the mind-consciousness element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*) are included in a reckoning, is "similarity" (*sabhāgatā*) in the sense of inclusion;
while that beginning with "arising together" (*ekuppāda*) and so forth is to be understood as "association" (*sampayoga*).
5. Explanation of the External Matrix (Bāhiramātikāvaṇṇanā) 5.

Because it is established outside the matrix of the *Dhātukathā*, the meaning is that it is placed externally, following after [the main text] by way of this method of arrangement, as indicated by the phrase: "All... [etc.
...the matrix. Or rather, by this method of arrangement, [it treats] the categories beginning with the wholesome (*kusala*) and ending with the non-conflict (*araṇa*).

The meaning is: having set aside here [the previous section], because this [present] treatise has been established as a matrix (*mātikā*) distinct from the matrices of other treatises outside the *Dhātukathā*, and because it has been presented in that manner.
Regarding [the categories] such as "inclusion" (*saṅgaha*) and "non-inclusion" (*asaṅgaha*), inclusion is of only one kind; why then is it said to be "fourfold"? [It is because] inclusion...
Because it was stated merely as a word whose meaning has not been determined, without explaining its specific sense.
Regarding the words "inclusion" (*saṅgaha*) and "non-inclusion" (*asaṅgaha*), etc., the meaning here is this: first, the word "inclusion" is fourfold according to its own respective meanings.

Alternatively, the meaning itself—when its particular distinctions have not been determined and has reached a state where it must be grasped in a general sense—is what is expressed as "inclusion" in such phrases as "inclusion and non-inclusion"; thus, there is no contradiction.
This is a fault. For if the specific distinction were excluded, there would be a single uniformity for it, and not [a variety] prior to that.

Because the word *jāti* (birth/class) is a term requiring a correlative, when it is said "the inclusion by birth" (*jāti-saṅgaho*), it is understood as "by its own birth," since no other related term has been stated.
Thus, what is called "inclusion by birth" (*jāti-saṅgaho*) in the *Rūpa-kaṇḍa* is actually an inclusion by genus (*sajāti-saṅgaho*).

Here, in the matrix of methods (*naya-mātikā*), the two [methods]—"inclusion" (*saṅgaha*) and "non-inclusion" (*asaṅgaha*), and "association" (*sampayoga*) and "dissociation" (*vippayoga*)"—are general enumerations of the methods for questioning and answering regarding phenomena (*dhamma*) without specifying the particularities of the phenomena to be questioned and answered. The remaining [methods], however, are [enumerated] after having specified them.
For instance, when it should have been stated as "the non-included by means of the included" or "the non-included by means of the non-included," only one [term] is used.

The elision of the word *asaṅgahita* (unincluded) is to be understood. By that [elision], the method of question and answer—characterized as "the state of being unincluded" (*asaṅgahitatā*)—is indicated, which depends upon a specific dhamma that is itself unincluded but distinguished by a qualifier that is included (*saṅgahita*). Furthermore, in the phrase "by what is included" (*saṅgahitena*), the instrumental case is to be understood as a qualifying term.
This same method applies to the series of indications of the methods beginning with the third and ending with the tenth.

[This applies] to those [categories] excluding the sixth. For in those as well, having established the determination of the specific qualities of the phenomena to be asked about and answered by means of two pairs of terms according to the method already stated, the methods of questioning and answering are indicated there at each point by a third term similar to the final one.

Among these, in the fourth and fifth [categories], there is a designation of the instrument (*karaṇa*) in the sense of the agent (*kattū*); and in the four beginning with the seventh, it occurs in connection with accompaniment (*sahayoga*).
It should be understood as such, and not like the qualifiers used in the second and third [sections], where there is a common substratum (*samānādhikaraṇa*).
For in those cases, one class of phenomena (*sabhāva*) is qualified by another class of phenomena; whereas in these [sections], one phenomenon (*dhamma*) is qualified by another phenomenon.
However, in the four sections beginning with the eleventh, the specific determination of the phenomena is made by the first phrase alone, while the others follow the method of question and answer.
They have been enumerated. And here, the use of the instrumental case should be understood specifically in the sense of "distinction.

For the states that serve as the basis for the questions and answers distinguish their own associated or dissociated nature by means of the instrumental factor consisting of distinctions such as being included [in a particular category] and so forth.

"By way of alternative" (*vikappato*) means by way of various conceptualizations; the meaning is "by way of classification. "By way of determination" (*sanniṭṭhānavasena*) means by way of association with resolve (*adhimokkha*).
And "all mental arousings spoken of by way of resolution" means all mental arousings spoken of by way of resolution;
the meaning here should be understood as "by way of their commonality.
For resolution is stated as common to all those mental arousings spoken of by way of resolution, while the others are common to all [mental states]. In that regard, they are common.
The *pasaṭā* and *pākaṭā* [categories] should be grasped first; therefore, the enumeration (*uddesa*) was made for the purpose of grasping their inclusion (*saṅgaha*) and so forth.

Furthermore, since those that are not common [to all] must also be grasped, *adhimokkha* (resolute conviction) was enumerated among them to show the inclusion and so forth of others as well, by way of its broad scope.
And it is stated in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī-aṭṭhakathā*: "It is spoken of by way of definitive determination (*sanniṭṭhāna*)."
It should be understood that this was stated with reference to the wording in the *Paṭiccasamuppādavibhaṅga*.

However, since there is a sense in which all those [mental factors] mentioned by way of definitive determination are common to all, when it comes to discussing those that are both common and uncommon,
it is stated [here] by way of that resolve (*adhimokkha*) which has a wide range among the uncommon ones, because it is common to all mental states mentioned.

Contact and the other [mental factors] are common to all [consciousnesses]; however, resolve (adhimokkha) is described here because it has a vast object among those factors that are not common [to all], since no other such factor exists—this is how the intended meaning should be understood.

Furthermore, the life-faculty (jīvitindriya) is not mentioned here because it is mixed with matter (rūpa); on the other hand, one-pointedness of mind (cittekaggatā) is not included because its nature is not that of concentration (samādhi).

Since there is no other state of the same nature as concentration that must be pervaded, excluded, or negated by the general term *sāmāñña* itself, or by the general and particular terms [of the three trainings],
it is to be described by means of general and particular terms that illuminate its distinctions— terms that indicate the divisions of that very phenomenon—
and not by terms whose characteristics are contrary to what has been stated, as is the case with feeling (*vedanā*), which has the nature of pleasure and so forth.

Because of the ambiguity between the general and specific terms, the word "one-pointedness of mind" (*cittekaggatā*)—being a general term that functions independently of a specific term regarding the intrinsic nature of concentration—would itself become a specific term and indicate only that which is not of the nature of concentration; whereas the other [term] would indicate only that which is of the nature of concentration.
Thus, one-pointedness of mind would be divided into two types, being both uncommon and having a limited scope; [this is not the case] here.

It does not merit inclusion in the summary (uddesa). Alternatively, because it lacks the manifest quality like contact (phassa) and the other [mental factors], and because it must be described as depending on another dhamma, it does not merit being called "life" (jīvita); thus, it was not included in the summary.
The commentary on the matrix (mātikā) is finished.
2. Commentary on the Exposition (Niddesavaṇṇanā) 1.
The First Method: Commentary on the Terms of Inclusion and Non-Inclusion 1.
Commentary on the Terms of the Aggregates (Khandhapadavaṇṇanā)
6. In the Great Treatise on the Aggregates, Bases, and Elements (*Khandhāyatanadhātu-mahāpakaraṇa*), these are stated as phenomena to be directly known (*abhiññeyya-dhamma*).

However, for the purpose of showing the specific qualities—such as being fully understood (*pariññeyyatā*)—of those phenomena already known through direct knowledge by way of their intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), the Truths (*sacca*) are stated; and for the purpose of showing the specific functions such as predominance (*adhipati-kicca*), the Faculties (*indriya*) and so forth are stated.

Thus, just like the distinction between the Truths and the rest, the distinction between what is included and what is not included (*saṅgaha-asaṅgaha-visesa*) is likewise dependent upon that which is to be directly known.
It should be understood that the matrix (mātikā) of the method—"Inclusion by three; non-inclusion by three"—was established so that it would be easy to understand when being explained.

And having done so, the conjunctions and disjunctions stated "by four" were answered after posing questions regarding the aggregates and so forth, which are the bases for what is to be directly known (abhiññeyya).
As for the statement, "The aggregate of form [is included] with one aggregate," those phenomena which are called "the aggregate of form" [are to be understood].
They are so called because they possess a commonality (*sabhāgatā*) by virtue of being the form-aggregate (*rūpakkhandha*) among the five aggregates;

thus, he demonstrates their inclusion and enumeration by means of what is termed the "state of being the form-aggregate" or the "designation of the form-aggregate. Therefore, he says, "Whatever... and so forth.
For by this, the phenomenon to be included is shown as the "form-aggregate. As for the inclusion by which it is included:
The statement "by one aggregate" refers to the seeing of that inclusion. The meaning here is that it is reckoned by one reckoning among the five reckonings of aggregates.
And because inclusion is expressed by terms such as "aggregate" and so forth, he will later say, "included by the inclusion of aggregates," and so on.

Regarding the "Exposition of the Method of Non-Inclusion" (*asaṅgahanayaniddesa*): this should be understood as being stated as a partial method of that very same method [of inclusion and non-inclusion]—namely, "inclusion and non-inclusion"—and not as a separate method.

Furthermore, since only the dyads, triads, and tetrads rooted in the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*) are shown here, it follows that when those rooted in the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*) are combined with the preceding [section], there is no difference; therefore, they are treated by the latter [section] alone.
This shows that the following are obtainable: three dyads, two triads, and one tetrad; two dyads and one triad rooted in the aggregate of perception (*saññā-khandha*);
and one dyad rooted in the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhāra-khandha*).

Furthermore, it should be understood that after the questions and answers regarding the pentads, the questions and answers for these [groups] are to be made in brief; or else, they can be known by the method already stated.
"Not included in the Pāḷi.
[This concludes] the commentary on the section beginning with the "Bases" (Āyatana). 40.
Regarding the phrase "And because among the pairs of Duka," although the answer is the same even for the single [Duka], it is nevertheless the case that for those where the answers are identical...
In the case of the eye-faculty, ear-faculty, pleasure-faculty, and so forth, dissimilar answers are seen among the dyads and other groupings.
Herein, there is no mutual similarity of answers between the dyads of the eye, the ear, and the pleasure-faculty, nor between the dyads and the triads;
however, in this instance, there is a mutual similarity of answers between the dyads of suffering, origin, and the path, as well as with the triads.
He states the reason for teaching the truth of the path immediately after the truth of origination as being the same mode of presentation applied to the three pairs [of truths].
6. Commentary on Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda): 61.
"Without beginning with a question, ignorance is associated with one aggregate; conditioned by ignorance, volitional formations are associated with one aggregate."
It should be understood that even though it ought to have been written, this statement "ignorance [is associated] with one aggregate" was not written down due to negligence.
Alternatively, by employing the *sarūpa-ekasesa* (the single remainder of identical forms) construction, the answer regarding ignorance is shown by the very word "ignorance.

Regarding the phrase "all resultant consciousness," no qualification should be made here by the inclusion of the term "resultant," for in the *Dhātukathā*, wholesome and other types of consciousness are also included.
The inclusion [of these factors] within the categories beginning with "consciousness conditioned by formations" is shown by their respective answers,
which are similar to the answer given for the phrase "resultant states" in the *Niddesa* on the categories of the dissociated,
the included, and the non-included; and here, by the statement regarding the inclusion of name-and-form within the eleven bases, it is understood that even those not born of karma are included.
71. Because birth, aging, and death are merely the states of being born, maturing, and dissolving respectively, they cannot be found when separated from the ultimate reality;

thus, they consist of the mere intrinsic nature of ultimate phenomena. Since these constitute the production, maturation, and dissolution of matter, they are apprehended by way of the state of being "malleable" (ruppana);
therefore, they share the same essential characteristic as the dhammas of the aggregate of matter. As for the immaterial [phenomena]...

However, because they arise together with the group of four aggregates (catukkhandha) as their state of origination and so forth—just as the types of material clusters (rūpakalāpa) arise together with the primary elements (bhūta)—the individual primary elements are not apprehended through the functions of feeling, perceiving, or cognizing, which are exclusively ultimate (paramattha) functions; rather, they are apprehended by the function of conditioning (abhisankharaṇa), which is a non-exclusive ultimate function.
Therefore, they share the same essential nature (dhammasabhāga) as the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha). This applies likewise to both types [of primary elements].

Since these [characteristics] are not grasped by the sense bases such as the eye-base—which have exclusively ultimate functions—and thus share the same nature as the dhamma-base, the dhamma-element, and dhammas in the sense of being "devoid of a sentient being," they are included within those aggregates and so forth;
therefore, it was said: "Birth is included in two aggregates," and so on.
The commentary on the section concerning inclusion and non-inclusion according to the first method is finished.
2. The Second Method: Explanation of the Terms "Included" and "Not Included.

171. Regarding the exposition of the terms "included" and "not included," that very class of phenomena (dhammajāta) which was determined as "not included"—being distinguished from what is "included" and thus requiring both questioning and answering in the summary—is precisely what is intended here.

Demonstrating this, he said: "Those phenomena which are included by the eye-base (cakkhāyatana) through inclusion by aggregates (khandha), but not included through inclusion by bases (āyatana) or elements (dhātu).

In all cases, because the generalities of inclusion by aggregates and so forth always depend on specific distinctions and because the questions and answers are based on such divisions, the enumeration of aggregates and so forth is purely with specific distinctions.
Therein, it is merely by means of the statement of what is included and what is not included [that the distinction is made].

Because specific categories of phenomena have been determined, those phenomena which are included by one or two of the three groupings (saṅgaha) but not by the others could have been shown merely by saying:
"They are included by the grouping of aggregates (khandha-saṅgaha), but not included by the groupings of bases (āyatana-saṅgaha) and elements (dhātu-saṅgaha).

However, since such cases are impossible, and because this matrix of methods (naya-mātikā) is intended to be viewed in relation to both the internal and external matrices, [the full analysis is necessary].

In the summary (uddesa) as well, it should be understood that whatever among the non-conflicting aggregates, such as the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha), serves as the inclusive factor, the "unincluded" is determined in relation to each of those;
thus, in order to specify and demonstrate the phenomena (dhamma) as determined by each respective inclusive factor, he says, "by the eye-base (cakkhāyatana)," and so forth.
For wherever there is a determination of the specific phenomena to be questioned and answered—
They are not [redundant], because in that first method and the sixth method they exist as the state of being the question and the answer;
and in the others, by way of determining each respective thing that is to be questioned and answered, the aggregates beginning with matter and ending with non-dispute have been enumerated.

In this context, in the phrases "by the eye-base... [and so on] ... by the tangible-element," the designation of the instrument (*karaṇa*) should be understood as having the sense of the agent (*kattū-attha*).

In the phrases "by the inclusion in the aggregates (*khandha-saṅgaha*), by the inclusion in the bases (*āyatana-saṅgaha*), and by the inclusion in the elements (*dhātu-saṅgaha*"), it is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇatthe*).

Furthermore, herein, for whichever specific inclusive category among the aggregates and so forth there may be something else—whether included or not included—that is to be included by that very category, that [is what is meant].

That very same [aggregate] is designated as the "comprehender" (saṅgāhaka) and the "comprehended" (asaṅgāhaka). However, there is no other dhamma to be comprehended by the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) through the inclusion of aggregates, nor likewise by the aggregates of feeling (vedanākkhandha) and so forth;
and that [aggregate] itself does not become either its own comprehender or its own non-comprehender.
As for what was stated—that "the aggregate of form is comprehended by one aggregate"—that too does not refer to that very same [aggregate].

This meaning is explained as follows: it was stated with reference to its being included by that [aggregate], but it was also stated with reference to its being grasped by the term "form aggregate" by virtue of its nature as the form aggregate.
And if only that were included by it, then in the exposition of the terms "associated with" and "dissociated from" what is included, [it would say]: "with the feeling aggregate... [and so forth].

"One might say: 'Those phenomena which are included by the inclusion of aggregates (khandha-saṅgaha) are also included by the inclusion of bases (āyatana-saṅgaha) and included by the inclusion of elements (dhātu-saṅgaha);
those phenomena are associated with three aggregates, one base, and seven elements,' and so forth;
yet this has not been stated. Therefore, just as consciousness (citta) is neither associated with nor dissociated from consciousness,"

Thus, the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) is neither included by nor excluded from the aggregate of form; likewise for the aggregates of feeling (vedanākkhandha) and the rest in relation to the aggregates of feeling and the rest.
For that very same thing cannot be both homogeneous and heterogeneous to itself.
Therefore, just as the aggregate of form [is not partially included by itself], a whole is neither the includer nor the non-includer of its own parts. As with the aggregate of form...

The sense base of mental objects (dhammāyatana) [is the commonality] of the aggregates beginning with feeling; the phenomena possessing a basis (saraṇā dhammā) are the commonality of the four aggregates.
For there is no differentiation among the parts that are included within a whole, by which those parts could be either similar or dissimilar to the whole;
likewise, the whole is not a subsumer of its own similar and dissimilar parts.

And it is an inclusive [category]. For example, the sense-base of mental phenomena (dhammāyatana) is included within the aggregate of aggregates by way of being similar to subtle matter and dissimilar to the aggregate of feeling and so forth;

likewise, the life-faculty (jīvitindriya) is included within the aggregate of aggregates by way of being similar to the life-force of both the material and immaterial, and dissimilar to a portion of the aggregate of matter and a portion of the aggregate of formations, excluding the life-faculty itself.
For that which is partially similar is not [necessarily] similar as a whole, nor is that which is partially dissimilar dissimilar as a whole.
Therefore, even though they are included within the self, belong to the self, and are partially similar to the self, they lack the quality of being inclusive of others;
since they do not include what is already included, they cannot themselves be the inclusive factors. Thus, due to the absence of inclusiveness...
In this way, the non-inclusion of such things should be understood.
As for what was stated— that "the dhammāyatana, excluding the unconditioned (asaṅkhata),
is included within four aggregates," and that "the eye-base and ear-base are included within one aggregate"— that does not refer to parts [of those bases].
It demonstrates the state of being a subsumer of the aggregate and the state of being a partial subsumer of the aggregate;

furthermore, it shows that the sense-sphere of mental objects (*dhammāyatana*) is fivefold, being divided according to the count of the four aggregates into what is to be counted and what is not to be counted, while the sense-spheres of the eye and so forth are of a single type because they are to be counted by means of a single aggregate-count. [This applies] to those things that are independent of being subsumers or non-subsumers.

For in the first method, there is merely the demonstration of counting by means of the respective counts for those things to be counted and those not to be counted, because there is only the mere performance of the action;

whereas in the second and subsequent methods, there is the demonstration of the non-counting, etc., of those included and not included by the inclusive and non-inclusive [categories], because there is the presence of the threefold action consisting of the agent, the instrument, and the act itself.

Likewise, in the first method, there is the presence or absence of the respective states of the aggregates (khandha), etc., which is characterized as the state of being counted or not counted in such and such a way.

Regarding "homogeneity and heterogeneity": in the case of the second and subsequent [questions], when viewing the phenomena as they have been defined, the state of having the same aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth between the grasper and the grasped is homogeneity (*sabhāgatā*), and the absence of that is heterogeneity (*visabhāgatā*). In the questions and answers, it is precisely the presence or absence of the state of each respective aggregate and so forth;
this is their distinction.
However, there are things similar to the faculty of pleasure (*sukhindriya*) that correspond to the truth of origination (*samudayasacca*) which ought to be included by them;

yet, because there is nothing similar that should be included but has not been included—due to the absence of anything non-inclusive—they have not been extracted [from the list]. As for things similar to the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*), since they consist of multiple aggregates (*khandha*) that form a heterogeneous collection distinct from those [truths], there is nothing among them that should be included by way of the aggregate-classification (*khandhasaṅgaha*) by those [truths] or that should not be included by others.

Because of the absence of being a collector and the absence of not being a collector. Thus, because of the absence of being a collector, the absence of not being a collector, and the absence of both, one should understand that only the eye-base and so forth were selected—without extracting those similar to what was previously stated—and this is due to the presence of being a collector and the presence of not being a collector.
In that context: "Those phenomena which are included by the eye-base through inclusion by aggregates..."

It should be understood that material phenomena (rūpadhammā), excluding the eye-base (cakkhāyatana), are included by way of inclusion within the aggregates (khandhasaṅgaha), but not as the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha).
For this demonstrates that a single part is not the inclusive whole.
In the commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), however, the phrase "by the word 'aggregate'" means "by the inclusion [expressed] by the word 'aggregate'," and not "by the inclusive [whole]."
"But by some kind of inclusion" (*kenaci saṅgāhakena*)—this, however, must be brought forward and stated.

Since that [inclusion] is not applicable to the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*) and the others, the meaning is that this answer is not applicable to the aggregates of form and so forth which act as the includers.

For, according to the method [stated in the text]: "Included by the aggregate of form...," it is the aggregate of form alone that is included by the eye-base (*cakkhāyatana*), and that [aggregate] consists of ten and a half [factors].

If it is argued that since there is nothing not included within the bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*), it follows that the eye-base (*cakkhāyatana*) and so forth should also not be taken [as distinct], we reply:
this does not follow. For the meaning of the word "only" (*eva*) is not merely the exclusion of others, but rather the exclusion of anything other than that which is inclusive.
Furthermore, the phrase "and that," etc., is not an independent statement; rather, it is dependent upon what is inclusive. How so?

For since the aggregate of form is included within the aggregate of form itself, there is no other thing besides the aggregate of form that is included by the inclusion of aggregates— which would not be included by the inclusions of bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*)— as there is in the case of the eye-base,
where things other than the eye-base are also included by the inclusion of aggregates.

Whatever might not be included by way of the inclusion of bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*), that very same form aggregate (*rūpakkhandha*) is indeed included by the form aggregate through the inclusion of aggregates (*khandha*).

This is the intended meaning here that is appropriate. However, one might think: "Let that very same form aggregate not be included by the form aggregate through the inclusions of bases and elements. To prevent this, he says: "And that [is included] by ten and a half..."
“There is nothing that is not included by way of the bases (āyatana) and elements (dhātu). And here, one should supply the phrase “by the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha).

In this context, the absence of non-inclusion is stated by this method: the aggregate of form is neither a subsumer nor a non-subsumer of the aggregate of form itself, or of its parts such as the eye and so forth, by way of the inclusion of bases and elements. Thus, there is no state of being uncomprised.
It is not logical that the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) is included within the aggregate of form, or within its own parts, by way of being included in eleven bases (āyatana) and elements (dhātu).
For such inclusion does not exist. If it did exist, then the aggregate of form would also have to be mentioned in the section describing "associated" and "dissociated" states by way of inclusion.
Therefore, by all three types of inclusion, the aggregate of form and its parts [are excluded].
Or they may be included, yet there is also their dissociation.

Thus, because there is no absence of inclusion due to non-inclusion, in the phrase "these and others," just as with the eye-base and so forth, there is no absence of inclusion for those things included by these and by others;
therefore, "these and others" [are so called] in whatever way that may be.
The intention is that these kinds of phrases—like those [already mentioned]—are not included as "comprehenders" because they involve an inappropriate application and exclusion.

Regarding this, what was stated—"for the aggregate of form is comprehended by the aggregate of form itself"—is refuted by demonstrating that there is no state of being either comprehended or not comprehended by means of that very same thing. As for the reason given here for their non-inclusion:

And while that [non-inclusion] exists even when there is inclusion, it would be appropriate [to speak of it] in the case of the truth of origin and so forth—since if something were included by them, the absence of non-inclusion by them would be understood—as being due to the absence of non-inclusion. However, there is nothing at all that is included by the aggregate of form and so forth;
how, then, could there be non-inclusion of it? Therefore, it is precisely the absence of being an includer that constitutes its non-grasping here.

The reason [for their non-inclusion] is appropriate. Although there is no lack of inclusion for that which is included within itself—such as the form-aggregate (*rūpakkhandha*) and so on, which are part of themselves and share a portion of their own nature—there is such a lack for other things.

Thus, it is not the case that the absence of both [inclusion and non-inclusion], as is the case with the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*) and others, serves as the reason for their non-inclusion here.
And this applies to the base of mental objects (*dhammāyatana*), the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*), and so forth.

When there is inclusion within the groupings such as the four aggregates and the pairs, there is no lack of inclusion for those included factors by means of those [other] groupings of bases and elements—such as the base of mental objects (dhammāyatana) and the life-faculty (jīvitindriya); thus, the absence of non-inclusion is not inconclusive.

Therefore, one should understand the reason for the non-inclusion of those previously mentioned [factors] that were not included, and the inclusion of those that were included, according to the method already stated.
Regarding the phrase "invisible but still impinging" (*anidassanaṃ punadeva sappaṭighaṃ*):

here, by connecting the term "invisible" (*anidassana*) with the word "impinging" (*sappaṭigha*) as it was used in the previous [category] "visible and impinging" (*sanidassanasappaṭighaṃ*), the category of "invisible and impinging" is shown.
By the phrase "again" (*punadeva*), one takes up the category of the "visible pair" (*sanidassanaduka*) while excluding the specific term "visible" (*sanidassana*) from that very same context.
This is shown. It cannot be said that "the eye-base alone is included by the eye-base.
For it cannot be said that "the eye-base is included by the eye-base through the inclusion of bases," nor can it be said that it is "not included";
this is the method demonstrated here. Thus, in all cases, there is the inclusion of that [whole] itself and of its parts by way of the inclusive inclusion (*saṅgāhaka-saṅgaha*).
Regarding the statement "not included by what is not inclusive" (*asaṅgāhaka-asaṅgahita*), the impossibility of such a designation within those statements must be applied.

For it is precisely because of the absence of being non-inclusive that the eye-base and so forth are not said to be "not included" by the eye-base and so forth; it is not because of the absence of being inclusive.
The commentary on the term "not included by what is included according to the second method" is finished.
3. The Third Method: Explanation of Terms Concerning the Unincluded and the Included.

179. In the exposition of terms concerning the unincluded and the included, regarding those things not included within the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*) by way of the inclusion of aggregates, there is a commonality of sense-base (*āyatana*) and element (*dhātu*) for the three aggregates beginning with feeling (*vedanā*), as well as for Nibbāna, together with subtle form (*sukhumarūpa*).
Even though only subtle matter constitutes the aggregate of form, there is no commonality of base (āyatana) or element (dhātu) with the aggregate of form;
therefore, those [bases and elements] are not included by it within the groupings of bases and elements.
Not only are they not included, they are also not excluded from those groupings because they share a commonality of base and element with that portion of the aggregate which is subtle matter.
However, what is intended here is precisely the state of being uncomprised;
since those things not comprised by the consciousness aggregate, the eye base, and so forth, are in no way mixed with them, they are therefore entirely uncomprised by them.

Furthermore, Nibbāna—which is not comprised by the inclusion of the aggregates as a collection consisting of the five aggregates—is [uncomprised] by the form aggregate, and so on, within the context of the truth of suffering and the rest.
Just as [something] is included by way of the inclusion of bases (āyatana) and elements (dhātu), it does not exist by way of those [categories];

therefore, one should understand that such things are not grasped because they lack the state of being inclusive, specifically because of the absence of inclusiveness in the case of indeterminate phenomena (abyākatadhamma) and so forth, which constitute an aggregate of the five aggregates together with nibbāna. For there is nothing whatsoever for which they [are inclusive].

There may be things that are not included by way of inclusion within the aggregates (*khandha-saṅgaha*), yet a part of itself cannot be non-included by itself nor share the same nature as a part of itself;
therefore, because they include what is not included by themselves, the feeling aggregate (*vedanā-khandha*) and the others are taken [as examples].
However, that which was stated in the Commentary—that "those phenomena included by the sphere of mental objects" (*dhammāyatana*)—cannot be maintained.
For there is no state (dhamma) included by any inclusion within the base of mental objects (dhammāyatana), because it consists of aggregates that are of a different class (visabhāga) and of Nibbāna;
nor does it itself become its own includer through the inclusion of aggregates. Thus, this method is shown by the absence of being an includer through the inclusions of bases and elements.
The meaning of "counted by the reckoning of the base of mental objects" is as follows: those [states]... pe ... are included.

By this [method], one should exclude: (1) terms such as the "bases of psychic power" (*iddhipāda*), which illustrate only a portion of the base of mental objects (*dhammāyatana*) mixed with consciousness; (2) terms such as the "aggregate of form" (*rūpakkhandha*), which illustrate [form] mixed with coarse matter;

(3) terms such as the "aggregate of consciousness" (*viññāṇakkhandha*) or the "eye-base" (*cakkhāyatana*), which do not illustrate the base of mental objects in its entirety; and (4) terms such as the "base of mental objects," which illustrate the entire base of mental objects.
Instead, one should [illustrate] a portion of the base of mental objects by means of the "base of the known" (*aññāyatana*).
This shows that they are taken as illustrating the unmixed [categories].
The commentary on the terms included under what is not included by the third method is finished.
4. The fourth method: commentary on the terms included under what is included.

191. In the exposition of the terms "included by what is included" and "not included by what is included," whereas the second and third methods were taught as "the not included by the included" and "the included by the not included" due to the distinction in the occurrence of inclusion and non-inclusion among the three types of inclusion, it is not so for the fourth and fifth.
For in those cases, there is only the occurrence of inclusion; thus, [it is taught] as "the included by the included."
It has been stated that because of the very occurrence of non-inclusion, that which is not included is "not included.
Therefore, in the absence of any distinction in the occurrence of inclusion, these two methods (nayā) are dependent upon the distinction between included phenomena and non-included phenomena.

In this context, when a particular phenomenon already included by some [category] is further included by another included phenomenon, it is to be asked as "included by what is included" (*saṅgahitena saṅgahito*) by virtue of its being included.
And it must be answered. To show that very point as it has been determined, he said: "Those phenomena included within the aggregates, etc., by the truth of origin;
those phenomena included within the aggregates, etc., by those phenomena.

And herein, those things which are not included by any of the three types of inclusion—such as the aggregate of form, the aggregate of consciousness, the base of mental objects, and the truth of suffering—are [to be understood].
Furthermore, those phenomena which are not included by the two-fold inclusion of bases and elements— such as the eye-base and so forth—

and those which are not included even by the single inclusion of aggregates or the inclusion of elements— such as the feeling aggregate and so forth, the truth of cessation, the life-faculty, and so forth,
as well as the eye-consciousness element and so forth— those phenomena, due to the presence of the absence of being inclusive, [are excluded] by way of their non-inclusiveness.
They were not included; however, those which are inclusive by way of all three types of inclusion have been included here because they possess the state of being inclusive.
For even when included by those [three], they are invariably inclusive of their own includer—that is, that of which further inclusion must be asked and answered.
In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, however, "by the entire term such as 'aggregate' (*khandha*), etc.
means by the term "matter-aggregate" (*rūpakkhandha*), etc., which expresses the whole.

As for what was stated—"that which, having included its own subsumptive factor, would again enter into a subsumption by that very same [factor]"—this should not be construed as "by that aggregate-term, etc."; rather, it refers to something else that has been subsumed.
It cannot be said that it does not exist. For when the inclusion of something by means of another is questioned, the answer given concerns its inclusion by that [category], and not merely by itself;
rather, it is by means of what includes it. Just as feeling (*vedanā*) and sound (*sadda*) are both aggregates (*khandha*) and bases (*āyatana*), subtle matter (*sukhumarūpa*) is not so;
rather, it is only a portion of the aggregates and bases. Therefore, [the question refers to] "a portion of subtle matter."
Rather than saying "or [the gross]," it is stated as "or the subtle form. And in all instances, it should be construed as "unmixed with anything else.
Furthermore, as for what was said—"referring to those very phenomena by which [the aggregates, etc.
are comprised under categories such as the aggregates"—that too cannot be stated in that way. For here, there is no inclusion of that which is already included by means of another inclusion.

When asked and answered, it is indeed a matter of inclusion; therefore, "by one aggregate" means by one reckoning of aggregates—this is the meaning here, not by way of an inclusive factor (*saṅgāhaka*). For a single aggregate does not include even its own constituent parts.
The commentary on the term "included by what is included by the fourth method" is finished.
5. The Fifth Method: Explanation of the Category of the Unincluded by the Unincluded (Asaṅgahitena-asaṅgahitapada-vaṇṇanā) 193.

In the exposition of the category of the unincluded by the unincluded, the demonstration of the phenomena as they have been determined should be understood according to the same method already stated.

And herein, those aggregates of phenomena together with subtle material form and consciousness—which are like the truth of suffering, the non-demonstrable, the non-reactive, the non-mental, the non-clinging, and so forth—[are to be understood].
Although some [factors] may not be included by one or two of the groupings because they cannot be included by all three, there is nonetheless nothing that cannot be included by them;
thus, they do not fail to provide a complete grouping. Nor are they non-inclusive in the same way as indeterminate (abyākata) phenomena, which cannot be included by any grouping whatsoever;
therefore, they are not extracted on account of being non-inclusive, whereas the others are extracted by way of the opposite case.

As for what is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: “For by such a term, Nibbāna would not fall under the inclusion of the aggregates (*khandhasaṅgaha*)”—this was said with reference to the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*).

However, among those things that are non-demonstrable, non-reacting, and non-inclusive, Nibbāna is included; yet it is not itself the inclusive category of that [truth]. This is according to the method of answering by way of similarity.

"Combined with those that have been made"—this means that when combined with the second question and so forth thus formulated, all thirty-four questions, beginning with the first question on name-and-form (nāmarūpa), amount to that number.

"That very word which was extracted from the question" refers to the specific words such as the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) and so on; it does not refer to the phenomena (dhamma) to be questioned once they have been isolated.
For those [phenomena] were shown by way of their characteristics (lakkhaṇa), not by way of their actual verbal form (sarūpa) through the word itself.
In this context, it should be understood that by the word "eva" (only) in the phrase "tadeva" (that very same), it is shown that what has been excluded is never not excluded;
thus, it demonstrates the certainty of the excluded being excluded and the uncertainty of anything else.
For in the phrase "tadeva yehi asaṅgahitaṃ" (that very same which is not included by those [categories]), the word "niyamato" (by necessity) can be supplied as an ellipsis. Now...

Or rather, it should be understood that the word *eva* (only/just) serves the purpose of determining the state of being excluded from inclusion precisely by virtue of its having been extracted in that question—
being of such a kind as was extracted in that question— and not for the purpose of precluding the state of being excluded from inclusion by anything else.
For that which is extracted in a question may indeed be accompanied by something else.

And that which is not included is uncomprised by what is not included. For while the aggregate of form and so forth are included when accompanied by others, the aggregates of consciousness and so forth are not included.
Regarding the statement "the remainder are included," this should be understood as meaning "the remainder are not uncomprised.

Even by those mental phenomena of consciousness, those very phenomena of form are not comprised by the three types of inclusion; thus, they are raised in the question as being non-comprisers even by all three types of inclusion.
The intention is that they are "not included" (*asaṅgahitā*) after having been offered. For even feelings (*vedanā*) and the rest, when not explicitly mentioned, are likewise not included.
And here, in the first method, it is stated that feelings and the rest are not included by consciousness; in the second, however, it is "material phenomena"—this is the distinction.

For feelings and the rest are not included in the aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth by means of the inclusion of material form and consciousness alone; [they are excluded] by means of gross material forms.
The meaning is that it is not included by consciousness, nor by any of the three [other] aggregates. For here, a portion of form is included by the term "form.
196. Regarding the fourth question, "the eye-base by the four [aggregates] beginning with feeling":
it should be understood that by the phrase "eye-base," he shows that which was raised in the question as being non-inclusive. However, by what is not included by the eye-base...
The ten coarse bases (*oḷārikāyatana*) are not included [in the sense-sphere aggregates], nor is it the eye-base alone.
By the phrase "matter and the mental-object base" (*rūpañca dhammāyatanaṃ*), that which is not included by any of the three types of inclusion is precisely consciousness;
and by means of that which is not included, he enumerates all those phenomena excluding consciousness as being likewise unincluded. For the answer is uniform.

Having recited them, they should be shown. Therein, when similar answers are presented together by means of the first aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*), other dissimilar answers are shown by way of providing a guiding principle (*nayadāna*).
Therefore he said: "Form and the sphere of mental objects (*dhammāyatana*)... [etc. ...are shown by being condensed in another manner.
Therein, "two existences" refers to the non-percipient existence (*asaññabhava*) and the single-aggregate existence (*ekavokārabhava*). "Two" refers to...
This was stated with reference specifically to external derived phenomena (*bāhirupādādhamma*).

That which delimits what is to be asked and what is to be answered—namely, the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*) and so forth, by means of which the non-inclusive and the non-comprised are determined—is called the "object" (*visaya*), because it serves as the basis for those questions and answers.
However, this is because the summary verse (*uddāna*) shown above provides merely the framework (*nayadāna*).
"Method" (*naya*) has been stated. There is also a reading, "And the twenty-two-fold method" (*dvevīsanayo ca*); the meaning is that this method consists of twenty-two terms.
The commentary on the terms "not included by what is not included" (*asaṅgahitena-asaṅgahita-pada*), which is not subsumed under the fifth method, is finished.
6. The sixth method: Commentary on the terms "conjunction" (*sampayoga*) and "disjunction" (*vippayoga*).
228. Regarding the terms "conjunction" (*sampayoga*) and "disjunction" (*vippayoga*), whatever is found and whatever is not found therein—all that is included within the question.

This was not stated with reference to the categories such as the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*) and so forth; rather, it should be understood as referring to the term "conjunction" and the term "disjunction.
For among the aggregates of form and so on, there are certain terms such as the base of mental objects (*dhammāyatana*) that are not found [in the others].

That [term] was not included even in the inquiry. However, although the term "association" (sampayoga) is not found among the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) and so forth, it is included in the inquiry formulated as:
"With how many... is the aggregate of form associated? On the other hand, [the term] is found among the aggregates of feeling (vedanākkhandha) and so forth.
Furthermore, the term "dissociation" (vippayoga) is found everywhere. As for the relation of material phenomena with matter or with Nibbāna, and that of Nibbāna...

It should be understood that by precluding association on the grounds that "there is no such thing as association with form," because of the absence of commonality in terms of simultaneous arising and so forth, that very state of simultaneous arising and so forth is shown to be their dissimilarity; thus, due to its absence, dissociation is also effectively precluded.
For the state of simultaneous arising and so forth, which exists among the four aggregates, [is absent] between those [and form].
There is commonality with respect to forms and Nibbānas, yet there is also mutual dissimilarity among those various forms and Nibbānas;

however, there is no such thing as their simultaneous arising and so forth between a portion of form and Nibbāna, by which there could be a dissimilarity between one portion of form and another portion of form or Nibbāna, or between Nibbāna and form.
It is for this very reason that it is said: "dissociation from the four."

Regarding the seven consciousness-elements (*viññāṇadhātu*), even if they are not dissociated from even one [of these qualities], just as the form-existence (*rūpabhava*) is illustrated by three consciousness-elements,

and those states that are neither-resultants-nor-dhammas-of-the-resultant-type by five, and those without applied thought and sustained thought (*avitakkavicāra*) by one, they illustrate states that are dissociated and without an object;
so too, without illustrating them thus, even if there is dissociation from even one, they are associated with all seven, and thus there are seven [qualities].

The intention is that they "illuminate those [factors]. For by the term *avippayutta* (unseparated), it is meant those factors which are not dissociated, and not those which are associated (*sampayutta*).
Therefore, this includes: (1) those terms such as *dhammāyatana* (the base of mental objects) and so forth which illuminate factors associated with them;

(2) those terms such as *acetasika* (non-mental) and so forth which illuminate what cannot be defined in terms of being either associated or dissociated; and (3) those which are associated yet cannot be so defined.

They illuminate the terms such as the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*) and so forth; thus, it is stated that there is no inclusion of any of those phenomena that illuminate both the non-objective (*anārammaṇa*) and the mixed (*missaka*).

For indeed, among the aggregates (*khandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*), there is neither association (*sampayoga*) nor dissociation (*vippayoga*) with any of the following: all consciousness-elements (*viññāṇadhātu*) that are non-objective, those that are mixed, those associated with them, or the collections of both.

If that were so, then in the exposition of the term "dissociated from the dissociated" (*vippayuttena-vippayutta-pada-niddesa*), one should not say: "Those phenomena which are dissociated from wholesome phenomena (*kusala-dhamma*), and those phenomena which are dissociated from those [wholesome] phenomena.
For would not unwholesome and indeterminate phenomena be both objectless (*anārammaṇa*) and mixed with both types of phenomena? No;
because it is stated that the aforementioned aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth possess neither association (*sampayoga*) nor dissociation (*vippayoga*). The aggregates and so forth...

For indeed, parts are not distinct from the whole, nor is there a distinction between one part of a whole and another part of that same whole; because there is no differentiation between the parts and the whole, there is no state of being "similar" (sabhāga) or "dissimilar" (visabhāga).

Consequently, there is no association (sampayoga) or dissociation (vippayoga) between them and the aggregates (khandha) and so forth. However, wholesome states (kusala-dhamma) are distinguished from unwholesome and indeterminate states, and those [unwholesome and indeterminate states] are distinguished from the wholesome;
yet they do not possess the status of being parts of a whole or parts of another whole consisting of those very parts.
Therefore, without referring to the aggregates and so forth, but merely by way of their dissociation,

it is stated that there is mutual dissociation between the unwholesome states and the others, and between the others and the wholesome states, because of the presence of dissimilarity; this same method applies to all such cases.
In the summary verse (*uddāna*), however, where it says "eighteen from that," it should have been said "sixteen"; and where it says "twenty-three," it should have been "twenty-one.

Furthermore, in all instances, certain portions of the formations aggregate (*saṅkhārakkhandha*), the mental-object base (*dhammāyatana*), and the mental-object element (*dhammadhātu*)—which consist of a convergence of many phenomena both with and without distinctions of time and continuity, such as the truth of origin (*samudayasacca*), the feeling aggregate (*vedanākkhandha*), and so forth—and certain portions mixed with other factors, such as the bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*) and so forth, [are included] along with those things that are without an object (*anārammaṇa*).

The aggregates of form and so forth, being unmixed, are indeed apprehended as distinguished from those with objects by way of their association or dissociation, and from those within the same continuum at the same time by way of being in different parts.

Thus, by virtue of being distinguished from those various things in different parts, they obtain association or dissociation as appropriate. For they possess the commonality of simultaneous arising and so forth.

And as for "heterogeneity" (*visabhāgatā*): it is because of this that it is stated here and there, "it is associated with one aggregate, one base, and one element by some [factors]," and "it is dissociated from one base and one element by some [factors].
Furthermore, the aggregates of feeling, perception, and consciousness, though they are collections occurring at different times, are each indeed single factors when they are present.

Therefore, because there is no division of that which exists at the same time, the pleasure faculty (*sukhindriya*) and the others do not constitute a division of the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*);

likewise, the eye-consciousness element (*cakkhuviññāṇadhātu*) and the others do not constitute a division of the aggregate of consciousness (*viññāṇakkhandha*) or the mind base (*manāyatana*). Consequently, it is said:
"The pleasure faculty is dissociated from one aggregate by some [factors]," and "the eye-consciousness element..."
It is not stated [in that context] as "dissociated from one aggregate, one base, and some [factors]," and so forth;
however, although consciousness is devoid of a division into aggregates and bases, it is indeed explained by way of a division into elements. Thus it is said: "The eye-consciousness element... pe...
the mind-consciousness element is dissociated from sixteen elements. In the same way, regarding the faculty of pleasure and the others, which are analyzed by way of a division into faculties:

In such passages as “those states dissociated from the faculty of pleasure,” dissociation should be understood according to the specific context, not as referring to the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha) in its undifferentiated state.
Just as, with reference to its state of association with those [other factors], it is said: “The truth of the origin is associated with three aggregates.”
If it is asked: "Since it was stated [in the *Paṭṭhāna*] with reference to that state of dissociation, why was it not stated there as 'dissociated from three aggregates'?

It is because a statement of dissociation from those [aggregates] is inappropriate when they are undifferentiated. For when they are differentiated, the truth of the origin (*samudayasacca*) is dissociated from the faculties of pleasure, pain, and grief, and from consciousness-elements other than the mind-consciousness-element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*).
It is appropriate to speak [of the distinction] precisely by way of differentiation, because they are comprised within the category of "dissimilarity" (*visabhāgatā*);

however, it is not appropriate [to speak of such a distinction] with respect to the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-khandha*) and so forth when they are devoid of differentiation, because while those [aggregates] exist, there is no absence of dissimilarity in the existence of that which has arisen.

For that conditioned thing (*saṅkhata*) which, like unarisen phenomena, does not undergo a division at the time of being touched [by contact], must be extracted [from the category of the present]; that is the state of being present (*paccuppanna-bhāva*).
It is extracted by way of being associated with or dissociated from [the object], and that [extraction] occurs because it must depend on the very state of existence in the present—
though devoid of temporal division— for the sake of the conditioned aggregates and so forth which are themselves devoid of such division.
For indeed, there can be no dependence of the non-existent upon the non-existent, nor of the non-existent upon the existent, nor of the existent upon the non-existent.

There is no association (*sampayoga*); however, when dissociation (*vippayoga*) is understood as a distinction that indicates non-existence, then by that very fact, dissimilarity (*visabhāgatā*) is also necessarily included.

But when dissociation is not so grasped, since dissimilarity is not grasped through those respective apprehensions, and because the similar is delimited among phenomena precisely through their existence when similarity exists, it follows that there is existence (*vijjamānatā*).
By the phrase "is shown," even "homogeneity" (sabhāgatā)—defined as the state of simultaneous arising and so forth—is indeed included.

And because that is included, only association (sampayoga) is obtained, not dissociation (vippayoga); therefore, the truth of the origin is stated as being associated with the aggregate of feeling and the others, not as being dissociated from them.
This same method applies to the truth of the path and the others as well.

262. Regarding the commentarial statement, "Excluding the investigation (vicāra) of the second jhāna, the rest are 'without initial application and with only sustained application' (avitakkavicāramatta)":

this shows that it is precisely those factors which, like the primary initial application (vitakka), do not adhere to other types of mental states arising within the same category, that are intended here by the term "without initial application and with only sustained application.

For this very reason, in the immediately following method, it is stated that they share the same destiny as the truth of origination (samudayasacca), and not with those states accompanied by both initial and sustained application (savitakkasavicāra).

These are not included. Furthermore, among the ten ways of non-association (*dasamosānanaya*), the dissociation from those dissociated factors and from the sixteen elements dissociated from them is stated as being comprised within the eighteen [ways].

However, when those [factors] associated with applied thought (*vitakka*) are included, since all of them are associated with sustained thought (*vicāra*), it is possible to say: "They are associated with one aggregate and with some [elements]."

To speak [of it as such]: for that aggregate (*samudāya*) is not associated with anything other than *vicāra*, having excluded *vitakka*. Indeed, there is no association of the aggregate with anything other than *vicāra* on the part of *vitakka*, which is but one part of it.

Just as, among the various types of consciousness-arising, the association of the aggregate of the bases of power (*iddhipāda*) with the three aggregates (*khandha*)—which are parts of the base of power—is [attributed] to the aggregate.

It does not exist; it should be understood in this way here as well. Just as among those [factors], since not even one is called "dissociated" from the aggregates of feeling and perception and from a portion of the aggregate of mental formations, the collection is said to be associated with them;
so too here, because there is nothing dissociated from investigation—namely, anything that possesses only investigation without applied thought—the collection is associated with that [investigation].

It cannot be said that it is not so. For it is not the case that associatedness cannot be predicated [of this state] in the same way as it cannot be predicated of those states whose roots are to be abandoned by vision (*dassanena-pahātabba-hetuka*), etc.

Just as among those states whose roots are to be abandoned by vision, some are associated with delusion (*moha*)—which is a portion of the aggregate of formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*)—while others are not, yet the totality is not associated with it, nor is anything else [so associated].
There exists a phenomenon (*dhamma*) by which that aggregate (*samudāya*) might be associated;
thus it is said, "there are no phenomena with roots to be abandoned by vision that are associated. The same applies to those with roots to be abandoned by cultivation, those with roots, and so forth.

However, there is no such thing among those states without applied thought but with sustained thought (*avitakkavicāramatta*) by which an aggregate without applied thought but with sustained thought could be associated.
Because there is no state that is not associated with any investigation whatsoever, it should therefore not be said that they are "not associated.

Furthermore, in all instances, the use of the plural form *kehi ci* (by some) even when referring to a single dharma should be understood as being employed because the number is not restricted by calculation.
The commentary on the sixth method, the section on association and dissociation, is finished.
7. Seventh Method: Commentary on the Section on the Associated and the Dissociated (Sampayuttena-vippayutta-pada-vaṇṇanā) 306.

In the exposition of the section on the associated and the dissociated (*sampayuttena-vippayutta-pada-niddesa*), the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*) and the others are not included because they lack association with those [mental factors].

Although the truth of origination (*samudayasacca*) and the others are associated with them, and are also dissociated from those that are associated, [they are excluded] from among the associated and the dissociated...

Because there is no dissociation from the aggregates and so forth. For indeed, among those other phenomena dissociated from the states of consciousness arising with greed—which are associated with the truth of origination—there is no dissociation from any [of the factors] within the aggregates and so forth.
But is it not the case that those very states of consciousness are themselves the four aggregates, one and a half bases, and one and a half elements?
Should their dissociation be stated? No, because those other factors possess the nature of aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth.
For it is not only those very factors that constitute the four aggregates; rather, they and others besides them do.
The same applies to the one-and-a-half bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*). Furthermore, parts of a composite whole are not dissociated from other composite wholes.
Because there is no dissociation. This same method applies to the path, the truths, the faculty of pleasure, and so forth.

Furthermore, when those states "without applied thought but with sustained thought" (*avitakkavicāramatta*) are intended to be included without exception, no reason is seen for their non-inclusion, since they share the same classification as those "with applied thought and sustained thought" (*savitakkasavicāra*).

However, in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), the phrase "such as these" (*evarūpāni*) refers to those in which, just as in the case of the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*), a detailed exposition (*vissajjana*) is not appropriate.

It should be understood that [the phrase] "such as these" is stated because they do not apply to others due to their lack of connection with the answer, and not because of an absence of association (*sampayutta*).
By the words "those terms which illustrate the states associated with the element of phenomena (*dhammadhātu*)," he indicates the terms for the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*) and so forth;
and by "consciousness unmixed with anything else," he indicates the terms for the aggregate of consciousness (*viññāṇakkhandha*), the mind-base (*manāyatana*), and so forth. Therein:
"Not mixed with another" means not mixed with what is dissociated; this is the meaning.
For here, even those phrases associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling are included because they indicate consciousness that is mixed with its associated factors.

By this characteristic, he shows that only such [phrases] are included, and not that only such [phrases] are included, because phrases such as the Truth of Origin and the Bases of Psychic Power (iddhipāda) are not included.
“Now, the ancient reading was: ‘Then the contact-septad [is explained] together with the associated terms.
However, considering this to be deficient, the reading was changed to: ‘Then the contact-septad; three in the triads, and seven in the intermediate [groups]. 309.
‘Together with the term extracted from the question, by way of the dissociated factors’—this refers to the term extracted from the question.”
It is stated thus because, while dissociated from their associated [mental factors], they are nevertheless dissociated along with them.

In the summary verse of the Pāḷi, the phrase "two associated with mind" refers to initial application (*vitakka*) and sustained application (*vicāra*), which are exclusively associated with the mind-element (*manodhātu*); thus it demonstrates both the state of having initial application and the state of having sustained application.
The commentary on the section concerning those associated with and dissociated from the seventh method is finished.
8. The eighth method: Commentary on the section concerning those associated with and dissociated from [the factors].

317. In the exposition of the section concerning those associated with and dissociated from [the factors], it refers specifically to that which is associated with and dissociated from the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*) and so forth.

Just as it has been determined that [such a thing] does not exist, rather than saying, "Those phenomena dissociated from the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) are associated with those [other] phenomena," it is stated: "Regarding those phenomena dissociated from the aggregate of form, with how many aggregates...
[etc. ...are they associated? There are none. By this, [it is shown that] for those things dissociated from the aggregate of form, by any...
Because there is no association with the aggregates and so forth, it shows that for what has been determined [in the previous method], there is simply no "associated-with-the-dissociated" state;
