how then could there be an association with the aggregates and so forth for that again?
The commentary on the eighth method, the "Associated-with-the-Dissociated," is concluded.
9. Commentary on the term *sampayuttena-asampayutta* (associated-with-the-associated). 319.
Regarding the commentary on the term *sampayuttena-asampayutta*, the compound phrase "by way of [any one of] the aggregates, etc. (*yaṃ-khandhādi-vasena*) is to be understood as follows:
the meaning is "by way of whichever aggregate, etc. The phrase "of that very same" (*tasseva*) means "of that very same aggregate, etc. This...

What is meant is this: that which is stated here as "associated" refers to whichever aggregate among the feeling-aggregate and so forth is associated with the form-aggregate and the others up to the consciousness-aggregate;
then, having again asked about the association of that very same feeling-aggregate and so forth with the aggregates and so forth, the answer is given.
For it is determined as "associated with what is associated" because it is associated with that which is itself associated.
By the phrase "or with form," it should be understood that non-association with cessation-truth, non-conditioned phenomena (asaṅkhata), and so forth is also stated;

likewise, by the phrase "or with those mixed with form," non-association with the unclung-to (anupādinna) and the not-to-be-clung-to (anupādāniya), as well as with those mixed with Nibbāna, is stated. For he will say:
"Nibbāna, moreover, belongs to the category of subtle form. By the phrase "with those comprising all aggregates of form," it refers only to those [aggregates] currently existing.

"Association is obtained" means by way of the immaterial becoming (*arūpabhava*) and so forth, which include the four aggregates (*catukkhandha*) without excluding even a single dhamma among those that are present. This is the summary here:
all those such as the aggregate of material form (*rūpakkhandha*) that do not obtain association are not included, while all others, such as the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*), are included.
The commentary on the term "associated" in the ninth method is concluded. 10.
The tenth method: Commentary on the term "dissociated" in relation to the dissociated. 353.

Regarding the description of the term "dissociated from the dissociated," those phenomena not included [in the previous categories], such as the base of mental objects (*dhammāyatana*) and so forth, are included because they exist as phenomena occurring within all states of consciousness that are mixed with non-objective factors.

Because there is no dissociation from those [factors], they are not included; for phenomena such as the truth of suffering, the four great elements, and the indeterminate, there is an absence of dissociation from the aggregates and so forth that are dissociated from those dissociated factors. This distinction should be understood.
The commentary on the term "dissociated from what is dissociated by the tenth method" is finished.
11. Explanation of the Terms "Associated" and "Dissociated" in the Eleventh Method (Ekādasamanaya) 409.

In the explanation of the eleventh method, the connection of these terms—“those [states] together with the remaining three aggregates, one mind-base, and seven consciousness-elements”—is with the phrase “are called associated. The word “by some” [refers to those states].

To demonstrate this point, by the phrase "excluding craving from the aggregate of formations (saṅkhārakkhandha) and from the base of mental phenomena (dhammāyatana) and the element of mental phenomena (dhammadhātu)," the specific factors included within the aggregates and so forth by the truth of origination (samudayasacca)— referred to by the words "and those"— are distinguished;

and for those very distinguished factors, [the inclusion] in the aggregate of formations, in craving, and in the base and element of mental phenomena is [specified] by the remaining categories excluding the self.
And with reference to its association with craving and with the aggregates of feeling and perception—which are capable of association—he said:
"It is called 'associated with some' because it is associated with the remaining [factors].
The commentary on the section regarding the associated and dissociated states, as included in the eleventh method, is concluded.
12. Commentary on the Terms Regarding What is Included and Not Included by Way of Association in the Twelfth Method. 417.
And since, as in the ninth method, only those factors capable of association are found in the twelfth method, it is said: "Those very same [factors] are extracted.
The commentary on the terms regarding what is included and not included by way of association in the twelfth method is finished.
13. Thirteenth Method: Explanation of the Terms "Not Included" and "Associated/Disassociated" 448.

In this explanation of the thirteenth method, those twenty-two phenomena which, by all three types of inclusion (*saṅgaha*), are not included and are exclusively consciousness (*viññāṇa*) alone, are shown in the Pāḷi by the summary verse beginning with "matter and the base of mental data" (*rūpañca dhammāyatanaṃ*). These are [included] by the aggregate of matter (*rūpakkhandha*).

...are said to be "questions similar to the formless realm. However, those which are not included by any of the three types of inclusion and are merely gross bases—just like the formless realm—all such remaining ones mentioned here are said to be "similar to the formless realm.
As for the "rest," these are the aggregates beginning with feeling mentioned in the fifth method; although they are not included [by the threefold inclusion], they are included here.

“They do not ascend to the answer” means they were not extracted. As for those phenomena such as the truth of suffering that are not included [in the aggregates], there is nothing at all to be said regarding them.
However, in order to show why the aggregate of feeling and so forth do not ascend [to the answer], he says, “By the aggregate of feeling,” and so on.
In that context, “there is no association between them” refers to the absence of association between material and immaterial phenomena.
The meaning is that there is no association due to the mixture [of factors] with those dissociated from consciousness.

However, if those immaterial phenomena (arūpadhammā) and material phenomena (rūpadhammā) were ever associated with any consciousness-element other than the wholesome ones, their dissociation would not be absent;
thus, it was not stated that "there is no dissociation," nor [was it stated] with regard to the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha).
It should be understood that this is because there is no dissociation for those things that are not included [in the aggregates].
For it is due to the absence of both [association and dissociation] that the aggregate of feeling and the others do not arise here. However, one might object here:

"Indeed, by way of the aggregates and so forth, the seven consciousness-elements and mental states (dhammas) that are mixed with non-objective factors are not included in the aggregate of feeling; and for these, there is neither association nor dissociation."

The reason for the absence of association (sampayoga) and dissociation (vippayoga) among all consciousness elements (viññāṇadhātu) together with their objectless states, all consciousness-element concomitants, and those phenomena belonging to both [consciousness and its concomitants]—
which are not included within the three groupings of the aggregate of feeling and so forth, the aggregate of consciousness and so forth, and the eye-base and so forth— is their non-arising (aruhaṇa).
This is due to dissociation by way of genus (jāti), dissociation by way of plane (bhūmi), dissociation by way of time (kāla), and dissociation by way of continuity (santāna).
Disjunction is fourfold. Therein, disjunction by way of kind refers to "wholesome states, unwholesome states," and so forth;

disjunction by way of plane refers to "belonging to the sense sphere, belonging to the fine-material sphere," and so forth; disjunction by way of time refers to "past states, future states," and so forth;
disjunction by way of continuity refers to "internal states, external states," and so forth. Thus, disjunction should be understood as fourfold.

The commentary on the section concerning those associated with and dissociated from what is included in the Thirteenth Method is finished. 14. Commentary on the Section Concerning What is Included and Not Included in What is Dissociated from Mind (the Fourteenth Method) 456. In the Fourteenth Method, because the bases such as the base of mental objects (*dhammāyatana*) consist of states that are non-objective and mixed with all types of consciousness-arising, they are dissociated from mind. Thus, they are included in what is dissociated from mind. However, because the remaining states—such as the aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations, as well as the materiality aggregate—are not non-objective, they are not included in what is dissociated from mind; rather, they are included in what is associated with mind. Therefore, they are not included in what is dissociated from mind. Furthermore, because the remaining states—such as the faculties, powers, path factors, jhāna factors, and so forth—are not non-objective, they are not included in what is dissociated from mind; rather, they are included in what is associated with mind. Consequently, they are not included in what is dissociated from mind. Moreover, because the remaining states—such as the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right endeavors, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eight path factors—are not non-objective, they are not included in what is dissociated from mind; rather, they are included in what is associated with mind. Therefore, they are not included in what is dissociated from mind.

Explanation of the Schedule (*Mātikāvaṇṇanā*)

1. Having shown the analysis of the aggregates and so forth for the phenomena included by way of triplets and dyads in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*, and having stated the distinctions such as inclusion and non-inclusion for those same phenomena analyzed and included in the *Dhātukathā*, [the author] now sets forth the following in order to show, in detail, that designation (*paññatti*) by which they are designated both according to their intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) and by way of derived qualities (*upādāya*): "Six..."

By the passage beginning with “designations,” the designation of a person (*puggalapaññatti*) is introduced. Therein, when certain phenomena (*dhammā*) occur in a temporal sequence, the designation of a person—such as “a person,” “a woman,” “a man,” “a deity,” or “a human”—arises by taking them as a collection of non-essential factors (*asabhāva*).

Furthermore, there is the making known (*paññāpanā*) of those [phenomena], as well as external matter (*rūpa*) and Nibbāna, by way of their being collections of essential factors (*sasabhāva*) and their distinctions as essential factors.
"Description of intrinsic nature" (sabhāvapaññatti) should be understood as fivefold, beginning with the description of the aggregates (khandha).

By this, all descriptions of intrinsic nature analyzed in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī* and other texts are included. However, "description of a person" (puggalapaññatti) is a description of what lacks intrinsic nature (asabhāvapaññatti).

And by means of that—referring to the phenomena within the continuum of a sentient being that possess such natures as "to be fully understood," which are divided into categories such as "liberated at times"—[the person is described].
By this [term], all designations of non-substantiality (*asabhāva-paññatti*)—such as "the dwelling is a bed" and so forth—are included within the designation for the exertion [of striving].
Up to this point, what is called designation (*paññatti*) consists of the designation of the existent (*vijjamāna-paññatti*) and the designation of the non-existent (*avijjamāna-paññatti*).
These two, along with the mixed (*vomiṣsā*) and the other four, constitute the total. Therefore, by showing these, all designations have been shown in this treatise.

It should be understood [as follows]. Among the six designations (paññatti), such as those of the aggregates (khandha) and so forth, it should be understood that the name "Puggalapaññatti" has been given to this treatise because it relies upon the person-designation (puggalapaññatti), whose specific classifications have not been shown elsewhere but are shown here alone.
The phrase "those phenomena (dhammā) which he wishes to designate here" means the intention is to show them as the objective bases (vatthu) for designation.
For in this treatise, one does not perform the act of making known; rather, one demonstrates designations by means of bases (*vatthu*).

Regarding the phrase "the making known as aggregates": this refers to all instances of making known through general and specific designations, such as "matter is an aggregate" or "earth," and it should be understood that it is said with reference to that. Furthermore, "making known" (*paññāpanā*) means showing or establishing.
These two are the meanings: their manifestation and their laying down (*nikkhipanā*).

In this context, the laying down is simply the making known—the act of arranging those respective categories by saying, "This has such a name," or "This has such a name"—as in the passage beginning, "The aggregate of form... [up to] the faculty of one who has already known is liberated by occasion.
It is not, however, the act of establishing a connection with a physical location, as in the case of beds and so forth that are to be designated. As for this which...
The designation of the agent is made in the phrase, “for the conceptual designation of names both shows and establishes.

This should be understood as being made with reference to the fact that those various phenomena are shown and established by means of a conceptual designation of names—whether existing as a state (*bhāva*) or as an instrument (*karaṇa*)—and thus having that [designation] as their cause.

By the statement beginning with “existing conceptual designation,” he says “by what is outside the Canon” (*pāḷimuttakena*), etc., with reference to its not being included in the canonical text (*pāḷi*).
“Of the wholesome and unwholesome alone” means as in the case of the wholesome and unwholesome. “Of that which exists” (vijjamānassa) has the sense of “being present” (sato);

its meaning is “that which has come into being” (sambhūtassa). Alternatively, “of that which exists and is present” (vijjamānassa sato) has the sense of “of that which has become existent” (vijjamānabhūtassa).
Showing this very meaning, he says “of that which has come into being. By this, he rejects the state of non-existence. Likewise, “of that which does not exist” (avijjamānassa)...

Just as wholesome states and so forth exist with a nature distinct from the nature of unwholesome states and so forth, and contact and so forth exist with a nature distinct from the nature of feeling and so forth;

likewise, having set aside those phenomena depending upon which there arises the perception "woman" or "man" regarding that which does not exist, there is no such thing as a female or male nature distinct from them, because it has not arisen—this is the meaning. That which...
Regarding this, some say the meaning is "that which does not exist in one mode but exists in another mode.
Whatever needs to be said about that has already been stated in the *Paññatti-duka* (Treatise on Designation).

Because there is the occurrence of apprehending [a person] as "woman" or "man" by means of a mind free from dogmatic adherence, following worldly convention even though the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) does not exist, it is said to be "established merely by worldly convention."

He said: However, that which is grasped by a mind characterized by dogmatic adherence—such as the fifth truth and so forth—is established neither by way of intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) nor by way of conventional designation (*saṅketa*).
Therefore, it is stated that "it is unapprehendable in every respect. Regarding the statement "in these...
they are found," this was said with reference to the fact that all three [truths] appear in their own form within this treatise.
However, the teachers' views should be reconciled with the method of the commentary as it has been stated above.

Therefore, regarding the statement "it is a designation in the sense of being designatable," since this [designation] lacks intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), the meaning is that it is a "designation" in the sense of being a mere object to be designated.
For even that which is to be designated possesses its own nature; because it acquires its specific ultimate name from that very source, it is not to be obtained from something else.
It receives the name "concept" (paññatti), but as for its non-substantiality, because it lacks intrinsic nature, it does not receive a name by way of its own intrinsic nature.
It receives the name "concept" in the sense of being a mere object to be designated by names such as "a being" (satta) and so forth;

yet beings and the like are non-substantial. For there is no state of having an unapprehendable intrinsic nature—whether through identity with or difference from form and the other aggregates—for that which possesses an intrinsic nature.

A *kirīṭa* is a crown; one who possesses it is a *kirīṭī*. And according to this teacher’s view, since there must be no deficiency in the characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*), a complete synthesis (*sabbasamorodha*) should be made.

For it is appropriate that such designations as "the second" or "the third"—which are designations by comparison (*upanidhāpaññatti*) and designations by proximity (*upanikkhittakapaññatti*)—partake of all six types of designation, because they have the concept (*saṅkhāta*) as their primary factor.
And the other [concepts] are, as appropriate, various designations (*paññatti*). However, there is no such thing as a "number" (*saṅkhā*)—such as "two," "three," and so forth—which exists in itself;

therefore, one should understand that these designations based on continuity (*santati*) are non-existent designations (*avijjamāna-paññatti*), while those other designations based on comparison (*upanidhā-paññatti*), as they have been demonstrated, are likewise non-existent designations because of their non-existence.
Thinking thus, he says: "The remaining [terms] belong to the category of the non-existent and to the category of the non-existent by means of the non-existent.

Regarding the designations of comparison (*upanidhā*) and juxtaposition (*upanikkhittaka*), such as "the second," "the third," "two," "three," and so forth, he conceives them as being precisely designations of the non-existent by means of the non-existent.
For that which is designated in dependence upon the first and so on, and having been juxtaposed with the second and so on, is indeed [so designated].
And that reckoning does not exist at all. Likewise with the designation of continuity (*santatipaññatti*); for eighty or eighty years do not exist [as a discrete entity].

"A certain designation of plane" refers to the designation of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) and so forth; the intention is that the sense-sphere and so forth are phenomena possessing intrinsic nature (*sabhāvadhamma*).
However, when "sense-sphere" is taken in the sense of a location, this must be a designation of the non-existent regarding what is non-existent.
When the aggregates produced by karma are apprehended, it is a designation of the existent based on the non-existent. Just as the designation of a person as "speaker"—
whether by way of the act consisting of speech or the volition that originates speech— belongs to the category of a designation of the non-existent based on the existent,
so too is the designation of persons and the like as "emaciated" or "corpulent" by means of shape, which is comprised within the sense-sphere of form (rūpāyatana).

A designation of what is non-existent by means of what is existent is appropriate. Alternatively, "shape" (saṇṭhāna), when not included within the sense-sphere of visible form (rūpāyatana), is a designation of the non-existent by means of the non-existent.

However, designations such as "form is contact," and so forth, should be subsumed under the designation of function (kicca-paññatti) by way of functions such as being affected (ruppana), or under the designation of individuality (paccatta-paññatti) by way of the names of individual phenomena.
When the designations of the existent and the non-existent have been stated, the other [designations] that occur by way of their combination are also implicitly stated;
thus, this teaching of the Master should be understood as being all-inclusive. 2.
In order to show the meaning of the passage beginning with “To whatever extent there are five aggregates,” he says: “By whatever means of designation,” and so forth.
In this context, "as far as the five aggregates" means from "the aggregate of form" … pe … "the aggregate of consciousness";

this is the designation of the aggregates as "aggregates. It should be understood that this meaning has been stated by way of both summary and classification, having thus constructed the textual connection: "as far as the five aggregates" and "the designation of the aggregates as aggregates."

For its meaning is shown by this [phrase]: "Insofar as it is designated in brief as 'the five aggregates,'" and by the following [phrase]—"Insofar as it is distinguished in detail as 'the aggregate of form,' etc."—it is shown by that which begins with "the aggregate of form" and so on. Therein, the mention of "the aggregate of form...
up to the aggregate of consciousness" is merely an indication of the classification. By means of that, everything not explicitly mentioned is also [included].

"It is included" means that it has been stated: "Therein, too, the aggregate of form belongs to the sense-sphere," and so forth. Alternatively, this is the construction of the meaning of the text here:

connecting the word "to whatever extent" with all the terms, it means that to whatever extent there are five aggregates, to that same extent there is the designation of aggregates for those aggregates.
To whatever extent there are the five aggregates and their subdivisions, such as the aggregate of form and the rest...

The analysis: by the phrase "how many is the analysis of the aggregates' designation of aggregates," he shows the analysis of the designation of aggregates according to the classification of bases as stated in another treatise.
This same method applies to the phrases "as far as the sense-bases" and so forth.
"By way of a single part" means by way of a mere summary.
The Commentary on the Matrix (Mātikāvaṇṇanā) is finished.
2. Commentary on the Exposition (Niddesavaṇṇanā). 1. Commentary on the Exposition of the Singlefold (Ekakaniddesavaṇṇanā).
1. By the intention that "the jhāna factors themselves are liberation," he says, "by the mental body co-nascent with liberation.
For by the passage beginning with "together with which," etc., he first explains the sense of being possessed [of them].

By the statement "it is indeed only when touched by contact that there is name," he explains the second sense, namely touching through contact, as stated in the passage beginning with "Moreover, this," etc.; by the others, the other senses.
In the sense of causality. For it is said that "contacting" (*phusanā*) refers to the state of being a cause through the act of possessing and touching.

Furthermore, because the first meaning is difficult to understand, he explains it by saying, "Therein, of this... and so forth. Regarding the statement, "Excluding those factors, the remaining fifty-six states," he says, "There are four aggregates (*khandhā*)," because the faculties of feeling (*vedanā-indriya*) and mental pleasure (*somanassa-indriya*) are included therein. This being so...

Is it not the case that because pleasure is to be touched by the faculties of feeling and mental joy (*vedanā-somanassindriya*), and because those three are not distinct from one another, it follows that the touching of the latter occurs by means of the former?

It does not follow, because it is stated that the attainment of the state of close contemplation (*upanijjhāyana-bhāva*) occurs through the sense of being the dominant factor over what is felt (*vedayitādhipati*).

Alternatively, the plural number is used because there are many factors, [the phrase] "setting aside those factors" (*ṭhapetvā tāni aṅgāni*) referring to the plurality of factors. Furthermore, among them, each individually...
The construction (*yojanā*) should be made by means of the phrase beginning with "having set aside initial application" (*vitakkaṃ ṭhapetvā*).

In that regard, according to this construction "having set aside pleasure" (*sukhaṃ ṭhapetvā*), there are the remaining three aggregates (*khandhā*); in the others, there are four. And in all constructions, having included three within, it is stated that "there are four aggregates."

2. One who is liberated from certain taints by means of non-temporal liberation (*asamayavimokkha*), and who, through the attainment of the support for non-temporal liberation, possesses the temporal liberation (*samayavimokkha*) in an especially eminent way—he alone is "liberated at times" (*samayavimutta*). For he is liberated by that [temporal liberation];

being a trainee (*sekkha*) who has attained meditative absorption (*jhāna*), he is one who will not return again to existence in the realms of form or formlessness, and is thus liberated in such a manner from sensual lust and the other defilements. This is the designation of "one liberated at times."
He is worthy to attain it. However, an ordinary person (puthujjana) who has attained jhāna is subject to returning again;

because he is not yet liberated from the manifestation of sensual lust and other defilements, he does not deserve the designation "liberated at times" (samaya-vimutta), and for that reason he is not called "liberated at times.
For an Arhat, however, there are no taints (āsava) remaining from which he would need to be liberated. It is merely a dwelling in happiness in this very life (diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra).
Indeed, for him there are the eight liberations. Therefore, those eight liberations are not the cause for his being designated as "liberated at times" or "liberated independent of time.
To demonstrate precisely that they are not the cause, it was said: "He does not...
[and so on] ...dwell," rather than to show that the dry-insight practitioner alone possesses the state of being liberated independent of time.

It should be understood thus: for every Arahant is one liberated irrespective of time (*asamayavimutta*). "External" means those things existing outside of the supramundane (*lokuttara*); the meaning is "mundane" (*lokiya*).
To show that the word "formless" (*arūpa*) does not denote merely the formless aggregates and Nibbāna, it is said: "other than form," and so forth.
"The casket of the mind" refers to concentration (*samādhi*), for concentration serves as the foundation for the states such as the direct knowledges (*abhiññā*).
It is like a casket. "To pervade the course" means to extend over a long period of time; the meaning is to set it in motion.
One should understand that because no heed was paid to the thought, "It must be swept," there is a breach of the duty (*vatta-bheda*).
However, a meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) lost through such a mere breach of duty is not to be retrieved for nothing, just as one that has been lost through sensual desire and so forth.
Because it is an obstacle to dullness, it must be brought back [to the mind] merely by performing the duties with composure; therefore, he said, "he sat down as soon as he had entered.
Even for those who spend their time in negligence appropriate to themselves, the attainment does not fail;
thus, one is not said to have "fallen away," because there is the capacity to enter that attainment as soon as one withdraws from each respective distraction—this is the intended meaning.
“But why, Bhante, would gain, honor, and fame be an obstacle for a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed?
For as to that unshakable liberation of mind, Ānanda, I do not say that gain, honor, and fame are an obstacle to it.
However, Ānanda, those pleasant dwellings in this very life that come to one who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute—”

However, in the Sutta, it should be understood that there is no contradiction with that statement because the intention was to say that gain, honor, and fame are an obstacle to those dwellings in the bliss of attainment— which must be maintained by entering them from time to time— since they fail to be accomplished during those various times of distraction.
5. Regarding the phrase "of phenomena" (*dhammānaṃ*)... [and so forth]... here it should be said "by means of phenomena.
For in this context, both the falling away and the non-falling away of a person from those attainments are stated by way of "phenomena.
Furthermore, therein, because those attainments might become disturbed due to the negligence of the person, the disturbance and non-disturbance of the phenomena are stated; however, for the person—

It should be understood that the distinction between the two modes of expression—whether by means of a mere difference in phrasing or a mere difference in the meaning of the words—is stated as being merely a difference in method (*pariyāya*), referring to the fact that "destruction" is said to apply only to those things subject to decline.

7–8. *Cetanā* (volition) consists of the volition of attainment and the exertion directed toward it. *Anurakkhaṇā* (guarding) is mindfulness accompanied by wisdom, which discerns what is beneficial and what is detrimental to the attainment.

Those who are capable of such volition and guarding are called "capable of volition" (*cetanābhabba*) and "capable of guarding" (*anurakkhaṇābhabba*) with respect to the attainments that are being willed and guarded.

10. "The lineage of worldlings" (*puthujjanagotta*) means that they have transcended the training of worldlings; the meaning is that they have transcended the three trainings pertaining to worldlings. For those [trainings] are called "the training of worldlings" because they do not effect the severance of the three fetters. 11.

One who stands on the path of arahantship, being terrified by the fear of the round of existence due to the surge of wisdom, is called "one who has desisted out of fear" (*bhayūparata*) because he has desisted from the higher fetters. Thus it is said: "The seven trainees are those who have desisted out of fear. 12.

Those devoid of the wisdom of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga-paññā*) are included by the phrase "possessed of the obstruction of kamma-result" (*vipākāvaraṇa*); these are those with a three-rooted rebirth-linking (*tihetuka-paṭisandhika*).
Showing that some are included by the term "lacking wisdom" (duppaññā), he said, "those who lack the supporting conditions for the attainment of the paths and fruits.
For without wisdom, there can be no such supporting condition.

14. Since fixed, unfixed, and mixed courses of existence occur only where there is such a process, it is only there that fixed phenomena exist. Showing that because this is absent in Uttarakuru, there is nothing there called "fixed," he said, "But as for those of Uttarakuru," and so forth.
16. Among the thirteen headings, the "obstacle heading" (*palibodha-sīsa*) and so forth are to be abandoned; the "resoluteness heading" (*adhimokkha-sīsa*) and so forth are the abandoners;
and the "range heading" (*gocara-sīsa*) is the fruit of abandonment. For that is the liberation consisting of the fruit within the objective field.

The "formations heading" (*saṅkhāra-sīsa*) is the object of both the path that abandons and its fruit; it is cessation, which is the seclusion from formations. Thus [are] those things to be abandoned.

In the *Paṭisambhidā*, thirteen "heads" (*sīsa*) are mentioned in order to show the state of being "equal-headed" (*samasīsibhāva*) through the demonstration that the exhaustion of the fruits and their objects occurs simultaneously.

However, here, based on the statement, "The exhaustion of the taints (*āsava*) and the exhaustion of life occur neither before nor after," he provides an application by way of the heads of the occurrence of defilements alone among those [thirteen], saying: "Therein, the head of defilement," and so forth.
In this context, although the Path— which is emerging from the round— exhausts even the head of the process of existence (*pavatta-sīsa*) by ensuring its non-occurrence after death,
it is nevertheless said that "the life-faculty, which is the head of the process, exhausts the death-consciousness," because the process continues until the moment of death.
However, through the exhaustion of the defilements (*kilesa-pariyādāna*), [the fruit] must be produced immediately following itself.
The sections on reviewing and the section on the exhaustion of the defilements deserve to be called the same.
For, according to the statement, "When liberated, the knowledge arises: 'It is liberated,'" the exhaustion of the defilements is said to be completed by the conclusion of the reviewing.
Furthermore, if that completion occurs through the death-consciousness, then by that very consciousness the life-span is also brought to its end.

Regarding the phrase "it occurs," he says "by way of equality of turns" because, through this equality of turns, there is no "first" or "last" in the exhaustion of the defilements (*kilesa*) and the exhaustion of life (*jīvita*).

As for the statement "having descended into the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), one attains final nibbāna (*parinibbāyati*)," it should be understood that here the very consciousness of final nibbāna is spoken of by way of its descent into the life-continuum.

17. *Mahāpayoga* means great activity; it is the destruction of the mode of existence of the great cloud that causes misfortune. *Tiṭṭheyya* means that the destruction would not proceed—that is the meaning. 18.
*Araṇīyattā* means because of being worthy of veneration (*payirupāsitabbattā*). 20.

When the state of having accomplished what was to be done occurs through the attainment of that supreme knowledge, the state of being "one possessing the three knowledges" (*tevijjatā*) is in its primary sense (*nippariyāyatā*). And since that is established by way of the lineage of transmission (*āgamanavasena*), it is the preeminent threefold knowledge; thus he said, "The burden is indeed to be brought [to completion]."

22. *Tattha ca*: the locative case is used here in the sense of a sign (*nimitta*), or in the sense of being the basis for the attainment of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*). For it is precisely there that one is said to have attained omniscience.
23. *Ananussutesu dhammesu*: the meaning is "in regard to truths not heard from others. 24.
Having stated the eight liberations (*vimokkha*), beginning with "one possessing form sees forms" and ending with the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), [it is said]: "From which..."

“Ānanda, when a bhikkhu dwells having personally realized these eight liberations with the body, and having seen them with wisdom, his taints are utterly destroyed. This, Ānanda, is called a bhikkhu liberated in both ways.
Although this was stated in the Mahānidāna Sutta, it was stated there with reference to the most excellent type of one liberated in both ways; therefore, here it is according to the Kīṭāgiri Sutta.
In order to include those liberated in both ways (*ubhatobhāgavimutta*), it is said: "Having attained the eight attainments together with their co-nascent mental body, he dwells therein.

For in the *Kīṭāgiri Sutta*: "Here, monks, a certain person dwells having personally touched with the body those peaceful liberations that are formless, transcending forms; and having seen them with wisdom, his taints are utterly destroyed."

“Monks, this person is called one liberated in both ways. Thus, four types of those liberated in both ways have been described by way of the formless attainments, as well as the supreme among those liberated in both ways, who possesses the aforementioned characteristics.
The same method applies to the body-witness (*kāyasakkhin*) as well.
"Having seen with wisdom, his taints are utterly destroyed": it is not that the taints see with wisdom;
rather, because they are destroyed by the cause of seeing, they are said to be "destroyed after having seen. For since their destruction is dependent upon seeing, seeing is the prior action.
"This one is supported by the name": this one liberated in both ways, having been freed from form, [is supported] by the name.
The meaning is as follows: because he stands having relied [on the formless] and is subsequently released from that, he is called "one who relies on the name" (*nāmanissitaka*);
and after stating the sutta that establishes this, it is said that he is "liberated in both ways" (*ubhatobhāgavimutta*) because of being well-liberated from the two bodies.

For in the sutta, regarding the brahmin Upasīva, who had attained the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*), the Blessed One declared: "The sage is proclaimed to be liberated in both ways, being liberated from the body of name (*nāmakāya*)."

In the first Elder’s exposition, one who is liberated by two parts is "liberated in both ways" (*ubhatobhāgavimutta*); in the second Elder’s exposition, one who is liberated from both parts is "liberated in both ways";
and in the third Elder’s exposition, one who is liberated by two parts on two occasions is [so called].
This is their distinction. In that context, "liberated" means liberated from defilements (*kilesa*) through the suppression and eradication of those defilements.

The meaning should be understood as "liberated from both bodies. However, the immaterial-sphere attainment is said to be "liberated from the mental body" (*nāmakāya*), which means it is liberated from the mental body consisting of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).

Because it is liberated from the mental body through the distancing of the hindrances, and liberated from the physical body (*rūpakāya*) through the suppression of craving for form, it is called "partially liberated on both sides" (*ekadesena ubhatobhāgavimutta*).

The intention [of the phrase] "it occurs" is that it is appropriate for it to serve as the cause for attaining the state known as "liberated in both ways" (*ubhatobhāgavimutta*), which is based upon the path of Arahatship.

For the intention is that if not even one among these possesses the attainment of the eight liberations (*aṭṭhavimokkha*), then they have not attained even a single liberation that is liberated from the form-body (*rūpakāya*), which is the cause for the state of being "liberated in both ways. Indeed, among those in the formless realm (*arūpāvacara*), not even one...

Because he has attained the state of one liberated in both ways through the acquisition of its causes, and because he is capable of being designated by that name due to possessing a portion of the eight liberations, he is called "one who has attained the eight liberations. Therefore, it was said: "But in the case of the immaterial-sphere jhānas," and so forth.

26. "He realizes the limit of what is touched": the end of what is touched (*phuṭṭhanta*) is the limit of what is touched; [it refers to] the limit of the touched, namely, the immaterial-sphere jhānas.
The intended meaning is "the immediately subsequent time. And here, the accusative case should be understood as expressing continuous connection (*accantasaṃyoga*).

What is meant is that one realizes precisely the time immediately following contact by means of the method to be realized. Alternatively, this may be a neuter abstract noun, as in expressions such as "he sat to one side" (*ekamantaṃ nisīdi*).
For he [realizes it] through the formless jhāna by way of suppression-liberation (*vikkhambhana-vimokkha*) from the material body and from a portion of the mental body.
Being liberated, by that [liberation] the release termed cessation becomes as if observed and illuminated, yet it has not been realized by means of the body.
However, when certain taints have been exhausted by taking cessation as the object, it is realized by him;
therefore, because he realizes the cessation to be realized exactly as it was observed by means of the mental body (*nāmakāya*), he is called a "body-witness" (*kāyasakkhī*).
It is said [he is "liberated"], yet he is not called "one who has attained liberation" because some of his taints (*āsava*) have not been fully exhausted.
27. Regarding the phrase "having seen, he has attained": by this, he illustrates the attainment of cessation through the vision characterized as the vision of the Four Noble Truths.
Alternatively, there is the reading "having reached the end of seeing" (*diṭṭhantaṃ patto*); immediately following the knowledge of the path of stream-entry, which is characterized as seeing—
"Attained" (patta) is what is meant. For from the first fruit up to the highest path, one is "attained to view" (diṭṭhippatto).

However, regarding the phrase "having rejected this method with 'no,'" it is stated here that there is a diversity of wisdom among those who have attained the states of being "attained to view" and "liberated by faith";
it is not stated that the specific distinction by which that distinction was reached has been described—this is the fault [in his position].

It should be understood that [the teaching] was rejected upon seeing [this]. By the phrase "in the commentaries on the Agamas," it should be known that he merely confirms the established diversity of what has come down in tradition for the sake of strengthening it.
With the words "one who has faith is liberated," he shows that even for one who is not liberated in every respect, there is a state of being liberated by means of mere faith.
Alternatively, "liberated through faith" (saddhā-vimutta) means "resolutely intent through faith" (saddhāya adhimutta).
29. "He carries wisdom" means he exercises wisdom pre-eminently; "wisdom carries this person" means it leads them toward Nibbāna.

31. Regarding the phrase "even at the moment of the Path," why was the word *api* (even/also) used? Does one not become endowed with the Noble Eightfold Path only at the moment of the Path, such that one would be called a *sotāpanna* only then? This is not the case.
For the name "stream" (sota) is given because it is a stream to a fruit—whether eightfold or sevenfold—that is similar to the Path itself;

thus, one who possesses that [fruit] is called a "stream-enterer" (sotāpanna). Alternatively, even one established in the fruit is said to possess the stream by means of the path, provided that the stream has not been lost and can still be made to proceed by the path. However, the stream is not entered anew at that moment as it was during the first moment of the path.
Therefore, because he has entered the stream, it is appropriate to call him a "stream-enterer" (sotāpanna) starting from the first fruit. For it is said:
"Bhikkhus, whoever has unwavering confidence in me, all of them are stream-enterers.

Of those stream-enterers, five find their final end here, and five find their final end after passing away from here. In that context, [this applies] to those established in the second fruit and so forth.
The phrase "there is a distinct name" means that only one who has attained the first fruit, being distinguished from the others, is appropriately called a "stream-enterer" (sotāpanna);

therefore, he alone is intended here. By the statement "he awakens by means of the path already attained," this shows that the path already attained serves as the decisive support (upanissaya) for the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths and other such practices. *Sambodhi* is the supreme resort (*ayana*) or support (*nissaya*).

"For *etassa* means 'for him whose destination is full enlightenment' (*sambodhiparāyaṇo*). In the second sense, he is 'one whose destination, path, and resort is full enlightenment' (*sambodhiparāyaṇo*).
32. Since the word *kula* alone refers specifically to a great family, he says: "The meaning is that he is reborn only in families of great wealth. 33.

What is called the "seed of the aggregates" (*khandhabīja*) is the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhiviññāṇa*). In this context, it is [discussed] solely by way of its being established here and its being subject to reflection (*nijjhānika*).
The meaning is this: one who has attained jhāna, even if they have not yet completely severed the internal fetters, is similar to a non-returner (anāgāmi) and is of a nature not to return;

such a person does not count here [in this context]. However, one who wanders both below and above, remaining within the realm of sense-desire (kāmabhava), and possesses only inferior jhāna, is what is intended here as one who "counts" [among those to be reckoned].
34. "That which is to be said" means that it would be appropriate to say: "The state of attenuation is to be understood by way of two causes," and so forth. 36.
"Either immediately upon rebirth" means that either this person becomes [attenuated] immediately upon rebirth, or else they generate the Noble Path immediately thereafter.
"Or before reaching the middle of the lifespan" refers to the measure of the lifespan of that person.
The meaning of the text here is that when [the life-span] has not yet reached the middle, one generates the Noble Path within that interval. However, in the Commentary,

in the phrase "without having reached the mountain, the river," it should be understood that the word *appattaṃ* (not reached) is used as a *vacanasesa* (elliptical expression), functioning as a word occurring after another word (*para*) in a compound construction, as in the case of "having not reached the middle of the life-span."

37. *Upahacca*: the meaning of this is "having approached. By this, both the passing beyond the middle [of life] and the approaching of death are included. Therefore it is said: "Having passed beyond the middle," and so forth. 40. *Uddhaṃvāhibhāvena*:
that which carries upward is "upward-carrying" (*uddhaṃvāhī*), namely the stream of craving or the stream of cyclic existence (*vaṭṭasota*).

Its state is "the state of being upward-carrying"; by that, "by the state of being upward-carrying" is what is meant. Even though one is an "upward-streamer" (*uddhaṃsota*) among the Aviha deities, if they attain final nibbāna there...

It does not matter where he goes to attain final nibbāna; rather, for one who attains final nibbāna, there exists both "attaining final nibbāna without exertion" (*asaṅkhāra-parinibbāyitā*) and "attaining final nibbāna with exertion" (*sasaṅkhāra-parinibbāyitā*).
It is on this basis that ten types of non-returners (*anāgāmin*) are described, and likewise in the case of the Atappa and other heavens.
"Without reaching the surface" (*anupahacca-tala*) means not having reached the surface. For those who attain final nibbāna without exertion and with exertion, their progress is swift and very swift.
Thus, their similarity to a fungus that burns up small or large amounts of grass and wood should be understood;

it is not like the superiority [of those who attain Nibbāna] immediately upon arising, nor like the lack of superiority [of those who attain Nibbāna] after reaching the ocean. Rather, there is a degree of superiority and lack of superiority among those who attain Nibbāna by collision in the intermediate state (*antarāparinibbāyin*) and those who go upstream (*uddhaṃsota*).
For it is precisely these who are the "those who attain Nibbāna without exertion" (*asaṅkhāraparinibbāyin*) and "those who attain Nibbāna with exertion" (*sasankhāraparinibbāyin*).
The expression "greater than great" is intended to show the bark capable of burning grass and wood, not to show an excess or a non-excess. "May there be nothing for me,
and may nothing be mine" refers to the fivefold causal series beginning with ignorance and volitional formations, and not to consciousness and so forth.
The meaning of "this fivefold fruit, while occurring, shall not be mine" is as follows:

By that, through the accomplishment of past existence and by showing the occurrence of this suffering from the origin of suffering, the practice of seeing the arising of the aggregates in the sense of the arising of conditions has been stated.
[The thought] "it will not be, it will not be mine" means: if, at present, this fivefold cause does not exist...
"In the future, the fivefold fruit will not be mine"—this is the meaning. By this, the practice of seeing vanishing (*vaya*) in the sense of the cessation of conditions has been stated.
Alternatively, the practice of emptiness (*suññatā*)—by way of warding off the notions of self and what belongs to self both now and in the future—has been stated by all four [truths].
"Whatever exists" (*yadatthi*) means that which exists. "Become" (*bhūta*) means having its own intrinsic nature (*sasabhāva*), or having arisen, according to the observed arising and passing away.
The meaning is that the five aggregates, as they have been seen in their emptiness, are merely name-and-form (nāmarūpa), devoid of any imagined state such as woman, man, or a sentient being.
With a mind turning away through the contemplation of turning away (vivaṭṭānupassanā), one attains equanimity, thinking, "I abandon that which has come to be";
it is thus said that one becomes equanimous by means of the knowledge of equanimity towards formations (saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇa).

Regarding the phrases "he does not delight in existence" (*bhave na rajjati*) and "he does not delight in origination" (*sambhave na rajjatīti*), some say that this means he does not delight in either non-distinct or distinct existence.
However, it should be understood that "existence" (*bhava*) refers to the present state, while "origination" (*sambhava*) refers to the future, which is included by the mention of "birth" (*jāti*).
Alternatively, "existence" (*bhava*) is said to be what has already come to be (*bhūta*), and "origination" (*sambhava*) is its nutriment; [the practitioner] does not delight in these two.
"He delights" shows the practice of one in training (*sekkhapaṭipatti*). For detachment from what has come to be and its origin is the practice of one in training.
As it is said: "Venerable sir, one sees with right wisdom, as it really is: 'This has come to be.

Having seen with right wisdom, as it really is, that 'This has come to be,' one practices for disenchantment with what has come to be, for its fading away, and for its cessation. Its nutriment and origin..."
"Having seen it as it truly is... [as before] ...he practices for disenchantment with that which arises from that nutriment...

Having seen as it truly is... [as before] ...that what has come to be through the cessation of that nutriment is subject to cessation, he practices for disenchantment with what is subject to cessation, for its fading away, and for its cessation.
In this way, venerable sir, one is a trainee. Then he spoke further:
Then, not being attached in this way, he gradually sees the further state of peace, Nibbāna, correctly with the wisdom of the path;
yet that state has not been fully realized by him in every respect, because it is to be realized by the fourth path alone,
and it has not yet been realized by him through that [third path].
The commentary on the Singlefold Exposition is finished.
2. Commentary on the Twofold Exposition. 63.
Because no defilement has been suppressed, the sense-sphere existence (kāmabhava) is not liberated in any way from anything; this constitutes the internal grasping.

“Specific condition” (*visesa-paccaya*) refers to what is internal (*ajjhatta*). In this context, “bondage” is the internal fetter (*ajjhatta-saṃyojana*); that which is associated with it is “possessing internal fetters. 83.
One whose mind functions with benevolence even without a cause is “kind without cause” (*akāraṇa-vacchala*).

Even when looking toward a future purpose, one who acts based on what was previously received or done is indeed called “grateful” (*kataññū*), but not “one who returns a prior favor” (*pubbakārī*); thus he said, “he will act... (*karissati*).
“...me,” and so forth. One who is devoted to darkness and light, yet performs meritorious deeds without depending on the fruit of merit, is called a “prior-doer” (*pubbakārī*).
“He makes the perception ‘I am giving a debt’”—the meaning is that even if he does not actually form such a perception, he is as if doing so.

86. Regarding “having obtained bear meat, one does not feel remorse thinking it is pig meat”: even though one knows it is bear meat, one does not feel remorse thinking it is pig meat; the point is that having crushed it [into an indistinguishable mass], one transgresses.
90. *Titta* means one who is free from anxiety due to having completed what was to be done.
The commentary on the Exposition of Pairs (*Dukaniddesa-vaṇṇanā*) is finished.
3. Commentary on the Exposition of Threes (*Tikaniddesa-vaṇṇanā*).

91. "By way of the distinction from the other restraints" means by way of the restraint of the mind (*manosaṃvara*), or by way of the distinctions such as the restraint of mindfulness (*satisaṃvara*).

"Possession of unwholesome virtue" refers to possessing that which was stated: "And what, householder, are unwholesome virtues? Unwholesome bodily action, unwholesome verbal action, and evil livelihood. For him... [omitted] ...
"his conduct is thus attended by apprehension" means his conduct is thus accompanied by apprehension.
94. The terms such as "body-witness" (*kāyasakkhī*) and so forth are stated by way of showing the distinction between individuals who possess similar objects of experience.

107. Or, "concentration is the beginning": since supramundane states are the Sāsana in the ultimate sense, the concentration that serves as their foundation is called its "beginning"; insight is mentioned because it is proximate to that [concentration]; and the Path is mentioned because it is a part of its root. 108.
A person of "shoulder-like wisdom" (*ucchaṅgapañña*) is to be understood as one whose wisdom resembles a shoulder; this is precisely because of the similarity of his wisdom to a shoulder.
Just as wisdom, so too is the person like a hollow; this is stated with the intention that therein phenomena do not remain for long.
For he will say: "The meaning is that wisdom is like a hollow.
And just as wisdom is like a hollow, it should likewise be understood to be like an overturned jar, because therein phenomena do not persist.

113. One who possesses anger-streaks produced by offenses that are like lines carved on stone—due to their long duration and stability—is "endowed with stone-lineage" (*pāsāṇalekhūpama*); thus he is called "stone-lined" (*pāsāṇalekhūpamo*). The same applies to the others as well. 118.
One who is devoid of the basis for learning and so forth, being empty like a reed, is called a "reed" (*naḷo*); one who is "raised up" (*uggata*) like a reed is "arrogant" (*unnaḷo*). 122.

Regarding the statement, "There will be talk of virtue for us," he says, "there is no talk of virtue at all," demonstrating that even the initial commencement of such talk does not occur when one is immoral.

123. "In this and that" means: in each of those instances—whether it be one who is to be assisted, one who is to be purified by wisdom, or one who is to be increased—he assists by means of the wisdom arisen in dependence upon superior virtue (*adhika-sīla*);
such is the meaning. 124. "Immorality is like a cesspool": by this, he shows that immorality is indeed similar to excrement.
130. "And they are not able to explain correctly": this refers to the sense that, for the most part, they are not able [to do so].
It is stated [either] that when a Tathāgata has arisen, one is unable to attain meditative absorption while making an effort to do so out of disrespect toward him;
or else, the sectarians such as Pūraṇa and others are intended.
The commentary on the Exposition of Threes is finished.
4. Commentary on the Exposition of the Tetrads 133.
Immorality committed by another through one’s own command and personal application is called "an heir to half of that evil" because one is an heir to [half of] the evil through such an injunction.
145. The word "this" refers to the method beginning with "the first among them," and so forth.

148. *Ñāṇugghāṭanaṃ* (the clearing away by knowledge) is the bringing of the phenomena within the range of knowledge through teaching. *Saha udāhaṭavelāyā* means "together with the moment of being uttered"; the meaning is that it occurs at that very time, without the interval having elapsed.

152. *Taṃ* refers to the immediately preceding statement. When it is asked, "What is the world? the reply, "The five aggregates of clinging," is a statement that stands by encompassing a great significance and is consistent with the meaning (*atthayutta*). The definition "it is called 'world' (*loka*) because it disintegrates" (*lujjati*) is consistent with the etymological cause (*kāraṇayutta*).
156. *Sahitāsahitassa* means "of the combined and the uncombined," or alternatively, "in the delimitation of the combined and the uncombined."
"Dveyeva" means only the second and the fourth. Because they possess the excellence of both teacher and disciple and are thus capable of awakening others, they are "dhamma-preachers by nature";
the meaning is that they are preachers of the true Dhamma. 157.

"Vāsadhura" refers to the cultivation of the perfuming of the mind with wholesome states. This "evil person" is mentioned as the fourth, not the first. For the first is intended here as one who does not wish to deceive, such as the Brahmin of Verañjā.
159. Regarding persons as well, "the noble ones' similarity in advancing and so forth" means that for persons, the acts of advancing and so forth are similar to those of the noble ones;
or alternatively, it means that the person is similar to the noble ones by way of their advancing and so forth, or that there is a similarity in the advancing and so forth.

166. When one says of an immoral person, "He is immoral," one speaks what is factual. When one does not say that he is immoral because of killing living beings or because of taking what is not given, but rather says it is because of killing living beings alone, one speaks what is true.
Regarding that which was called "at the proper time," in order to show the nature of the one who is said to "speak at the proper time" with respect to that statement:
Showing that the passage beginning with “he knows the right time” has been stated, he says: “Regarding that which was said as ‘at the right time,’ there is the person...,” and so forth.
(168) “Failure of arrival” refers to the [sexual] act; “failure of antecedent conditions” refers to the semen and blood.

“Conditions for occurrence” means the conditions for what occurs, namely food and so forth. “Joti” means that which illuminates; it is light. By means of the excellence of family and other such factors...
And while shining, the light moves as light.

173. By means of reviewing the defilements that have been abandoned and those that remain, there is the very vision of liberation through seeing those defilements from which one is liberated and those from which one is not;
thus it is said: "The knowledge and vision of liberation is nineteenfold."
"Knowledge of reviewing. 174. "Whatever [garments] are woven on a loom": this means whatever garments among those woven on a loom; thus it is said.
"Sāyatatiyo" means that which has a third part consisting of *sāya* (evening). "Anuyogo" means application. "One who is devoted to that" (*taṃ-anuyutto*) is the accusative case.
It should be seen, or it is a neuter gerundive. 178.
Therein, "by way of training" means by way of training in the training and in the livelihood (*sājīva*). "Fulfilling the training" means fulfilling the restraint of virtue (*sīla-saṃvara*).
And "not transgressing the livelihood" refers to [the study of] the collection of names (*nāmakāya*), the collection of phrases (*padakāya*), and the collection of etymologies (*niruttikāya*).
The meaning is: "being one who does not transgress the training rule spoken by the Blessed One, namely, 'the body of phonemes'.
And it is precisely this pair that is called "training" (*sikkhanā*). In that regard, non-transgression of the communal life (*sājīva*) is the condition for the fulfillment of the training rules;

for from that [non-transgression], there arises the fulfillment of restraint (*saṃvara*) up to the [attainment of the] path. "From the state of destruction" means from the state of harming. "Turmeric-dye" (*haliddirāga*).

Regarding the phrase "it does not remain firm like [something]," the similarity to turmeric dye (*haliddirāga*) should be understood here through the instability of the *kathā* (discourse or description), not through the instability of the person.
179. As for "a wooden māsaka": by the word "iti" (thus), he indicates such types as those that enter into common transaction.

"Exchanging one thing for another after showing it" means, for example, showing a pair of garments worth ten coins and giving them to someone who does not know it to be so, in exchange for something worth five coins.
181. *Avikiṇṇasukhaṃ*: Unscattered happiness; that is, happiness that has not become diffused by way of the conceptualization of beauty and so forth regarding forms and other sense objects.
187. Insight (*vipassanā*) that proceeds by way of impermanence and so forth regarding the phenomena of the aggregates is said to be "obtained" through the attainment of the path and its fruits;

because it does not persist in the absence of such attainment, only one who has attained the path and its fruits is called "one who has obtained the higher wisdom of insight into phenomena" (*adhipaññādhammavipassanālābhī*).
The knowledge of the path and its fruits (*maggaphalañāṇa*) should be understood as "insight into phenomena through higher wisdom" (*adhipaññādhammavipassanā*), because it possesses superior wisdom,
or because it possesses a distinguished vision regarding the Dharma of the Four Truths, or indeed regarding Nibbāna, which is the supreme among all phenomena.
(189) "Not endowed with what has been heard" means not being possessed of either the [teachings] as they were heard or their meaning.
The commentary on the Exposition of the Tetrads is finished.
5. Commentary on the Exposition of the Pentads 191.
Since the classification of individuals is understood from the mere enumeration in the first pentad, [the following explains] how one should practice toward them.
Explaining that practice, he said, "In this regard, as for that which... and so forth. "The word *ārambha*" means a word expressive of the activity of undertaking (*ārambhakiriyā*).
He said, "The function of the path is completed by the arising of the fruit," meaning that "the fruit itself is stated by way of the function of the path.
"Excellent through entreaty" means excellent through [acts such as] praise and so forth.
192. From the beginning, that which is to be placed (ādheyya) is the "receptacle" (ādhāra).

"Mouth" (mukha) should be understood as the grasping that proceeds by way of seeing, hearing, and giving a reply, just like [speech] proceeding from the mouth. That mouth is the receptacle; or rather, the natural mouth itself is the receptacle for the purpose of grasping.

One whose [grasping] has that as its receptacle is "one who has the mouth as the receptacle" (ādheyyamukho); what is meant is one who grasps by means of the initial statement alone, without further investigation.
194. *Rajaggasmiṃ* means in the state of being a dust-cloud. 199.

The construction is not "milk is declared the best of cows"; rather, after showing the five products of the cow from their origin, the passage beginning with "milk from the cow" was stated for the purpose of demonstrating that clarified butter (*sappimaṇḍa*) is the foremost among them. Therefore he said:
“Cows have what is called milk,” and so forth.
The commentary on the Exposition of the Pentads is finished.
6. Commentary on the Exposition of the Hexads.

202. In order to show that the Perfectly Enlightened Ones and others are individuals who possess the aforementioned qualities in an absolute sense, he said, "By that, the Perfectly Enlightened One is to be seen," and so forth. Therein, "by that" means by all of this taken together:

namely, his own direct realization of the Truths, his attainment of mastery over the powers consisting in the acquisition of omniscience, and [the rest]. "By the knowledge of omniscience" (sabbaññutaññāṇena).

However, when this is stated, all of this is included because there is no omniscience (sabbaññutaññāṇa) without the personal realization of the truths and the attainment of mastery over the powers (balas).
Therefore, in the commentary (aṭṭhakathā), only this much was said: "by means of omniscience.
In that context, by the expression "not derived from a teacher, arisen by oneself," the fact that omniscience has a teacher is [implied].
He denies arising from another, but not the omniscient knowledge of our Teacher which was produced by others;
for there is no such [knowledge] as that which ought to be denied.
The commentary on the Exposition of the Sixfold Set is finished.
7. Explanation of the Set of Seven (Sattakaniddesa) 203.

Regarding the phrase "faith is called 'well-acquired,' it emerges": by this, it is shown that faith—which is included among wholesome states (*kusala-dhamma*) or which constitutes resolution (*adhimokkha*) among the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiya-dhamma*)—is wholesome as it emerges, being regarded as "good. The same applies to moral shame (*hirī*) and the other [faculties].
Regarding the phrase "in wholesome states" (*kusalesu dhammesu*): here, the locative case is to be understood as indicating either inclusion within them or assistance toward them.
Furthermore, by such statements as "Faith emerges well in wholesome states," etc., [the text] shows the arising of faith and the other qualities through the wisdom of their emergence.
For this very reason it is said: "That faith of his does not even remain," and so forth.

Having stated the vision of benefits that assists in emerging—namely, “Excellent is faith in wholesome states”—it should be understood that by the words “emerges,” it is precisely faith, so designated, that is shown as the emergence. “Caṅkavāra” refers to the alkaline vats of washermen.
A single mental cycle (cittavāra) is the continuity of rebirth-linking, life-continuum, and death, produced by a single kamma.
It is said, "by the second mental moment," because the second [moment] follows immediately after the first, just as it was grasped.
One should understand that there are many individuals who, having emerged and remained [in the stream], do not realize *arahantship* in that particular birth;
however, even one who does realize it may, during the prior stage, pass through the state of being the third individual and so forth, and finally become the seventh individual.
The commentary on the Exposition of the Septads is finished.
10. Commentary on the Exposition of the Decads. 209.
Regarding the phrase "the end for five here, the end for five here having left [this world]": herein, those who are stream-enterers and so forth...

Those who, having been reborn in the fine-material or immaterial realms, will attain final nibbāna there— even though they belong to the class of those who reach their goal after departing from this world—
are not included among those reborn in a state common to worldlings, because their internal fetters have not been eradicated. However,

it is by way of being reborn in a state not shared with worldlings that those such as the "one who attains nibbāna in the interval" (antarāparinibbāyī) and others are described as "reaching their goal after departing from here."
"They have been stated" means they are to be understood.
The commentary on the Exposition of the Decads is finished.
The Root Commentary on the *Puggalapaññatti* treatise is completed.
Commentary on the Introduction to the *Mūlaṭīkā* of the *Kathāvatthuppakaraṇa*:

Regarding the phrase "because they are the basis (*vatthu*) for the discussions," it refers to the fact that the collection of discussions, which constitutes this treatise (*pakaraṇa*), serves as the locus or occasion for its own constituent parts.
He speaks. For within a whole, its parts are included. Showing the manner in which he taught it in brief, he said:
"It was established by the very laying down of the matrix (mātikā).
This concludes the commentary on the Nidānakathā.
"He attained final Nibbāna through the element of Nibbāna without residue remaining" (*anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbāyi*):
the term "final Nibbāna" is stated here as the instrument (*karaṇabhāvena*) for the purpose of distinguishing it from the mere act of passing away (*parinibbāna*).

Alternatively, that element of Nibbāna by means of which the final consciousness becomes free from rebirth-linking (*appaṭisandhika*) is stated as the instrument for that cessation of rebirth-linking. "The weak side" (*dubbalapakkhaṃ*).
They say it is not as powerful as the *Kāḷāsoka*, but rather it is "of a single circle" (*ekamaṇḍalika*).

However, its weakness is stated due to the absence of wisdom capable of generating the distinction between those who speak according to the Dhamma and those who speak against the Dhamma. "Of them alone" means of the Bāhulikas themselves;

they are also called the Bahussutikas. "Those who have split" (*bhinna-kā*) means they have split from the original recitation (*mūla-saṅgīti*) or the original school (*mūla-nikāya*), [differing] in their tenets, suttas, and grammatical forms.
And the meaning is that they have reached a state of dissimilarity.
"The compendium of the root" refers to the Council of Five Hundred. Regarding the phrase "except for those compiled," and so forth:

from among the Long Discourses and others, having extracted this or that particular discourse from what was already compiled elsewhere, it is said that they "made them elsewhere. From what had been compiled...
Or else, they composed a discourse not included elsewhere, or they composed it somewhere other than [where it now stands]; this is the meaning of "elsewhere.
"The meaning and the Dhamma" means the meaning of the Pāḷi and the Pāḷi itself. "In the Vinaya and in the five Nikāyas" means in the Vinaya and in the remaining five Nikāyas.
“Ānanda, ‘feeling’ has been taught by me in a figurative sense,” and so forth—this is what is taught figuratively.
For here the figurative sense is that the Blessed One spoke of equanimity-feeling as “peaceful” and “sublime. “Bhikkhus, there are these three feelings:
pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and equanimous feeling”—and so forth—this is what is taught non-figuratively. For the intrinsic nature of feeling is indeed threefold.
Herein, this is the non-figurative sense (*nippariyāyatā*). “Even pleasant feeling is impermanent and conditioned,” and so forth, is of direct meaning (*nītattha*).
“Whatever is felt, all that is suffering,” and so forth, is of indirect meaning (*neyyattha*).
Passages such as, “Monks, in three respects the people of Jambudīpa surpass the people of Uttarakuru and the gods of the Tāvatiṃsa heaven,” refer to something else.

Having taken what was spoken, they established another meaning. Regarding such suttas as "There is no living of the holy life among the devas," they took what was spoken with reference to one thing and established another meaning; this is how the meaning here should be understood.

By means of the mere shadow of the phrasing, they destroyed much of the subtle and refined meaning, such as emptiness (suññatā) and so forth, in passages beginning with, "There is a certain person who practices for his own benefit."
"Profound in the Vinaya" means setting aside a certain portion of what is profound in the Vinaya;
or alternatively, it means setting aside a certain portion of the Sutta that is profound by virtue of its removal of defilements (*kilesavinaya*).
"Appropriate" refers to a Sutta that accords with one's own intention, or a non-Sutta that merely resembles a Sutta. Some [commentators] expounded only the section on the Aṭṭhakathā, while others...
He said, "The entire Abhidhamma Piṭaka," meaning "the Abhidhamma as the extraction of meanings (atthuddhāra) consisting of the six treatises (chappakaraṇa).
Although the *Kathāvatthu* is subject to dispute (*savivāda*), the six treatises—which are free from dispute (*avivādāni*)—should have been recited;
however, they did not come forth, and it was for the purpose of showing this that he said "the six treatises. Or else, [it refers to] those that were circulating prior to the Third Council.
By way of this [sixfold classification], it is called the "Six Treatises" (*chappakaraṇa*). "Others" refers to other treatises such as those of the Abhidhamma.

"Name" refers to the name of a Nikāya, such as *Mañjusirī*, which is not connected with [the names of] the Buddha and so forth. "Characteristic" (*liṅga*) refers to a specific shape produced by distinctions such as the lower garment, the upper robe, and so on.
"Requisites" refers to items such as the training staff (*sikkā*). "Demeanor" (*ākappa*) should be understood as the specific manner of arranging the limbs during standing and other postures.
*Karaṇa* refers to specific duties such as sewing robes and so forth.
*Saṅkantika* means those who have split away from a particular school (*nikāya*) or tenet (*vāda*).
The meaning is that the divisions of the *saṅkantikas*—namely the *Suttavādins*—gradually split apart and did split apart. *Bhinnavādena* means "by one in whom various tenets have split."
It is said that there are eighteen [schools] together with that undivided Theravāda, including the divided doctrines (*bhinnavāda*).

Alternatively, "by the divided doctrine" means that there are eighteen through their divided tenets (*laddhi*); the meaning is that all of them are included by the word "together. Regarding the phrase "the supreme among the Theravādins," here *thera* is a nominative form without a case ending.
It is called *thera* because it belongs to the elders (*therānaṃ ayaṃ*). What is that? It is the doctrine (*vāda*). Thus, the meaning here is: "the elder among doctrines" (*thero vādānam uttamo*).

With reference to the doctrines that have already arisen, it is said: "the crushing of the doctrines of others. Because it has the characteristic of refuting doctrines that will arise in the future, it is called "characterized by the future.
The commentary on the Nidānakathā is finished.
The Mahāvagga.
1. Discourse on the Person (Puggalakathā) 1.1.
The Purely Real Meaning (Suddhasaccikaṭṭha) 1.1.1.
Explanation by Way of Conformity and Opposition (Anulomapaccanīkavaṇṇanā)
1. Illusions such as a non-jewel appearing in the form of a jewel and so forth are called "illusion" (*māyā*).

Illusions, mirages, and the like—which are apprehended through unreal forms such as jewels or water—are not the ultimate truth (*asaccikaṭṭha*) because they possess the aspect of an unreal object of knowledge (*abhūtaññeyyākāra*).

Showing that what does not exist in that way is the ultimate truth, he said: "Illusion... [is] the real meaning" (*bhūtattha*). Even when apprehended by means of hearsay and so forth, it is likewise...

"It is otherwise as well" means it should be understood as being of such a kind, not the ultimate reality (*paramattha*); however, showing that the ultimate reality is what is directly perceived by oneself (*attapaccakkha*), he said:
"From hearsay... [etc. ...the supreme goal. Regarding "of the sophist" (*chalavāda*):
because of the commonality of the word "exists," when "exists" is stated, it refers to the common expression used for form and so forth which have been stated as existing.

This is the intended meaning (*adhippāya*). Furthermore, because of the statement, “Having taken up that conviction (*laddhi*), he acknowledges, ‘I am so,’” it cannot be said that he is a “quibbler” (*chalavāda*).
For a conviction is not a quibble. “Not giving an opportunity” means cutting off his standing ground.
If [the self] were apprehended in the sense of ultimate reality (*saccikaṭṭha*), it would be apprehended like form and so forth; however, since it is not apprehended in that way...
The intention is that he turns [the opponent] back by saying, "Your argument does not hold.

With reference to that, he shows that the "ultimate reality" (saccikaṭṭha) mentioned here in the phrase "that which is ultimate reality" is the same as the "classification of phenomena" (dhammappabheda) found in such passages as "matter is apprehended," which is demonstrated by way of its having conditions and so forth.
Having said, “In that sense of the true and ultimate meaning,” for one who says, “in that manner,” this is the intended meaning:
that which is apprehended by way of the mode of the true and ultimate meaning is what is called “apprehended in the sense of the true and ultimate meaning.

Otherwise, instead of saying “tattha” (therein), it would have to be said “tassa tenākārena” (of that, in that manner). What, then, is the distinction between this [question] and the previous question? Regarding the previous question—
It was stated that just as the seventy-fivefold classification of phenomena (dhamma) is apprehended by way of its actual intrinsic nature (sabhāva), so too is the person (puggala) apprehended.

However, in this context, one must consider: by whatever mode—such as being subject to change (ruppana) or having conditions—that classification of phenomena is apprehended when it is being apprehended by way of its actual intrinsic nature, is the person also apprehended by that same mode?

This is the distinction. Furthermore, just as feeling—which is perceived as having the intrinsic nature of an element (bhūtasabhāva) like material form—is not perceived by way of the mode of being affected (ruppanākāra), so too the person (puggala)—which is perceived as having the intrinsic nature of an element like the various categories of phenomena (dhamma)—is not perceived by way of such modes as being affected or possessing conditions;
thus, it can be asserted by the opponent, and this [objection] is not to be censured.

It may be so. And since contempt for him is appropriate, no refutation should be made. However, because no other ultimate reality apart from the differentiation of phenomena is established, he challenges [the opponent] precisely by way of the differentiation of phenomena. By means of that very contempt, he demonstrates the refutation.
These are the positions of acceptance and contempt, the positions of affirmation and denial through general and specific characteristics, and the positions of direct and inverse order.
The distinction between these two methods—the first and the second—should be understood as follows.
