When one says, "Indeed, you ought to say this," one incurs the fault of failing to state what ought to be stated;

it should be understood that this is expressed by the phrase "because of having incurred a censure" (*niggahassa pāpitattā*). Thus, this [method] is both a censure and a matter of direct and reverse order.
It is stated: "Because it is said that there is the imposition of four evils, [the group] beginning with this is called the 'forward pentad' (*anulomapañcaka*).
However, from both the forward and reverse orders, there ought to be seven [groups] including two instances of setting aside (*ṭhapanā*);
or else, the reason for excluding those must be stated. As for what will be said: "'Setting aside' (*ṭhapanā*) is so called because of the setting aside of the opponent's position; 'this..."
"It is merely for the purpose of showing 'this is your fault'; it does not serve to make evident either a refutation or a counter-argument.

With this intention, he also avoids the two types of *ṭhapanā* here. Just as in that case he will speak of the fourfold nature of the counter-argument (*paṭikamma*) without mentioning the fivefold nature of the counter-argument, so too here the fourfold nature of the refutation (*niggaha*) ought to be stated.
However, because the *suddhikaniggaha* (pure defeat) is dominated by the element of defeat itself, it should be understood that the defeat alone is stated separately as the subject of the summary.
As for those who say, "Because it is a defeat regarding what is not as it truly is (*ayathābhūta*),

no counter-argument (*paṭikamma*) is stated there separately," for them it would follow that in the second "gate of debate" (*vādamukha*), there would be four types of defeat and five types of counter-argument.
2. "‘The very ultimate meaning intended by oneself’—the intention here is with reference to conventional truth (sammutisacca). For he will say:
‘The opponent’s further inquiry, “What is the ultimate meaning? is directed toward either pure conventional truth or conventional truth mixed with the ultimate meaning.
In that context, if the opponent maintains that the ultimate meaning intended by himself is conventional truth,"
One who asserts that a person is apprehended in the mode of conventional truth (*sammutisacca*) should not be refuted as being of the same position;
rather, this discussion itself should not have been initiated. Alternatively, the meaning is this:

the proponent of the other side (*paravādin*) spoke the words beginning with "that which is the ultimate reality" (*saccikaṭṭha*) while referring precisely to the ultimate reality intended by the proponent himself. For the proponent [holds that] conventional truth alone is the ultimate reality.
It follows that [the term] "intended" (adhippetam) is used. If both were intended, it would not be necessary to say again:

"Or, having grouped conventional truth and ultimate truth together, he spoke thus. Furthermore, if both truths are indeed "ultimate in the sense of being the true state" (saccikaṭṭha-paramattha), then for one who wishes to maintain that the person is apprehended by way of a portion of that "true state," [the claim] "the person is apprehended as an ultimate in the sense of the true state," and so forth, [would be untenable].
An inquiry should not be made, nor is it appropriate to inquire by means of a partial aspect of the ultimate truth (*saccikaṭṭha*).
For feeling, which is apprehended in the mode of being felt, cannot be inquired into as if it were apprehended in the mode of being affected (*ruppana*);

furthermore, the opponent does not accept a person (*puggala*) whose intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) consists of being affected and so forth, but rather [accepts] only the ultimate reality (*paramattha-sacca*). [This applies] to anything other than the ultimate truth.
When that which is the "actual reality" (*saccikaṭṭha*) is present, one need not investigate whether it possesses ultimate truth (*paramatthasacca*).

For those who say, "Having attributed the designation 'actual reality' to what is not actual reality, he asks with reference to that," it is illogical for the "actual reality" as expressed by their own conventional usage to be the same as the "actual reality" they themselves intend.

Furthermore, regarding the status of being "actual reality" for both [types]—the "actual reality" as expressed conventionally and the "actual reality" as the ultimate—the method already stated applies.
Fault. And that which is apprehended in the mode of conventional truth (sammutisacca) might or might not be apprehended in the sense of being a real intrinsic nature (bhūtasabhāva).

If it is apprehended in the sense of being a real intrinsic nature, then one who asserts that the person (puggala) is also apprehended as a true ultimate reality (saccikaṭṭha-paramattha) should not be questioned. But if it is not apprehended in the sense of being a real intrinsic nature, then [the person] apart from that... [of conventional truth].

The mode of the true, ultimate reality cannot be predicated because it is unestablished. And he will say: "Just as form and so forth exist by way of their individual characteristics and general characteristics, the person does not exist in that way.
Therefore, the intended meaning here must be sought.
Regarding the phrase "of the two truths," this might be conceded because [the person] is not apprehended through the mode of either of the two truths.

Or rather, nothing need be said. For just as being unapprehendable in part by way of the ultimate mode (*paramattha-ākāra*) is not a reason for assent, so too being apprehendable in part by way of the conventional mode (*sammuti-ākāra*) is not a reason for denial;
this is how the intended meaning (*adhippāya*) should be sought here as well. The statement "it is not apprehended" is merely a commonality of expression; it is this very expression that is [meant].
The intention is: "By resorting to this fallacious argument (*chalavāda*) that 'it is both permitted and prohibited.

Just as one might say, "I am to be refuted by the very same permissions and prohibitions through which [the opponent] perceives it," so too, "you [are to be refuted] by the very same permissions and prohibitions through which he does not perceive it.
Thus, here, the fabrication of what is impossible based on what is possible through a generalization is a fallacious argument (*chalavāda*).
It ought to be so. Therefore, it should be understood that the phrase "it is not apprehended" is merely a commonality of expression;
because it serves as the basis for a quibble (*chala-vāda*), it is called "quibbling. Alternatively, the meaning may be: "relying upon both the mere commonality of expression and the quibble.
It remains to be examined whether the act of setting aside (*ṭhapanā*) does not constitute the making manifest of the refutation (*niggaha*) and its remedy (*paṭikamma*).

For it is not possible to charge that "the denial of the latter after having admitted the former, or the admission of the former while denying the latter, is wrong," without first establishing the two opposing positions.
3. Regarding the words *tava* (of you) and *paṭijānantaṃ* (admitting):
with the intention that these are respectively the genitive and accusative cases used as possessive attributes, he said, "you yourself admitting."

4–5. Because he was subjected to a censure by means of four reproaches and imputations of fault—namely, when he said, "The censure you have inflicted upon me with the words 'We are difficult to restrain;

indeed, we are so! and so forth, is as false as the censure you have inflicted upon yourself"—thus, by that same method, the fact of his censure being a *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing) was established through those four reproaches and imputations of fault made during the fivefold conformable questioning, by means of the censure he himself had previously inflicted.
The meaning should be understood as: "because it was brought along with the state of being non-refutable," or "because it was admitted that there was no state of refutation.

In the same way, when one says, "In that case, since you have refuted [me], if indeed... [etc. ...this of yours is wrong," this should be understood as the fourfold conclusion regarding the very conclusion of the state of non-refutation.
The commentary on the positive-negative method is finished.
2. Commentary on the Reverse and Direct Order (Paccanīkānulomavaṇṇanā) 7–10.

Having stated, "The admission [of the person] belongs to the opponent's doctrine based on one's own tenet," it was further said, "The negation [of the person] belongs to the opponent's doctrine because of the non-existence of a person from the perspective of ultimate reality. In this regard, this negation belongs to oneself...

If it is done according to his own tenet (*laddhi*), then it follows that his tenet is: "The person is apprehended in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*) by way of another ultimate sense, namely, the ultimate sense of what is established as real.
This being so, he should not be refuted by one who seeks to establish the apprehension [of the person] by way of conventional truth (*sammutisacca*).
Alternatively, if he conceals his own tenet and denies [the person] by way of the other's tenet, then [he contradicts] his previous admission.
Because it is not contradictory, he should not be refuted; for no fault is incurred in one who states the tenets of both oneself and another.

However, the intended meaning here may be that one who, having first affirmed his own tenet, then rejects the tenet of another, has abandoned his own tenet and adopted the tenet of another, and thus he should be refuted.
The commentary on the reverse and direct order is finished.
The commentary on the pure ultimate meaning is finished.
2. The ultimate meaning as location.
1. Explanation of the Direct and Reverse Order (Anulomapaccanīkavaṇṇanā) 11.
“In all places” (*sabbattha*): showing that the meaning is “in the entire body,” he says, “with reference to the body.
“Therein” (*tattha*) means in that abbreviated recension (*saṃkhittapāṭha*). Since it was said, with reference to the body, “it is not found anywhere,” [the full text follows].
When this is said, it follows that [the person] is apprehended outside the body; therefore, the opponent’s rejection of this is the position of our own side (sakavādin).

By this, the meaning expressed is that the person is not apprehended by way of any intrinsic nature (sabhāva), for there is no location for the apprehension of something apprehended by way of any intrinsic nature that is released from being either the body or other than the body.
3. The Meaning of Reality in Terms of Time 1.
Commentary on the Positive-Negative Order 12.

"And at the time of the preceding and succeeding births": [this refers to] that very same thing which is apprehended at the time of the middle birth, [being considered] at the times of its preceding and succeeding births.
The intention is: "with reference to apprehension. The rest is exactly as stated in the first method;

that is to say, it is similar to what was stated in the first of these three methods, namely, in the method concerning "everywhere" (*sabbattha*). What is that? The meaning is: the brevity of the text.
For here too, because when it is said "it is not apprehended at all times," it follows that it *is* apprehended at some time, therefore—
It should be understood that the negation of the contrary belongs to the proponent (sakavādī). 4.
The Meaning of the Truth of the Parts. 1.
Commentary on the Positive-Negative [Analysis].

13. And in the third method, since it is stated that “it is not found in all,” one would imply that it is found in at least one; therefore, it should be connected thus: the denial in the counter-argument belongs to the proponent himself (sakavādī). Hence he said, “exactly like that. [End of] Section 2:
Explanation of the Counter-Argument and the Conformity to the Occasion and so forth. The True Meaning of the Occasion and so forth. The Commentary on the Counter-Argument and the Conformity.

14. Regarding the phrase "of the fivefold sequence in conformity" (*anulomapañcaka*) and so forth: it should be understood that the "fivefold sequence in conformity" refers to the pentad of refutation (*niggaha-pañcaka*), and that the "counter-position" (*paccanīka*) is stated as the counter-remedy (*paṭikamma*).

Therein, the meaning of the "fivefold sequence in conformity"—beginning with "In all respects, a person is not apprehended"—is [to be understood] even though it has not been stated in its own form, having arrived by way of an abbreviated version of the canonical text beginning with "In all respects, a person is not apprehended."

It should be understood according to the method stated in the passage beginning with “because [it was said] with reference to the body,” and by way of providing a counter-argument to the opposing view expressed in such statements as “a person is apprehended everywhere,” which was stated for the purpose of performing a refutation; thus,

having condensed the Pāḷi of the refutation and so forth, it is found in the introductory portion that shows only the beginning, in the positive sequence starting with “a person is apprehended,” where it says “everywhere.”
The meaning should be understood in the manner stated by the passage beginning, “The inquiry regarding the body refers to one’s own doctrine,” and so forth.
Alternatively, instead of taking the meaning as “in that which has been commenced,” the meaning should be taken as “therein, among those three doors.
And here, the entire Pāḷi of the positive-negative pentad based on the positive pentad is rooted in the positive pentad.
It is said that there is a "Pāḷi" [text], as well as a "Pāḷi of the Reverse and Direct Pentads," which is the Pāḷi of the reverse order.
Having condensed that, it is stated that the meaning of the reverses— such as "the person is not apprehended"— and the direct order— such as "it is apprehended"—

which appear by way of counter-action even though they are not explicitly stated in their own form, should be understood in the same manner as was explained below regarding the "pure" and "actual" meanings.
The commentary on the *Saccikaṭṭha* is finished.
5. Commentary on the *Suddhikasaṃsandana*:
"The correlation of the *saccikaṭṭha* with form and so forth" refers to the correlation of the person (*puggala*) who is the *saccikaṭṭha* with form and the other aggregates.
The intended meaning is either a convergence [of the person] with the truths, or a convergence of the person with form and so forth in their actual reality.
Because the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "the person and form" has the sense of conjunction, the meaning stated by way of illustration—just as "form"—is to be investigated.
The tenet and position is that it cannot be said whether the person is other than or not other than form and so forth.
The sutta beginning with, “‘The soul is one thing, the body another’—this was left undeclared by the Blessed One,” and so forth.
He said, “seeing the contradiction with the *Samaya-sutta*,” referring to the fact that if [the opponent’s position] were accepted, it would result in a contradiction between those two.

“From the standpoint of the Dhamma” means from the standpoint of the Pāḷi. By those who say, “The *Paṭikamma-catuṅka* and so forth are abbreviated; the arguments of the opponent... have been shown,” etc.
"A person is not apprehended" … [as before] … "understand the counter-argument"—here one will have seen the reading "ājānāhi niggahaṃ" (understand the refutation).

"For the purpose of making him acknowledge otherness": the meaning is that it is for the purpose of challenging him by means of his acknowledgment of otherness, such that "just as otherness must be stated by me, so too must it be stated by you. Of the conventional and the ultimate...
The meaning of "the question regarding unity and diversity being set aside" is that it is undeclared (*abyākata*).

If [the opponent] were to reject [the question] because it is to be set aside, then since the rejection would have been made by him as well based on the very same doctrine that it is to be set aside, he too should not be censured.
However, the other person—that is, the individual—takes some specific nature (*sabhāva*) as a basis and maintains that it is to be set aside; yet, if such a nature exists...

The opponent should be rebuked for saying that "the state of being set aside" (ṭhapanīyatā) is not logical. However, there is no intrinsic nature (sabhāva) whatsoever in conventional designation (sammuti).

Therefore, the proponent's rejection—stating that one who asserts the state of being set aside regarding the question of identity and difference (ekattanānatta) should not be rebuked—is the interpretation that is appropriate here.
The commentary on the Discussion of the Pure [Case] is finished.
6. Commentary on the Discussion of Similes (28–36):
"The inquiry into otherness by way of the commonality of apprehension"—this is a similarity between the two, not an identity.
One should investigate whether it is logical as a cause, or rather, whether it is apprehendable as a distinct individual essence in the sense of ultimate reality (*saccikaṭṭha-paramattha*).
The original reading was "twenty-one" (*ekavīsādhikāni*), but it should instead be read as "twenty" (*vīsādhikāni*). 37–45.
One who allows the Sutta stating "there is a person" to be accepted is, in their thinking, allowing for the apprehension [of a self] to be accepted.
He said: "Having applied the commonality of apprehension. Thus, nine hundred and twenty methods of settlement (*paṭikamma*) have been shown;
by this, it is understood that even in the *Suddhika-saṃsandana*, the reading is simply "understand the settlement" (*ājānāhi paṭikamma*).

And as for what was stated among the "heads of disputes" (*vādamukha*) regarding the pure and the actual fact (*suddhika-saccikaṭṭha*) as the "fourfold settlement" (*paṭikamma-catukka*), that too is [included within] the "fivefold settlement" (*paṭikamma-pañcaka*).
The commentary on the correlation of similes is finished.
7. Commentary on the correlation of the fourfold method (catukkanaya). §§46–52.
One who does not desire even a difference in a single dhamma [from the ultimate] should not be engaged in discussion by way of individual dhammas such as form (rūpa) and so forth.
For he who, not desiring otherness in the aggregate as a whole, yet rejecting non-otherness in its parts, would not be subject to censure;
in order to preclude such an opportunity for speech, [the author] said, "And this inquiry," and so forth.

"The whole" refers to the entire classification of phenomena consisting of fifty-seven types, whether it be the person (*puggala*) or the ultimate truth (*paramatthasacca*)—it is with reference to such a whole that [the objection was raised].

The meaning is as follows: Having thus reflected upon the entirety of ultimate reality (*paramattha*), and because the characteristic of the application (*anuyoga*) has been established by way of the continuum (*tantravasena*), and because there exists no "true state" (*saccikaṭṭha*) other than the entirety of ultimate reality, it is logical to impose a refutation upon one who rejects the question "Is form the person?
on the grounds that the person cannot be something other than that [ultimate reality] in its true state. This is the meaning.
“By way of dissociation from what is homogeneous” means that it is not of the same nature as matter (*rūpa*). “All phenomena” refers to all phenomena with the exception of matter.

Regarding the statement “the person is in matter,” he says “and out of fear of the view of annihilation” with the underlying intention that one rejects [this idea] due to the fear of falling into annihilation when the support [of matter] perishes.
However, in the three [other] instances, the rejection is due to contradiction with the [accepted] positions.
This is what is intended. For it is not correct to say that he desires the view of a personal entity (sakkāyadiṭṭhi), but rather rejects it out of fear of the eternalist view (sassatadiṭṭhi).
Indeed, among the views of a personal entity, only five are annihilationist views (ucchedadiṭṭhi); the rest are eternalist views.
Furthermore, in the phrase "apart from form" (aññatra rūpā), it should be understood that the meaning "a person possessing form" (rūpavā puggalo) is included.
The commentary on the *Catukkanayasaṃsandanavaṇṇanā* is finished.
Also finished is the commentary on the discourse on the *saṃsandanakathā*.
8. The commentary on the *Lakkhaṇayutti*.
54. Regarding "the reverse and the conformable": this does not accord with what will be said later, namely, “But it should be stated by way of the sixfold method:
‘Understand the counter-measure,’ and so forth. For in the reverse-and-conformable method, when it is the reverse, one should say “understand the refutation,” and not “the counter-measure.”
The commentary on the analysis of characteristics (*lakkhaṇayuttivaṇṇanā*) is finished.
9. Commentary on the Purification of Words (*vacanasodhanavaṇṇanā*), §§55–59.
Regarding the statement that the two phrases "the person is apprehended" (*puggalo upalabbhati*) are identical in meaning: here, that very identity is [challenged] by the opponent.

This must be investigated: whether it is accepted or not accepted. For if one asserts that while the person (*puggala*) is indivisible, this [term] "is found" (*upalabbhati*) is divisible, how could one accept the identity in meaning between the words *puggala* and *upalabbhati*, which refer respectively to what is divisible and what is indivisible?
And just as with the meanings of what is divisible and what is indivisible...
When one speaks of the distinction between those forms that are perceived and those that are not, the objection— that some form is perceived while some is not—
does not arise; likewise, when one speaks of this [object] according to the aforementioned distinction,
it should be sought here that the objection as previously raised does not apply.
60. Regarding the statement, “Behold the world as empty,” it is said that this implies in meaning that there is no person (*puggala*); thus he says, “it is also said that ‘there is not’.
The commentary on the clarification of the words is finished.
10. Commentary on the Inquiry into Designations (*paññattānuyoga*).
61–66. With reference to the non-separation from the form-body (*rūpakāya*), he says, "because of the existence of the form-body.

With reference to the designation (*paññatti*) as it occurs in the Sutta, "whether possessing form or formless," he says, "and because of the existence of such a designation. Because of the absence of the state of one possessed of desire (*kāmī*):

since being a possessor of desire is not an invariable characteristic and because there is an absence of dependence on the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*), one cannot be called "a possessor of desire."
"He rejects" is the intended meaning.
67. "By means of body-contemplation" (kāyānupassanāya) is a statement of the cause; the sense is that he has acquired such a view precisely because of body-contemplation acting as the cause.
"Spoken directly" means it was spoken directly [by the Buddha] thus: "It has not been declared by me that the soul is one thing and the body another."
The commentary on the inquiry into designations (*paññattānuyoga*) is finished.
11. Commentary on the Inquiry into Destinations (*gatianuyoga*) §§69–72:

It was stated: “Showing [the fault], he said: ‘In that case, a person wanders on,’ and so forth. However, it should rather have been: “Showing [the fault], he said: ‘It should not be said that a person wanders on,’ and so forth,” or else, “Having shown [the fault], he said...”.
91. Regarding the statement, "It goes together with the body designated as 'form'":

here, since one who says "it goes together with form" has not admitted that "the person is form," they must be asked in what manner they fall into the position that "the soul is that same as the body.
[The phrase] "with reference to rebirth in the non-percipient realm" means: of a person who has gone to hell and is about to go to the non-percipient realm.

And since one does not admit an intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) for those who have reached the formless realm, the meaning should be understood as referring to rebirth immediately following death.
However, for those who— taking it that perception exists among non-percipient beings both at the time of death and at the time of rebirth—
might wish to admit an intermediate existence for one who has reached the non-percipient realm, [it would follow] from the very nature of the intermediate existence...
“It is not possible to say that ‘rebirth in the non-percipient realm is without feeling.

(92) Regarding the phrases beginning with “without feeling,” the term “other than that” refers to a rebirth in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, which is distinct from the state of perception. For they maintain that even in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, it cannot be said that perception exists.

(93) He speaks according to the view that since a person does not exist apart from phenomena such as form, the person—like a fire dependent on fuel—is dependent upon the fuel of form and so forth, and thus does not exist apart from form and the rest.
The commentary on the application of the investigation into going is finished.
12. Commentary on the Application of the Investigation into Designation by Means of Grasping (Upādāpaññattānuyogavaṇṇanā) 97.

Regarding the phrase "in such cases as 'blue' being designated in dependence upon blue form," the meaning is: "In the case of the statement, 'The designation of a person as "blue" is in dependence upon blue form,'" it refers to those instances where one who is questioned is designated as "blue" in dependence upon what is blue, and so forth.

98. “With reference to the state of being skilled” means it was stated with reference to the state of being skilled (*chekaṭṭha*), not as a designation for the wholesome (*kusala*). The meaning should be understood as: “One who conceives [the idea] that ‘it is by depending on a wholesome feeling’ asserts [that position].
112. Now, in order to show... [etc. he said, “Just as a tree,” and so forth; thus it is said that, having shown the prima facie argument (*pubbapakkha*), he states the reply (*uttara*). 115.
Having cited the statement from the reply-position (*uttarapakkha*)—“He who has form is one possessing form”—he said, “Because,” and so forth.

116. "By way of contemplation of mind" (cittānupassanāvasena): the intended meaning is by way of the association with minds such as those possessed of lust, which has been explained by way of the contemplation of mind.

118. "By means of which" (yena): the sense faculty called the eye is the instrument referred to by the word "by means of which"; thus the meaning is "the eye. He speaks with reference to the fact that it is the eye itself that sees form; for the very act of the eye assuming the state of being the support for consciousness is what is termed "seeing.
The commentary on the application of the designation based on derived phenomena (upādāpaññatti) is concluded.
13. Explanation of the Application of Human Effort (Purisakārānuyoga) 123.
"Mere doing" refers to the aggregates that function by way of being the producers and instigators of kamma. 124.

With the intention that there is no birth for a person without prior kamma, and that for one who is born there is no engagement—whether right or wrong—in the fields of knowledge and so forth, he said: "It is prior kamma alone that [produces it]," and so on.

125. Regarding the phrase "of the cycle of action" (*kammavaṭṭassa*): here, they say that there must be no interruption of the cycle of action, such that whoever is the agent of one act must perform another act, and the agent of that [second] act must perform yet another.
It should be examined whether the agent of a person becomes the agent of the action. [This is so] because of being produced by his mother and father, and so forth; [this refers to] his agent.
Furthermore, this must be investigated: does one who intends fall into a succession of agents among those who perform the action?

(170) "Out of fear of contradiction with the Suttas" means out of fear of contradicting such passages as: "That it is the same person who acts and the same person who experiences [the result], O Brahmin, is one extreme.
(171) From the statement, "He rejoices here and he rejoices after passing away," [it follows that] at the time of performing the action and at the time of experiencing the ripening...
The intention is that he admits, "And it is that very same [self]. However, when asked, "Is pleasure and pain self-made?
he rejects it, because it would contradict such suttas as: "What do you think, Kassapa, is pleasure and pain self-made? Do not say so, Kassapa. (DN 2.33).
"It is merely a matter of opinion" means that the statement "it is neither that very same [self] nor another" does not exist at all; therefore...
The intention [of the text] is that by speaking thus, one falls into the position that there is no self-agency (*asayaṃkāra*), and so forth.
Furthermore, with the words "Moreover" (*apica*) and so on, this is shown: the inquiry as to whether "he acts" and so forth was not stated merely according to the desire of another;

rather, for one who does not accept one alternative among "he acts" and so on, another follows, and for one who does not accept that either, yet another follows. Thus, regarding the desire for an agent and an experiencer...
Having stood [at the beginning], [the phrase] "he does that," and so forth, is used even in the sense of having fallen into [an offense] against one's own will.

Alternatively, it shows that this investigation is undertaken not merely because all [statements] such as "he does that" have been established, but rather because each individual [statement] has been established.
By the phrase "in the same manner as before," [it is shown that] the entire sequence beginning with "he rejoices here" constitutes the grounds for admission and so forth.
This shows that they should be applied on one side.
The commentary on the application of human effort is finished.
The Section on the Beautiful is finished.
14. Commentary on the Application of the Higher Knowledges (Abhiññānuyogavaṇṇanā) 193.

Regarding the statement, "Arahatta is accomplished by means of the application of the higher knowledges (*abhiññānuyoga*) and so forth," here, the application of the higher knowledges is: "Is it not the case that there is someone who exercises psychic power (*iddhi*)?
The establishing [of the proposition] is: "Indeed, there is someone who exercises psychic power. And [the refutation begins with] "By that very person, indeed... and so forth.
And the meaning of "pāpanā" should be understood as being included by the word "ādi.

Since the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhayañāṇa*) is here called a direct higher knowledge (*abhiññā*), he says "the accomplishment of arahantship" (*arahattasādhanā*) because it is the accomplishment for an Arahant who possesses that direct higher knowledge; for the accomplishment of an Arahant is indeed the accomplishment of that state.
The commentary on the application of the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) is finished.
15–18. Commentary on the application of relatives (*ñātaka*), etc. 209.
"Of such a kind" means that the third category, which is the true reality (*saccikaṭṭha*), does not exist; this is the intended meaning. However, in this way...
If one were to speak of a person who constitutes the third extreme—the state that is not the ultimate truth (asaccikaṭṭha)—while desiring such a person, one would indeed be refuted by the Sutta. Why?
Because there is no such ultimate reality (saccikaṭṭha), and because no such intrinsic nature (sabhāva) exists; thus, being subject to refutation, one conceals one's own tenets.
The meaning should be understood as follows: the refutation belongs to the opponent.
The commentary on the inquiry regarding relatives and so forth is concluded.
19. Commentary on the Inquiry Regarding Penetration and So Forth.

218. By the expression "appropriated feeling," it is shown that there is no knowing or understanding of unappropriated feeling such as "I am happy" or "I am suffering," and it also demonstrates the practitioner's capacity to delimit even subtle feelings. 228. Regarding the statement on characteristics:
the intention is that entering within the material form constitutes being together with the material form, whereas exiting externally constitutes being without the material form.

"‘These indeed’: ‘the gross acquisition of a self,’ ‘the mind-made acquisition of a self,’ and ‘the formless acquisition of a self’—these are the conventional designations of the world by which a Tathāgata employs speech without misapprehending them, whether they be true or false.
Even though a self is not found therein, because that [self] is not found, he does not give rise to misapprehension or the view of a self."
"In the world, one uses the conventional expression ‘acquisition of a self’ merely by way of worldly discourse; this is the meaning here.

And in this context, by refuting the existence of a person (*puggala*) according to its specific and general characteristics and asserting existence only by way of worldly convention, it is stated that there is no such thing as a 'person' as an intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).
For if such a thing existed, its existence would have to be described by way of its own intrinsic nature."
"It may be, not by worldly convention"—by this, however, one should connect the preceding commentary on the meaning in such a way that it accords with reality and is free from misapprehension.

"The cause of worldly consensus" means that because it proceeds by way of worldly consensus, it is therefore called "truth. "The characteristic of suchness" means the cause of suchness; because it proceeds by way of the suchness of phenomena, it shows that it is "truth."
The commentary on the section concerning the application to penetration is finished.
The commentary on the discussion of persons is finished.
2. The Discussion on Decline.
1. Commentary on the Discourse on the Loss of Eloquence in Debate (Vādayuttiparihānikathāvaṇṇanā) 239. Regarding the sutta:
“Bhikkhus, these two things lead to the decline of a bhikkhu who is still in training (sekkha),” this is not a basis for the attainment of decline in an Arahant;
rather, it concerns the attainment of decline in those such as Non-returners (anāgāmī) and others.

Therefore, regarding the statement "they maintain that even an Arahant can fall away," the word *pi* (also/even) should be construed here as "even for a Non-returner (*anāgāmī*) and even for a Once-returner (*sakadāgāmī*).
The earlier reading states: "In the third [case] as well, only those of dull faculties are intended; for it is their doctrine that there is no falling away for any of them.
However, if only those of dull faculties were intended, no such restriction (*parikkhepa*) would need to be made.
And thus they recite: "Therefore, even in the third [case], it is only those with sharp faculties who are intended.
For their view is that there is no falling away for any of them.
Having grasped the meaning in an improper way: [the opponent thinks] that since it was stated that the stream-enterer alone is fixed, only he does not fall away, but...

They say that by taking the meaning as "the others," and not taking the stated meaning as "for the sake of the higher paths," one grasps the sense that "one who is fixed" does not fall away from the fruit of stream-entry.
The commentary on the discussion regarding the loss of the arguments for the doctrine is finished.
2. Exposition of the Convergence of Noble Persons and of Decline. 241.
Regarding the passage beginning with "But as for that here," it refers to one who, having stood in the fruit of the path of seeing, subsequently attains Arahantship;
then, desiring to decline from that and stand again therein, he attains Arahantship immediately thereafter through renewed effort.
"It does not desire" — this must be investigated.
(262) "One who has attained mastery and has obtained jhāna" should be understood as referring to a trainee (*sekha*).

However, the worldling (*puthujjana*)—whether he has attained mastery or not—is not included here according to the classification of those liberated by occasion (*samaya-vimutta*) and those liberated unconditionally (*asamaya-vimutta*). But when he is analyzed, [he is included] among those for whom attainments have been suppressed.
It is said that one might partake in the state of being "liberated by occasion" (samaya-vimutta) due to the influence of the defilements (kilesa).
The commentary on the comparison of noble persons (ariya-puggala) and their decline is finished.
3. Commentary on the Proof by Sutta regarding Decline.

265. The distinction between the superior and the inferior is stated according to such suttas as: “In this regard, that path which is pleasant and leads to swift direct knowledge is declared to be excellent in both respects.
As in the phrase “seen, heard, and sensed,” the word *muta* here refers to what is to be reached;
thus he says, “worthy of contact.”

267. They lead to the loss of what has not yet been attained; the intention is that this refers to one who is liberated by occasion (*samaya-vimutta*) and who has reached a conclusion according to his own practice.
The commentary on the exposition of the loss of what has been accomplished through the suttas is finished.
The commentary on the discussion of loss is finished.
3. Discourse on the Holy Life (Brahmacariyakathā) 1. Explanation of the Discourse on the Pure Holy Life (Suddhabrahmacariyakathāvaṇṇanā) 269.

Although it was stated, "starting from the Paranimmitavasavatti devas and above," the statement in the sutta, "By three grounds, bhikkhus... indicates that they do not even accept the cultivation of the path for the realms below that level.
270. It was stated that "the denial refers to the acquisition of the path by certain householders and some devas.
However, when asked regarding the location where [the path] does not exist, it is not appropriate to deny it in terms of a specific person.
And if this were his intended meaning, he should not be defeated, because his intention would be identical to that of the proponent himself.
271. *Ekantarikapañhā* (Questions with Alternating Intervals): These are questions consisting of alternating intervals between the proponents of opposing views and the proponent of one's own view.
The commentary on the Discourse on Pure Conduct is finished.
2. Commentary on the Discourse on the Convergence of Conduct.

273. One must investigate how this [statement]—that "by means of the path of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara-magga), he becomes one who has reached his final destination while remaining here"—accords with the exposition of the attainment [of the fruit], such as:
"For a non-returner (anāgāmī) who has developed the path here is called one who has reached his final destination while remaining here.
Previously, only the non-returner was referred to as "non-returner," whereas here the intention is that the term includes the non-returner through jhāna, the stream-enterer (sotāpanna), and so forth.
Here, one who, having developed the path to arahantship, realizes the fruit right here, is called "one who attains final nibbāna here.
On the other hand, one who, having developed the path here, realizes the fruit there, is called "an arahant who attains final nibbāna there.
The commentary on the discourse on the comparison of the holy life is finished.
The commentary on the Discourse on the Religious Life (*Brahmacariyakathā*) is finished.
4. Commentary on the Discourse on Specificity (*Odhisokathāvaṇṇanā*) 274.
In order to show the meaning of the phrase "specifically, specifically" (*odhiso odhiso*), he said: "part by part."
The commentary on the Discourse on What Has Been Done is finished.
4. Commentary on the Discourse on Abandoning. 1.
Commentary on the Discourse on Not Quoting Sutta.
280. "The presence of what is to be done" (*kiccasabbhāva*) refers to the state of having abandoned that which is to be abandoned by the three [paths].

However, if one holds the view that this task is accomplished by that very path, it does not accord with the view that sensual lust and ill will are abandoned at the stage of an ordinary person (*puthujjana*).
Therefore, even though they were abandoned at the stage of an ordinary person, because they do not arise again at any time once the path of seeing has arisen, for those three—
The intention is that the function of the paths arises.
The commentary on the discussion regarding the citation of suttas is finished.
The commentary on the discussion regarding "abandoning" (jahati) is finished.
5. The Discourse on "Everything Exists" (Sabbamatthītikathā) 1. Explanation of the Logical Method (Vādayuttivaṇṇanā) 282.
Regarding the phrase "everything in the whole body": "everything" refers to such things as the head, the feet at the back, and the eyes; thus, everything exists everywhere.
"It exists" (atthi) is the meaning. "At all times" means that in childhood there is youthfulness, and in old age there is childhood;
thus, in every time, everything [is present]. "In every manner" means that by way of a blue aspect there is yellow, and by way of a yellow aspect there is red;
thus it is. "In all phenomena" means that in the eye there is the ear, and in the ear there is the nose; thus it is. He says "inappropriate" (ayutta) means devoid of connection (yoga).
But that [yoga] has a single nature. To demonstrate how there can be an absence of yoga for that which has a single nature, he says, "For among things of diverse natures," and so forth.
For two fingers or two rams, which have diverse natures, possess a mutual conjunction (*aññamaññayogo*), but not that which exists as a single entity alone.
Therefore, it is said that the "absence of yoga" (*ayoga*) is that which is devoid of the conjunction that occurs among things of diverse natures, being itself of a single nature.

"This person asks" means that, having grasped the state of wrong view in the opponent's doctrine, it is stated that there exists the state of right view in one's own view that has arisen [in response].
The commentary on the application of the method of debate is finished.
2. Explanation of the Synthesis of Time (Kālasaṃsandana-vaṇṇanā) 285.

"Having set aside the past and the future, and having treated only present form as undesirable and indivisible"—by this it is meant that both the term "present" (*paccuppanna*) and the term "form" (*rūpa*) must be understood as referring exclusively to present form. Regarding the designation (*paññatti*):

By the phrase "because it does not depart," this is understood: unlike the designation of matter (*rūpa-paññatti*), the designation of the physical basis (*vatthu-paññatti*) does not function as a designation of an existing thing defined by its own intrinsic nature;
rather, it is a designation of a non-existent thing (*avijjamāna-paññatti*) that functions by depending upon a collection of matter occurring through a sequence of before and after.
Therefore, when the state of being the physical basis has ceased—due to the disappearance of the state of being white—it must necessarily cease as well.
"It is joined [to the present], but not when the present state of material form has ceased.
The commentary on the correlation of time is finished.
The commentary on the clarification of the terminology follows.

288. Regarding the statement, "The future or the present comes to be having been," it should be understood as follows: the future comes to be having been the future, and then, becoming the present, it "comes to be";
likewise, the present comes to be having been the present, and previously having been the future, it becomes the present—thus it is said to "come to be having been. What do you say to that?

The intention behind the question—"having been, does it become?"—is appropriate because it asks about the non-cessation and non-interruption of the state of "having been and becoming," due to the non-disappearance of that state.

As for the phrase "from the non-existence of what has become after having been": this refers to the future; that is, from the non-existence of the present state after that which was present has again become the future.

The intended meaning is this: since that which has been a past entity (*bhūta*) becomes present, and since that which was not yet future becomes present and thus receives the designation "having been, it comes to be" (*hutvā hoti*), therefore he asserts that the expression "having been, it comes to be" is applicable for a second time as well.

However, for one who speaks thus of the non-cessation of the state of "having been, it comes to be" regarding phenomena (*dhamma*), [the same would apply] to non-phenomena (*adhamma*), such as a rabbit's horn.
With the intention that "having not been, it does not reach the cessation of its state of being," he said, "Then, no," and so forth.
"By the method of negation" means by way of the difference in time. "By the method of affirmation" means by way of the non-difference in meaning.

Even for one who accepts the non-difference in meaning, the state of being in the present is stated regarding what has not yet come, and [the state of being] in the future is stated regarding what is present.
It must be investigated how one who has spoken [of existence] can admit non-existence.
For by that [statement], only the non-difference of the object is admitted, not the present state of what is future, nor the future state of what is present.

"Having turned back the question previously rejected" means that the fault already stated—namely, that for a question which has been admitted, there is the fault [of the argument] "having been, it is"—is now applied to the fault not yet stated.
The meaning is that, having set aside a question that was rejected, one takes it up again and challenges with it.

And here, since "it exists" is said by way of a difference in state (*atthānānatta*), how can there be a rejection of the future as being present simply because of a difference in time (*kālanānatta*)?
The intention is that this is due to the very same person’s simultaneous admission and rejection.
Regarding the phrase "each one, not having been, does not exist," this refers to both the future and the present;

thus it is said, "each one, not having been, does not exist; not having been, does not exist. It does not mean that each one alone, not having been, does not exist, and then again, not having been, does not exist.
This same method applies to the previous statement: "each one, having been, exists; having been, exists. [This concerns] the future...
For by including both names—namely, "having been, it comes to be" (*hutvā hotī*) for the present, and "it comes to be having been" (*hutvā hoti hutvā hotī*)—the objection is raised;
likewise, the intention is that "not having been, it does not come to be" (*na hutvā na hoti na hutvā na hotī*) is also included.
By the phrase "as if completely enveloped in darkness from all sides," he shows that one ought to admit what is not so enveloped.
And here, in the first method, it is urged that what has already existed comes to exist again; in the second method, each of the future and so forth is given the designation "has come to exist.
This is the distinction. The commentary on the clarification of the terminology is concluded.
Commentary on the Discussion of Knowledge of the Past, etc. (290).
When it is asked again... "he admits its existence," one must investigate here how it is stated by the phrase "present knowledge" through this relative expression which follows upon it.
The commentary on the discussion of knowledge of the past, etc., is finished.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Arahant, etc. (291):

Contradiction by reasoning should be understood as [the following]: that an Arahant would possess lust and so forth; that there would be no distinction between him and an ordinary worldling (*puthujjana*); that living the holy life (*brahmacariya*) would be fruitless; and so on.
The commentary on the discussion of the Arahant, etc., is finished.
Commentary on the Discussion on the Purification of Words (Padasodhanakathāvaṇṇanā) 295. "For that reason" means:

because the words *atīta* (past) and *atthi* (is/exists) have the same meaning, and because the meaning of the word *atthi* is the state of having passed away (*nvātītabhāva*), it is said, "The past is what has passed away; what has passed away is the past. In this context, however, there is the existence of the past and so forth.
This fault applies only to the opponent who speaks [in that manner], and not to the proponent who says, "Nirvana exists";
it should be demonstrated accordingly.
The commentary on the discussion for purifying the words is finished.
The commentary on the Discourse on "Everything Exists" is finished.
7. The Discourse on "Some Things Exist.
1. Commentary on the Discourse on "Some [Things] Past, etc."
299. Regarding the phrase "of the three groups": these are the unripened-result, the ripened-result, and the non-resultant.

One should consider how one who asserts the existence of unripened-results by way of conventional usage should be questioned, [thinking]: "They maintain that there is a formation dissociated from consciousness which is an accumulation of kamma.
The commentary on the discussion of the partial-existence theory is concluded.
8. Commentary on the Discourse on the Foundations of Mindfulness (Satipaṭṭhānakathāvaṇṇanā) 301. "In order to ask about the supramundane state" means:

because right mindfulness—whether mundane or supramundane—is a foundation of mindfulness, or because it is only the supramundane that is the foundation of mindfulness in the ultimate sense, he asks about the supramundane state by way of that [mindfulness].

The meaning. "By way of a question concerning the classification" means by way of a question concerning the classifications of the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), which consist of the mundane and supramundane foundations of mindfulness taken together.

9. Commentary on the Discussion of the "Whatever" Meaning (Hevatthikathāvaṇṇanā) 304.

Regarding the phrase “because it was established inappropriately” (*ayoniso paṭṭhāpitattā*): the meaning should be understood as having been established by means of what is not to be stated and what is to be regarded with equanimity (*upekkhitabba*).
The commentary on the discussion of the "whatever" meaning is concluded.
The commentary on the Mahāvagga is finished.
2. The Second Chapter: 1.
Commentary on the Section on Bringing from Others.
307. The emission of semen by those who are conceited (adhimānika) must be examined.
For it is said that even for outsiders who have abandoned passion for sense-pleasures through concentration and insight, there is no emission of semen;
thus, those who were previously conceited are likely intended here.

308. *Vacasāyattha* means in the sense of certainty; however, because the question "for what reason" (*kiṃ kāraṇā*) asks for a cause, it is appropriate to take it in the sense of a cause, as in the case of the discourse on the holy life (*brahmacariyakathā*).
The commentary on the presentation by another is finished.
5. Commentary on the Discourse on the Distinction of Speech.
326. In this discussion on the differentiation of speech, the statement “he has attained the supramundane first jhāna” refers to the first path (magga).
Because he contemplates [the aggregates] as suffering, he utters the words “suffering” alone; the intention is that he does not utter [the words] “origin” and so forth.
328. Regarding the phrase “by which he hears that sound”: this is appropriate if it is intended or asserted that he hears this sound at the very moment of the vocal intimation’s arising.
332. At the moment of the supramundane path, the intention must be stated for one who desires vocal expression when reciting the *Abhibhu Sutta* to another.
The commentary on the discussion of vocal expression is finished.
7. Commentary on the Discussion of the Stability of Consciousness.
335. In the discussion on the stability of consciousness (*cittatthitikathā*), the passage beginning with "eighty-four...
and so forth is rejected because it is understood that such a state of remaining for the full duration of one's lifespan is spoken of only in the formless realm (*ārūpya*) and not elsewhere.

By this, however, the second half of the commentary should also be considered: "But they do not remain even for that long, being struck down by two [types of] consciousness. And this follows from the previous allowance of states such as a hundred years.

The lack of contradiction must be made clear. The statement "moment by moment" was spoken as if the question had been asked by the proponent (sakavādin), but it should be understood that it was actually asked by the opponent (paravādin).
The commentary on the discussion of the stability of consciousness is concluded.
9. Commentary on the Discourse on Gradual Realization (Anupubbābhisamaya-kathāvaṇṇanā) 339.

In this discourse on gradual realization, by the words "or else" and so forth, he shows this: because the four knowledges constitute a single path, there is no occurrence of a single path having a plurality of natures;
and it is acknowledged that one develops the stream-entry path gradually, which is thus established.
344. When that vision has been brought to completion. 345.

Regarding the phrase "by means of the eight knowledges": here, when the eight [knowledges] are taken together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), one must investigate how the realization of the fruit of stream-entry occurs by means of the analytical knowledges of language (*nirutti*) and ingenuity (*paṭibhāna*).
The commentary on the discussion of successive realization is finished.
10. Commentary on the Discussion of Conventional Usage (Vohārakathāvaṇṇanā) 347. In this discussion of conventional usage, [the question] "Or rather, the ear and so forth too...

implies that among the exclusively mundane objects and subjects, it is only the object that possesses the supramundane nature, and not the subject; however, there is no reason for this. And just as the subjects possess the supramundane nature...
It is unestablished; likewise for the object, the sense-base of sound.

In that regard, just as the supramundane nature of that [consciousness]—whose supramundane state is unestablished—is [claimed], so too it would follow for the ear and the rest. Thus, the meaning should be understood as:

"How could those [bases] also be supramundane? One must not accept the meaning that "if it were to strike against the supramundane, it would itself be supramundane," for [it does not strike] in the supramundane.
"It strikes back" (paṭihaññati) means that even when [the sound] is merely imagined, the supramundane nature of the sound exists; this is the intended meaning.

"By mundane knowledge" (lokīyena ñāṇena) was extracted [from the commentary], but the canonical text (pāḷi) reads "by consciousness" (viññāṇena); and since that consciousness, by its connection with the ear, is understood to be ear-consciousness (sotaviññāṇa).
"The lack of exclusivity" (anekantatā) refers to the reason "it is mundane because it is to be known by mundane knowledge"; [this applies] to the mundane...
The intention is that, in the supramundane realm, there may be a state of indeterminacy due to the possibility [of multiple factors].
The commentary on the Discussion of Conventional Designation is finished.
11. Commentary on the Discussion of Cessation.
353. "He does not desire two truths of suffering" means that he does not desire those two truths of suffering for which there ought to be two cessations.

By the passage beginning, "Those which, having been analyzed by supramundane knowledge, have not ceased," etc., he shows that the formations which have ceased without analysis—that is, which do not manifest—are "ceased without analysis."
They do not cease after having arisen. By this, it is shown that there is cessation through non-reflection and cessation through non-occurrence.
The commentary on the discussion of cessation is finished.
The commentary on the second chapter is finished.
3. Third Chapter: 1. Explanation of the Discourse on Powers (Balakathāvaṇṇanā) 354.
Regarding the phrase "the knowledge of the degrees of the faculties is uncommon": this refers to it in its entirety, in all its aspects, according to the detailed exposition.

Even those who do not know the possible and the impossible understand, by way of mere enumeration and in brief, what is possible and what is impossible through such statements as: "It is impossible, it is out of the question, that a person possessed of right view should regard any conditioned phenomenon as permanent.

However, they do not understand the mastery over the faculties of others even by means of mere enumeration, as in the phrases: "He knows their underlying tendencies; he knows their latent dispositions," and so forth.

He says it is "unshared" because [the Buddha] knows [this]. However, the Elder spoke thus—"I understand, as it really is, the degrees of the faculties of beings"—referring merely to the knowledge of the sharpness or dullness of the faculties such as faith;
one should see that the intention here is that the knowledge of the degrees of the faculties of beings, as previously described, is not the Tathāgata-power. "By way of summary..."

It is said that [the Tathāgata] "claims [his knowledge] by way of knowing the mere fact of what is possible and what is impossible. But if one who claims this were to likewise claim that "the power of a Tathāgata is shared with disciples," how could he be challenged? 356.

Regarding the rejection of the remaining [powers], the intention is that because the knowledge of what is possible and impossible and so forth are shared or unshared among the members of our own school (sakavādin), the rejection applies there specifically with reference to the position that they are shared.
The commentary on the Discourse on the Story of Bāla is finished.
2. Commentary on the Discourse on the Noble One (Ariyanti-kathā). 357.
For one who asserts [the existence of a self] with reference to formations (saṅkhāra), how could there be a convergence of two types of contact?
This should be investigated according to the method already stated. A being is called a "resolution" (paṇidhi) because it is to be established after having been projected by way of conceptualization.

However, since that [being] is not to be established even when projected upon a single [object], its being devoid of that which is to be established even when projected upon a single object is what is expressed.
The commentary on the Discourse on the Noble End is finished.
4. Commentary on the Discourse on Being Liberated. 366.
At the moment of the Path, the mind—which was liberated by the liberation through suppression via jhāna—is [further] liberated by the liberation through eradication.
One must investigate: "What is the fault in this doctrine that [the path] is called 'being liberated'?
If there is a fault in the description of the "dissociated" (vippakatā), then even there, because of its state of being liberated by that [process], it is stated as "liberated and being liberated.

And if there were a fault, one should not challenge the expression "liberated and being liberated" on the grounds that it is "liberated" at the moment of arising (uppādakkhaṇa) and "being liberated" at the moment of passing away (vayakkhaṇa).

It might be so; however, it is simply the word "being liberated. Because for one who is being liberated in part, or regarding a part, the action of liberation is a qualifier of that part, it is called a "feminine past participle" (*bhāvanapuṃsaka*). "Mats and so forth" means mats, cloths, and so on.
"By a single consciousness" intends "by a single resultant consciousness."
The commentary on the discussion of "being liberated" is finished.
5. Commentary on the Discussion of the Eighth [Person] (Aṭṭhamaka): 368.

He employs the mention of "conformity" (anuloma) and "lineage" (gotrabhu) with the intention of refuting the following view that has arisen: "Even at the moment of conformity and lineage, those [defilements] which do not manifest would indeed be called 'abandoned' even at the moment of the Path."
The commentary on the discussion of the eighth person is finished.
6. Commentary on the Discussion of the Faculties of the Eighth Person: 371.

“He acquires the faculties” means that because he has not yet acquired the faculties, he acquires the leading faculties such as faith and so forth—which were previously non-faculties—by developing them; the intention is that he does not [merely] develop faculties that already exist.
The commentary on the discussion of the faculties of the eighth person is finished.
7. Commentary on the Discussion of the Divine Eye. 373.
"Well-established" means that it becomes distinguished by its objects, powers, and spheres of activity, just as it is by way of its condition.
The meaning is "the bestowing of power. "Only that much" means that the preceding physical eye (*maṃsacakkhu*) alone does not become supported by the Dhamma.
"Not come within range" means it has not reached the range of what is to be grasped by the physical eye.
And here, while describing the incomparability of the power and domain of the [divine] eyes themselves, he indicates the object of the physical eye as follows:
The phrase "the object" (*visaya*) refers to the apprehension of the object, not for the purpose of showing a specific distinction among objects;

rather, it indicates that it is for the purpose of showing such a form-object as possesses specific distinctions of power and range. Or, the specific distinction belongs to the power and range of a similar object.
Furthermore, he does not maintain that the fleshly eye itself is the divine eye; thus, at the time when [the vision] is supported by the Dhamma, it is the former, the fleshly eye, that is meant.

The intended meaning is that he does not accept this. The statement that "the arising of the fleshly eye is the path" was said solely for the purpose of showing its status as a condition for the fleshly eye, not for the purpose of establishing its non-clung-to (anupādinnatā) nature.

His intention is that those [great elements] which have arisen by way of the condition of fine-material-sphere jhāna are "fine-material-sphere. This same method applies to the phrase "of the immaterial-sphere" (*arūpāvacarikānaṃ*).
"Even here": because of the absence of fine-material-sphere consciousness at the moment of the immaterial-sphere consciousness, he rejects it;
the intention is that he rejects it on the grounds that at that very moment, having been a fine-material-sphere consciousness, it has not arisen as an immaterial-sphere consciousness.

(374) Although he does not accept that the divine eye becomes the eye of wisdom when it is supported by the Dhamma—by which [he means] that the three eyes would become different types of eyes through support by the Dhamma—this is his intention.
The commentary on the Discourse on the Divine Eye is finished.
9. Commentary on the Discourse on the Knowledge of Beings Passing According to Their Karma 377.

Regarding the statement, "With the divine eye, he understands beings as they pass according to their karma," this refers to the proximate cause (upanissaya) for the knowledge of beings passing according to their karma.
The exposition of the instrument was made with respect to the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*), not with respect to the function of knowing beings according to their deeds (*yathākammūpagata*).
However, since others imagine that exposition of the instrument applies to that very function, [the author] said, "having grasped it erroneously.

By the statement, "The doctrine is that the knowledge of beings according to their deeds is itself the divine eye," [it is shown that] the divine eye is thus [identified with] the knowledge of beings according to their deeds.
It must be so. And the word "eva" (only/just), standing in an inappropriate place, should be construed after the term "divine eye.

For it precludes the knowledge of the destination according to karma from being something other than the divine eye; for there is no such thing as the "knowledge of the destination according to karma" apart from the divine eye.
The commentary on the discussion of the knowledge of the destination according to karma is finished.
10. Commentary on the Discourse on Restraint (Saṃvarakathāvaṇṇanā) 379.
Since the existence of both restraint and non-restraint among the deities of the Four Great Kings is made manifest by the Āṭānāṭiya Sutta, he said, “beginning with the Tāvatiṃsa devas.
This being so, in the discourse on the happy destinies (*sugatikathā*), [the phrase] “of the former deities included among the Tāvatiṃsa” [is used].
It must be said: "The drinking of liquor by the Sakka-devas is heard of; therefore, that drinking of liquor by them does not constitute non-restraint.
The commentary on the discussion of restraint is finished.
The commentary on the Third Chapter is finished.
4. The Fourth Chapter: 1.
Commentary on the Discussion of Whether a Layperson Can Be an Arahant.

387. Regarding the phrase "by way of being associated with the fetters of a householder": this demonstrates that one is called a "householder" precisely because of being associated with desire and lust for household life, and not merely by way of outward appearance.
The commentary on the discussion of whether an arahant can be a householder is finished.
2. Commentary on the Discussion of Rebirth.

388. “By way of non-maternal birth” means that he is of spontaneous birth (*opapātika*); the intention is that one should understand the meaning as: “there, through that very rebirth, he attains final Nibbāna.
The commentary on the discussion of rebirth is finished. 4.
Commentary on the Discussion of Endowment (*Samannāgata-kathā*).

393. In the discussion on "endowment" (*samannāgata*), one who asserts [the endowment] with reference to acquisition (*patti*) does not speak of an endowment with the four aggregates as if they were [simultaneously] present. Therefore, it must be explained how the undesirable consequence of his [asserting] an endowment with the four—contact and so forth—would otherwise follow.
The commentary on the discussion on endowment is finished.
5. Commentary on the Discussion on Endowment with Equanimity (*upekkhā*).
397. "By this same method" means that everything beginning with "therein, two kinds of possession" should be applied accordingly.

Therein, the "attainment-dhamma" (patti-dhamma) refers to the acquisition of the first jhāna and so forth by one who reaches any particular plane among the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) and others by way of the first jhāna and so forth.
It is a formation dissociated from consciousness because it does not cease even when the first jhāna and so forth have ceased.
They say that one is said to be "endowed with those" because of them when sleeping and when engaged in recitation and so forth.
The commentary on the discussion of being endowed with equanimity is finished.
6. Commentary on the Discussion of Whether One is Awake or Asleep at the Bodhi Tree.
398. Therefore, because the two aforementioned types of knowledge constitute enlightenment (*bodhi*), the construction should be understood as follows:

the question and the inquiry belong to the proponent (*sakavādī*) with reference to those who hold the view that one is a Buddha because he possesses enlightenment, [arguing] that enlightenment does not exist by way of a dharma attained apart from those two.
The commentary on the discussion regarding the Buddha’s awakening is finished.
7. Commentary on the Discussion of the Marks (Lakkhaṇakathāvaṇṇanā).
402. Since this was stated specifically with reference to a bodhisatta, one must exclude those who possess the marks but are not bodhisattas.
This sutta was spoken specifically with reference to a Bodhisatta; it does not mean that there is no one other than a Bodhisatta who possesses the marks.
Nor does it mean that everyone who possesses the marks is a Bodhisatta. Therefore, the intention is that [the possession of the marks] is not a conclusive proof.
The commentary on the discussion of the marks is finished.
8. Commentary on the Discussion of Entering the Path of Certainty (Niyāmokkantikathāvaṇṇanā) 403.

"Except for the fulfillment of the perfections" (*pāramīpūraṇa*) means that it is shown that it is precisely through the fulfillment of the perfections that those people are called "beings destined for enlightenment" (*bodhiyā niyatā*). For, as indicated by the phrase "merely because of their death," etc., they do not give a prediction (*byākaronti*) because no one has yet arisen who is designated as having entered the path of certainty (*niyāmaka*).
The commentary on the discussion of entering the path of certainty is concluded.
10. Explanation of the Discourse on the Abandoning of All Fetters (Sabbasaṃyojanappahānakathāvaṇṇanā) 413.

"In the direct sense alone" means that because there is nothing further remaining to be abandoned, one does not take this figurative expression "abandoning of all fetters," but rather takes it as meaning "precisely by abandoning [them] through the path of Arahatship. This is what is intended.
They say that he admits [the absence of defilements] because of the non-existence of what remains to be abandoned (*appahīnassa abhāvā*);
likewise regarding the term "abandonment without remainder" (*anavasesappahāna*). If this were so, it would follow that he has discarded his own tenet and admitted the tenet of the opponent.
The commentary on the Discourse on the Abandoning of All Fetters is finished.
The commentary on the Fourth Chapter is finished.
5. The Fifth Chapter.
1. Commentary on the Discussion of Liberation (Vimuttikathāvaṇṇanā) 418.

Regarding the statement "there is no knowledge of fruition": the intention is that they should not be called "liberated" because they lack the state of liberation-by-its-own-nature (*tadaṅgavimutti*) and so forth, nor should they be called "unliberated" because those defilements abandoned by the Path do not arise again.
And herein, the knowledge of the lineage-change (*gotrabhuñāṇa*)— [...]* *Note: The provided source text ends abruptly; this translation reflects the available portion.*
It should be understood that this is included by the mention of insight (vipassanā).
The commentary on the Discussion of Liberation is finished.
2. Commentary on the Discussion of the Knowledge of the Adept (asekha-ñāṇa).

421. "But this is not of one beyond training" (na pan' etaṃ asekkhaṃ): by this [statement], he shows the meaning that for another [teacher] there is the view that "knowledge is indeed of one beyond training" because its object is the domain of one beyond training, but it is not [the knowledge] of one beyond training.
The commentary on the discussion of the knowledge of one beyond training is finished.
3. Commentary on the Discussion of Perversions (Viparīta-kathā-vaṇṇanā).
"424. 'Not earth alone' means that it is neither the earth characterized by its specific marks (lakkhaṇa-pathavī) nor the earth consisting of material components (sasambhāra-pathavī).

Furthermore, it should be understood that the statement regarding the inversion of perceiving the impermanent as permanent and so forth as 'misconception' (viparīta-ñāṇa) applies even to non-knowledge (aññāṇa), having attributed the conventional designation of 'knowledge' (ñāṇa-vohāra) to it."
The commentary on the Discourse on Perversions is finished.
4. Commentary on the Discourse on Certainty (Niyāmakathāvaṇṇanā) 428–431.
There is knowledge that conforms to the truths and follows the path-knowledge; seeing this, the Blessed One said, "He is capable."
The view is that one knows [the future]. Regarding the phrase "making the first question itself the fourth":
here, he says "the fourth" by counting from the point where the erroneous application begins with the words "for the fixed [person] to go on the wrong path.
The commentary on the discussion of the fixed course (niyāma) is finished.
5. Explanation of the Discourse on the Analytical Knowledges (Paṭisambhidākathāvaṇṇanā) 432–433.

Even for one who holds that whatever knowledge belongs to the Noble Ones is exclusively supramundane, it cannot be said that all knowledge is analytical knowledge (paṭisambhidā). For even the knowledge of non-Noble Ones is indeed knowledge; thus, its quality as knowledge remains.

"It should not be said that he does not desire it. Regarding the phrase "with reference to the knowledge of attainment in the conventional designation of the earth-kasiṇa," the intended meaning may be that this refers to the knowledge of a non-noble person (*anariya*).
The commentary on the *Paṭisambhidāmagga* is concluded.
6. Commentary on the Discussion of Conventional Knowledge (Sammutiñāṇakathāvaṇṇanā) 434–435.
Showing that he speaks by taking both [types of truth] as having the commonality of being "truth" through the commonality of the word *sacca*, he says, “In that regard,” and so forth.
The commentary on the discussion of conventional knowledge is finished.
7. Explanation of the Discussion on the Mental Object (Cittārammaṇakathāvaṇṇanā) 436–438.

By the statement, "One attends to the characteristic of touching of contact," it is shown that the previous admission of what is to be said was made with reference to a collective attention (*samudāyamanasikāra*) distinct from the attention to successive phenomena (*anupadadhammamanasikāra*).
The explanation of the discussion on the mental object is concluded.
8. Explanation of the Discussion on Knowledge of the Future (Anāgatañāṇakathāvaṇṇanā) 439–440.

Regarding the phrase "from all [knowledge]," it is stated that there is knowledge of the future in such passages as "of Pāṭaliputta, indeed. Thus, it is said that they maintain there is knowledge even of the immediate future by virtue of the commonality of its being "future.
The explanation of the discussion on knowledge of the future is finished.
9. Explanation of the Discussion on Knowledge of the Present (Paṭuppannañāṇakathāvaṇṇanā) 441–442.

"Depending on the word" means depending on the word implied by the sense, or depending on the word of permission. "With reference to continuity" means with reference to the continuity of contemplation as dissolution from the perspective of dissolution; this is the intended meaning.
The explanation of the discussion on knowledge of the present is finished.
10. Explanation of the Discussion on Knowledge of the Fruits (Phalañāṇakathāvaṇṇanā) 443–444.

"Just as the Buddhas" means that just as the Buddhas know the fruits by their own power through the knowledge of the higher and lower states of all types of fruition, so too [does this person]; this is what is meant.
The explanation of the discussion on knowledge of the fruits is finished.
The commentary on the Fifth Chapter is finished.
The Great Fifty-Section is complete.
6. The Sixth Chapter.
1. Commentary on the Discussion of Certainty (Niyāmakathāvaṇṇanā) 445–447.

"There is no such thing as 'uncertainty'" means that just as for one who is certain of falsehood there is what is called uncertainty in another existence, so too for this [person], there is never any state of uncertainty; the intention is that such certainty is unconditioned (asaṅkhata).
The commentary on the discussion of certainty is finished.
2. Commentary on the Discourse on Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppādakathāvaṇṇanā) 451.

"Established in the sense of a cause" means simply the state of being a cause. By this, he shows that the causal nature of phenomena is the "establishment of phenomena" (*dhammaṭṭhitatā*). The same applies to the term "the fixed order of phenomena" (*dhammaniyāmatā*).
The commentary on the discourse on dependent origination is concluded.
3. Commentary on the Discourse on Truths (Saccakathāvaṇṇanā) 452–454.

The truth of the basis (*vatthusacca*) consists of birth and so forth, sensual craving and so forth, and right view and so forth. The truth of characteristics (*lakkhaṇasacca*) consists of the characteristics of oppression, origination, and deliverance, namely oppression and the rest.
The commentary on the discourse on truths is finished.
5. Commentary on the Discussion of the Attainment of Cessation (Nirodhasamāpatti) 457–459.

“Being performed, it is performed” means that the non-arising of the immaterial aggregates (*arūpakkhandha*), which are currently occurring, is accomplished through the successive sequence of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).
However, one who says this [is so] because of the absence of the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṅkhata*) and the unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*)...
It negates the status of being a dhamma possessing intrinsic nature (*sabhāvadhammatā*). Furthermore, "cleansing" (*vodāna*) is merely a synonym for "emergence.
The intention is that there is no cause for the state of being unconditioned (*asaṅkhatabhāva*), because [the argument] establishes [only] the status of being a dhamma possessing intrinsic nature.
The commentary on the discussion of the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is finished.
The commentary on the sixth chapter is finished.
7. The seventh chapter: 1.
Commentary on the Discussion on What is Included.
471–472. "Associated" means "connected.
The commentary on the discourse on association is finished.
2. Commentary on the Discourse on Conjunction.

473–474. By stating that there is no "determination of diversity" (*nānattavavatthāna*), it shows that the statement "oil has entered into the sesame seed" would be untenable; thus, [the opponent] rejects it, saying, "Certainly not.
The commentary on the discussion of association (*sampayutta*) is concluded.
3. Commentary on the Discussion of Mental Factors (*cetasika*).

475–477. Since there is no co-nascence (sahajātatā) among contact and the other [mental factors] that is devoid of simultaneous arising and so forth, he said: "with reference to associated co-nascence" (*sampayutta-sahajātataṃ sandhāyā*).
The commentary on the Discussion of Mental Factors (*cetasika-kathā*) is finished.
4. Commentary on the Discussion of Giving (*dāna-kathā*).

478. "To urge by way of the object to be given" means: if the mental factor (*cetasika*) alone is the gift (*dāna*), then by the definition "it is a gift because it is worthy of being given," the status of being a gift would also follow for the mental factor alone; this is the meaning of the objection. 479.
The passage beginning with "unwanted fruit" (*aniṭṭhaphala*) is stated for the purpose of illustrating that non-mental factors can also be gifts;

it should be understood that it is not stated for the purpose of illustrating the giving of a fruit [by the mental factor alone]. By the phrase "unwanted fruit" and so forth, the giving of a fruit by a non-mental factor is shown.
