It is as if it were said; there is no state of giving [intrinsic to the act], and this was stated for the purpose of precluding that.

And having established this, he immediately says: "For a non-mental phenomenon such as food does not yield a result in the future. Regarding the phrase "for the purpose of determining the state of desirable fruit":
unlike the object given, there is no way in which the gift itself can have an undesirable fruit; rather, it is exclusively of desirable fruit.
The meaning is "for the purpose of restriction.
"By the other" refers to the method [of etymological derivation] beginning with "it is called *dāna* because it is worthy (*diyyati*).

However, in order to refute the proponent's own position—that "the gift is merely the object to be given"—by means of a single definition, [the author] provides scriptural proof in the opponent's position, beginning with "faith, moral shame," and so forth.

It is appropriate [to say] that "here someone gives food," and so forth; and it is appropriate for the proponent's own position (sakavāda) to state "faith, moral shame (hiri), and so forth" in order to refute the claim that "merely a mental state (cetasika-dhamma) is giving" and to establish that "a mental state is giving.
Alternatively, it is appropriate to establish that "the object to be given (deyyadhamma) is giving" by means of such statements as "here someone gives food," and so forth. Thus...
It should be understood that the statement, "but not by a single meaning," was made with reference to the diversity of the means for turning back [from unwholesome states].

In this context, just as in the doctrine of the opponent, when the question is asked regarding the purpose of establishing the Sutta—"Should it not be said that a mental state (cetasika-dhamma) is giving?"—the meaning should be understood as "it is a mental state";
likewise, in the case of the statement, "Should it not be said that the object to be given (deyyadhamma) is giving? [the same principle applies].

And regarding the phrase "the object of giving" (*deyyadhamma*) in the question: since it was stated that "the object of giving is a desirable fruit," this merely rejects the absence of a desirable fruit;

therefore, in this context, the reading should be "merely the state of being a desirable fruit is rejected. Or rather, it should be said: "it was rejected upon seeing merely the absence of a desirable fruit.
[The term *deyyadhamma*] is used for the purpose of releasing [the mind] from the state of confusion, in the sense that the mental factor (*cetasika*) is something to be given.
And because the object to be given possesses the quality of yielding a desirable fruit, it is said that its purpose is the liberation through the state of giving.
The commentary on the discourse on giving is finished.
5. Commentary on the Discourse on Merit Consisting in Use.

483. The tenet is that there exists merit consisting in enjoyment (*paribhogamaya*) which is dissociated from consciousness (*cittavippayutta*). For they say, with reference to that, "Merit consisting in enjoyment increases"—this is the intended meaning.

485. "By way of that too" means by way of that tenet as well. They say he asserts, "There may be a simultaneous occurrence (*samodhāna*) for these [mental factors] just as there is for the five types of sensory consciousness.
However, this refers specifically to the simultaneous occurrence of the contact and other factors associated with the five sensory consciousnesses.
The intended meaning is that he acknowledges [the gift].
(486) By the phrase "even when not used," it is shown that "the recipient, having accepted it, does not use it but discards it," and so forth.
When the object to be given is not used, because it remains a source of merit, the merit consisting of actual usage increases.
This position is defeated. When it is defeated, the proponent’s own position becomes strong.

The intention is that the meritorious nature [of an act] is established in this way through the volition of relinquishment (*cāgacetanā*) alone. Even when the object to be given has not yet been consumed, since its meritorious nature exists solely through the volition of relinquishment, he says: "The proponent’s own position alone is strong."
The commentary on the discourse concerning merit consisting of enjoyment is finished.
6. Commentary on the Discourse Concerning What is Given Here (Itodinnakathāvaṇṇanā) 488–491.
“They subsist by means of that” means they subsist by means of that very robe and so forth, or they subsist by means of that very gift of robes and so forth.
The intended meaning is that [they would not be sustained] even without the karma performed by themselves. "For this reason" means:
even for one who establishes the view, "If they were not sustained by whatever robes and so forth given from here, how could they rejoice... [and so on]... how could they obtain gladness?
The commentary on the discussion of what is given from here is finished.
7. Commentary on the Discussion of the Triple Division of the Ripening of Kamma Concerning Earth (Pathavī-kamma-vipāka-otika-kathā-vaṇṇanā) 492.

Since contact (*phassa*) is divided into that which is to be experienced as pleasant and so forth, after showing by means of contact all ripening of kamma, the passage beginning with “And that [contact], as well as perception and the rest” was stated in order to show the association [of these factors] with those [mental states] excluding the self. And there are these...
This was said with reference to the concomitant phenomena such as eye-consciousness that arise in one who is reproaching.

"The aspiration for whatever desirable result occurs therein" indicates that aspiration which serves as a decisive support (*upanissaya*) for karma— that is, performing an action after having formed an aspiration specifically for a desirable result—
or it refers to craving conditioned by present feeling by way of producing grasping and so forth.

It is produced from suffering. "Root-thirst" refers either to former thirst which serves as the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for the karma that produces the present cycle of kamma-results, or to that which, acting as an assistant to the karma, serves as the decisive support for the kamma-result.
To show that the censure is employed according to their own tenets, he said: "And of their doctrine," and so forth.
494. "By way of acquisition" means that when there is karma, there is the acquisition of earth and so forth; thus it shows that such karma is called "conducive to that.
The commentary on the discussion of the triad of earth as the result of karmic ripening is finished.
8. Commentary on the Discussion of the Triad of Aging and Death as Ripening.
495. "Because of the absence of the characteristic of association" means the intention is that there is an absence of this characteristic of association, namely, "having a single object.

496. "There is no alternative way" means that there was no alternative way for the proponent himself to state [the position]; thus he shows that the question was not asked in terms of the indeterminate (abyākata) for the purpose of excluding aging and death as a result of maturation (vipāka) among the indeterminate states.

497. Some say that "the state of being ill-favored in color is aging itself"; however, that is incorrect, because it is the same as the demonstration of the ugliness of matter itself through such statements as "that unwholesome kamma is the source of matter," and so forth.
The commentary on the discussion of the maturation of aging and death is finished.
9. Commentary on the Discussion of the Maturation of Noble Dhamma: 500.
They "turn" refers to the cycle of karma and so forth.
The commentary on the discourse on the ripening of noble qualities is finished.
10. Commentary on the Discourse on Ripening and the State of Being Subject to Ripening 501.

"By way of that condition" means: by way of that condition which consists in being a mutual condition for one ripening [of consciousness] with respect to another ripening. "By way of that condition" also refers to the state of being a mutual condition.
This is the intention. By the words "for that" (*so hi*) and so forth, he shows that this objection is the reason for the previous admission.

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "in the sense of a condition among mutual conditions, etc.," he includes co-nascent conditions and others, thereby showing [the objection applies] through each respective mode of being a condition among them.
The commentary on the discussion regarding "resultant and states subject to result" is finished.
The commentary on the Seventh Chapter is finished.
8. The Eighth Chapter: 1.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Six Destinations.
503–504. "Color" (*vaṇṇa*) refers to both the appearance of color and shape; thus it is said, "having a similar form and shape.
The commentary on the discussion of the six classes of beings is concluded.
2. Commentary on the Discussion of the Intermediate State (*antarābhava*).
505. [The intermediate state exists] because it sees places that are very distant, obstructed, or yet to be reached, like one possessing the divine eye;

and because it travels through the air, piercing through the spaces between the earth, like one possessed of psychic power (*iddhimā*). Regarding the phrase "not by way of a natural process" (*na sahadhammena*):
the intention is that if that being did not exist in the interval, there would be no reason for the negation "it is not called an intermediate existence" (*antarābhavo*).

506. Regarding the phrase "not desiring birth, aging, death, as well as the succession of death and rebirth-linking": by this, he does not accept that there is an intermediate state (antarābhava) consisting of the aggregates immediately following death;
nor does he accept that what is currently occurring is "birth"; nor does he accept that "death" consists of vanishing immediately after having entered the mother’s womb.

507. Just as there is a succession of death and rebirth-linking through repeated passing away and arising here and there within the realms of sense-desire existence and so forth, so too [the text] shows that one does not desire that [existence] there.
The commentary on the discussion of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is finished.
3. Commentary on the Discussion of the Strands of Sensual Pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*).
510. By the sense of "desiring," the state of sensual existence (*kāmabhava*) refers to all aggregates and so forth belonging to the sense sphere;

this is how it should be understood according to this intention. However, in the *Dhātukathā*, the state of sensual existence is shown only with respect to the appropriated aggregates, not by way of the sense of "desiring.
This is merely because of the statement: "Bhikkhus, there are these five strands of sensual pleasure."

"Depending on" (nissāya) means: since the fivefold division of sensual pleasures is called "sensual pleasure" (kāma), the expression "the sensual element" (kāmadhātu) is nothing other than a synonym for that;
it is with this very intention that the word is used in this way.
The commentary on the discussion of the strands of sensual pleasure is finished.

5. Commentary on the Discussion of the Form Element (Rūpadhātu-kathā-vaṇṇanā) 515–516. Regarding this discussion of the form element, because of the statement "the form element," one should recognize the tenet that the form element must consist exclusively of material phenomena (rūpī-dhamma).
In the Suttas, the delimitation of planes is restricted to specific levels, as in such passages as "these three existences" (tayo ime bhavā).
They also state that there is a delimitation of karma, beginning with the words, “having made the Avīci hell its lower limit.
The commentary on the Discourse on the Form Realm is finished.
6. Commentary on the Discourse on the Formless Realm.

517–518. "By this means" means that just as in the preceding discussion material phenomena (*rūpadhammā*) were spoken of without distinction as the "form element" (*rūpadhātu*), so too here immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhammā*) are spoken of without distinction as the "immaterial element" (*arūpadhātu*);
thus the intended meaning is that the method explained there applies here as well.
The commentary on the Discourse on the Formless Realm is finished.
7. Commentary on the Discourse on the Bases in the Form Realm 519.

“The signs of the nose, etc.”—this should be stated as “the signs of the nose, tongue, body, and so forth. By “sign” (*nimitta*), it refers to a collection of material form characterized by a particular shape, which is distinguished by being the location (*okāsa*) for the nose and the other sense organs.
The commentary on the discussion of the bases within the fine-material element is finished.
8. Commentary on the Discussion of Form in the Immaterial Realm (Arūpa-rūpa-kathā-vaṇṇanā) 524–526.
Subtle form exists; the intention is that the immaterial realm is so called because it is the escape from that [subtle form].
The commentary on the Discussion of Formless Form is finished.
9. Commentary on the Discussion of Form as Being Kamma: 527–537.
“Exerting” (pakappayamānā) means striving; the meaning is that they exercise a predominant activity among the associated [mental states].
In the first position, he states this question: "Whatever form is originated by an unwholesome mind, all that is unwholesome.
The commentary on the Discussion of Form as Kamma is finished.
10. Commentary on the Discussion of the Life-faculty.
540. Regarding the question on the life-faculty of the formless (*arūpajīvitindriya*), he speaks by taking the final part of the question beginning with, "Is there a life-span for formless phenomena?
He maintains that there exists a continuum of the life-faculty dissociated from consciousness for formless phenomena.
In this context, since he accepts it for both material and immaterial phenomena, it is appropriate to say that he accepts it for immaterial phenomena.
It should be understood that the phrase "of immaterial phenomena" (*arūpadhammānaṃ*) is what is being stated.

541. It should also be known that by saying "whether there be material phenomena in the continuity of a being," etc., he is likewise referring to that very same continuity of the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*).

542. "With reference to the prior and subsequent parts": the intention is that because of the proximity of the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), even at that time [of death], one has indeed entered into attainment.

544–545. Regarding the two life-faculties (*jīvitindriya*): the earlier reading states, "The question belongs to the proponent (*sakavādin*), the admission belongs to the other"; the later reading states, "The question belongs to the opponent (*paravādin*), the admission belongs to the proponent," and this [latter] is correct.
The commentary on the discussion of the life-faculty is concluded.
11. Commentary on the Discussion of Karma as a Cause (*kammahetukathā*).
546. "They know [the cause] for the performance of such kamma as the taking of life" refers back to the preceding inquiry regarding stream-enterers and so forth.
As for the phrase "handahī" (well then), this cannot be said to be a word of acceptance used by the proponent himself;

rather, it would be more appropriate to say that the proponent speaks thus in order to make the opponent accept [the answer], namely, "for the cause of which kamma? Thus, it is logical that he says this to induce the opponent's assent.

"Having caused [the opponent] to accept" means not taking the sense as "having caused him to acknowledge a position," but rather the sense should be understood as "having caused the proponent of another doctrine to adopt his own view.
The commentary on the discussion of the cause of kamma is finished.
The commentary on the eighth chapter is finished.
9. The ninth chapter: 1.
Commentary on the Discourse on Seeing the Advantage.
"547. For the purpose of showing the distinction (*vibhāga*) means for the purpose of showing the difference (*visabhāga*); this is what is meant.
One should consider how it is appropriate to crush the intention of one who asserts [the two views] by way of different mental states (*nānācitta*).

For it is appropriate that this [treatise] was undertaken to show the absence of those two [mental states] in one who speaks of the two kinds of seeing simultaneously by way of their objects (*ārammaṇa*). By the words 'by way of hearsay' (*anussava*), etc."
It is shown that insight (vipassanā) is not only knowledge whose object is impermanence and so forth, but also the perception of the benefits in Nibbāna, such as "Non-arising is security" and so on.
The commentary to the Discourse on Perceiving Benefits is finished.
2. Commentary on the Discussion of the Deathless Object (Amatārammaṇakathāvaṇṇanā) 549.

Regarding the phrase "out of fear of the Sutta": it should be understood as being out of fear of the Sutta because [the Buddha] stated that the state of being secure and so forth refers to the state of being non-fettering and so on, based on the passage: "Monks, 'the further shore, secure, free from fear'—this, monks, is a designation for Nibbāna. Thus it should be seen as being out of fear of the Sutta.
The commentary on the discussion concerning the object of the deathless is finished.
3. Commentary on the Discussion Concerning Matter as Having an Object: 552–553.

"For the purpose of showing the classification of the meaning of 'object'": this refers to the classification [of the term *ārammaṇa*] as "the sense of condition" (*paccayattha*) and "the sense of being clung to" (*olubbhattha*).

The meaning is stated as follows: even though there is an object of clinging because of the presence of conditions, one should not conclude that [consciousness] "has an object" simply because it has an object of clinging—whether one assumes or does not assume the absence of distinction among those who cling to existing conditions.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of whether form has an object.
4. Commentary on the Discussion of Latent Dispositions Having No Object (Anusayānārammaṇātikathāvaṇṇanā) 554–556.
The intention is that they are said to "exist" merely because they have not been abandoned, and not because they are actually present.
The commentary on the discussion of latent dispositions having no object is concluded.
5. Commentary on the Discussion Concerning Whether Knowledge Is Without an Object (Ñāṇaanārammaṇantikathāvaṇṇanā) 557–8.
"Of that knowledge" means, they say, "of path-knowledge.
The commentary on the discussion concerning whether knowledge is without an object is finished.
7. Commentary on the Discussion of Thoughts that Have Entered (Vitakkānupatitakathāvaṇṇanā) 562.
“Without distinction” means by both ways: through the object and through association.
The commentary on the discussion of thoughts that have entered is finished.
8. Commentary on the Discussion of the Sound of the Expansion of Thought (Vitakkavipphārasaddakathāvaṇṇanā) 563.

Regarding the phrase "in all cases" (*sabbaso*), he says, "even at the time of the occurrence of the mind-element (*manodhātu*)," showing that this refers to the meaning: everywhere, at all times, and in all instances among states of consciousness accompanied by thought (*savitakkacitta*). "Mere expansion of thought" (*vitakkavipphāramatta*) means the mere occurrence of thought; this is the intended sense.
The commentary on the discussion of the sound of the expansion of thought is finished.
9. Commentary on the Discussion Regarding Speech Not Corresponding to One’s Mind (Nayathācittassavācātikathāvaṇṇanā) 565.
“There is no offense” means that because there is an absence of the intention to deceive, it does not constitute false speech (musāvāda).
This concludes the commentary on the discussion regarding speech not corresponding to one’s mind.
11. Commentary on the Discussion Concerning Possession of the Past and Future (568–570).
"In those" means in those designations. One is called "possessed" by way of the designation of possession; one is called "an obtainer" by way of the designation of obtaining.
That which is called "possessed" is what is known as the designation of possession. That which is called "an obtainer" is...
Or rather, the intended meaning should be construed as: "This is called the designation of acquisition.
The commentary on the discussion of possession in the past and future is finished.
The commentary on the ninth chapter is finished.
10. The Tenth Chapter. 1. Explanation of the Discourse on Cessation (Nirodhakathāvaṇṇanā) 571–2.

By stating "simultaneously with the moment of dissolution of the life-continuum consciousness" (*bhavaṅgacitta*), [the author] refers to the moment of dissolution of the functional aggregates (*kiriya-khandha*).
It should be stated that the aggregates belonging to rebirth arise together with [the moment of] rebirth;

likewise, those belonging to rebirth [arise] together with the moment of their dissolution, and functional states (*kiriyā*) [arise] together with the moment of their dissolution. By the inclusion of the four functional aggregates, eye-consciousness and the others are included.
"Knowledge" (*ñāṇa*) is appropriately understood here as path-knowledge (*magga-ñāṇa*).
The commentary on the Discussion of Cessation is finished.
3. Commentary on the Discussion of the Path for One Possessing the Five Consciousnesses:
576. Its characteristic is stated not by saying "six consciousnesses," but rather "the five consciousnesses have arisen bases," and so forth.

The characteristic has been stated. However, the non-statement here of "six consciousnesses" is intended as the reason for the statement beginning with "Indeed, it should not be said, O friend... (No ca vata re vattabbe).

(577) "Worldly" refers to insight and the path. Regarding that which is called "signless" therein: the intention is that at the moment one is possessed of eye-consciousness, that which is grasped as signless is precisely what is meant by "emptiness," since one is then described as "not grasping a sign."
The commentary on the discussion of the path for one possessing the fivefold sense-consciousness is finished.
5. Commentary on the Discussion of the Fivefold Sense-Consciousness Being Without Volition (Asābhoga) §§584–586.
"It is bent by way of the wholesome and unwholesome" means that it proceeds having been bent—that is, directed—by the state of being wholesome or unwholesome.

Furthermore, that [mental factor] should be understood as the apprehension of the mode of the object, by means of which there is association with non-greed and so forth, as well as with greed and so forth—
as in the cases of such phrases as "a portion of the mind [perceiving] 'this is pleasant'" and so on.
The commentary to the discussion on the lack of volitional effort in the fivefold sense-consciousness is concluded.

6. Commentary on the Discussion of the Two Kinds of Virtue (Sīla) §§587–589 [The cessation] is the cessation through momentary dissolution (*khaṇabhaṅga*), not the cessation through non-arising (*appavatti*), nor the cessation through the transgression of virtue (*sīlavītikkama*).

"Just like a transgression" means that just as one is called "immoral" (*dussīla*) when a transgression has been committed, so too is one [called immoral] when [the virtue] has ceased; thus it refers to those who are inclined toward transgression.
The meaning is "observing.
The commentary on the discussion regarding the two types of virtue is concluded. 7.
Commentary on the Discussion Regarding Virtue Not Being a Mental Concomitant (acetasika).

590–594. "By which he is indeed called virtuous": the intention is that by means of that accumulation which is dissociated from consciousness and present, one who possesses unwholesome or neutral states of consciousness is nevertheless called virtuous.
The rest here should be understood according to the method already stated in the discussion on "Giving is not mental," though that discussion must be sought out.
The commentary on the discussion of whether virtue is mental concomitant is finished.
9. Commentary on the Discussion of the Cause of Undertaking (598–600).
Regarding this discussion on the cause of undertaking, it should be understood that its similarity to the preceding discussion consists in its partial resemblance to the discussion on utilization.
The commentary on the discussion of the cause of undertaking is finished.
11. Commentary on the Discussion of the Limit of Immorality Without Intimation (Aviññatti-dussīlyantika-kathāvaṇṇanā) 603–604.
Regarding the completion of the factors for killing living beings and so forth through a command: when one who was commanded on one day [commits the act] on another...
For one who commits the destruction of life during the day, at that time that command constitutes an *aṅga* (factor) even without a formal communication (*viññatti*);
thus, the intention is that non-communication is a breach of moral discipline (*dussīlya*). The commentary on the discussion of non-communicative breach of moral discipline is concluded.
The commentary on the Tenth Chapter is finished.
The Second Fifty is completed.
11. The Eleventh Chapter.
4. Commentary on the Discussion of Knowledge (Ñāṇakathāvaṇṇanā) 614–615. Regarding the phrase "just as the Mahāsāṅghikas [say]" in the discussion of knowledge:

other than the Andhakas mentioned previously in the discussion on whether knowledge is without an object (*anārammaṇa*), these might be the Mahāsāṅghikas referred to here. If [it is argued that] the fading away of lust (*rāgavigama*) occurs through the phrase "when there is no more ignorance" (*aññāṇe vigate*) and so forth...
This shows that, just as with the designation "one free from lust," the disappearance of ignorance is the cause for the designation "one possessing knowledge.
For one is not called "possessing knowledge" (ñāṇī) because knowledge exists in him; rather, he is called "possessing knowledge" by way of being the opposite of one who possesses ignorance.

And regarding the phrase "by the acquisition of knowledge," the meaning should be understood as follows: because ignorance has vanished through the acquisition of knowledge, he comes to be designated as "one possessing knowledge."
The commentary on the Discussion of Knowledge is finished.
6. Commentary on the Discussion of "This is Suffering" (Idaṃ-dukkhaṃtika-kathā).
618–620. As for the phrase "in his own system," the opponent means "in his own doctrine."
The commentary on the discussion of "this is the end of suffering" is finished.
7. Commentary on the Discussion of the Power of Psychic Potency (Iddhibala). 621–624.
"By way of the ripening of kamma" is said with reference specifically to hell; for it is there that the divisions such as the *abbuda* and so forth exist.
This is stated by way of such a ripening of kamma. "Or by calculation of years" refers to humans and the gods of the Four Great Kings and so forth;
for even their kamma capable of yielding a result for an incalculable period of time is delimited by a calculation of years.
The commentary on the discussion of the power of psychic potency is finished.
8. Explanation of the Discourse on Concentration (Samādhikathāvaṇṇanā) 625–626.
“In the sense of composing” means that one does not take it as if there were a separate mental factor called concentration in the sense of placing [the mind] evenly.
“By way of deception” refers to the fact that both eye-consciousness and the jhāna-consciousness exist for only a single moment of consciousness.
"And there is no distinction whatsoever"—by this, the intention is "merely by way of generality.
The commentary on the Discussion of Concentration is finished.
9. Commentary on the Discussion of the Stability of Phenomena (Dhammaṭṭhitatā).
627. "And as the condition of immediate succession (*anantarapaccayatā*)," etc.: ignorance is the immediate condition for volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*).
From that stability which belongs to ignorance, there arises a stability characterized by the state of being an immediate condition; this is the intended meaning.
And here, the mention of "immediate condition" is for the purpose of showing a single condition that is devoid of the state of being a mutual condition (*aññamaññapaccaya*).
It should be seen. For by that, every such condition is demonstrated. And as for "mutual conditionality":
ignorance is a condition for volitional formations, and volitional formations are a condition for ignorance.

In this context, through the stability of ignorance—which consists in its being a condition for volitional formations—there is the stability of volitional formations which consists in their being a condition for ignorance; and the same applies reciprocally. This is the intended meaning.
The commentary on the Discussion of the Stability of the Dhamma is finished.
10. Commentary on the Discussion of Impermanence: 628.
"They are fully established" means that like form and so forth, they are fully established because they arise and cease together with form and the other aggregates.

The meaning is as follows. Regarding the phrase "by way of applying oneself to the analysis of impermanence": they say that just as the designation "staff" applies to all three sections of a staff, so too the designation "impermanence" applies to all three characteristics;
thus, it is by way of applying oneself to the analysis of that [impermanence].
The commentary on the discussion of impermanence is concluded.
The commentary on the eleventh chapter is finished.
12. The twelfth chapter: 1. Commentary on the Discussion of the Formal Act of Restraint (Saṃvarokammantikathāvaṇṇanā).
630–632. "The door of ripening" refers to the movement of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*). "The door of karma" refers to wholesome and unwholesome mental states.
The commentary on the discussion of restraint and non-restraint is finished.
2. Commentary on the Discussion of Karma.

633–635. Regarding the phrase "the rejection is made with reference to the indeterminate," they say that this means the rejection was made according to the characteristics of one's own school (sakasamaya).
Thinking that since volition without result (avipāka-cetanā) has been shown in its true nature, volition with result (savipāka-cetanā) is also effectively shown, he says:
"In order to show volition both with and without result in its true nature."
The commentary on the Discussion of Kamma is finished.
3. Commentary on the Discussion of Sound as Resultant: §§636–637.

By the statement beginning with “Immaterial phenomena originated by kamma,” it is shown that even in the case of the eye and other faculties originated by kamma, the designation “resultant” does not apply; how much less so, then, for sound, which is not originated by kamma?
The commentary on the discussion of the sixfold maturation is finished.
4. Commentary on the Discussion of the Six Bases (Saḷāyatanakathā). 638–640.
Therefore, it is stated that there are those whose doctrine holds that "the six bases are, without distinction, maturation" (*vipāka*).
The commentary on the Discourse on the Six Sense Bases is finished.
5. Commentary on the Discourse on the Seven Times at Most: 641–645.
"One who is fixed as to being seven times at most" means one who is destined (niyata) to [attain liberation] within seven existences at the very most. This is the analysis.
"This distinction. But when it says, "Do you, however, desire his entry into the fixed course (niyāma)?

the meaning is: do you desire the fixed course in some other state of being "seven-times-at-most" (sattakkhattuparama), rather than through the attainment of the fruit of the nature of not falling into the states of loss (avinipātadhammatā)?
"The absence of immediate retribution (ānantariya)" refers to that immediate karma by which one becomes "capable" (bhabba) through the realization of the Dhamma.
The meaning is that they do not exist; or rather, there is an absence of the state of being an immediate offender (*ānantariya*) for the person.
But will he realize the Dhamma in the interval? Some say: "One who has seven births at most does not exceed the seventh existence, but there is no prohibition regarding those before it. Others say:
"For one who was prophesied by the Blessed One through the power of his knowledge, realization occurs in the interval."
Although there is no such fixed destiny (niyāma), nevertheless, because there is no certainty regarding any future existence for him, he is called "one capable [of attaining liberation].

Just as wholesome volitions associated with direct knowledge (*abhiññā-cetanā*), even when they do not occasionally yield a result, are termed "states characterized by ripening" (*vipākadhamma-dhammā*) due to their capacity to yield a result when the causes are present;
so too, due to the flexibility of his faculties, he is "one who has seven births at most," neither because of a fixed destiny nor because of anything ordained by the Blessed One.
Because it is indeterminate (*abyākata*), and because the malleability of the faculties (*indriya-mudutā*) is not a state that produces incapacity, it is not called "incapable.

Furthermore, here the absence of incapacity is negated due to the non-existence of any state that produces incapacity; however, the capacity to realize [the truths] in the interim has not been stated.

For if one who is "limited to seven births" were to realize them in the interim, he would become a "one who goes from family to family" (*kolaṅkola*). But this is said without making such a distinction, on account of the nature of being capable.

"It is appropriate to say 'he is capable' (*bhabbo*). Regarding the phrase "nothing that determines existence" (*na bhavaniyāmakaṃ kiñci*), the words "having seen" (*passitvā*) are to be supplied as an ellipsis, or it is connected with "he explains" (*byākaroti*).
The commentary on the discussion concerning "one who has seven births at most" (*sattakkhattuparama*) is finished.
The commentary on the twelfth chapter (*dvādasama-vagga*) is finished.
13. The Thirteenth Chapter. 1.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Kappaṭṭha: 654–657.
In the commentary on the kappaṭṭha, "below" refers to the discussion on the power of psychic potency (iddhi).
The commentary on the *Kappaṭṭha-kathā* is finished.
3. Commentary on the *Anantarāpayutta-kathā* (660–662).

Regarding the *Anantarāpayutta-kathā*: it is called *anantarāpayutta* because one is engaged (*payutta*) in what is immediate (*ānantariya*); thus, it refers to the state of being engaged in the immediate [karmas].
It should be understood that the meaning [of this] is stated in the Commentary after having supplied the word *anantara*. The reading “*anantarapayutto*” is also seen in the Pāḷi.
The commentary on the discussion of the immediately preceding (*anantarāpayutta*) is finished.
4. Commentary on the Discussion of the Determination of the Determined (*niyatassa-niyāma-kathā-vaṇṇanā*).

663–664. Regarding the statement, "The remaining phenomena of the three planes are called 'undetermined' (aniyata)": here, the term "phenomena of the three planes" is said with reference to those phenomena for which the fixed course (niyāma) has not been reached.
Indeed, it is with reference to these very phenomena that it is stated: "Even one possessed of them is still undetermined.
Thus, taking this as a mere conventional designation, [it is said]: "A Bodhisatta who is fixed and in his final existence is capable of realizing the Dhamma."
The construction of the meaning is as follows: the view of those who hold that "one enters into the fixed course" (niyāmaṃ okkamatī) is based on the intention [of the word] "to enter.

However, in this way, the mere existence of conventional designation (vohāramatta) is stated as the reason for the expression "fixed" (niyato), while the capacity to realize the Dhamma is stated as the reason for the expression "enters into the fixed course" (niyāmaṃ okkamatī). Indeed, it is this very capacity that is the reason for both.
It is logical. "By another" means: if one who is fixed-in-falsity were to enter the fixed course of rightness, or if one who is fixed-in-rightness were to enter the fixed course of falsity;
since that does not exist, this is for the purpose of demonstrating that.
The commentary on the discussion of the fixed-in-falsity is finished.
8. Explanation of the Discourse on Lust for the Unpleasant (Asātarāgakathāvaṇṇanā) 674.

Regarding the discourse on lust for the unpleasant, the phrase "lust" (*rāga*) is intended here to mean greed (*lobha*) as it occurs in the form: "O, may this very thing be mine!"—it shows that it is not otherwise. 675.
However, the word "of the sutta" (*suttassa*) is connected with the word "the intention" (*adhippāyo*).
The commentary on the discussion of lust for what is unpleasant is finished.
9. Commentary on the Discussion of Whether Craving for Phenomena is Indeterminate (676–680).
Since it is stated that "craving for phenomena" exists, therefore, among wholesome states—both mundane and supramundane—it is indeterminate.
Alternatively, by taking craving for all [phenomena] as "craving for phenomena" (*dhammataṇhā*), he shows the position that because it is craving, it is not wholesome;
yet because it occurs with respect to phenomena (*dhamma*), it is not unwholesome, and is therefore indeterminate (*abyākata*).

Thus, having condensed the six types of craving into three categories, the intention is that even craving for phenomena is not indeterminate, since it exists within the state of craving for sense-pleasures (*kāmataṇhā*) and so forth.
The commentary on the discussion concerning whether craving for existence is indeterminate is finished.
The commentary on the Thirteenth Chapter is finished.
14. The Fourteenth Chapter.
1. Explanation of the Discourse on the Linking of the Wholesome and Unwholesome (Kusalākusalapaṭisandahanakathāvaṇṇanā) §§686–690.

The word "that" (*taṃ*) should be understood as being connected separately with both "the wholesome" and "the unwholesome. Alternatively, there is an ellipsis, and it refers to "both of those" (*taṃ ubhayaṃ*). "Links together" (*paṭisandahati*) means it joins; what is meant is that it causes [the next state] to arise immediately after.
The explanation of the discourse on the linking of the wholesome and unwholesome is finished.
2. Commentary on the Discussion of the Arising of the Six Bases (Saḷāyatanuppattikathāvaṇṇanā) 691–692.

Some proponents assert that "in the sprout, the mere seed of trees and such, complete with branches, twigs, and so forth, becomes manifest. To provide an illustration for their position, he said, "of those [trees] complete with branches and twigs," and so on.
The commentary on the discussion of the arising of the six bases is concluded.
3. Explanation of the Discussion on the Condition of Immediate Proximity (Anantara-paccaya-kathā-vaṇṇanā) §§693–697.
Regarding the statement, "Dependent upon the eye and forms, ear-consciousness arises," here [the author] says, "He acknowledges it by way of its acquisition.
Even while observing the immediate arising [of consciousness], he does not maintain that the ear-consciousness has the visible form as its object within the eye.
Then, because it has entered [into its object] by way of the immediate acquisition [of the object], it is appropriate to say that it "acknowledges" the sound-object within the ear itself.
The commentary on the discussion of the immediate condition (*anantara-paccaya*) is finished.
4. Commentary on the Discussion of Noble Form (*ariya-rūpa*).
698–699. One who maintains that the path consists of right speech and so forth also says it is "of the nature of the Noble Ones" (*ariyarūpa*).
The commentary on the discussion of the nature of the Noble Ones is finished.
5. Commentary on the Discussion: Is there another underlying tendency? (*Añño-anusayo-ti-kathā-vaṇṇanā*)
700–701. “‘With lust’ and so forth, however, means that at that time it is to be called ‘with lust’ because lust has not been abandoned”;

“‘With underlying tendency’ and so forth, however, means that at that time it is to be called ‘with underlying tendency’ because the underlying tendency has not been abandoned”—this is the former reading.
The latter reading is also appropriate; for that [state] is not something other than the manifestation of the underlying tendency.
Therefore, it is said: "That is not a proof; it is associated with this. The commentary on the discussion regarding whether there is another underlying tendency (*anuśaya*) is finished.
6. Commentary on the Discussion Regarding Whether Obsession (*paryavasthāna*) is Dissociated from Mind.

702. Since lust and the other defilements arise even for one who attends to the impermanence and so forth [of phenomena], and yet they are not associated with insight (vipassanā), the intended meaning is that the position is held to be that "obsession (pariyuṭṭhāna) is dissociated from consciousness.
The commentary on the discussion regarding obsession being dissociated from consciousness is finished.
7. Commentary on the Discussion of the Included (Pariyāpanna).

703–705. "Threefold" means by way of the defilements (*kilesa*), the bases (*vatthu*), and the spheres (*okāsa*); or alternatively, it is threefold by way of sensual lust (*kāmarāga*), sensual thought (*kāmavitakka*), and phenomena belonging to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara-dhamma*).
"By way of the defilement of sensuality" means by way of being the sensual element (*kāmadhātu*) which consists of the defilement of sensuality; this is what is meant.

"Not perceiving the intended meaning" refers to [the view] that it underlies [the mind] by way of being accompanied by the form element (*rūpadhātu*), [thinking] that it exists as one of the phenomena belonging to the form element.
The meaning is that he does not perceive the fact that [the question] was asked as being "included within the realm of form" (*rūpadhātupariyāpanna*).
The commentary on the discussion of inclusion is finished.
8. Commentary on the Discussion of the Undeclared (*abyākata*).

706–708. The connection is as follows: the speculative view (*diṭṭhigata*) is called "undeclared" (*abyākata*) because it was not stated by way of its being eternal and so forth, in the passage, "Vaccha, 'the world is eternal'—this has been left undeclared. However, in this context, it is not the speculative view itself that is called "undeclared";
rather, it is shown that "this question is to be set aside" (*ṭhapanīyo eso pañho*). Therefore, in every respect, the speculative view is "undeclared."
"It should not be said" is appropriate.
The commentary on the discussion of the indeterminate (abyākata) is finished.
9. Commentary on the discussion of the non-included (apariyāpanna).

709–710. Therefore, they explain the meaning as follows: since one is called "free from lust" (*vītarāga*) even though the suppression of views and lust is equal, but one is not called "free from views" (*vigatadiṭṭhika*), it follows that view is not included within the mundane (*lokiya*).
However, because of the absence of views regarding form (*rūpa*), there must be a view included within the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*). And if it were indeed included [in the sense-sphere],...
If that were so, then just as sensual lust (kāmarāga) disappears for one who has attained jhāna, so too would [wrong] view disappear;
thus he might be called "one whose views have vanished" (vigatadiṭṭhika). But he is not so called; therefore, it should be understood that he says:

"The view is not included (apariyāpannā), for that view of his has not vanished like sensual lust, which—being a view of sensuality (kāmadiṭṭhi)—would be included within the sense-sphere realm (kāmadhātu)."
The commentary on the Discourse on the Unincluded is finished.
The commentary on the Fourteenth Chapter is finished.
15. The Fifteenth Chapter.
1. Commentary on the Discussion of Conditionality (Paccayatākathāvaṇṇanā) 711–717.
Therefore, since conditionality is fixed, it means that for a state that has become a root-condition (hetupaccaya), its status as a root-condition alone is fixed;

it cannot simultaneously possess the status of a predominance-condition (adhipatipaccaya) and so forth, just as it cannot possess the status of an object-condition (ārammaṇapaccaya) and so forth. Thus, its nature as a root-condition is what is determined.
The commentary on the Discussion of Conditionality is finished.
2. Commentary on the Discussion of the Mutuality Condition (Aññamañña-paccaya). 718–719.
Only the unwholesome volitional formation (apuññābhisaṅkhāra) is included because it was stated: "Is not ignorance co-nascent with the formations?"
This is the intended meaning (*adhippāya*). Regarding the phrase "by way of co-nascence, mutuality, presence, non-disappearance, and association":

here, since the support condition (*nissaya*) is already included by the inclusion of "presence" (*atthi*) according to its various divisions, it is not mentioned separately. It should be understood that the nutriment of karma (*kammāhāra*) is excluded because it is not common [to all]. For he will say:
"The three types of clinging (*upādāna*) are conditions for craving (*taṇhā*), just as volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) are for ignorance (*avijjā*). Therefore, [the nutriment of] clinging...
In this context, the conditionality of formations is shown to be exactly the same.
The commentary on the discussion of mutual conditionality is finished.
9. Commentary on the Third Discussion of Perception and Feeling.

732. In the third discussion on perception and feeling (*saññā-vedayita-kathā*), "with reference to other beings" means that the intention is to refer to those five-aggregate beings (*pañcavokāra-satta*) other than those who have attained cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), for whom the attainment of cessation must occur;

or alternatively, it means "with reference to all other beings," since even for non-percipient beings (*asañña-satta*), death is held to occur upon the arising of perception. "The body's own process" (*sarīra-pakati*) refers to such a [state].
"This body: in such a body even the touch of a hand moves," and so forth.
"There might be a contradiction with the Sutta"—this should be said after having first made the opponent admit [the point].
The commentary on the discussion of the third perception and feeling is finished.
10. Explanation of the Discussion on the Non-percipient Beings (Asaññasattupikākathāvaṇṇanā) 735.
Regarding the enumeration of the attainments of non-perception (*asaññasamāpatti*), the cultivation that proceeds by way of the fading away of perception is the attainment of the fourth jhāna;

yet, instead of taking that cultivation proceeding by way of the fading away of perception—which is the attainment of the fourth jhāna—to be the "attainment of non-perception," they claim that [the state of] non-perception is also [that attainment].
This shows that the opponent’s position is that it is indeed the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saññā-vedayita-nirodha-samāpatti*) [that is meant].

Because non-greed and the other [wholesome roots] exist for one who has entered the attainment of non-perception (*asañña-samāpatti*), the attainment of the fourth jhāna established in our own system is here called the "attainment of non-perception.

It is said with reference specifically to the attainment of the fourth jhāna, because it is "non-perceptive" due to being attained through the fading away of perception (*saññā-virāga*), and not because of the total absence of perception.
The commentary on the discussion concerning the non-percipient beings is finished.
11. Commentary on the Discussion Concerning the Accumulation of Karma. 738–739.

Regarding the questions, "Is it co-arisen with karma? [the author] rejects [this] with reference to the accumulation of karma (*kammūpacaya*), [as it is] dissociated from consciousness (*cittavippayutta*).

In some places the reading is, “He denies with reference to [the mind] associated with consciousness, and he affirms with reference to [the mind] dissociated from consciousness”; in other places it is, “He denies with reference to [the mind] associated with consciousness, and he affirms with reference to [the mind] dissociated from consciousness.
Both of these should be investigated. 741.
Therefore, the intended meaning should be understood as follows: because all three exist simultaneously and because of the convergence of the three types of contact, he asks about their identity.
The commentary on the Discussion of the Accumulation of Kamma is finished.
The commentary on the Fifteenth Chapter is finished.
The Third Fifty is completed.
16. The Sixteenth Chapter. 3. Explanation of the Discourse on the Bestowing of Happiness (Sukhānuppadānakathāvaṇṇanā) 747–748.
Regarding the phrase "that which is of such a kind" in the discourse on the bestowing of happiness: that which belongs neither to oneself, nor to others, nor to him.

The intention is that he admits, by way of mere opinion, that such a thing as this cannot possibly be given to another because it is impossible for anyone else to do so, rather than through logical reasoning.
The commentary on the discussion regarding the giving of happiness is finished.
4. Explanation of the Discourse on the Attention of Grasping (Adhigayhamāna-manasikāra-kathāvaṇṇanā) §§749–753.
"By way of being that-mind" (*taṃcittatāya*): that very mind which has become the object belongs to this [mind], thus it is "that-mind" (*taṃcitto*);

the state of that is "being that-mind" (*taṃcittatā*); by means of that, it is "by way of being that-mind. Alternatively, that mind which is both the grasper and the graspable is "that-mind" (*taṃcittaṃ*).
The state of that [mind] is its very nature as both the subject and the object, its being that same mind; the meaning is "to urge by means of that.
The commentary on the discussion of mental attention (manasikāra) involving grasping is finished.
9. Commentary on the Discussion of Form as Ending with the Fine-Material and Immaterial Realms.

768–770. Regarding the discussion on whether form belongs to the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) or the immaterial sphere (*arūpāvacara*), "below" refers to the discussion on what is included [in the aggregates] as presented in the fourteenth chapter.
The passage beginning with "for the sake of attainment" (*samāpatti-atthiya*) follows the same method already stated.

Furthermore, as for the statement here that "there is form belonging to the immaterial sphere," which refers to form produced by the performance of immaterial-sphere kamma, whatever needs to be said regarding that has already been explained according to the same method in the eighth chapter’s discussion on form in the immaterial realm (*arūpe-rūpakathā*).
The commentary on the discussion concerning the limits of the fine-material and immaterial spheres is finished.
The commentary on the sixteenth chapter is finished.
17. The seventeenth chapter.
1. Commentary on the Discussion of the Accumulation of Merit by an Arahat (Atthi-araha-to-puññūpacaya-kathā-vaṇṇanā) §§776–779.

“Without taking up a consciousness”: this means “without taking up a functional consciousness (kiriyacitta),” which is indeterminate (abyākata), because it is stated that the occurrence of giving and so forth exists through a functional consciousness.
The commentary on the discussion of the accumulation of merit by an Arahat is finished.
2. Commentary on the Discourse on the Absence of Untimely Death for an Arahant 780.
"Having grasped it in a wrong way" means having grasped the sense that one does not say there is an exhaustion of even those kamma-formations whose results have not yet been experienced;
this is the intended meaning. Some, however, [interpret it as] the exhaustion of a person without their having experienced the result of the kamma.
They say, "I do not say [it]," having thus grasped the meaning in an improper way (*ayoniso*).
"Does it not proceed so long? means he rejects it on the basis of the view that "it does not proceed so long"; "does it proceed beyond that?
means he rejects it on the basis of the view that "it proceeds beyond that. Here, it is said: "While life remains, while there is a remainder of life, one deprives [the being] of life."
The teachers say that there is no taking of life for one who strikes or cuts off the head of someone who is dying either by their own words or through their own natural disposition.

The intention is that even though the being is a living creature, the perception of it as such exists, and the murderous intent and the effort are present, there is no taking of life because the person has not died by that specific effort. However, while dying in this way, [the victim] does not, for even a single moment of consciousness...
It is difficult to discern whether one is "not dead" prior to death by way of natural law (*dhammatā-maraṇa*).
The commentary on the discussion regarding the absence of untimely death for an Arahant is finished.
3. Commentary on the Discussion: "All this is due to kamma."

784. "Just as a sprout does not arise from what is not a seed": just as there is no arising of a sprout from what is not its seed, so too there is no arising of the present process from what is not karma or from the ripening of karma;
it is with reference to this that [the opponent] rejects [the position]. This is the intended meaning.
"He asks about the fruit of giving by way of the object to be given" means: by way of the object to be given, whatever volition one gives with—that is the fruit of that gift.
"He asks" means he asks regarding the object to be given; this is what is intended.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion concerning "all this as an act.
4. Commentary on the Discussion Concerning the Binding of the Faculties (*indriya*).

788. "Even without impermanence" means that, as in the passage beginning "as painful as the hells," it is intended that suffering can also be described by virtue of its having suffering as its object.
The commentary on the discussion regarding the bondage of the faculties is finished.
7. Commentary on the Discussion of Whether It Should Not Be Said That the Saṅgha Purifies Offerings.
793–794. Regarding the discussion on whether the Saṅgha purifies the offering (*dakkhiṇā*):

the intention is that those [paths and fruits] are not able to purify the offering in the same way that an individual is able to purify it by performing the purification of virtue (*sīla-parisodhana*) and so forth, and even by attaining cessation (*nirodha*). Alternatively, it is because they do not receive [the gift].
The commentary on the discussion of what is not to be declared—that the Saṅgha purifies the offering—is finished.
11. Commentary on the Discussion of the Purification of Offerings (Dakkhiṇāvisuddhikathā): 800–801.
In this discussion on the purification of offerings, while demonstrating the meaning of the phrase "it may be purified," [the Blessed One said]: "It is of great fruit..."
[He] said, “It would be so. The purity of mind of the donor alone is what yields the result;

thus, the intention is that it is independent of the recipient—it brings about the state of being a volition of great result by the donor alone, even without the recipient acting as a condition—and therefore it yields the result independently of the recipient.
If there were another person who performed [the act] for another, such as the so-called "volition of giving" belonging to the donor...
Why was it said, "If it were performed by the recipient, it would be appropriate"?
Is it not stated in the *Laddhikittana* that "the gift is given by the donor, and the result is produced by the recipient; thus one would be the agent for another"?
True, that is so. However, even the production of the result by the recipient would only occur if it were through the production of the volition of giving (*dānacetanā*).
The intention is that, this being so, it would be logical for one thing to be the agent of another.
The commentary on the Discussion of the Purity of the Offering is finished.
The commentary on the Seventeenth Chapter is finished.
18. The Eighteenth Chapter: 1.
Explanation of the Discourse on the Human World; 802–803.
Regarding the phrase "improperly" (*ayoniso*): this was said with reference to such apprehensions as "with reference to the Tusita heaven," and so forth.
The commentary on the Discourse on the Human World is finished.
2. Commentary on the Discourse on the Teaching of the Dhamma (804–806).
It is said that after he had accepted his teaching, it was taught by the Venerable Ānanda Thera himself.
The commentary on the discourse on the teaching of the Dhamma is finished.
6. Commentary on the Discourse on the Transition of Jhānas (813–816).
Regarding the discourse on the transition of jhānas, "out of order" means that after emerging from the first jhāna, [one enters] without applied thought and sustained thought (*vitakka-vicāra*).

They should be attended to as being fraught with danger; therefore, one must attain the second jhāna—such is the sequence for the access concentrations and the jhānas, and it means that [the practice] is not possible without this.
The commentary on the discussion of the transition between jhānas is finished.
7. Commentary on the Discussion of the Intermediate Jhāna (Jhānantarika-kathāvaṇṇanā) 817–819.
"This is called the 'intermediate jhāna' (jhānantarikā)" means that because it lacks the specific state of any one of the first jhānas and so forth, it is not a jhāna;

rather, it is called the "intermediate jhāna" because it is like the intermediate space between directions such as south and east. Which one is it? It is this state which possesses only vicāra and is devoid of vitakka.
It should be connected with "in concentration.
The commentary on the discussion of the intermediate jhāna is finished.
9. Commentary on the Discussion of Whether One Sees Form with the Eye.

826–827. “With reference to the admission [of seeing]”: the intended meaning is that this refers to the admission of mental consciousness (manoviññāṇa) as stated in the passage beginning, “Having seen a form with the eye, one grasps at its signs,” and so forth. Therefore, it must be investigated:
“This being so, if form falls within the domain of mental consciousness, how then can the admission of mental consciousness be the act of seeing form?”
The commentary on the discussion of “one sees visible form with the eye” is finished.
The commentary on the eighteenth chapter is finished.
19. The nineteenth chapter.

1. Commentary on the Discussion of the Abandoning of Defilements (Kilesapajahanakathāvaṇṇanā) §§828–831. “They do not arise even when unarisen” means they are called “abandoned”; therefore, he rejects the notion that there is an abandoning of defilements.
However, those [defilements] have neither arisen and passed away, nor will they arise, nor have they arisen in the past.
He shows that it cannot be said that "one abandons defilements," and so forth.
The commentary on the Discussion of the Abandoning of Defilements is finished.
2. Commentary on the Discussion of Emptiness (*Suññatā*).
832. First, regarding the phrase "the characteristic of non-self for some": this refers to the characteristic of non-self of the immaterial aggregates (*arūpakkhandha*).
"By one method" means by way of the method of the state of aging and death (*jarāmaraṇabhāva*) as the characteristic of non-self; so they say.

For, in the case of the material aggregate (*rūpakkhandha*) and the others, the state of being subject to lack of mastery—expressed as "may it not age, may it not die"—is non-selfhood (*anattatā*); and in its actual meaning, that is simply aging and death itself.

And because it is stated that "this aging-and-death is comprised within two aggregates," their intention is that the aging-and-death of the formless aggregates is included within the aggregate of formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*).
The commentary on the Discourse on Emptiness is finished.
3. Commentary on the Discourse on the Fruits of Recluseship (Sāmaññaphala-kathāvaṇṇanā) 835–836.
"The arising of the fruit" refers to the dhamma that has been attained.
The commentary on the Discourse on the Fruits of Recluseship is finished.
5. Commentary on the Discussion of Suchness (Tathatākathāvaṇṇanā) 841–843.

Regarding the phrase "reckoned as the intrinsic nature of form and so forth" (*rūpādisabhāvatāsaṅkhātā*): here, the meaning should be understood as "the intrinsic nature of form and so forth" (*rūpādisabhāvatā*). For he says that suchness (*tathatā*) is the very state of being (*bhāva*), not the conjunction with a state of being (*bhāvayoga*).
The commentary on the discussion of suchness is concluded.
6. Commentary on the Discussion of the Wholesome (Kusalakathāvaṇṇanā) 844–846.
Nibbāna is wholesome merely by virtue of its blameless nature. Whatever is wholesome, all that is so merely by virtue of its blameless nature; therefore, it is said that nibbāna is wholesome.
The commentary on the discussion of the wholesome is finished.
7. Commentary on the Discussion of the Ultimate Determination (Accantaniyāmakathāvaṇṇanā) 847.
Regarding the statement, “Once submerged, he remains submerged,” based on that Sutta:

one might think that the restriction made with reference to the non-arising of supramundane faith and the other faculties in that particular birth was made with reference to his being like a mere husk within *saṃsāra*.
"This is the absolute certainty of the worldling (puthujjana), namely, his fixed wrong view"—

thus he says, "there is an absolute certainty for the worldling. One should investigate and understand that the arising of doubt and the arising of another [wrong] certainty are what turn one away from absolute certainty.
The commentary on the discussion of absolute certainty is finished.
8. Commentary on the Discussion of the Faculties (Indriyakathā): 853–856.
"Of the mundane as well" means that, just as with the supramundane states, it is shown that even the mundane states—faith and the rest—possess the very nature of the faculty of faith and so forth.

The meaning should be understood as follows: it was stated for the purpose of showing that faith and the other [faculties] themselves constitute the state of the mundane faculty of faith and so forth, in order to establish their status as mundane faculties of faith and the rest.
The commentary on the discussion of the faculties is finished.
The commentary on the nineteenth chapter is finished.
20. The twentieth chapter: 2.
Commentary on the Discourse on Knowledge.
863–865. In the discussion on knowledge (*ñāṇakathā*), the statement "one fully understands suffering" indicates only supramundane path-knowledge.
Thus, when you say "one fully understands suffering," this statement of yours indicates only supramundane path-knowledge, not the status of that [knowledge] as such. Why?
Because it is not the case that only supramundane knowledge [is involved]; therefore, it has been stated that this is not a proving factor.
The commentary on the Discussion of Knowledge is finished.
3. Commentary on the Discussion of the Hell-Wardens (Nirayapālakathāvaṇṇanā) 867–868. *Paṇunnaṃ* means driven away; the meaning is "completely cast out."
The commentary on the Discourse on the Hell-Wardens is finished.
4. Commentary on the Discourse on Animals (Tiracchānakathāvaṇṇanā) 869–871.
Regarding the phrase “in acknowledgment of its existence,” it should be construed separately as “in acknowledgment of the existence of that elephant-nāga and of the divine vehicle.”
The commentary on the talk about trivial matters is finished.
6. Commentary on the Talk about Knowledge (Ñāṇakathāvaṇṇanā) 876–877.
Regarding the phrase "if that [knowledge] has twelve bases" in the talk about knowledge, the word "supramundane" (*lokuttara*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.

That supramundane knowledge, if it has twelve bases—that is the meaning. "To be fully understood" refers to the preliminary stage (pubbabhāga), while "fully understood" refers to the subsequent stage (aparabhāga).
However, since the knowledge of the truths also performs its function of full understanding and so forth at the moment of the path, he said:
"together with the preliminary and subsequent stages."
The commentary on the Discussion of Knowledge is finished.
The commentary on the twentieth chapter is finished.
The fourth fiftieth section is completed.
21. The Twenty-first Chapter. 1. Explanation of the Discourse on the Teaching (Sāsanakathā). 878.

Regarding the statement "it was spoken for the purpose of exhortation in all three questions": this means that in all three questions, the words beginning with "the teaching" (*sāsana*) were spoken; thus, it should be understood that the parts are stated by way of being the basis for the whole.
The commentary on the Discourse on the Dispensation is finished.
4. Commentary on the Discourse on Psychic Power (Iddhikathā).

883–884. Regarding the discourse on psychic power: "There is psychic power by way of intention" means that there is a type of psychic power named "intention," so called because it succeeds through the influence of intention.
The commentary on the Discourse on Supernormal Power is finished.
7. Commentary on the Discourse on the Dhamma: 887–888.
In this discourse on the Dhamma, if it were said that there is a fixed order of form (*rūpa-niyāma*) because no form exists other than from the standpoint of form itself, [that would be so].
Since there is no such thing as a "form-factor" (rūpaṭṭha) that is distinct from form itself, there is no form apart from the form-factor;
therefore, with the intention that form is simply form and not of the nature of feeling and so forth, it should be said: "Form is determined by way of its form-factor.
It is not intended that it is determined by some other fixed rule regarding the form-factor. In this context, since there is no form-factor distinct from form—
When the non-existence of any form other than the state of form (rūpaṭṭha) is demonstrated, it is indeed as if the non-existence of any state of form other than that very form has been demonstrated.
Thus, in order to demonstrate that very non-existence of any state of form other than form, he said, "The intrinsic nature of form," and so forth.

"This conventional expression" means: taking them as if they were distinct, the conventional expression "the intrinsic nature of form" (*rūpasabhāva*) occurs as the intrinsic nature of form, and the conventional expression "the state of form" (*rūpaṭṭha*) occurs as the state of form.

The meaning is that the conventional expression "the state of being form" (rūpaṭṭha) serves to indicate the distinctness [of form] from feeling and the rest, as its specific nature; thus it is for the purpose of making known their difference.

Therefore, because of the non-identity of form with respect to the state of being form—that is, because form is not of the same nature as feeling and so on—when one says, "Form is only form, not the nature of feeling and so on," rather than saying "Form is determined by the state of being form," that statement is faulty in the manner already described.

Now, as for the question, "Why does he, while stating that 'matter is fixed in its aspect as matter'—meaning it should be said that matter is matter alone and not of the nature of feeling and so forth—affirm that 'matter is fixed in its aspect as matter'?", the meaning should be understood as follows:
Is it not the case that since this was stated by himself and not by another, one should not say "he affirms"? No; for even oneself is [considered] another.
"From the statement 'as it were' (*viya*). Or rather, "to be stated" means that it is to be stated by the proponent himself; this is what is intended.
And if he acknowledges that this matter is indeed to be stated by him, then for what reason does the proponent acknowledge it? This is the meaning here. "By way of another meaning":
having concealed the very reason already stated therein, [the opponent] challenges [the proponent]; thus, it is that same reason [which is being addressed].
Having shown this, he turns back the objection. "In a way other than this" means that apart from the mere intrinsic nature of form and so forth, there is nothing fixed imagined by him;
thus, for the purpose of turning back that imagination, he says "fixed in falsehood," etc., in order to object again according to that same method.
This concludes the commentary on the Discourse on the Dhamma.
The commentary on the twenty-first chapter is finished.
22. The twenty-second chapter: 2.
Commentary on the Discussion of Wholesome Consciousness.
894–895. In the discussion on wholesome consciousness, "at the moment of impulsion" (javana-khaṇe) refers to the moment of impulsion preceding the consciousness of final Nibbāna.
The commentary on the discussion of wholesome consciousness is concluded.
3. Commentary on the Discussion of the Imperturbable (Āneñja).

896. Regarding "the life-continuum consciousness" (*bhavaṅgacitta*): because it occurs at the conclusion of the life-continuum process, the death-consciousness (*cuticitta*) is called "life-continuum consciousness.
The commentary on the Discourse on the Imperturbable (*Āneñjakathā*) is finished.
5–7. Commentary on the Discourse on the Three (*Tissopikathā*).

898–900. Having seen a seven-year-old fetus, one thinks: "There exists within the womb itself the maturation of the faculties that serves as the cause for attaining Arahantship," and thus one imagines:
"The attainment of Arahantship also exists. The intention is that, having seen a dream of the sky, one imagines:
"Just like the supernormal powers such as traveling through the sky, there exists the realization of the Dhamma and the attainment of Arahantship."
The commentary on the story of Tisso-pika is finished.
9. Commentary on the Discussion of the Condition of Repetition (Āsevanapaccaya) 903–905.

“No one indeed ‘repeats’ the condition of repetition” means that just as a seed does not take on the state of the four sweets, so too there is no one who, while taking up the condition of repetition known as cultivation (*bhāvanā*), is said to be “repeating. This is the meaning.
The commentary on the discussion of the condition of repetition (*āsevanapaccaya*) is finished.
10. Commentary on the Discussion of Moments (Khaṇikakathāvaṇṇanā) 906–907.
The establishment of the continuity of matter (*rūpasantati*) is such that among material phenomena such as earth and so forth, some arise while others cease.

It exists. For there are no conditions such as "immediate" (anantara) and so forth for material phenomena by which the continuity of matter might proceed in the same way as the continuity of the immaterial;
thus, regarding consciousness, it was objected: "The great earth is established within consciousness," and so on.
The commentary on the discussion of the momentary (khaṇika-kathā) is finished.
The commentary on the twenty-second chapter is finished.
23. The twenty-third chapter: 1.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Single Intention.
908. "Having a single intention through the intention of compassion" means that it has an intention other than the intention of lust; this is what is meant.

Regarding the phrase "a single intention," the word *eka* (one) should be understood here in the sense of "oneness. For when there is a state of equality, even in the case of an intention of lust, there exists "single-intentionality" (*ekādhippāyatā*) by virtue of being "with a single intention" (*ekādhippāyena*).
The commentary on the discussion of a single intention is finished.
3–7. Commentary on the discussion of acting according to one’s will through power (issariyakāmakārikā).
910–914. Acting according to one’s will through power is the doing of what is intended by means of power. "She might go" refers to entering the womb.

One might go [to such extremes]. Regarding the statement, "The practice of austerities for the sake of exercising power is performed through wrong view," the meaning here should be understood as follows:
when the practice of austerities is performed for the sake of exercising power, it is to be seen as being performed through wrong view;
or alternatively, that there is no such thing as practicing austerities for the sake of exercising power without wrong view.
The commentary on the discussion of exercising power according to one’s will is finished.
8. Commentary on the Discussion of Counterfeits (Patirūpakathāvaṇṇanā) 915–916.

With reference to loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables], they say: “Just as there is no lust that is a counterfeit of loving-kindness and so forth, one takes ‘lust’ itself [to be the subject]; likewise for hatred.”
The commentary on the Discourse on the Appropriate is finished.
9. Commentary on the Discourse on the Unproduced. 917–918.
Regarding the phrase “not the state of impermanence, etc.”: here, that which has impermanence and so forth as its state is called “the state of impermanence, etc.,” namely, form (*rūpa*).

It has been said: by stating, "For it is not only the first Truth that is suffering," it is shown that the question was asked with reference to the Truth of Suffering (*dukkhasacca*) in the sense that "suffering alone is fully established" (*parinipphanna*).

This being so, he would not have been able to say, "The eye-base (*cakkhāyatana*) is not fully established," and so forth; for the eye-base and the other [bases] are not unclung-to (*anupādinnāni*) supramundane (*lokuttara*).
Or: "That" refers to the statement, "Suffering alone is fully established, but matter is not";
the meaning is that, because matter is suffering, it certainly ought not to be so called.
The commentary on the discussion of non-establishment is finished.
The commentary on the twenty-third chapter is finished.
The *Mūlaṭīkā* (Root Commentary) on the *Kathāvatthu-pakaraṇa* is completed.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
Commentary on the Opening of the Yamakapakaraṇa-mūlaṭīkā:
Having prevented the grasping of phenomena in a distorted manner through the brief teaching provided in the Kathāvatthu-pakaraṇa, [the author proceeds] with respect to those very same phenomena...

When the *Dhammasaṅgaṇi* and other treatises have been expounded among the teachings (*dhamma*), the *Yamaka-pakaraṇa* (The Book of Pairs) was commenced for the purpose of removing various kinds of afflictions by means of resolving doubts regarding the bases consisting of phenomena (*dhamma*), persons (*puggala*), locations (*okāsa*), and so forth.

Having shown that [work] precisely through its occasion (*samaya*) and teacher (*desaka*), and because the sequence of its commentary has now arrived, the commentary upon it is undertaken with the thought: "The burden that has come must necessarily be borne."
Declaring this, he said, "In brief," and so forth.

Therein, "that which is beyond his domain" means that while birth exists, death occurs; thus, birth—or the five aggregates of clinging—is his domain, and he has transcended it by abandoning its origin (samudaya). Alternatively, death is the domain of King Yama.

He has passed beyond the region where his commands prevail. He is one who knows the six regions—the "six regions" being those of the six things incapable of being done, as stated in the phrase "incapable of doing the six impossible things.
Thus, he is a "knower of the six regions" (*chaṭṭhānadesaka*). His body hairs are each individual, turned upward, blue-black, and stainless;
thus he is "one whose body hairs are individually turned upward, blue-black, and stainless" (*ayamāvattanīlāmalatanuruho*).
The commentary on the commencement of the work is finished.
1. The Root Pairs (Mūlayamaka):
Commentary on the Section of Enumeration (Uddesavāra).

1. By the phrase "because it is taught by way of pairs" (yamaka), he shows that this entire treatise—consisting of ten sections, each containing a collection of pairs, as well as the collection itself—is designated as such on account of its pairs.

If it is argued that the designation "meaning-pair" (atthayamaka) is applied because of two meanings consisting of the wholesome and unwholesome roots, and that this would result in the status of a "pair" being applied only to the specific proposition, "Whatever states are wholesome, all those are wholesome roots," [the answer is: it does not so result.

This is because the state of being a "meaning-yamaka" (atthayamaka) has been stated by way of the distinctions between the wholesome and the wholesome roots as expressed in the second and first questions—
desiring to know those [distinctions]— or alternatively, by way of the wholesome and wholesome roots included in the words of determination in the first and second questions,

which are desired to be known through the distinctions of the wholesome roots and the wholesome. For distinctions that are desired to be known necessarily depend upon that which possesses those distinctions.

Or rather, because the state of predominance belongs here to that specific quality (*visesavatam*) and to those phenomena (*dhammānam*) which depend upon that specific quality, only one meaning is included for each individual question.
Furthermore, the word "meaning" (*attha*) here does not denote the phenomena themselves, nor does it denote causes, fruits, and so forth;
rather, it denotes the meaning of the textual passage (*pāḷiattha*). For this very reason, he says: "of those very meanings," and so on.

The statement "taking all three terms together" is said merely with reference to the fact that the term *nāma* (name) includes [the categories] beginning with the wholesome (*kusala*), and not with reference to its inclusion of them exhaustively.
Furthermore, because the term *nāma* was stated for the purpose of including all wholesome factors and so forth, it is said:
"in four places within the matrix of the wholesome triad (*kusalattika-mātikā*)."
The commentary on the Section of Enumeration (Uddesavāra-vaṇṇanā) is finished.

Commentary on the Section of Exposition (Niddesavāra-vaṇṇanā): 52. Regarding the phrase "without asking which among those that are wholesome," in this *Aññamaññayamaka* (Mutual Pairs), just as in the second *Yamaka*: "whichever... [and so forth].

The intention is that, instead of asking "the roots of the wholesome," one should ask "whatever is wholesome," because by taking up something new that is distinct from the previous set of dyads (yamaka), the subsequent dyad does not occur [redundantly].
Some say it is "because of being in accordance with the nature of the reverse inquiry. However, [this is said] by way of the meaning of the previous inquiry.
The final question ought to correspond to that [preceding one], because doubt arises regarding the reverse order once the forward order has been understood without uncertainty;
therefore, it is not the case that the prior question must correspond to the final question—this is the appropriate intended meaning here.
Furthermore, since this very meaning is possible through these words as well, it is not possible [to claim otherwise].
...to speak. For the meaning of the wholesome expression (*kusala-vyañjana*) is not the same as the meaning of the single-rooted expression associated with the wholesome root (*kusalamūla*).
