Therefore, the answer also becomes inconsistent. For when the question is posed using the wholesome expression, at this point [where it says] "the remainder," one must say "the remaining wholesome phenomena" (*avasesā kusalā dhammā*);
otherwise, one would have to say "the remaining phenomena co-arising with the wholesome roots. It is not [the latter].
And those statements have the same meaning because they both illuminate the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the indeterminate. However, this may be the intended sense here:

since the meaning expressed by the phrasing "whatever are wholesome" is already possible through the phrasing "whatever share the same root as a wholesome root," the question "whatever share the same root as a wholesome root" was asked without first asking [the former], just as in the second dyad (yamaka).

For there are no other wholesome states that share a single root with the wholesome roots in the same way that they do with the wholesome roots themselves; rather, there are others besides those wholesome states.
In the commentary on the reverse inquiry, it is stated that if the question "Are they rooted in the same root as the wholesome roots?
were asked, the answer should be given according to the method explained below: "The roots are those which arise together."
That too cannot be said in that way. For when it is asked, "Are all those states which have mutual roots by way of a wholesome root also rooted in the same root as the wholesome root?

the answer must simply be "Yes. This is because among those states that have mutual roots by way of a wholesome root, there is nothing that does not share the same root; for if there were, it would be like the case of the direct (anuloma) inquiry.
A distinction should be made. Where the three wholesome roots arise, they have mutual roots and a single root, because each pair has mutual roots and a single root with respect to the other.
However, where only two arise, they have only mutual roots and not a single root;
it is for the purpose of excluding such a [mis]conception that [the text says] "roots."
If it is argued that the answer should be given by the passage beginning, "Those which arise together," etc., we say no;

for that [objection] is already precluded by the very answer, "Yes (āmantā)," and because the reciprocal relationship of being a single root between two or three roots arising together is determined by the answer to the positive inquiry (*anulomapucchā*).
For in the case of those things that are mutual roots, there is indeed a commonality of root.
It is questioned by means of the expression "having a single root," not because of a mutual identity of roots; yet there is indeed a commonality of roots between two [roots].
For among those, each one has that same root as the other root and as the other roots derived from it.
However, since their mutual rootedness is determined, there is no doubt regarding their having a single root; thus: "All those states [arise] from a wholesome root..."

It should be understood that the question "having a single root" (*ekamūlā*) was not asked [separately]. Regarding the two expressions: "they have each other as their roots" (*aññamaññassa mūlā etesaṃ*), thus they are "mutually rooted" (*aññamaññamūlā*);
and "they have one and the same root" (*samānatthena ekaṃ mūlaṃ etesaṃ*), thus they are "single-rooted" (*ekamūlā*). Both statements speak precisely of the connection with roots;

for that very reason, in both cases it is said, "by means of the wholesome root" (*kusalamūlena*). In that context, regarding the state of being single-rooted within the commonality of the application of roots:
When that specific [quality] is determined, the state of being mutual roots is not yet determined; thus, the question regarding the *anuloma* (conformity) proceeds.

However, when the state of being mutual roots is determined within the specific application of roots (*mūlayoga*), since there is no state of being mutual roots without a single root, the commonality of the application of roots—the state of having a single root—is indeed determined.
Therefore, instead of asking "Are they of a single root? as was done with the statement regarding wholesome roots (*kusalamūla*), [the text proceeds as follows].
Since a statement of a single root does not indicate the state of being wholesome (*kusala*), there is doubt regarding the state of being wholesome;

therefore, in the first and second pairs of questions, the reverse question, "Are all those states wholesome? is posed. Likewise, since a statement of mutual roots does not indicate the state of being wholesome, there is doubt regarding the state of being wholesome;
and because the context of what is wholesome continues to apply, [the question] "All... [is asked].
The question "Are those states wholesome? is thus formulated as a reverse inquiry.
53–61. Having stated the meaning according to the Root Method (Mūlanaya), the Root-of-Roots Method (Mūlamūlanaya) is presented by means of this alternative approach:

to clarify the meaning through the qualification of the root by way of its being a wholesome root, through the commonality of the root, and through the demonstration of the connection between roots by means of one root with another root.

It is stated [thus]. By means of the letter *ka* at the end of a compound whose referent is another word (*aññapadattha*), the "root method" (*mūlakanaya*) is stated in all three dyads precisely to illustrate the root-conjunction (*mūlayoga*).
The manner of expression for the "root-of-roots method" (*mūlamūlakanaya*) is exactly as previously described. 74–85.

"Having made it non-designative" (*abbōhārikaṃ katvā*) means: because it is obtained together with those that do not possess the state of having a single root, it is devoid of the designation "with-root" (*sahetuka*).
It is not that "indeterminate" (abbohārika) is used here in the sense of the presence or absence of the root-condition (*hetupaccaya*), as it is in the "Duo of With-Root" (*sahetuka-duka*);
rather, it is called "indeterminate" because it receives only the designation "with-root" (*sahetuka*) and not the designation "without-root" (*ahetuka*).

"By way of what is obtained together" means: by way of the material phenomena (*rūpa*) that are obtained together with those cittas that arise without roots and with Nibbāna, which are devoid of the root-condition.
86–97. In that textual passage where the reading appears as, “That which is rootless does not share the same root with the root of name;

that which has roots shares the same root with the root of name,” it should be understood that because names have been specifically determined by the phrase “whatever mental states (nāma-dhammā),” the word “name” is already implied when “rootless” or “having roots” is stated, and thus it was not explicitly mentioned. However, where...
There is also the reading: “Name is without cause; name is with cause. In that context, it is called “name” for the purpose of making its meaning clearly manifest.
The commentary on the section of the Exposition is finished.
The commentary on the Root Pairs is finished.
2. The Khanda-Yamaka (Pairs on Aggregates) 1.
The Section on Designations (Paṇṇattivāra) Commentary on the Section of Enunciation (Uddesavāravaṇṇanā)

2–3. In the *Khandhayamaka*, regarding the six divisions of time, the arising and cessation of the aggregates (*khandha*), as well as their full comprehension (*pariññā*), should be explained by way of persons, space, and both persons and space. Those aggregates are designated by five terms, beginning with "the aggregate of form" (*rūpakkhandha*);
they have ten constituent terms. Among these, is that very phenomenon (*dhamma*) expressed by the constituent terms such as "form" and so forth also [expressed] by the collective term?

The meaning is as follows: regarding this point of doubt—namely, whether that which is expressed by a collective term (*samudāyapada*) is the same as that expressed by its constituent member terms (*avayavapada*)—it is shown that the meaning of the collective terms is either a single part expressed by the constituent member terms such as "form" (*rūpa*), etc., or the whole;

whereas that which is expressed by the collective terms is exclusively the meaning of the constituent member terms such as "form," etc. To demonstrate this point, [the text says]: "Form is the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandho*)."
The section on the purification of terms beginning with “the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandho) is ‘form’ (rūpan)’” has been stated.

Furthermore, because compound terms such as “the aggregate of form” have the meaning of the final member as their primary significance, and because there is the possibility of both the word *khandha*—which constitutes that primary meaning—and the meaning of the subordinate term (*upapada*) such as *vedanā*, [it is explained] regarding this term “the aggregate of form”: ... [text continues] ...just as in this case of “the aggregate of form,” [the analysis proceeds].

In this context, the status of being the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*) belongs to that which is expressed by the word "form" (*rūpa*) as a member of the aggregate, because the words "form" and "aggregate" stand in a relationship of grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*);

likewise, the status of being the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*) and so forth belongs to that which is expressed by the word "aggregate" as a member of the aggregate, because the words "feeling" and so forth stand in a relationship of coreferentiality with the word "aggregate. Thus it is there.

In order to show this point— that at a place of doubt, a phenomenon (dhamma) stated by a term for a component of an aggregate (khandha-avayava-pada) may be expressed by some aggregate-term (samudāya-pada), but not every [component] is expressed by every [aggregate-term]—

the Wheel of Terms (pada-sodhana-mūla-cakkavāra) beginning with “Rūpaṃ rūpakkhandho, khandhā vedanākkhandho” was stated. And by showing it in this way, [it is shown] that the word *rūpa* and so forth function as qualifiers (*visesana*), while the word *khandha*...
The state of being qualified and the state of having a common substratum between the qualifier and the qualified are thus demonstrated.
Consequently, a doubt arises here: is there matter other than the aggregates from which this matter is excluded so as to serve as a qualifier for the aggregates?
And are all the aggregates themselves to be qualified by that matter which serves as their qualifier?

But what is that "matter" which constitutes a specific instance of the aggregate? It is matter consisting of the primary elements and derived matter, because it is precisely that which is being grasped.
In the *Niddesa*, having cited the phrase "the aggregates: the aggregate of matter," an answer is given. Thus, in this point of doubt, there is no matter other than the aggregate;
for by that very word "matter," when it is spoken of with the pure word "aggregate," [it is understood as such].
It is said that not all aggregates (khandhas) need to be qualified by matter (rūpa), which serves as a specific qualification for some of them; therefore, they must be analyzed accordingly.

This same method applies to the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha) and the others as well. To demonstrate this point, the section on the "pure aggregates" is stated, beginning with: "Matter is an aggregate; aggregates are matter," and so forth.

Then, when it is admitted that "form is an aggregate" (*rūpaṃ khandho*), there arises a doubt regarding the application of the term "aggregate" to form as a specific instance, following the determination that form possesses the nature of an aggregate—namely, the doubt: "Is this word 'aggregate' restricted only to form, or does it also apply to specific instances such as feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth?
In this regard, not all aggregates are connected with specific instances such as feeling; rather, some are connected with certain [specific instances].
The Wheel-Section on the Pure Aggregates (Suddhakhandhamūlacakkavāra) was stated in order to show that they "yoke by means of a qualification.

Thus, it should be understood that the Section on Designations (Paṇṇattivāra) was stated for the purpose of determining those aggregates for which the arising and so forth must be explained, by way of purifying their designations.
Regarding the phrase "having bound four wheels each," here the term "wheels" refers to the pairs [of questions], because they constitute the constituent parts of a wheel.
"Having bound four pairs [of terms] to each root of the aggregates. For it must be understood that this is the meaning here.
Or rather, the meaning should be seen as: "having bound four pairs [of terms] in such a way that they have each aggregate as their root.
In that context, taking the basic term "form is the aggregate of form," and so forth, as the hub, [the word] "aggregates" [is established].

This should be understood as stating that the nature of a wheel (*cakkabhāva*) is expressed by taking "this is the rim" (*idaṃ nemiṃ*) and "the aggregate of feeling" (*vedanākkhandho*) and so forth as the spokes (*are*), rather than by way of their connection as a circle (*maṇḍalabhāvena*).
For even in the sections beginning with "rooted in the aggregate of feeling," the reading proceeds only after purifying the preceding [terms], not by way of a circular connection.
And for that very reason, having taken merely the attainment of the pure aggregates (*suddhakhandhalābhamattam*), [it is used] as a qualification of the aggregates.
The meaning is that, instead of remaining at the mere level of "form" and so forth within the category of form and the rest,

the term is extracted in the manner of "the aggregate of form" (rūpakkhandho) and so on by joining it with the word "aggregate" (khandha) in order to show the meaning of form and the rest as characterized by their specific status as aggregates;
thus, the meaning is analyzed.
The commentary on the section of the summary is finished.
Commentary on the section of the exposition: 26.
Regarding "the lovely form, the pleasant form": "In the world, the eye is a lovely form... [and so on] ...forms in the world... [and so on] ...eye-consciousness... [and so on]."
"Eye-contact... [and so on] ...feeling born of eye-contact... [and so on] ...perception of forms... [and so on] ...volition regarding forms... [and so on] ...craving for forms...

[and so on] ...thought directed toward forms... [and so on] ...examination of forms"—thus it should be understood that what is spoken of here is the threefold existence (tebhūmaka) which serves as the basis for craving;
therefore, that which consists of the aggregate of the five aggregates and is pleasant and agreeable in nature is [the object of clinging] in one respect.

He said, "It is the aggregate of form," [meaning] "that which is pleasant in form, agreeable in form, is form, but not the aggregate of form. Or rather, because it shares the nature of being dear, the aggregate of form enters into what is pleasant in form, and not by way of its essential nature of being subject to change (ruppana); thus it was said, "That which is pleasant in form, agreeable in form, is form, but not the aggregate of form.
In the *Saññāyamaka*, first, regarding "perception of views" (*diṭṭhisaññā*), the words "distinction" (*visesa*) are to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.
In this context, "perception" (saññā) is itself the "perception of views" (diṭṭhisaññā).

For in such passages as, “A person who has undertaken vows goes from high to low, being bound by perception,” and “For one who is detached from perception, there are no fetters,” it is indeed "view" that is called "perception. 28. [Question:
“Is it not the case that they are aggregates, yet not the aggregate of feeling? [Answer: “Yes. Thus, in the absence of the application of the term "aggregate" (khandha),...
It should be understood that by stating there is an absence of the designation "feeling-aggregate," one is merely performing a purification of the concept;

it is not the presence of some other dhamma that serves as the authority here. And having established this, he will later say: "Is it not the case that they are not bases, yet not the ear-base? Yes. 39.
Regarding the statement "feeling and the others are other than form," feeling and the others here should be understood as supramundane. For those are of a pleasant nature.
And because they are not objects for craving, they do not possess the nature of pleasure; thus, they are other than form.

As for the statement, "the remainder, excluding both form and the aggregates," this too should be understood as being said merely with reference to the non-occurrence of the word *na* (not) together with these [terms].
And having done so, [it is said]: "Excluding both the eye and the bases, the remainder are neither..."
He will say, "The eye is not a base," and so forth. For in that context, there is nothing whatsoever to be included by way of the phrase "the remainder.

If there were such a thing, it would have to be the base of mental objects (*dhammāyatana*). For he will say: "Is the base of mental objects [included]? Yes. Furthermore, it could not be a basis for craving.
If it were such a basis, then because it would possess the nature of being pleasant and agreeable, it would be form (*rūpa*), as in: "Form..."
Because of the statement, "It is an aggregate (khandha)? Yes," it is also called an aggregate.

However, in the Commentary, although [the term] is not present there, one should understand that the inclusion of "designation" (paññatti) in the phrase "the remainder" was made with reference to the actual existence of the apprehension of "woman," "man," and so forth, based on what is actually present.
The commentary on the section of the Exposition (Niddesavāra) is finished.

2. Commentary on the Section on Occurrence (Pavattivāra) [50–205]. In the Section on Occurrence, the triplets, dyads, and single pairs based on the aggregate of feeling and so forth are stated only in conjunction with the subsequent [conjunction], not with the preceding one. Why?
Because there is no difference in meaning among the sections concerning unmixed [factors] and the divisions of time.

For if the coupling of the latter with the former were stated in reverse order by coupling the latter with the former—just as the coupling of the former with the latter has already been done—there would be no difference in the meaning.

There is likewise no difference in the questions and answers; therefore, that particular arrangement was not made. However, only six variations are mentioned here due to the difference in time: the present [is coupled] with the past, ...
Regarding the statements "the present by means of the future" and "the past by means of the future," these three are merely variations of mixed time-periods as already shown;

they do not exist separately and thus are not included [as distinct categories]. For in various places, through reverse-order questions, the distinctions of time such as the present by means of the past have been shown;
and by that same method, it is said: "For whom the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) had arisen..."

It is possible to apply [the formula] beginning with, “His aggregate of feeling arises,” and so forth. For this very reason, in the cases of mixed temporal divisions, the *Yamaka* (Pairs) were stated by joining each subsequent aggregate with each preceding one;

whereas in the cases of unmixed temporal divisions, they were stated by joining them with the last one only, both for the sake of ease of comprehension and according to the method of selection employed.
By the phrase "by this very characteristic," etc., he shows the reason why they are called "prior questions" and "subsequent questions.

For that question for which there is an answer by way of showing its essential nature (*sarūpa*) is called a "complete question" (*paripuṇṇa-pañha*), because it encompasses the matter to be answered in its entirety.
However, regarding the answer to that [complete question], by means of its prior section...

It is called the "prior question" (*purepañha*) because its meaning is similar [to the subsequent], and it is called the "subsequent question" (*pacchāpañha*) because its meaning is similar to the latter portion.

This similarity of meaning should be understood in the prior question by way of the mere commonality of the arising, ceasing, and acquisition of the aggregates (*khandha*) as comprised by a single term, without investigating the distinctions between the terms of certainty and doubt. [This applies] to that which is comprised by the term of certainty...
Or rather, it is appropriate that the previous question was stated by way of the allowance for a [certain] aggregate (*khandha*).

Rejection (*paṭikkhepa*) is the denial of that which has the sense of certainty; prohibition (*paṭisedha*) is the warding off of that which has the sense of doubt—this is the distinction between rejection and prohibition.
"Remaining as the very words of the Canon" refers to that which is in the question-text of the Canon: "it does not arise."
The word has been stated; the meaning is that it becomes that very same word, though devoid of the syllable *na*.

In this regard, it should be understood that while the answer follows the course of the text for the purpose of negating the negation of arising and cessation, the answer is actually made by means of a negation for the purpose of negating arising and cessation themselves.
It should be understood that the inclusion of the four questions and the five answers within twenty-seven instances is stated by way of partial inclusion.
For it is only a complete question, together with its answer as shown in its own form,
that is to be included in the twenty-seven instances.
"What indeed can be done beyond this?"—by showing the demarcation of the text from this point onward, he demonstrates the absence of anything else that could possibly be accomplished.

By the statement, "For those Pure Abodes (suddhāvāsa), neither the aggregate of form nor the aggregate of feeling had arisen there," it is made known that within the planes of the Pure Abodes, there is no second rebirth even on a single plane. From the moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi)...
For from birth until death, this teaching proceeds by taking the continuity of the karma-born stream as a single unity and showing its arising and cessation.
For when that [stream] is uninterrupted, there is the occurrence of wholesome states and so forth; when it is interrupted, there is no occurrence.
Thus, arising and cessation are demonstrated by that very [continuity]. Therefore, from the moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) of that single being—
As long as there is no cessation of death, so long there is no pastness; nor has the kamma-born continuity ever arisen therein by way of rebirth-linking prior to that [moment].
Thus, both aggregates are stated as "had not arisen.
But why is it not understood from this passage that there is no second rebirth-linking anywhere in the Pure Abodes? Because of the existence of the *uddhaṃsota* (one who goes upstream) passage.
For indeed, two textual traditions (pāḷi) must be reconciled.

Regarding the statement, "For those non-percipient beings, the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) will arise there," one should take only those non-percipient beings who are distinguished by the definitive determination (sanniṭṭhāna) of the other passage: "For whomsoever, wherever, the aggregate of form will arise. Thus, having taken them [the non-percipient beings] alone...
It is said, “of non-percipient beings. By this, it refers to those who are excluded by way of their definite destiny;
having gone from there to the five-aggregate realm, they will attain final nibbāna, and for them there is no possibility of rebirth again in the non-percipient state. With reference to them, he said:
“For those in their final existence, neither the aggregate of form nor the aggregate of feeling will arise there.”
“...will not arise. Here, is there some final existence (*pacchimabhava*)—like the five-aggregate existence (*pañcavokārabhava*) and so forth—in which their non-arising will occur?

No; rather, it is with reference to those destined for a final existence who abide in any of the five-aggregate existences or elsewhere, that there is this definitive conclusion: “For whom the aggregate of form will not arise in such-and-such a place.”
Because they are included therein. And in order to acknowledge that for them there is no arising of the other [aggregates] in that state, he said, "the aggregate of feeling will not arise.

This phrase, "for those attaining final nibbāna in the Suddhāvāsa [heavens]," should be understood as being stated with reference to the parinibbāna of the aggregates in their respective planes for both those who possess rebirth-linking and those who do not, among the inhabitants of the Suddhāvāsa. For all of them, in that state...

"The aggregate of feeling did not arise. However, whereas the expression "will cease" applies even to the present moment when one is possessed of the moment of arising, the expression "did arise" does not apply to the present;
rather, it applies only to the past that has already arisen and passed away. Therefore, it was said: "For those who have attained final Nibbāna, [feeling] did not arise."

Because that which has arisen has not yet passed away from its continuity. Since world-systems are infinite, because space is unlimited, there is no delimitation even for the arising and cessation of phenomena described in terms of space; thus, there is a state of intermingling.
Therefore it is said: "Where the aggregate of feeling arises, does the aggregate of perception cease there? Yes."
The commentary on the Section on Occurrence (Pavattivāra) is finished.
3. Commentary on the Section on Full Understanding (Pariññāvāra). 206–208.

Why was it said, "even though the Section on Persons and Bases (Puggalokāsavāra) is not obtained"? Is it not the case that if the Section on Bases (Okāsavāra) is not obtained, that [Section on Persons] is also not obtained?
Is it to be understood that [the base] must exist by way of non-acquisition? No; because in that context, there is a statement regarding the full understanding (*pariññā*) of the person alone.
For even in the section on the bases of the person (*puggalokāsa*), it is the full understanding of the person within the base that is spoken of, not the full understanding of the base itself.

And if the section on the bases were also to be mentioned, it would have been stated as "wherein one fully understands the aggregate of form," thus expressing the full understanding of the person with respect to the base.
Therefore, it is stated that [the full comprehension] is obtainable only in the section on persons (*puggala*), and not in the section on bases (*okāsa*). Hence he said: “Yes...

it may be. Precisely for that reason—that is, because of obtaining the three time-periods (*addhāna*) by way of the moments of consciousness during the course of existence (*pavatta*)—and otherwise because there is no full comprehension of the aggregate of form at the moments of death and rebirth-linking, [it is said]:
“He who fully comprehends the aggregate of form [fully comprehends the aggregate of feeling].”
Regarding the statement, "He fully understands," there ought to have been a response of "No" (natthi), yet "Yes" (āmantā) was given.

By saying, "In the moment of the supramundane path," and so forth, he shows that the acquisition of full understandings—which are comprised of both definitive and doubtful states—occurs precisely during the moments of consciousness in the course of existence (pavatta).
This is said with reference to the ordinary person (puthujjana) in response to the question, "Does he not fully understand?"
The statement "it is said [that he] addresses" is spoken because an ordinary person (puthujjana) lacks the duty of full comprehension (pariññā) in every respect.
"An Arahant does not comprehend the aggregate of form, yet he has not failed to comprehend the aggregate of feeling;
with the exception of one possessing the highest path and an Arahant, all remaining persons do not comprehend the aggregate of form, nor do they comprehend the aggregate of feeling."
By the statement "he has not fully understood," it is shown that there is no one else who can fully understand except for one who possesses the highest path (*aggamaggasamaṅgī*);
therefore, it should be understood that the reply "Yes" was spoken with reference to the remaining persons.
The commentary on the section on full understanding (*pariññāvāra*) is concluded.
The commentary on the *Khandha-yamaka* is finished.

Commentary on the Section on Enumerations (Uddesavāra-vaṇṇanā) 1–9.

Regarding the *Āyatanayamaka* and others, the reason for stating the "Section on Designations" (*Paṇṇattivāra*) before the "Section on Purifying the Words" (*Padasodhanavāra*) and so forth should be understood by the same method explained in the *Khandhayamaka*.
In some places, it is stated: "By making eleven times eleven, there are one hundred and thirty-three pairs (*yamaka*)," and so on.
The enumeration written in the manuscripts is not [correctly] so; it is written elsewhere as "one hundred and thirty-two," and so forth.
The commentary on the section of the summary (uddesavāra) is finished.
The commentary on the section of the exposition (niddesavāra).
10–17. "In the sense of blowing" means in the sense of expansion, or in the sense of being manifest.

When everything spoken of as "the body is a phenomenon" (dhamma) is indeed a base (āyatana) possessing its own intrinsic nature, it is stated here with regard to "the body is a base" and "phenomena are a base" that "it is so" (āmantā).
However, there is nothing whatsoever possessing its own intrinsic nature that is not spoken of by the term "body" or by the term "phenomena."
Regarding the statement, “It is not the body, nor the sense-base; it is not the mental object, nor the sense-base,” the answer given is simply, “Yes.

The Section on Occurrence (Pavattivāra).
1. Commentary on the Chapter on Arising (Uppādavāra) 18–21.

In the section on the process of existence (pavattivāra), regarding the statement on the arising and cessation of the clung-to process (upādinnapavatta) based on the eye-base (*cakkhāyatana*)—which consists of eleven [factors]—even those answers not obtainable therein form a "pair" (*yamaka*) together with the sound-base (*saddāyatana*).
It should be understood that he speaks after having won them over merely by means of their questions. Regarding the phrase "sixty-six pairs":

here, from among those rooted in the sense bases of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and visible form, one pair each must be excluded, as well as the five pairs rooted in the sense base of sound; thus, eleven pairs are to be omitted by way of answer.
For he will say: "Because the sense base of sound does not arise at the moment of rebirth-linking, there is no answering of a pair together with it."

In the second [section], although the response is similar to the first and so forth, it should be understood that this was stated specifically with reference to the section on persons (*puggalavāra*).
However, because the response in the section on bases (*okāsavāra*) is dissimilar, it was stated [there] to make it known that "it is not the case that the response is similar everywhere";
thus, it was also answered in the section on persons. Together with the sense bases of odors, tastes, and tangibles, there are three pairs of identical questions (*yamaka*).

"Similar answers" (*sadisavissajjanā*) is stated because the answer must be given with reference to beings of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara-satta*) by way of such formulations as "those who possess the eye but lack the nose," and so forth.

For in their case, since the seed of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi-bīja*), produced by karma that is dispassionate toward sense-desires, possesses such an intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), the nose and other faculties, as well as odors and other objects, do not exist.
[This is said] because they provide similar answers in the *Ghānāyatana-yamaka* (The Pairs on the Nose Base) among those [treatises] rooted in the eye base (*cakkhāyatana*).
The meaning is that there is a similarity of response together with the *Yamakapaṇḥā* on the sense-base of the nose (*ghānāyatana*).
But was it not the case that in that [text] the response proceeded by way of "for those being reborn who possess the eye-base but lack the nose-base," and so forth;
whereas here, regarding those based on the nose-base, the response is given as: "For whom the nose-base arises, does the tongue-base arise? Yes."?
Is it not the case that there must be similar answers? True;

however, just as the dyads on the sense-base of the nose (*ghānāyatana*) have similar answers while the dyads on the sense-bases of the tongue and body (*jivhākāyāyatana*) do not, so too here the dyads on the sense-bases of the tongue and body have similar answers.
Therefore, the reason why similar answers are not recorded in the Canon for those specific cases is by way of illustration.

However, showing that the reason for providing the identical answers for those [questions] based on the eye-base (*cakkhāyatana*)—which were already taken up—is precisely by way of illustration, he said:

"Because of the identical answering in the *Ghānāyatanayamaka*. And here, the state of having identical answers should be understood as prevailing in the majority of cases among those [questions] based on the nose-base (*ghānāyatana*), specifically in the *Jivhākāyāyatanayamaka*. For in those [cases],...
For the three questions, there must be an answer of "Yes" (āmantā), while for the final question, it is "for those being reborn who possess bodies but lack noses," and so forth.

Alternatively, just as in the case of the dyads (yamaka) beginning with the aggregate of perception (saññā-khandha) based on the aggregate of feeling (vedanā-khandha) and others, regarding the unmixed [factors] and the distinctions of time—
In the three [sections], by the response "Yes" (āmantā), the admission that the aforementioned statement constitutes a response must be made;
however, because there is nothing new to be said, no further answer was given.
Likewise here, the Jivhāyatana Yamaka based on the Ghānāyatana is not included in the Pāḷi because there is nothing new to be said—this matter is self-evident.

The *Kāyāyatanayamaka*, however, should be answered by way of the second inquiry; and that [second inquiry] has an answer similar to the *Ghānāyatanayamaka* among those based on the eye-base (*cakkhāyatana*).
Therefore, since the answer to whichever inquiry is to be given is similar to the answer in the *Ghānāyatanayamaka*, its specific details have not been included in the text; such is the meaning here.
It should be understood. The term "likewise" (tathā) is stated here by way of the commonality of not being included in the canonical text (*pāḷi*), and not by way of a commonality of reason.

However, because the sense bases of the nose, tongue, and body—which function in those born from non-womb birth (*agabbhaseyyaka*) as well as in those born from womb birth (*gabbhaseyyaka*)—are indistinguishable and lack any distinction in their concomitance at the time of the completion of the sense bases, when one answer is given in the *Ghānāyatana-yamaka*, the other two [the tongue and body] follow accordingly.
It should be understood that when the questions based on the nose-base (*ghānāyatana*) have been answered, those based on the other two bases are not to be answered.

Regarding the phrase "together with the visible-form base and the mind base": the intended meaning is "together with the visible-form base and the mind base" as stated in response to the question, "For whom the visible-form base arises, for that person does the mind base arise?"

For, among the pairs beginning with the mind-base (manāyatana) which have the visible-form base (rūpāyatana) as their root, the fact that the answers to the initial questions in the pairs beginning with odor, flavor, and the tangible are similar is stated as the reason for not providing separate answers for those pairs.

Since there ought to be answers by way of a counter-question for the second questions, an answer should not be given according to the method previously stated; and likewise, no answer should be given for the initial questions.

Regarding the phrase "because the answers are similar to those below": here, for the pairs concerning taste and tangibility rooted in the odor base, and for the pair concerning tangibility rooted in the taste base, there must be answers given by way of the very same replies as were provided previously;
thus, the answers should not be formulated in the manner stated before. As for those [pairs] that must be formulated, they are those rooted in odor, taste, and tangibility.

The meaning is that the pairs concerning the mind-base (*manāyatana*) and the mental-object-base (*dhammāyatana*) have answers identical to those of the pairs concerning the mind-base and the mental-object-base rooted in the five bases beginning with the eye. All the pairs concerning the sound-base rooted in the eye-base and so forth,
as well as all those rooted in the sound-base itself, are said to be "answered" by means of non-answer— that is, by demonstrating that no answer can be obtained.
He said, "Sixty pairs of questions have been answered.
Regarding the phrase "one blind from birth and one deaf from birth," it should be understood that by the mention of "deaf from birth," one who is both blind and deaf from birth is included.
The expression "those with noses and those with eyes" is stated with reference specifically to a being of spontaneous birth (*opapātika*) whose sense bases are complete.
Here, the word *eva* should be construed after the phrase "spoken regarding this.
Just as the statement "of those with noses but no eyes" was spoken with reference to one whose sense bases are incomplete, it is not so with the statement "of those with noses and eyes.
Rather, the meaning should be understood as follows: this [latter] was indeed spoken with reference to one whose sense bases are complete. By that, even one who is deaf from birth...
The fact that it was spoken with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*) is not precluded.

22–254. Since he asks about the "eye-base" (*cakkhāyatana*) specifically as the world of form-brahmās (*rūpībrahmaloka*), he speaks while observing merely the simultaneous arising of the eye and ear in that [realm] as a rule;
however, in the section on the "bases" (*okāsa*), because the person (*puggala*) is not referred to therein, where—
"In the sense-sphere realm (kāmadhātu) and the fine-material realm (rūpadhātu), the eye-base (cakkhāyatana) arises;
does the ear-base (sotāyatana) also necessarily arise there? "Yes," it is said.
Or again: "For whom the visible-object-base (rūpāyatana) will arise, for him the eye-base will arise? "Yes."

Why was this admitted? Is it not the case that for one who, having entered the state of lying in the womb, will attain final nibbāna, the visible base (*rūpāyatana*) will arise at rebirth-linking, but the eye base (*cakkhāyatana*) will not?
For that person in that state in whom the visible base will arise, after the arising of the visible base, there is the non-arising of the continuity of the eye base.

Because even during the course of existence (*pavatti*), one must admit that which is yet to arise. Now, why was it admitted [in the text] that "for whom the visible-object base (*rūpāyatana*) will not arise, for him the eye-base (*cakkhāyatana*) will not arise"?
Is it not the case that for a being in the final existence (*pacchimabhavika*) lying in the womb, while still before the eleventh week from conception, the visible-object base will not arise?
And [is it the case that] the eye-base will not arise? No, because the arising that is to occur in that existence is not spoken of as such by virtue of its being in the future.

For in another existence, whatever initial arising of the continuum of each respective base is yet to come—whether in the process of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) or in the course of existence (*pavatta*)—that future arising is spoken of as such by virtue of its being that [state], because it is included within the "present of duration" (*addhā-paccuppanna*).

However, that which will arise within the course of that very same existence is called "future arising" because it is included within the present time-period (*addhāpaccuppanna*). For here, by way of the time-periods, the division of the present and other times for the process born of karma is intended. And having done so, in the *Indriyayamaka*: "For whom the female faculty arises, will the male faculty arise for him? [The answer is: No. Why? Because it is not possible for both to arise simultaneously in one and the same continuity. But for whom the female faculty has arisen, will the male faculty arise for him? Yes. Why? Because it is possible for both to arise in different continuities. Thus, the future arising is stated in relation to the continuity of a specific individual. It is not stated as a general rule for all beings. Therefore, there is no contradiction with the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*. Furthermore, the future arising is stated in relation to the continuity of a specific individual, not in relation to the arising of a new existence (*bhava*). If it were stated in relation to the arising of a new existence, then for one who has attained the fruit of Non-Returner (*anāgāmiphala*) in this life and will attain Parinibbāna in that same existence, the five aggregates would have to be stated as "future arising," because they will arise in that very existence. Yet, they are not stated as such. Therefore, it is clear that the future arising is stated in relation to the continuity of a specific individual. Thus, the meaning is established. This is the section on the future arising. Now follows the section on the present arising. Herein, the present arising is stated in relation to the continuity of a specific individual, not in relation to the arising of a new existence. If it were stated in relation to the arising of a new existence, then for one who has attained the fruit of Stream-Entry (*sotāpattiphala*) in this life and will attain Parinibbāna in that same existence, the five aggregates would have to be stated as "present arising," because they are present in that very existence. Yet, they are not stated as such. Therefore, it is clear that the present arising is stated in relation to the continuity of a specific individual. Thus, the meaning is established. This is the section on the present arising. Now follows the section on the past arising. Herein, the past arising is stated in relation to the continuity of a specific individual, not in relation to the arising of a new existence. If it were stated in relation to the arising of a new existence, then for one who has attained the fruit of Arhatship (*arahattaphala*) in this life and will attain Parinibbāna in that same existence, the five aggregates would have to be stated as "past arising," because they have passed away in that very existence. Yet, they are not stated as such. Therefore, it is clear that the past arising is stated in relation to the continuity of a specific individual. Thus, the meaning is established. This is the section on the past arising. Now follows the section on the non-arising. If it were stated in relation to the arising of a new existence, then for one who has attained the fruit of Arhatship in this life and will attain Parinibbāna in that same existence, the five aggregates would have to be stated as "non-arising," because they will not arise in that very existence. Yet, they are not stated as such. Therefore, it is clear that the non-arising is stated in relation to the continuity of a specific individual. Thus, the meaning is established. This is the section on the non-arising. Now follows the section on the past and present arising. If it were stated in relation to the arising of a new existence, then for one who has attained the fruit of Arhatship in this life and will attain Parinibbāna in that same existence, the five aggregates would have to be stated as "past and present arising," because they have passed away and are present in that very existence. Yet, they are not stated as such. Therefore, it is clear that the past and present arising is stated in relation to the continuity of a specific individual. Thus, the meaning is established. This is the section on the past and present arising. Now follows the section on the future and present arising. Herein, the future and present arising is stated in relation to the continuity of a specific individual, not in relation to the arising of a new existence. If it were stated in relation to the arising of a new existence, then for one who has attained the fruit of Non-Returner in this life and will attain Parinibbāna in that same existence, the five aggregates would have to be stated as "future and present arising," because they will arise and are present in that very existence. Yet, they are not stated as such. Therefore, it is clear that the future and present arising is stated in relation to the continuity of a specific individual. Thus, the meaning is established. This is the section on the future and present arising. Now follows the section on the past, future, and present arising. Herein, the past, future, and present arising is stated in relation to the continuity of a specific individual, not in relation to the arising of a new existence. If it were stated in relation to the arising of a new existence, then for one who has attained the fruit of Arhatship in this life and will attain Parinibbāna in that same existence, the five aggregates would have to be stated as "past, future, and present arising," because they have passed away, will arise, and are present in that very existence. Yet, they are not stated as such. Therefore, it is clear that the past, future, and present arising is stated in relation to the continuity of a specific individual. Thus, the meaning is established. Herein, the non-arising of the past, future, and present is stated in relation to the continuity of a specific individual, not in relation to the arising of a new existence. If it were stated in relation to the arising of a new existence, then for one who has attained the fruit of Arhatship in this life and will attain Parinibbāna in that same existence, the five aggregates would have to be stated as "non-arising of the past, future, and present," because they have passed away, will not arise, and are not present in that very existence. Yet, they are not stated as such. Therefore, it is clear that the non-arising of the past, future, and present is stated in relation to the continuity of a specific individual. Thus, the meaning is established. This is the section on the non-arising of the past, future, and present. Now follows the section on the past and non-arising. Herein, the past and non-arising is stated in relation to the continuity of a specific individual, not in relation to the arising of a new existence. If it were stated in relation to the arising of a new existence, then for one who has attained the fruit of Arhatship in this life and will attain Parinibbāna in that same existence, the five aggregates would have to be stated as "past and non-arising," because they have passed away and will not arise in that very existence. Yet, they are not stated as such. Therefore, it is clear that the past and non-arising is stated in relation to the continuity of a specific individual. Thus, the meaning is established. This is the section on the past and non-arising. Now follows the section on the future and non-arising. Herein, the future and non-arising is stated in relation to the continuity of a specific individual, not in relation to the arising of a new existence. If it were stated in relation to the arising of a new existence, then for one who has attained the fruit of Arhatship in this life and will attain Parinibbāna in that same existence, the five aggregates would have to be stated as "future and non-arising," because they will not arise in that very existence. If it were stated in relation to the arising of a new existence, then for one who has attained the fruit of Arhatship in this life and will attain Parinibbāna in that same existence, the five aggregates would have to be stated as "present and non-arising," because they are present and will not arise in that very existence. Yet, they are not stated as such. Therefore, it is clear that the present and non-arising is stated in relation to the continuity of a specific individual. Thus, the meaning is established. For those women who are in their final existence (*pacchimabhavika*) at the moment of rebirth, and for those women who, having been reborn in the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) or the immaterial sphere (*arūpāvacara*),
will attain final nibbāna there, and for those women who will attain final nibbāna after manifesting only a few more existences in this very same female state—
for all these women at the moment of rebirth, the female faculty (*itthindriya*) arises; yet [the masculinity faculty] does not arise for them.

It is said: "The male faculty will arise. For it is not the case that the male faculty will not arise during the course of that existence for all of them, since there is the possibility of a change of sex;
however, with reference to the absence of its initial arising in another existence, it is said:
"And the male faculty will not arise for them. For in another existence, the initial arising [of the male faculty] has not yet occurred.
“Intended” means: having made it thus, the term “existence” (*bhava*) is employed in the phrase “having shown some existences.

However, when the meaning is understood according to the statement, “Birth is the acquisition of the sense-bases (*āyatana*),” then [birth] arises for one who has taken rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) by means of the karma that produces this or that sense-base, lasting until the completion of the sense-bases, during which time the sense-bases necessarily come to be.
The answer to the two questions is thus well-established. And this being so, [regarding the question]:

"For whom ear-base will not arise, for that person eye-base does not arise?"—for those final-existence beings reborn in the five-aggregate realm, and for those who, having been reborn in the formless realm, will attain final nibbāna at the moment of rebirth—for these, the ear-base...
In such passages as, "It will not arise, and yet for them the eye-base does not arise," those being reborn—such as those in the womb or those in their final existence—are included.
And having done so, [the following] from the *Indriyayamaka* is also [accounted for]:
"Or, for whomsoever the faculty of mental joy arises, does the eye-faculty arise for him? Yes."

This is appropriate. Because the karma that produces the faculty of mental joy (*somanassindriya*) invariably produces the faculty of the eye (*cakkhundriya*), it is to be rejoiced in as something arising even within the womb until the faculty of the eye arises.

Furthermore, regarding the statement: "Or else, for whomsoever the sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*) has arisen in a certain place, for him the sphere of the nose (*ghānāyatana*) [arises] there..."

Regarding the statement: "Does it arise?"—for those passing away from the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), for those being reborn in the sense-sphere who are noseless (*aghānaka*), and for those of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*), the visible-object base (*rūpāyatana*) has arisen there, but the nose-base (*ghānāyatana*) does not arise there for them.
Here, the phrase "for those being reborn in the sense-sphere who are noseless" refers to those [beings] during the eleventh week [of gestation].
It should be understood that this is stated with reference to those who will die here and take rebirth through a kamma that produces the nose-base (*ghānāyatana*).
“Is it the case that for whomsoever the nose-base does not cease at a certain place, for him the visible-object-base (*rūpāyatana*) will not cease there? [Yes.
For those being reborn in the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), and for those sense-sphere beings who are without a nose.”
Regarding the statement, "For those passing away from the form realm, the nose base does not cease there,

yet it is not the case that the visible-object base will not cease for them there," the phrase "for those passing away from the sense-sphere realm who are without a nose" indicates that there is death for womb-born beings even while the nose base has not yet arisen. For [this is not the case] in the sense-sphere realm.

There is no other being besides one born from a womb who lacks a nose; for it is not stated in the *Dhammahadayavibhaṅga* that "at the moment of rebirth in the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*), eight bases manifest for anyone.

Now, why is it not understood why, with reference to beings of spontaneous birth (*opapātika*) alone, the answers "Yes" (*āmantā*) are given here and in the *Indriyayamaka* to the questions as they have been shown?

Because no answer is given to a question whose meaning has been grasped through a definitive conclusion in the *Yamaka*, due to the possibility that a portion of its meaning might still be subject to doubt.
For when there is something yet to be analyzed, no answer is provided; if such an answer were given, it would not constitute a complete response.
Now, why [is it said]: "Or for whomsoever the faculty of mental joy (*somanassindriya*) arises, for him the faculty of the eye (*cakkhundriya*)..."?
“Does it arise? “Yes. By this, is it not understood that “there is no rebirth-linking with mental joy for those lying in the womb”?
“At the moment of rebirth in the sense-sphere realm, for whom do ten faculties become manifest?
For beings lying in the womb who are possessed of roots and associated with knowledge, at the moment of rebirth, ten faculties become manifest: the body faculty...”

This is because of such statements as: "the mind-faculty, or the female-faculty, or the male-faculty, or the life-faculty, or the joy-faculty, or the equanimity-faculty, or the faith-faculty," and so forth.
In the section on cessation, regarding the division of future time, just as the cessation of that very same consciousness exists by way of its future state...

Just as it was stated regarding the moment of arising, so too the cessation of that very same kamma-born continuity (santāna) must be stated in terms of its future state at the moment of its arising; thus, in all cases, this is stated in that way only for those who are about to be reborn, not for those already born.
For those already born, however, the cessation of another, future continuity must be stated in terms of its future state, and not of that [present] one itself. Of that...

For it is said that cessation indeed begins immediately after arising. Therefore, even though the ear and eye are destroyed during the course of existence for Arahants, by way of apprehending the future time [of their destruction], one asks:
"Will the ear-base be destroyed for him for whom the eye-base will be destroyed? Yes. Or rather, will the eye-base be destroyed for him for whom the ear-base will be destroyed? Yes.
"Will the eye-base cease?"— to this, the two-fold answer is indeed appropriate. And because cessation is said to commence immediately after rebirth,
yet the term "cessation" is applied to death because it is the finality of that [rebirth],

therefore, even when [the process] has ceased during the course of existence, based on that which has not yet ceased in a certain portion of the continuum, it is called "cessation not yet completed" by way of death alone.
"Its cessation" is what is said. For it will be stated: "In one whose faculty of mental joy (somanassindriya) ceases, does his eye-faculty (cakkhundriya) cease?

Yes. Therefore, here too, since only the cessation at the moment of death (cuti) is intended, that which would cease during the course of existence (pavatta) is said to cease through death itself by way of its final conclusion.
“Āmantā” (Yes) is the appropriate affirmative reply. In the phrases beginning with “of those possessing eyes,” the meaning is understood as “of those who have acquired the eye-faculty,” and so forth.
“If the eye-base does not cease for someone, will the ear-base not cease for them?
For all those being reborn, and for those passing away who do not possess the eye-faculty, the eye-base does not cease, yet [the ear-base may still cease].”

In the phrase, "their ear-base will not cease," it should be understood that all those being reborn—with the exception of those in their final existence in the formless realm—and those passing away without eye-faculty, are included.
For they are subsumed under the second category; thus, because of this dependence [on that category], the term "all" and the term "without eye-faculty" are used here with a remainder (sāvasesa).
[The phrase refers to] "those in their final existence in the formless realm."

And here it should be understood that those who do not go from the formless realm to the five-aggregate realm, even though they have no other rebirth, are nevertheless included under the term "those in their final existence in the formless realm" (*arūpe pacchimabhavikā*).
This same method applies to others of a similar kind as well.
The commentary on the section on the process of existence (*pavattivāra*) is finished.
The commentary on the *Āyatanayamaka* is finished.
4. *Dhātuyamaka*. 1–19.

Regarding the phrase "of those that are obtainable": this is stated with reference to the fact that, in the section on occurrence (*pavattivāra*), the *yamakas* connected with the sound-element (*saddhadhātu*) and those connected with the eye-consciousness-element (*cakkhuviññāṇadhātu*), etc., are not obtainable by way of death and rebirth-linking (*cuti-paṭisandhi*).
The Commentary on the *Dhātuyamaka* is finished.
5. The *Saccayamaka*. 1.
The Section on Designations (*Paṇṇattivāra*).
Commentary on the Section of Exegesis (Niddesavāravaṇṇanā) 10–26:

Regarding the question, “Is suffering the truth of suffering? Yes,” although the term *dukkha* applies to all three—suffering as pain (*dukkhadukkha*), suffering in formations (*saṅkhāradukkha*), and suffering in change (*vipariṇāmadukkha*)—it is applied to birth and so forth by such statements as, “Birth, too, is suffering.”
Furthermore, when that [suffering] occurs other than as the suffering of suffering (*dukkhadukkha*), it does not occur independently of other factors.
Here, by taking up the bare term "suffering" as independent of others, he clarifies the designation:

thus, because it has the nature of suffering in the primary sense, this word "suffering" applies to that which is the suffering of suffering, and that is exclusively the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*).

“Yes, they are,” it is said. In the section on pure truth (*suddhasacca*), among the origins (*samudaya*) mentioned in the *Saccavibhaṅga*, there is none that exists among the states of fruition (*phaladhamma*);
nor is there any cessation (*nirodha*) said to exist among the states of fruition.

Furthermore, the term “path” (*magga*) applies to the fruits and the factors of the path because of their being the path and the fruit, not because of the presence of the function of the path itself; for those [fruits] have already completed the function of leading out (*niyyāna*).

Furthermore, the word "path" (*magga*) here denotes the way out (*niyyāna*), not the fruit of the way out; therefore, regarding the statements "the origin is a truth," "cessation is a truth," and "the path is a truth," the answer given is likewise "Yes" (*āmantā*).
Alternatively, when the terms have been purified through the purification of the words, the terms such as "suffering" (*dukkha*) and so forth function here specifically as qualifiers of "truth."

They are understood as "taken. However, in order to illustrate that these [terms] are exclusively qualifiers of the truths (*sacca*) and to show the specific application of those qualifiers to the truths, the "Pure Truths Chapter" (*suddhasaccavāra*) was stated.
Because suffering and the others—which are qualifiers of the truths—are exclusively truths themselves, it was stated: "Is suffering a truth... pe ...
Is the path a truth? Yes. And just as it is here, so it is in the *Khandhayamaka* and other such works.

In the sections concerning the pure aggregates (*suddhakhandha*) and so forth, it is appropriate to take only those forms (*rūpa*) and other phenomena that serve as the specific qualifications of the aggregates and so on.

However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, by means of the statement: "Because whether it be form reckoned as 'the nature of the dear' (*piyarūpa*) or 'the nature of the pleasant' (*sātarūpa*), or even the primary elements (*bhūta*) and derived matter (*upādārūpa*), all are included within the five aggregates; therefore, he assents with 'Yes,'" [it is shown that] there is the inclusion of forms and so on, the eye and so on, and suffering and so on.
In the sections on the "pure aggregates" and so forth as well, this point is illustrated: that other [aggregates] are also included because they are distinguished from the aggregates and so on;
therefore, the other meaning was stated by way of their corresponding nature.
The commentary on the section of the Exposition (Niddesa-vāra) is finished.
2. Commentary on the Section on Occurrence (Pavattivāra) [27–164].
“Even including the Suddhāvāsa deities” is stated because there might be a suspicion that, due to their being noble ones (ariya), they could be reborn through the truth of suffering (dukkhasacca).
“A consciousness dissociated from craving” should be understood here specifically in terms of the fivefold plane of existence (pañcavokāra).
It has been stated. However, by this definitive determination—namely, "for whom the truth of suffering arises"—all those who are reborn are included:

those in the fourfold existence (*catuvokāra*) during the course of existence (*pavatti*) who possess the moment of arising of any consciousness other than the path or fruit, and those in the fivefold existence (*pañcavokāra*) who possess the moment of arising of all consciousnesses.
It is precisely within those individuals thus determined by that definition [that the following applies].

Some explain that by the phrase "at the moment of arising of a consciousness dissociated from craving during the course of existence" (*pavatte taṇhāvippayuttacittassa uppādakkhaṇe*), those who possess the occurrence of one portion of both suffering and its origin are indicated;

for this is a demonstration of a division within what has already been grasped by way of a definitive determination (*sanniṭṭhāna*). Therefore, it is indeed appropriate that those belonging to the four-aggregate beings (*catuvokāra*) are also included.
For there is no possibility of their being included among those who possess the arising of the Path and its Fruit, since those [four-aggregate beings] do not possess such [Path and Fruit].

"Because it is not included by way of determination. This means that "this should not be taken here"—that is, the consciousness of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*) in the fourfold existence (*catuvokāra*)—is stated to be not included here in the statement regarding the arising of the Truths.
And herein, the phrase "of all those being reborn" is stated by way of showing the first arising of the process born of karma (*kammaja-pavatta*).

The non-percipient beings (*asaññasatta*) are also included here. The phrase "at the moment of arising of a consciousness dissociated from craving during the course of existence" (*pavatte*) is stated by way of showing the arising of the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*) unmixed with the arising of the truth of origin (*samudayasacca*).
The phrase "at the moment of arising of craving" refers to that [arising of suffering] mixed with the arising of the truth of origin, which is accompanied by craving. Of these two...
In the process of existence (*pavatti*) of non-percipient beings (*asaññasatta*), the arising of the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*) is not included anywhere, nor is its cessation likewise.
The same method applies to the *Maggasaccayamaka* (the Dilemma on the Truth of the Path). It is stated that in this context, the occasion should be understood by way of moments (*khaṇa*), namely:

at the moment of their rebirth and at the moment of the arising of a consciousness dissociated from craving (*taṇhāvippayuttacitta*). And this being so, "for whom, where, the truth of suffering... [and so forth].
In the final section of the answer to the question, "For one in whom suffering-truth arises there, will origination-truth arise there?", the statement:
"For others who are being reborn into the four-aggregate or five-aggregate realms, and during the phase of the arising of consciousness in the course of existence (pavatta),
for them suffering-truth arises there and origination-truth will also arise there"— would not be tenable.
For the truth of origination (*samudayasacca*) will not arise at the moment of rebirth (*upapatti-khaṇa*) nor at the moment of the arising of consciousness (*cittuppatti-khaṇa*).

Therefore, for those persons who possess a mind dissociated from craving at the moment of rebirth and at the moment of the arising of consciousness, the word *tattha* (there) is appropriate here in the sense of the "place" (*okāsa*), meaning:
in whichever sphere—such as the sense-sphere realm (*kāmāvacara*)—that rebirth and that arising of consciousness occur for them. For this is a section concerning persons and spheres. In that regard:

The phrase "of all those being reborn," and so forth, was stated for the purpose of specifying particular individuals; however, the location where they [are reborn] is precisely that [place]. Regarding the statement:

"For all those passing away, at the moment of the dissolution of consciousness during the course of existence (pavatta), and at the moments of the arising of the Path and the Fruit in the formless realm (ārūpa), neither the Truth of Origin nor the Truth of Suffering arises for them. Herein—

However, some say that because it functions in dependence upon the mind, only mind-born materiality (*cittaja-rūpa*) is intended here— specifically in the context of the statement, "At the moment of the cessation of consciousness during the course of existence, the truth of suffering does not arise"— and not materiality born of kamma (*kammaja-rūpa*) and so forth,
since the latter arises independently of the mind. But by the definitive conclusion of the passage, "Or for whom the truth of origin does not arise," [it is shown otherwise].
The person who is grasped is not grasped merely by reference to the mind; rather, it is whoever is of such a nature.
Therefore, by the statement "suffering-truth does not arise for him," suffering-truth is not described as being dependent solely on the mind;
rather, the meaning is that at the moment of the mind's dissolution, whatever suffering-truth there might be does not arise.
"It is understood. For there is no question that remains unanalyzed when the *Yamaka* (Book of Pairs) is being analyzed.

The statement, "When the second consciousness has arisen in the Suddhāvāsa [deities]," is said by way of showing the ultimate limit of that for whom the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*) had arisen, but not the truth of origin (*samudayasacca*), at whichever place it occurred. However, in that case...
Because they share the same destiny as that which was shown by him, all those who possessed the preceding consciousnesses are thereby shown along with the second unwholesome consciousness.
For even in their case, it is said: "Suffering-truth (dukkha-sacca) had arisen there for them, but origination-truth (samudaya-sacca) had not arisen there for them.
And having established this, the phrase "of the others, [namely] those of the fourfold and fivefold aggregates" refers to what has been stated above.
The Suddhāvāsa deities are not included. Just as in the answer to the question, "For whom, where suffering-truth arises,

has origination-truth arisen for them there?"— namely, "At the moment of the arising of the rebirth-consciousness of the Suddhāvāsas"— by this alone, those who possess the same destiny as one at the moment of the arising of the rebirth-consciousness [are included],
as well as those who possess all preceding moments of consciousness prior to the second unwholesome consciousness.
Since they have already been shown, they are not included by the phrase "of the others"; it should be understood in this way here as well.
The expression "of the others" is for the purpose of qualifying the five-aggregate beings (*pañcavokāra*), not the four-aggregate beings (*catuvokāra*).

For those [four-aggregate beings] mentioned previously do not exist as something to be excluded, unlike the five-aggregate beings such as the aforementioned Suddhāvāsa deities. "For those who have fully realized [the truths], there [in that realm], the truth of suffering..."
By this definitive statement—"the path-truth had arisen"—it should be understood that the person and the location are grasped as mutually delimited;
thus, those in whatever location have realized [the truth] are to be understood by the term "those who have realized.

Therefore, those who have realized in the sense-sphere realm (*kāmāvacara*), the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*), or the immaterial sphere (*arūpāvacara*)—[referring to] the fine-material sphere...
Or those reborn in the formless realm (arūpāvacara) are not included here for as long as the realization (abhisamaya) has not yet arisen there;

however, they are not mentioned separately because they belong to the same category as those in the first group—those in the Pure Abodes (suddhāvāsa) who have not yet attained realization—as shown by the phrase: "when the second consciousness is occurring in the Pure Abodes. [This refers to] "those who have not yet realized" (anabhisametāvīnaṃ).

Regarding those who have attained [the path] everywhere but have not yet fully realized it there, the phrase "while the second consciousness of the Suddhāvāsas is occurring" is stated for the purpose of specifying the particular time of their attainment among the Suddhāvāsas.
By the statement "after which consciousness they will obtain the highest path," those who possess the consciousness of purification (vodānacitta) are shown to share the same destiny.
It should be understood that this refers to everyone from those possessing the very first preceding consciousness up to those possessing the consciousness associated with the final craving.
This same method applies to other similar cases.

In instances where "at the moment of the dissolution of consciousness during the course of existence" (pavatte) occurs, the moment of dissolution of the rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhicitta) is also included.

Likewise, in the passage where it says "during the arising moment of consciousness in the course of existence" (*pavatte cittassa uppādakkhaṇe*), it should be understood as referring to the arising moment of the death-consciousness (*cuticitta*) as well.
Furthermore, in the answer to the question, "For whom the truth of suffering does not cease, for that person will the truth of the origin not cease?", in both sections it is stated simply:
"In the formless realm, at the moment of the dissolution of the path and its fruit" (*arūpe maggassa ca phalassa ca bhaṅgakkhaṇe*).
It was stated, but not specified. Why? Because even for a single path and fruit, one who possesses them at the moment of their dissolution partakes of both categories.

For among those included by the definitive statement "for whom the truth of suffering does not cease," there are certain individuals in the formless realms who, at the moment of the dissolution of the paths and fruits, possess three fruits and two paths.

For those who, while possessing the moment of the destruction [of the path], do not continuously suppress the craving for insight (*vipassanā-nikanti*) and the craving for existence (*bhava-nikanti*),
but instead give rise to them from time to time and will subsequently produce the higher paths— for such persons, the truth of the origin (*samudaya-sacca*) will cease.

Furthermore, for certain others who, without giving rise to craving in the interim, produce the higher paths and possess the moment of the destruction of the path and its fruits (*maggaphala-bhaṅgakkhaṇa*), [the same applies].
"Origination-truth will not cease. By this general statement, it is shown that when a preceding section is being discussed, there is an exclusion of what is to be stated in the subsequent section;
thus, this method has been demonstrated. The commentary on the Section on Occurrence (Pavattivāra) is finished.
3. Commentary on the Section on Full Understanding (Pariññāvāra), §§165–170. Regarding the section on full understanding... [and so forth] ... "three kinds of full understanding are found here":

this qualification is for the purpose of showing that all the truths are not to be fully understood through the modes of realization and development, just as all the aggregates and so forth are not to be fully understood in the *Khandha-yamaka* and other such works.

And for the purpose of showing the non-occurrence of this [craving] alternative: "The holy life is lived under the Blessed One for the sake of the full understanding of suffering and for the sake of the abandoning of its origin. To show that full understanding and abandoning among the Truths, "full understanding by way of investigation" (*tīraṇapariññā*) is stated with respect to suffering, not "full understanding by way of abandoning" (*pahānapariññā*).

And with respect to the origin, "full understanding by way of abandoning" is intended, not "full understanding by way of investigation. [This is] "full understanding by way of knowing" (*ñātapariññā*).

However, they are said to be "common" in both cases. For path-knowledge (magga-ñāṇa) clarifies both suffering and its origin; thus, it constitutes the full understanding through knowledge (*ñāta-pariññā*).

Because it accomplishes the function of investigating suffering, it is the full understanding through investigation (*tīraṇa-pariññā*), and because it brings about the non-arising of the origin, it is the full understanding through abandoning (*pahāna-pariññā*).
Thus, all three types of full understanding should be applied precisely at the moment of the Path.
The commentary on the Section on Full Understanding is finished.
The commentary on the Twin Verses on the Truths is finished.
6. The Twin Verses on Formations (Saṅkhārayamaka).
1. Commentary on the Section on Designations (Paṇṇattivāra-vaṇṇanā) 1.

Just as the aggregates and so forth were previously unanalyzed, the bodily formations and so forth have likewise not been explained; therefore, because they are not yet understood, he analyzes the three formations beginning with, "In-breathing and out-breathing are the bodily formation.
In the first sense, [the compound] *kāyasaṅkhāro* means "the formation of the body" (*kāyassa saṅkhāro*), which is a genitive (possessive) compound.

Thus, in the first sense, it is a genitive case; in the second sense, in the sense of the agent (*kattuatthe*), it is a genitive case. "The formation of speech" (*vaci-saṅkhāro*) is a genitive case in the sense of the object (*kammatthe*).
"The formation of the mind" (*citta-saṅkhāro*) is likewise only in the sense of the agent. However, since that [formation] is considered to have the meaning of the instrumental case, it is stated:
"having made it a genitive case in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇatthe*)."
2–7. Regarding the absence of meaning by way of each single pure term (*suddhika-ekeka-padavasena*):

even though a meaning has been shown by the wheel-turnings rooted in the purification of terms, such as a single [factor] like inhalation or exhalation obtainable through two terms, it cannot be expressed by the pure terms of "body" (*kāya*) and so forth, nor by the pure term "formations" (*saṅkhāra*).
This is because, just as a portion of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-khandha*) is not [the whole] denoted by the term "aggregate" (*khandha*), [so too is this case].

The intention is this: just as the aggregate of the [five] aggregates (*khandha-samudāya*) demonstrates that the intended meaning exists when the words are purified, so too there is no intended meaning for each individual word.
However, it might be argued that "body" (*kāya*) and "bodily formation" (*kāyasaṅkhāra*), and so forth, ought to be stated;
for if the term *kāyasaṅkhāra*, taken collectively rather than being explained separately, indicates a single meaning. The term *kāyasaṅkhāra*...

He speaks with the intention that, just as the word *khandha* when occurring in the sense of bodily formation (*kāyasaṅkhāra*) must be specified by the word "body" (*kāya*)— just as [it is] by the word "form" (*rūpa*)—
this is because this section on pure formations (*suddhasaṅkhāravāra*) takes up only those meanings intended as they were shown through the purification of the words in this section;
and since those [terms] were not included by the words "body" and so forth, [there would otherwise be no point in] the statement "the body is the bodily formation," and so on.

This demonstrates the improper application. However, here in the *Saṅkhāra-Yamaka*, because the terms "body" (*kāya*) and so forth and the term "volitional formations" (*saṅkhāra*) do not share a common locus (*asamānādhikaraṇa*), if one were to say, "The body is volitional formation; volitional formations are the body," there would be an abandonment of the intended meaning and an inclusion of what is unintended.

Therefore, the wheel-turning based on the pure state of volitional formations was not stated. [This is because it is excluded] by the wheel-turnings based on the purification of terms and the purification of the states.
However, because the word *saṅkhāra* has been shown to be qualified by the non-co-referential terms *kāya* and so forth, a doubt arises:

"Is this *kāyasaṅkhāra*, which is qualified by the word *kāya* occurring in a different sense, the same as that which is qualified by speech and mind (*vacīcitta*) occurring in different senses, or is it something else?
The same applies to the remaining [terms]. Here, for the purpose of showing them elsewhere:
It should be understood that six pairs (yamakas) have been stated by way of direct and reverse order, beginning with “bodily formation, verbal formation,” and so forth.
However, because this method is presented in the place of the section on pure formations (suddha-saṅkhāra-vāra) in the Commentary, it is called the “section on pure formations.
The commentary on the section on designations (paṇṇatti-vāra) is concluded.
2. Commentary on the Section on Occurrence (Pavattivāra-vaṇṇanā) 19.
