In the Section on Occurrence, because it provides the scope for both mental formations (saṅkhārā) and persons (puggala), jhāna and the planes (bhūmi) are taken separately as distinct scopes.
Thus, in the Section on Persons (Puggalavāra), by way of taking persons according to their scope, these two scopes are treated accordingly.

There is a grasping [of the object]; therefore, it should be understood that the persons included by way of the second and third jhānas—namely, "at the moment of the arising of inhalation and exhalation without initial and sustained application" (vitakka-vicāra)—are shown as being distinguished [from others].

Again, "those who have attained the first jhāna" indicates the person by way of the jhāna-sphere, while "those belonging to the sense-sphere" (kāmāvacara) indicates them by way of the plane-sphere (bhūmi). This applies to both types as well.
However, for the purpose of qualifying them, he says: "At the moment of arising of the in-breaths and out-breaths.
By this, he excludes those who have attained the first jhāna in the fine-material and immaterial realms, as well as those in the sense-sphere realm such as those in the womb and so forth.

For even among those in the sense-sphere realm, such as those in the womb and so forth, there is the arising of applied and sustained thought (vitakka-vicāra) without in-breaths and out-breaths. [Thus it is said] in the Commentary.

However, because they are exclusive [to those realms], the fine-material and immaterial-sphere beings have been indicated. By the phrase "at the moment of the arising of applied and sustained thought without breath-in and breath-out," the persons indicated should be understood as those in the occasion of the first jhāna and those in the occasions of the sense-sphere and so forth, distinguished by the absence of breath-in and breath-out.
In this manner, the classification of persons is to be understood in all instances.

21. Regarding the phrase "in the first jhāna of the sense-sphere" (*kāmāvacare paṭhamajjhāne*), it is stated in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*) that this refers to "the first jhāna arisen on the plane of the sense-sphere.

However, if this meaning were accepted, then in the passage, "In the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere and the immaterial sphere, there arises there a mental formation (*cittasaṅkhāra*), but there does not arise there a bodily formation (*kāyasaṅkhāra*)," the same would have to apply here as well—namely, that [the formations] arise in the planes of the fine-material and immaterial spheres.

The meaning would be "in the fourth jhāna," but that is undesirable because it results in not grasping the status of the planes as locations, and because it results in not grasping all fourth jhānas by way of their location.
Therefore, without conflating the jhānas, the planes, and the locations, the status of being a location must be applied separately.
For even in the location of the first jhāna, there is the bodily formation (kāyasaṅkhāra).

And the verbal formation arises, and [it] arises in the sense-sphere plane. Although the pair does not arise in every first jhāna and in every sense-sphere plane, it should be understood that this was stated thus because the arising of that pair exists therein.
And because they are distinct locations, the statement beginning with "but here, by way of the mere factor" [is made].

"It is not to be said" means that, in this *yamaka* (pairing), the second jhāna—which is "without applied thought but with sustained thought"—is to be understood as being included within the first jhāna by virtue of its sustained thought (*vicāra*).
Alternatively, it may be understood that the second jhāna, taken in its most eminent form, is not included [in the first].
In the *Yassayatthaka*, the phrase "those who have attained cessation" (*nirodhasamāpannānaṃ*) is not applicable; for indeed—
"They exist in space like non-percipient beings.

(37) "When the second consciousness of the Pure Abodes is occurring" means that when, from their first [consciousness] which is without applied thought and sustained thought, the second— which is with applied thought and sustained thought—
is occurring during the adverting of the desire for existence (*bhavanikanti*), he shows that both [the material body and the mental aggregates] have not yet arisen.
Thus, it is already shown that [the verbal formation] did not arise even in the preceding moments of consciousness.
Just as "for those being reborn in the Suddhāvāsa" was stated for the purpose of showing the beginning of the mental formation (cittasaṅkhāra),
so too "while the second moment of consciousness is occurring" should be understood as stated for the purpose of showing the beginning of the verbal formation (vacīsaṅkhāra).
The commentary on the Pavattivāra is finished.
The commentary on the Saṅkhārayamaka is finished.
7. The Anusayayamaka.
Commentary on the Section on Enumeration Distinguished by its Divisions:

1. "Full understanding through knowledge culminates in the discernment of conditions" means that, having elucidated full understanding through knowledge by means of the Root Yāmaka which illustrates conditions, and having elucidated full understanding through investigation by means of the Aggregates Yāmaka and others due to the predominance of investigation regarding the aggregates and so forth, [the text proceeds] until the abandoning of the underlying tendencies.

Regarding "full understanding as abandoning" (*pahānapariññā*): the *Anusaya-yamaka* (the "Pairs on Latent Tendencies") is undertaken in order to clarify full understanding as abandoning by means of the latent tendencies that constitute the basis for what is to be abandoned.
"By way of those that are found" means by way of those things that are found in the state of being latent tendencies.

The apprehension of latent tendencies through three modes is necessary because, if they were not apprehended in that manner, the textual passage beginning with the section on latent tendencies would be difficult to comprehend.
"But here, 'among the former'" means "among these [sections], such as the section on those with underlying tendencies (sānusayavāra), etc. Since there is no difference in meaning, one might ask:

"If it were not stated in such terms as 'for one being reborn in the sense-sphere realm (kāmadhātu) after passing away from the sense-sphere realm,' or 'for one being reborn in the fine-material-sphere realm (rūpadhātu) after passing away from the sense-sphere realm,' how could this be a presentation of the *Yamaka*? It is not so.

The teaching on the pairs (*yamaka-desanā*); furthermore, it is the demonstration of the delimitation of the bases for the underlying tendencies (*anusaya-ṭṭhāna-pariccheda*) by way of death and rebirth for those underlying tendencies taught through the preceding pairs.
Because of the abundance of teachings on pairs, the entire collection of all the sections should be understood as having the name "Pairs of Underlying Tendencies" (*anusaya-yamaka*).
Alternatively, even the inverse questions are obtained according to their meaning.

However, because there is no specific distinction in meaning, it is not explicitly stated; rather, this teaching should be understood as a "teaching by pairs" (*yamakadesanā*) by way of their being present.
By the phrase "they arise having obtained a corresponding cause," he shows that they are capable of arising when a cause is obtained.
For the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*), which have not yet been abandoned, arise when a cause is present. And [the teaching continues] until their incapacity for arising through the Path.
They are called "latent tendencies" (*anusaya*) because they have not yet been abandoned, such that they are of this very nature.
This specific nature is grasped by the word "arises" (*uppajjati*), and not in the sense of "being in the process of arising" as found in the *Khandha-yamaka* and other texts.

For this very reason, in the section on "Arising" (*uppajjanavāra*), such as the question, "Does the latent tendency of sensual lust arise for whomsoever the latent tendency of aversion arises?"—the answer being "Yes"—there is no difference from the section on "Latent Tendencies" (*anusayavāra*).

[They] have been analyzed. However, those [defilements] that have arisen and are arising once they have obtained a corresponding cause have become, and continue to be, firmly established in the sense of not having been abandoned. Furthermore, they have arisen and arise precisely because they are fit to arise;
there are no others called "fit to arise" apart from the past, future, and present. Therefore, all [of them], whether past, future, or present—
Sensual lust and the other [defilements] are called "latent tendencies" (*anusaya*). For latent tendencies exist only in the sense of being unabandoned;

and it is precisely those [defilements] of the past and so forth that are unabandoned. However, the abandoning of the latent tendencies occurs through the Path’s bringing about the state of non-arising for such things.
The "unabandoned aspect" is an aspect of a phenomenon (*dhamma*), not the phenomenon itself; and it is the phenomenon itself that arises. With this intention, he said: "the unabandoned aspect."

"And it is not logical to say that [the underlying tendency] arises. Regarding the phrase "underlying tendencies of beings" (*sattānusaya*): if they are called "underlying tendencies" because they lie latent within the continuum in the sense of being unabandoned, then why are only beings mentioned? Is it not the case that other defilements also possess the status of an underlying tendency because they too are unabandoned?
It does not follow; for the status of an underlying tendency belongs only to that which is unabandoned.
Because it has not been stated [otherwise]. For it has been said: "Furthermore, 'latent tendency' (*anusaya*) refers to a defilement that has become firmly rooted in the sense of being unabandoned.
Therefore, it is logical that a defilement which has become firmly rooted by way of being unabandoned is precisely what is called a "latent tendency.

And "firmly rooted" should be understood as its specific nature (*sabhāva*), which is not shared with others. For it was these very things that were designated as "latent tendencies" by the Tathāgata, who has awakened to the specific nature of phenomena.
It has been stated. "Firmly established" means one who possesses latent tendencies (*anusaya*).

Since the sections on the arising of latent tendencies share the same logical status, just as the expression "lies latent" indicates the mode of being unabandoned, so too might the expression "arises" [indicate the same].
Thus, by way of the section on arising, the expression "arises" is not explicitly stated [as redundant].
If it is argued that [the two terms] can be used interchangeably, that is not so, because those two have been stated with a distinction in their verbal meanings.

For although the meaning "it arises having obtained a suitable cause" is undifferentiated in both cases, the word "underlies" (*anuseti*) indicates that the underlying tendency has become firmly established within the continuum.
If that very same expression were to indicate "it arises," there would be no distinction for anyone.
The section on arising (*uppajjanavāra*) would not be applicable to non-existence; however, the expression "arises" indicates that which is capable of arising.

Why? Because the section on arising demonstrates that which is capable of arising. Furthermore, since the word *anusaya* refers to a latent state (*aparinipphanna-sayana*) that exists at all times, [the term "arising"] is used for the purpose of precluding the notion of a state of being firmly established (*thāmagatabhāva*) that is unworthy of arising.

The intention is that the statement regarding their arising—namely, "they arise having obtained a corresponding cause" (*anusentīti anurūpaṃ kāraṇaṃ labhitvā uppajjanti*)—which was spoken in order to show the meaning of the intended abode, is indeed well-spoken. The connection is that this too is well-spoken according to this measure of the *tanti*.
For by means of the three *tantis*, the state of being associated with consciousness (*cittasampayuttatā*) is illuminated.
The commentary on the section on the analysis of the divisions is finished.
Commentary on the section on the place of origin: 2.
"In two feelings of the sense-sphere" means in the sense-sphere plane, namely, in pleasant feeling and equanimous feeling; thus it is stated in the Aṭṭhakathā.
The mention of the sense-sphere element (kāmadhātu) is stated as a qualification for two types of feeling;

this being so, it would not have been stated that the sense-sphere element is the locus for the underlying tendency to sensual lust (kāmarāgānusaya). However, since among the two types of lust, the underlying tendency to existence-lust (bhavarāga) is stated to have the three elements—the fine-material and immaterial elements—as its loci—it follows that the sense-sphere element is the locus for the underlying tendency to sensual lust.

It should be stated thus. For the locus of the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) has been described as being threefold, by way of the elements (*dhātu*), feelings (*vedanā*), and everything included within the personality-sphere (*sakkāya*).

Therefore, among the three elements, in the sense-sphere element (*kāmadhātu*), and among the three feelings, in two feelings—here, the underlying tendency of sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) underlies;
thus, the status of the locus of the underlying tendency should be applied separately to both the element and the feelings. And as for the phrase "in two feelings," this...

The latent tendency of sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*), while persisting within feelings (*vedanā*), persists only in two [types of feeling] and not in three; this was stated solely for the purpose of precluding its presence in all three.

Thus, there is no instance where it persists in both [unpleasant and neutral feelings]. Therefore, there is no purpose in mentioning the "desire realm" (*kāmadhātu*) as a qualification of the feelings.

For the unconditioned (*apariyāpanna*) state of the body (*sakkāya*), which is neither a locus nor a non-locus for the latent tendencies of lust for existence (*bhavarāgānusaya*), [is what is intended].
It is evident that this is not a basis for the underlying tendency of sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*).

And just as when it is said, "in two feelings," two feelings other than the basis for the underlying tendency of aversion (*paṭighānusaya*) are understood, so too, in this case, those [feelings] other than the basis for the underlying tendency of existence-lust (*bhavarāgānusaya*) are understood.

And here, among other pleasant and agreeable forms associated with the two feelings, as well as among desirable forms and so forth, the underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) arises through a craving for pleasure and happiness; thus, its lying latent in those two feelings is stated.
For even when it arises elsewhere, it lies dormant following after these two feelings, thinking only "pleasure."

"He acquires" means: thus, when the underlying tendency to aversion (*paṭighānusaya*) arises in relation to feelings associated with pain (*dukkhavedanā*), as well as other unpleasant or disagreeable forms and undesirable objects, it strikes against them as being painful and repulsive;

therefore, having followed after the feeling of pain itself, it lies latent. It is for this reason that its "lying latent" (*anusayana*) in that [feeling] has been stated. Thus, regarding sensual lust (*kāmarāga*) and aversion (*paṭigha*) in the three [feelings]...

By the mention of "underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) toward feelings," it is shown that sensual lust (*kāmarāga*) and aversion (*paṭigha*) arise with respect to those things apprehended as desirable and so forth—by way of both the natural state of the object and by way of distorted perception (*viparītasaññā*).

For when they arise therein, they are said to "underlie" (*anusenti*) within the three types of feeling. Or rather, here, by means of the triad of feelings, [the nature of] the desirable and so forth is [demonstrated].

The apprehension of objects should be understood; by the mention of the sense-sphere element (*kāmadhātu*) and so forth, the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*) and others, which serve as the bases for the gratification of sensual desire (*kāmasāda*) and so on, are intended.

Therein, the underlying tendency of sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*), while lying latent through the gratification of existence (*bhavassāda*), underlies the sense-sphere element; while lying latent through the gratification of sensual pleasure (*kāmasukha*), it underlies pleasant and neutral feelings.
As for aversion (*paṭigha*), it occurs solely through the warding off of suffering; thus, wherever [it arises]...

Therein, even when being struck by it, one underlies only painful feeling. However, since there is no occurrence of sensual gratification (*kāmassāda*) regarding the realms of form and formlessness, nor regarding the phenomena belonging to the fine-material and immaterial spheres, the lust that underlies therein should be understood as "lust for existence" (*bhavarāga*).

Furthermore, because the inclusion of the three elements and the three feelings encompasses all that is comprised within the personality-view (*sakkāya*), [the text states]: "Wherein the underlying tendency to sensual lust..."

In the explanations of such passages as, "He does not underlie [them]; therein the underlying tendency to views (diṭṭhānusaya) does not underlie," it should be understood that no location for the underlying tendencies of views and so forth is stated apart from the three elements and the three feelings.

But is it not the case that for one who arouses longing for the unsurpassed liberations, the underlying tendency to aversion (paṭighānusaya) does not underlie the mental distress (domanassa) arisen with longing as its condition; and likewise in the case of joy and equanimity based on renunciation?

Regarding the statement "one should not lie latent with sensual lust": since there are other sense-sphere feelings that serve as bases for the underlying tendency of views (*diṭṭhānusaya*)—apart from those where sensual lust lies latent—let them be so.
However, there is no basis for that [sensual lust] other than the three elements and the three types of feeling;
therefore, it was not mentioned. But because [the text says]: "Where the underlying tendency of sensual lust and the underlying tendency of aversion..."
It is said: "Are the underlying tendencies of conceit (*mānānusaya*) not latent there, while the underlying tendencies of views (*diṭṭhānusaya*) and doubt (*vicikicchānusaya*) are not latent?

[The answer is] "Yes. Therefore, it should be understood that this was stated by taking suffering in general as the basis for the latency of the underlying tendency to aversion (*paṭighānusaya*), considering it in its collective sense. Likewise, mundane pleasure and equanimity are the bases for the latency of the underlying tendencies to sensual lust (*kāmarāga*) and conceit (*māna*).
Furthermore, in the Sutta it is said: "Here, friend Visākha, a bhikkhu reflects thus: 'When indeed shall I abandon mental distress?
Having reflected thus, he abandons aversion by means of that [reflection]; no underlying tendency to aversion lies latent therein.
Thus, having generated a mental distress based on renunciation, having suppressed it, and having exerted energy, [he abandons it] by means of the path of non-returning.

This was said with reference to the total eradication of aversion (*paṭigha*). For there is no such thing as the abandoning of aversion by means of aversion itself, nor the abandoning of mental distress (*domanassa*) by means of mental distress.

However, it should be understood that because all suffering here is a basis for the arising of aversion, it is called "the place where the underlying tendency to aversion lies latent. This is indeed a teaching given in its direct, non-figurative sense (*nippariyāya*).

But that is a teaching by way of a method (*pariyāyadesanā*). And having established it thus, with reference to the eradication by the path of non-returning (*anāgāmimagga*) of the underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*)—which was previously suppressed by the first jhāna and remained suppressed in that state—it is said: "Quite secluded...
he enters and dwells in the first jhāna; by means of that, he abandons lust; no underlying tendency to lust underlies there."

Thus it was said. Having likewise suppressed the underlying tendency to ignorance (avijjānusaya) that is suppressed by the fourth jhāna, with reference to its total eradication by the path of Arahantship, it is said: "With the abandoning of pleasure... [etc. ...he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna;
by means of that he abandons ignorance, and the underlying tendency to ignorance does not underlie therein. For indeed, it is not [the case that it is abandoned]...
It can be said that the underlying tendency to ignorance (*avijjānusaya*) does not underlie the equanimity of the fourth mundane jhāna in any way, because it has been stated:

"In all phenomena included within the category of personal existence (*sakkāya*), the underlying tendency to ignorance underlies them. Therefore, while the equanimity of the fourth jhāna is indeed the basis for the underlying tendency to ignorance, the sorrow based on renunciation (*nekkhammassita-domanassa*) is not *not* the basis for the underlying tendency to aversion (*paṭighānusaya*); thus, that tendency also underlies it there.
This should be understood. For here, "underlying tendency" (*anusaya*) is not spoken of in the sense of a state of lying latent;

nor is it according to the method stated in the Suttantas, because [here] it refers to the fact that the path which eradicates it is its direct opposite and possesses a powerful supporting condition (*upanissaya*).

And in this context, when there is a basis for an underlying tendency in an object, all greed—except for attachment to existence (*bhavarāga*)—is the underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*).
It is not possible to say so. For even when associated with the underlying tendency of views (*diṭṭhānusaya*) that underlies painful feeling and the form and formless realms, greed is simply greed;
it is not the underlying tendency of sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*). If it were so, then its locus would have to be stated just as that of the underlying tendency of views is.
However, the locus of the underlying tendency is defined by its inclination toward that [object] through the influence of one's disposition (*ajjhāsaya*).

It has been said: Just as when one regards desirable forms and so forth, or pleasant feeling, as either unobtained or as not being obtained, or as previously obtained but now past, ceased, vanished, and transformed—the aversion that arises functions solely by way of striking against suffering;
thus, suffering alone is the locus for its underlying tendency (*anusaya*).

It has been stated that it is not clung to; likewise, even when associated with the underlying tendency of views (*diṭṭhānusaya*) arising through the mode of misapprehension regarding suffering and so forth, greed (*lobha*) proceeds solely by way of attachment to pleasure. Thus, only the pair of pleasant and neutral [feeling] is stated to be its locus for the underlying tendency (*anusaya-ṭṭhāna*).

Consequently, there is no contradiction in all greed—excluding the lust for existence (*bhavarāga*)—being the underlying tendency of sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*), since they reside in one and the same [locus].
And they become attached to and repelled by an object. In this regard, attachment has a tendency toward pleasure, while aversion has a tendency toward pain;

thus, there is a difference in the basis for their underlying tendencies (*anusaya*). And having established this, [the question arises]: "Where the underlying tendency of sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) underlies, does the underlying tendency of aversion (*paṭighānusaya*) also underlie there? The answer is: "No."
Thus it is said. However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, after stating that grief arises toward the two types of feeling and toward desirable objects, it says:
"That is merely grief itself; it is not the underlying tendency of aversion (*paṭighānusaya*).

Therefore, just as in that case aversion is not the underlying tendency of aversion, so too, greed co-arising with the underlying tendency of views (*diṭṭhānusaya*) that arises toward suffering and so forth—
It is understood simply that the underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) does not exist.

As for what was said—that "it is merely grief (*domanassa*), and not the underlying tendency to aversion (*paṭighānusaya*)"—here, the phrase "not the underlying tendency to aversion" should be understood to mean that the underlying tendency to aversion is absent.
For there is no possibility of suspecting that grief itself possesses the nature of the underlying tendency to aversion.

The teaching might appear to be confused; for it would seem as though the arising of existence-taint (bhavarāga) in the two types of feeling within the sense-sphere (kāmadhātu) was stated merely by way of making those feelings its object.

Therefore, the intention is that this teaching was formulated precisely to show the distinction [of bhavarāga] by means of its specific object, since there is no difference in its co-nascent feeling (sahajātavedanā).
The commentary on the section on the bases of arising is finished.
Great Section 1:
Commentary on the Section on Latent Tendencies (*anusaya*).

3. "Underlies" (*anuseti*) and "arises" (*uppajjati*): these conventional expressions regarding the present should be understood in terms of their occurrence and cessation. For it is only by means of the Path that the cessation and interruption of the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) occurs, and not prior to that.
20. "Nor do they arise in a single place, nor do they take a single phenomenon as their object":

here, by the former [phrase], arising within a single thought-moment (*cittuppāda*) is excluded; by the latter, [arising] in relation to a single object (*ārammaṇa*) is excluded—this is the distinction. [This concludes] the section on the person and the world-sphere (*puggalokāsavāra*).
In the reverse order, the state of those various individuals not being subject to this or that underlying tendency (anusaya) should be understood by way of their natural abandonment [of it]:

"In three types of persons, regarding painful feeling, the underlying tendency to sensual lust (kāmarāgānusaya) does not underlie there, yet the underlying tendency to aversion (paṭighānusaya) does not fail to underlie there for them; for those same persons, in the form element..."

The statement, "In the formless realm and in the unconditioned (apariyāpanna), neither the latent tendency of sensual lust nor the latent tendency of aversion underlies those [states]," was said with reference to the fact that, by their very nature, suffering and so forth are not the basis for the underlying tendencies of sensual lust and so on.
Likewise, the statement, "In both types of persons, in all cases, neither the latent tendency of sensual lust nor the latent tendency of aversion underlies," was said for the same reason.

By the abandoning of the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*). Here, according to the first method, having considered the occasion, it is stated that there is no underlying tendency for those underlying tendencies existing in a person;
according to the second method, having considered the person, it is stated that there is no occasion for the occasion—namely, the sense-sphere element (*kāmadhātu*) and so forth.
The commentary on the section on underlying tendencies is concluded.

2. Commentary on the Section on Those Possessing Latent Tendencies (Sānusayavāravaṇṇanā) §§66–131. In the sections on "Possessing Latent Tendencies," "Abandoning," and "Full Understanding," the person (*puggala*) is spoken of as "possessing latent tendencies," "abandoning," and "fully understanding.

Regarding the person, the phrase "possessing latent tendencies" in this life may be stated either by way of a specific state of existence (*bhava*) or by way of this specific latent tendency of sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*).

"Is one with underlying tendencies (sānusaya) in this [feeling] or in others?"—thus, there is no such thing as being "with underlying tendencies" or "without underlying tendencies" based on a distinction between the underlying tendency to existence (bhavānusaya).
Likewise, the claim that "one is with the underlying tendency of sensual lust (kāmarāgānusaya) in two types of feeling, but without that tendency in painful feeling" is also not the case.
For feelings do not belong to the person; rather, they belong to the underlying tendencies themselves. As for the underlying tendency...

Each respective occasion for a latent tendency (*anusaya*) is the cause for a particular person’s state of having that latent tendency, as well as the sign for the abandonment and full understanding of that specific tendency;
conversely, an occasion where there is no latent tendency is the cause for the state of being free from latent tendencies and so forth.

Therefore, in the sections concerning these occasions, instead of using a locative designation (*bhummavacana*), the ablative form "from this or that" (*yato tato*) is used in the sense of a sign (*nimitta*).
It is said [in this way], or else in the sections on the full understanding of abandoning, it refers specifically to the sense of "non-appropriation" (*apādāna*).
For "abandoning" (*pajahana*) and "full understanding" (*parijānana*) consist in causing the departure from, and the destruction of, [defilements] from their respective locations.

In that context, "from which" (*yato*) means from whichever location of latent tendencies (*anusaya*), or conversely, from whichever location there is no latent tendency (*an-anusaya*). This refers precisely to the presence or absence of latent tendencies.

Indeed, for the purpose of demonstrating the state of being the basis (*nimitta*) and the point of departure (*apādāna*), in such passages as "In the fine-material element (*rūpadhātu*) and the immaterial element (*arūpadhātu*), one is possessed of the underlying tendency (*anusaya*) to conceit (*mānānusaya*);
[there] one abandons it," and "In painful feeling (*dukkhā vedanā*), one is not possessed of the underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*);
[there] one does not abandon it," the fine-material element and so forth are indicated precisely by means of the locative case (*bhummavacana*).

In the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), however, since the locus of the underlying tendency (*anusaya*) was shown in its specific form through the answer to the fourth question, the meaning of that [locus] was clarified even in the first question by stating "from which" (*yato*) as the locus of the underlying tendency.
Then, in order to show the literal meaning of this term "from which," it was stated: "one who has an underlying tendency because of the arisen underlying tendency of sensual lust."

That appears as if it were written by mistake. For one cannot say that "one who has latent tendencies" (*sānusaya*) refers to one with a latent tendency already arisen, using the ablative case (*nissakkavacana*) in reference to the place where the arising occurs. This is because the unconditioned (*apariyāpanna*) states are not places where latent tendencies arise;
thus, it is seen exactly as it stands. However, the meaning here should be understood in this way: "from which [place] having arisen" means "from which, having arisen."
"It must be so" (*bhavitabbaṃ, tena*); thus, the ablative case is employed in reference to the place of arising.

Likewise, [the phrase] "by that which arises among all phenomena" (*sabbadhammesu uppajjanakena*). Since non-arising is not desired when the negation of arising has not been made, one indeed causes it to depart from the state of non-arising by means of that which has attained the state of arising among all phenomena.
As for the term *sabbattha*, it means "from all places" (*sabbaṭṭhānato*).
This meaning is not impossible; for grammarians maintain that the letter *ttha* can signify a location other than the earth.
The commentary on the section on "With Underlying Tendencies" is concluded.
3. Commentary on the Section on "Abandoning."

132–197. In the section on abandoning (*pajahana-vāra*), one cannot state with certainty that "he abandons those [latent tendencies] by which the latent tendency of sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) and the others are abandoned with a remainder," because there exists the possibility of not abandoning them.

Therefore, regarding this certainty, it is stated that only he who abandons them without remainder abandons them. Consequently: "Is it the case that whoever abandons the latent tendency of conceit (*mānānusaya*) also abandons the latent tendency of sensual lust?"

"No," it is said. However, because the phrase "doubt" asks merely about the act of abandoning and does not provide a definitive conclusion, it is stated—with reference to abandonment as it actually exists—"He who abandons the underlying tendency to sensual lust, does he abandon the underlying tendency to conceit?
He abandons that which is associated with it. In the reverse order, however, "he does not abandon" refers to the absence of abandonment.

Thus, having been determined by both the words of certainty and the words of doubt, and having been questioned, those for whom there is no abandoning—meaning those who abandon without remainder—are excluded;

the rest are said not to abandon simply because of the presence of non-abandoning, and it should not be understood that they are excluded solely on account of an abandonment that actually exists. [This applies to] one who possesses the path of the non-returner...

Regarding the statement, "With the exception of the one at the eighth stage, the remaining persons do not abandon the underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) and do not abandon the underlying tendency to doubt (*vicikicchānusaya*)," it is said in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) that "the worldling (*puthujjana*) does not abandon them due to the absence of full understanding through abandoning (*pahānapariññā*),
while the others [do not abandon them] because those underlying tendencies have already been abandoned."

In this regard, although for some there is the underlying tendency of doubt (*vicikicchānusaya*) and for others both [tendencies], and thus there is the state of their having been abandoned, nevertheless, for stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*) and the rest, the abandonment of the underlying tendency of doubt is not the cause for the non-abandonment of both.
Therefore, it cannot be said that they "do not abandon" because of its being abandoned; rather, [this applies] to the underlying tendency of sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) as well.
The phrase "they do not abandon" is stated for the purpose of showing that those individuals are included by way of this definitive determination;
therefore, no further reason needs to be given for that. However, a reason must be given for the doubt regarding what was asked.

If that were so, would it not have to be said that "the rest [of the fetters] are abandoned because of the abandoning of that underlying tendency"? It should not be said that "one who [abandons] the underlying tendency to sensual lust..."

Having rejected [the proposition] with the words, "One who does not abandon [the latent tendency of sensual desire] does not abandon the latent tendency of views and the latent tendency of doubt," and having been asked [a follow-up question], since a corresponding answer must be given regarding the latent tendencies of views and doubt, it is said:
"Because those latent tendencies have been abandoned"; thus, because those latent tendencies of views and doubt have been abandoned, they are comprised within the category of "doubt."
The meaning should be understood as "they do not abandon the underlying tendencies.
The commentary on the section on abandoning is finished.
5. Commentary on the Section on What Has Been Abandoned.

264–274. It is said with reference to the *anuloma* (direct order) that in the section on "abandoned" (*pahīna*), the teaching is undertaken solely from the standpoint of those established in the fruits (*phalaṭṭha*).

For in the *paṭiloma* (inverse order), the teaching is also taken from the standpoint of worldlings (*puthujjana*). Furthermore, by the general expression "solely from the standpoint of those established in the fruits," it indicates that those who possess the path (*maggasamaṅgī*) are not included;
for [the abandonment of] the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) occurs in a single moment of consciousness for those possessing the path, as they are the absolute antidotes to them.

No underlying tendency (anusaya) is capable of arising, nor has it been rendered incapable of arising; therefore, they are not included in the sections concerning the abandonment or arising of underlying tendencies. 275–296.

In the section on the bases (okāsa), each respective underlying tendency is abandoned when it has been rendered incapable of arising within its own specific base, and it is unabandoned when that state has not been attained.
Thus, the expressions "abandoned" and "unabandoned" indicate only those respective bases. Therefore...

It is stated that in a non-open space (*anokāsa*), both [the robe and the person] must be returned. "In a common place, it is said to be abandoned along with him" means that in a shared location, it is abandoned together with him;
it does not mean it is abandoned at the same time. The commentary on the section concerning abandonment is finished.
7. Explanation of the Section on Elements (Dhātuvāra), §§ 332–340.
"Lying down following along with the continuum" means that they lie down by following along within whichever continuum they have not been abandoned;

the sense is that they lie down in the state of being ready for arising by virtue of their un-abandoned status within that continuum. It is precisely because they are capable of arising [that they are said to lie down].
For it is appropriate here as well that [phenomena] arise having obtained a corresponding cause.
Furthermore, in this context, the six negations such as "not from the sense-sphere" (*kāmadhātu*) are not intended as exclusions specifying the realms;

for if one were to say, "for one who has passed away from the sense-sphere and is not being reborn in the sense-sphere," etc., it would not be understood that "one is being reborn in this very [realm]."

Therefore, having first applied the formulation based on that [root] as: "for one who has passed away from the sense-sphere (*kāmadhātu*) and is being reborn in the sense-sphere, the fine-material sphere (*rūpadhātu*), or the immaterial sphere (*arūpadhātu*)," the subsequent formulations beginning with "for one not being reborn in the sense-sphere" were then made in successive order.
For in this way, by means of the terms "sense-sphere" and so forth, only those elements already mentioned are grasped, and nothing else.

It is understood. Just as it was stated in the section on latent tendencies (*anusaya*) that "the meaning of the word 'they lie latent' is taken as 'they arise'," there too, one cannot take "they arise" as referring merely to that which is currently arising, because of such statements as:
"In one for whom the latent tendency of sensual lust lies latent, does the latent tendency of aversion also lie latent? Yes. Furthermore, [it refers to] the state of not being abandoned.
The meaning "they arise with reference to [a particular object]" is what is understood there; here too, that is not inappropriate.

"Bhaṅgā" means they are to be broken, i.e., they are to be made twofold. But surely, there is no underlying tendency (anusaya) such that for one in whom it arises, it both underlies and does not underlie;
thus, why should they be made twofold? Why, then, is it said right there: "How many underlying tendencies are there as breakages? There are no underlying tendencies as breakages"?

The answers to the questions have been given. Is it not the case that doubt is not appropriate when there is no other alternative? No, it is not inappropriate, because the absence of the "breakdown" (bhaṅga) is not understood unless it is stated that "there are no breakdowns of underlying tendencies" (anusaya).
The commentary on the Section on Elements (Dhātuvāra) is finished.
The commentary on the *Anusaya-yamaka* is concluded.
8. The *Citta-yamaka*:
Commentary on the Section of Enunciation.
1–62. In the commentary on the *Cittayamaka*, there are three pure (*suddhika*) great sections from the very beginning;

thus, these three great sections consist of both mixed (*missaka*) and pure states, such as those with lust (*sarāga*) and the wholesome (*kusala*), etc. Among them, the meaning is that the pure ones come first.
Within each of the mixed states—namely, the minds mixed with lust and so forth—there are three great sections each, which are stated in their respective places.
Having combined them, it is said, "The sixteen sections on persons," and so forth; they were not stated without interruption.

Because each question is presented through the conjunction of arising and cessation with the present and future times—as in, "For whom consciousness arises but does not cease, for that one consciousness will cease but will not arise"—it is called "the section on the blending of arising, cessation, and time."
Thus it was said. In this manner, the respective names of the remaining sections should be understood by following the text (*pāḷi*).
The commentary on the section of the summary (*uddesavāra*) is finished.
The commentary on the section of the exposition (*niddesavāra*).
63. Regarding the phrase "referring to the mind of one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) of such a kind":

this should be understood as having been stated with reference to a person possessing the final consciousness at the moment of arising (*uppādakkhaṇa*), taking it for granted that such a mind is indeed intended here.

As for the statement "even the final consciousness of an Arahant does not arise and does not cease," this was said specifically with reference to one who possesses [that consciousness] at the moment of dissolution (*bhaṅgakkhaṇa*).

65–82. In the second answer to the question in the Chapter on Arising (*Uppādavāra*): "At the moment of the dissolution of consciousness, for those who have attained cessation, and for non-percipient beings, their consciousness had arisen, but their consciousness does not arise.

Herein, regarding the statement "at the moment of the dissolution of consciousness, their consciousness had arisen," [it means that] for all [beings], consciousness is only present by way of the moment (*khaṇapaccuppanna*).
The meaning stated is: "Because it has passed beyond the moment of its arising, it is said to have 'arisen' (uppajjittha).

Regarding the statement that at the moment of consciousness's arising, "that consciousness both has arisen and is arising," these two cannot be asserted in this way because, although it has attained arising, it has not yet passed away; thus it is "arising. For [this] is not the case in the present moment.

“There was arising” is a conventional expression used for the past. If that were the case, then regarding the statement, “Whatever consciousness has arisen, that consciousness arises,” one would not say “No,” but rather it should be analyzed.
Likewise, regarding the statement, “Whatever consciousness arises, that consciousness has arisen,” one would not say “No,” but rather it should be answered “Yes. [Regarding] “of consciousness...”
The phrase "at the moment of dissolution" refers to a person possessing a mind that is currently dissolving; for such a person, past mind has arisen, but no present mind arises.
The phrase "at the moment of arising of the mind" refers to a person possessing a mind that is currently arising;
for him too, past mind has arisen, and that mind is indeed arising. Thus it is in this context.
The meaning should be understood as follows: for "consciousness" (*citta*) is a general term that applies to both the singular and the plural according to the specific instance grasped.
In the passage, "Or, for whom consciousness will arise, for him does consciousness arise?
At the moment of the dissolution of consciousness," the phrase "for whom consciousness will arise" refers specifically to the person already determined by that very definition.
"At the moment of the mind's dissolution"—thus, in all instances, the restriction should be understood as being by way of definitive determination (*sanniṭṭhāna*).
The sections on "arisen and arising" and "ceased and ceasing" are taught and explained without any difference in the three sections beginning with the "person-section" (*puggalavāra*).
Therein, in the person-section, referring generally to any such person without distinction, it says: "arisen and arising," and so forth.

It has been stated that in the section on phenomena (*dhamma-vāra*), it is mind alone; whereas in the section on persons and phenomena (*puggala-dhamma-vāra*), it is both person and mind—this distinction should be observed here.
83. In the section on the "time elapsed" (*atikkanta-kāla-vāra*), because this belongs to the section on persons, the person is questioned;
therefore, the answer must be given in terms of the person alone. Just as by the question "whose mind arose," no person is excluded, so too...
"Is there no person whose consciousness, as it arises, has not already transcended moment by moment—that is, transcended the time [of arising]?
By this definitive statement, no one is excluded. For there is no such person for whom the moment of the arising of consciousness has not passed;
and yet, those whose consciousness has passed the moment of ceasing are not non-existent. Thus, the first question is to be answered: "Yes."

It may be so for the second and third [questions]. But the fourth should be answered thus: "At the moment of dissolution of the final consciousness, their consciousness has not transcended the moment of dissolution, yet their consciousness has not transcended the moment of arising;
for others, however, their consciousness has not transcended both the moment of dissolution and the moment of arising."
If that were so, why would the mind alone be analyzed in all instances without being relinquished [as a separate category]?

Because the person is defined by means of the mind. For, by the expression "the time has passed" due to the lapse of a moment, the person is said to have a mind that has passed the moment of arising (*uppādakkhaṇa*)—that is, a past mind—and in that context, the former [mind] does not refer to the moment of dissolution (*bhaṅgakkhaṇa*).

The classification of persons—beginning with "one who has transgressed" and "one who has not transgressed"—is shown by way of demonstrating, for that consciousness by means of which the person is defined, the transgression or non-transgression at each respective moment;
thus, in all the answers, it is consciousness itself that is analyzed. Alternatively, it is not merely a distinction of phenomena (dhamma) here...
The person was questioned, but rather it was the mind distinguished by the person; therefore, it should be understood that it is the mind itself that was answered.
Even if the question has the person as its primary focus, or even if it has the mind as its primary focus, in either case, the answer to the second question should have been "Yes" (*āmantā*).
Yet, instead of saying that, [the Master] stated that because the moment of cessation has passed, it is a time already elapsed.

It should be understood that the phrase "past consciousness" is stated for the purpose of showing that there is no "existence" (atthi) in the case of what is currently occurring, as there is in the case of having transcended a time by passing beyond the moment of arising. Regarding the expression "whose consciousness is not arising," the meaning is:
whose consciousness does not exist having passed beyond each and every moment of arising—that is, having transcended the time [of arising]. This same method applies to...
The same applies here to the phrase "ceasing.
In the mixed sections (114–116), the question— "For one whose mind with lust arises but does not cease,
will that mind cease but not arise?"— and the answer, "No," are shown in the Aṭṭhakathā.

In the Pāḷi, however, because it is stated in the laying down of the matrix (*mātikā*) as: “For whom a mind accompanied by lust arises and does not cease, for him that mind accompanied by lust will cease and will not arise,” the questions in the answer (*vissajjana*) are likewise extracted according to the sense of certainty and doubt regarding minds mixed with lust and so forth, starting from the moment of arising of the final mind accompanied by lust: “At the moment of arising of the final mind accompanied by lust...”
“For them, a lustful consciousness arises and does not cease; it will cease and will not arise.
For others, at the moment of the arising of a lustful consciousness, a lustful consciousness arises and does not cease;
it will both cease and arise. In this manner, the answer is for the most part identical to that of the pure section (*suddhikavāra*).
"Having been made to be done," it is understood as "abbreviated.
The commentary on the section of the exposition is finished.
The commentary on the *Cittayamaka* (The Pairs on Consciousness) is finished.
9. Dhammayamakaṃ 1.
Paṇṇattivāra: Explanation of the Section on Enumeration (Uddesavāravaṇṇanā)
1–16. Regarding the commentary on the *Dhammayamaka*:

having established the matrix (*mātikā*) of wholesome and other phenomena—meaning that they were not taught here in the same manner as they are taught in the *Mūlayamaka*, nor in the alternative way they are taught in the *Khandhayamaka* and so forth by grouping them under categories such as "the five aggregates"—but rather [in the manner of] the matrix for wholesome and other phenomena beginning with "wholesome and unwholesome phenomena" (*kusalākusalā dhammā*).
The *mātikā* (matrix); the meaning is that it has been taught here by placing that [matrix] at the beginning.
The commentary on the section on the enumeration (*uddesavāra*) is finished.
2. Commentary on the section on occurrence (*pavattivāra*).

33–34. Regarding the answer to the question, "When wholesome states arise for someone, do indeterminate states arise for that person?", it is stated in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā): "And 'indeterminate' is said by way of mind-originated matter.
However, in this present inquiry, matter originated by kamma and so forth is also obtained; that [matter] is, moreover, [discussed] in the answer to the reverse section.
"For all those passing away, at the moment of the cessation of consciousness during the course of existence, and for those in the formless realm at the moment of the arising of unwholesome states,
neither wholesome nor indeterminate states arise. Here,

having not included the matter originated by karma and so forth that is actually arising at the moment of the cessation of consciousness during the course of existence, [the text says] "neither indeterminate states..."
Because it is stated that "states do not arise," it is only mind-originated matter (*cittasamuṭṭhānarūpa*) that is intended here.

Some say that regarding matter originated by kamma and so forth, there is neither an affirmation nor a negation; likewise, it is with reference specifically to mind-originated matter that it is stated:
"When wholesome states arise for someone, do indeterminate states cease for him? No."

However, it is not possible to assert this [that matter arises at the moment of the mind's dissolution], because such claims are refuted by canonical texts stating that even for matter originated by kamma, there is arising at the moment of its own arising and cessation at the moment of its own cessation, and so forth. And as for those who say:
"Just as in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, in the discussion on cessation, it is said: 'At the moment of the stream-entry path, [the aggregates] born... [and so on].

In such passages as, "All phenomena, with the exception of mind-originated matter, are fading away (virāga), have fading away as their object, have fading away as their domain, are produced by fading away,
and are established in fading away," it is stated "with the exception of mind-originated matter" rather than "with the exception of matter" because mind-born matter is dependent on the mind;
likewise here too, [it is so stated] because it is dependent on the mind.

"It is said that only mind-born matter [is meant]," but that is not so. For those things for which the path of stream-entry (*sotāpattimagga*) is the co-nascent condition (*sahajātapaccaya*), and in which there is the possibility of [confusing] dispassion (*virāga*) and so forth, those phenomena co-nascent with the path of stream-entry are stated therein as "phenomena born at the moment of the path of stream-entry.
Indeed, the expression "born at the moment of the path of stream-entry" refers to their being born within the path.

It illuminates [the meaning]: kamma-born matter and the others do not deserve to be designated as "arisen at the moment of the path" when they arise outside the path, because they lack the state of being co-nascent conditions for that [path-consciousness] at the moment of the stream-entry path.
Therefore, in order to exclude them from among the phenomena co-nascent with the path at the moment of the path, it is said:
"excluding mind-originated matter. However, here [in this context], wholesome and other such phenomena...

For whichever person and in whichever location [mental] states arise and cease, the dependence or independence of the arising and ceasing of those indeterminate (abyākata) phenomena upon wholesome (kusala) and other [unwholesome or neutral] factors has been touched upon;
and it is not that matter born of kamma (kammaja-rūpa) and so forth is not indeterminate.
Therefore, regarding the arising and ceasing in the person or location grasped by way of such determination:
Among those [factors] that exist, they should be understood as indeterminate; among those that do not exist, they should be denied.

Furthermore, it can be said that those which are not dependent on mind are not included here as "indeterminate," because there is mention of the arising and ceasing of [the aggregates] for those who have attained cessation and for non-percipient beings.

In the fourth question, regarding the phrase "at the moment of arising of an unwholesome or indeterminate consciousness during the course of existence" (*pavatte akusalābyākatacittassa uppādakkhaṇe*), this refers to: "For whomsoever, moreover, the indeterminate..."
This was said with reference to those possessing the moment of arising of unwholesome or indeterminate consciousnesses in the five-aggregate plane,
and of indeterminate consciousness alone in the four-aggregate plane, as determined by the definitive conclusion [of the text] "mental phenomena arise. Thus, in all instances,
the distinction should be understood by way of such a definitive conclusion.

79. It was stated, “of that which has arisen by means of a single adverting [consciousness]”; however, this characteristic—namely, “at the moment of arising, unwholesome states will not arise for them, but wholesome states do not fail to arise for them”—is indeed obtainable even for that which has arisen in the javana-sequences prior to that [adverting consciousness] by means of various adverting [consciousnesses].
Therefore, it possesses a characteristic identical to this characteristic.

It should be understood that by this very conclusion regarding the state of future wholesomeness— namely, "at the moment of arising of that consciousness immediately after which they will attain the supreme path"— that state of having identical characteristics is illustrated.
This same method applies to the beginning of the sections on the state of past unwholesomeness and the state of past indeterminate states, where it says, "in the second unwholesome [consciousness]."
Regarding the phrase "in the second consciousness" and similar instances:
just as in the section on development (bhāvanāvāra), by means of the final path of development which abandons [defilements], the earlier abandonments through development are also shown;
so too here, each [consciousness] is shown by its respective beginning and end.

100. Regarding the statement, "At the moment of the dissolution of unwholesome states in the five-constituent existence (pañcavokāra), both unwholesome states and indeterminate states cease," it is understood that this refers to the sixteenth consciousness from the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhicitta*), or even to the subsequent existence-attachment consciousness (*bhavanikanticitta*);
it is understood that there is no [cessation] prior to that.
The commentary on the section on the process of existence (pavattivāra) is finished.
The commentary on the Dhamma-pairings (dhammayamaka) is finished.
10. The Faculties-Pairings (indriyayamaka).
1. The Section on Designations (Paṇṇattivāra). Commentary on the Section of Enumeration (Uddesavāravaṇṇanā):

In the Vibhaṅga of the *Indriyayamaka*, the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) is not indicated immediately after the mind-faculty (*manindriya*), but rather immediately after the male-faculty (*purisindriya*).
It was taught in the Sutta according to the order of exposition: "Bhikkhus, there are these three faculties. Which three? The female faculty, the male faculty, and the life faculty.

For in the section on the process of existence (*pavattivāra*), the life faculty is the protector of the pleasure faculty and the others—whether born of karma or not born of karma—which arise exclusively within the course of existence, during the moments of death and rebirth-linking.

It should be understood that for those [factors] arising from karma that are currently occurring, the pairs of dyads rooted in them must be stated by way of death, rebirth-linking, and the course of existence. However,
among the faculties beginning with the eye-faculty and ending with the masculinity-faculty, excluding the mind-faculty— which is not rooted in anything else—
the remaining ones rooted in those [other faculties] should be stated only by way of death and rebirth-linking, as in the *Āyatana-yamaka*.
Therefore, the life-faculty (jīvitindriya) is not mentioned among them, but is listed at the end.
The commentary on the section of enumeration (uddesavāra) is finished.
Commentary on the section of exposition (niddesavāra).

94. Regarding the phrase "the female is the female-faculty" (*itthī itthindriyan*): since there is no such thing as a "female" as an intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), yet the apprehension of a "female" does not fail to occur by depending upon phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth;
therefore, although the apprehension of a "female" is non-existent, it is treated as if it were existent because it proceeds by way of that [conventional] apprehension.
Thus, rather than saying "it does not exist," it is said "it is not" (*no*) with reference to that which is so apprehended. Regarding pleasure (*sukha*)...

And by making a distinction between pleasure and mental joy (*somanassa*), and between pain and mental grief (*domanassa*) through the very statement that "pleasure is mental joy" and "pain is mental grief," this specific difference is indeed grasped:
that pleasant feeling other than mental joy is pleasure, and painful feeling other than mental grief is pain.
Therefore, regarding the passage "Pleasure is the pleasure faculty; pain is the pain faculty," it is stated: "Yes, it is so."

140. In the section on the pure faculties (*suddhindriya*), regarding the statement "the eye is a faculty," it is said "yes" because here the divine eye and the eye of wisdom are both considered the faculty of wisdom (*paññindriya*). The remainder, "the ear," refers specifically to the stream of craving (*taṇhāsota*).
The commentary on the section of the exposition (*niddesavāra*) is concluded.
2. Commentary on the Section on Occurrence (*pavattivāra*).

186. In the section on occurrence (*pavattivāra*), the mind-faculty (*manindriya*) is enumerated here according to the method stated in the Sutta: "Bhikkhus, there are these six faculties. Which six? The eye-faculty... [etc. ...the body-faculty, and the mind-faculty.

This mind-faculty, as it occurs during death, rebirth-linking, and the course of existence, comes into association with all [minds] born of kamma and not born of kamma; however, it does not do so in the same way as the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*).
It is to be grasped by means of dependence on other phenomena; it is primary merely because it is the precursor.

Therefore, like a ridge-pole among rafters, it is placed at the end and joined as the meeting place for all the faculties. Having grasped the occurrence in those things rooted in the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) and so forth, when they have passed away, [the question is asked]:
"Does the pleasure-faculty (*sukhindriya*) arise in one in whom the life-faculty arises? [The answer is: "In all [of them]."
“For those being reborn, at the moment of the arising of a consciousness dissociated from the pleasure faculty during the course of existence,
the life faculty arises for them, but the pleasure faculty does not arise for them; at the moment of the arising of a consciousness associated with the pleasure faculty,
both the life faculty and the pleasure faculty arise for them,” and so forth, [regarding] the faculties of pleasure, pain, and mental grief.

Connection is obtained with the supramundane faculties; likewise, there are the methods based on those [faculties], such as: "When the faculty of pleasure arises in someone, does the faculty of pain arise in that same person?

No. However, connection with those arising only during the course of existence (pavatti), and the methods based on those, refers to the mental joy faculty (somanassindriya) and the others occurring during death, rebirth-linking, and the course of existence.

It should be understood that [these cases] were not mentioned because they are already evident through the method based on the life-faculty and the other methods. As for what was stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*:
"‘Among those with eyes but without mental joy’ refers to the four great resultant rebirth-linkings accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhā-sahagata*)";
this was said by way of illustrating rebirth-linking with eyes but devoid of mental joy.

It should be understood that this is what was stated. For no restriction was made to "only four"; therefore, the limited-sphere resultant and fine-material-sphere rebirth-linkings, which possess characteristics identical to those, are also shown by it.
Therein, among the sense-sphere rebirths, an illustration is given by means of the four great resultants because of their identity with rebirth-linking accompanied by mental joy (*somanassa*);
thus, just as those with rebirth-linking accompanied by mental joy do not lack eyes, so too are those with the other great resultant rebirth-linkings.

This meaning has been shown. Furthermore, by demonstrating that those born from a womb who possess eyes and so forth necessarily possess them at the moment of rebirth-linking, it is shown that for those passing away while in the womb—before the eyes and other faculties have arisen—they possess rootless rebirth-linking, whereas those of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) who possess roots do possess eyes and so forth.
Indeed, with reference even to those born from a womb, it is said: "But for whomsoever the faculty of mental joy (somanassindriya) arises..."
Regarding the statement, "Does the eye-faculty arise?"—the answer is "Yes. This is shown in the *Āyatanayamaka* (The Pairs on the Bases) according to how it is logically consistent.

For there is no reason to exclude those conceived in the womb (*gabbhaseyyaka*) who are included by way of a definitive determination (*sanniṭṭhāna*), since they are indeed mentioned in such passages as, "of women who are without noses and who are being reborn," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "of those with equanimity but no eye," it should be understood that this is stated by way of rootless rebirth-linking; herein, it demonstrates both the rebirth-linking of the sense-sphere which possesses equanimity but lacks the eye, and the formless-sphere rebirth-linking which shares its characteristics.
Furthermore, in some manuscripts the reading "by way of rootless formless rebirth-linking" is found, and that alone is preferable.
For it is said therein: “In that [state], faith, mindfulness, and wisdom are entirely absent, but concentration and energy have not yet reached the status of faculties.
However, if concentration and energy do exist there, one cannot say they “have not reached the status of faculties,” as it is asked:
“Is concentration the faculty of concentration? “Yes. “Is energy the faculty of energy? “Yes.”
According to the word. And in the rootless rebirth-consciousness, just as there is a trace of concentration in the form of one-pointedness, there is no such trace of energy;

therefore, it might be said here: "For in that case, faith, energy, mindfulness, and wisdom are entirely absent, whereas one-pointedness is indeed a trace of concentration. However, the intended meaning here might be this: just as...

In certain other rootless consciousnesses (*ahetuka-citta*), concentration (*samādhi*) and energy (*vīriya*) have reached the status of faculties (*indriya*); yet here, concentration and energy do not reach the status of faculties.
Thus, by showing the very absence of the faculties of concentration and energy, he distinguishes this from the other rootless types.

In that context, although it should have been said, "but concentration and energy are not present," the addition of the word "faculties" (*indriya*) serves as a qualification for the term "concentration."

This was stated because of the actual existence [of these qualities] even in one who has not yet attained the state of the faculty of concentration (*samādhindriya*), and not because of a mere trace of energy (*vīriya*).

For a qualifier applies only to that which is to be qualified. However, in those manuscripts where the reading is, "In that case, faith, energy, mindfulness, and wisdom are absolutely absent," that alone is more excellent.
"Until the eye-faculty arises, there exists the state of being eyeless for those in the womb"—it is with this intention that he says:
"For those who possess causes but lack the eye, [this is] stated both with reference to those lying in the womb and to those in the formless realm.
However, it should be understood that even among those lying in the womb, none are found who will inevitably develop the eye-faculty.
The phrase "for those with eyes who are dissociated from knowledge" is stated by way of those in the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*) who possess a two-root rebirth-linking;
thus, here too, those with rootless rebirth-linking and those without eyes are indeed included.
Furthermore, the arising and cessation of the female and male faculties is shown by way of their general prevalence through the modes of rebirth and death; for at times these [faculties]...
Arising and cessation occur even during the course of existence, as in the case of the beings of the first eon and others. Herein,

among the sets of roots of faculties beginning with the masculinity faculty, because they are determined by the eye-faculty and so forth— which are grasped by the definitive conclusions in the first questions and which proceed according to rebirth and death—
even though the life-faculty and others are obtained by way of their course of existence, they are [treated] only by way of rebirth and death.
In the second set of questions, the apprehension [of the object] should be understood through the definitive conclusions. 190.

The material life-faculty belongs to the same category as the eye-faculty and so forth; it proceeds solely by way of death and rebirth-linking, because it demonstrates the arising and cessation of the continuity [of existence].
Therefore, he said: "At the moment of the arising of a consciousness dissociated from joy during the course of existence (*pavatta*)."

"It was said with reference to the immaterial life-faculty. Regarding the phrase "according to the occurrence of these and other five faculties," here the "occurrence according to what is obtained" (yathālābha) should be understood as follows:
for these [faculties] beginning with the life-faculty, it refers to their occurrence at the moments of death, rebirth-linking, and the course of existence;

and for the others, such as the eye-faculty and so on, it refers to their occurrence at the moments of death and rebirth-linking. However, in the phrase "this, moreover, is only for cutting," regarding that specific [faculty]:

When a question has been fully answered by providing the specific characteristics for each respective part, it should be understood that this is called the "cutting off of the final portion" once the answer has been given.
Or again: For whomsoever the faculty of mental joy (somanassindriya) does not arise, does the faculty of life (jīvitindriya) not arise for him?

For those being reborn without mental joy (*somanassa*), and at the moment of the arising of a consciousness dissociated from mental joy during the course of existence (*pavatta*), the faculty of mental joy does not arise;
yet it is not the case that the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) does not arise for them.

Herein, the non-mention of "those who have attained cessation" (*nirodhasamāpanna*) and "non-percipient beings" (*asaññasatta*) indicates that the material life-faculty shares the same logical status as the eye-faculty and the others.

It illuminates this point, for its arising must indeed be stated in relation to rebirth itself. In the phrase "for those being reborn without mental joy (*somanassa*)," the non-percipient beings (*asaññasatta*) are included;
however, those who have attained the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpanna*) are not mentioned because they do not exist in the mode of active occurrence (*pavatti*).
Furthermore, its non-arising (*anuppāda*) should also be stated only in relation to death and rebirth, not in relation to active occurrence. In the final section as well, "of all... [is said].
"For those passing away, at the moment of the cessation of the mind during its course, neither the faculty of mental joy nor the life-faculty arises.

Thus, by including non-percipient beings (asaññasatta) within the phrase "for all those passing away," and by way of their [ordinary] course of existence, both those [non-percipient beings] and those who have attained the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpanna) are not mentioned.
Furthermore, in the *Yassayatthaka* [section], those who have attained the attainment of cessation should not be shown.

The meaning is that it should not be accepted. For the expression “of those who have attained cessation” does not indicate a location like the expression “of non-percipient beings,” nor does it indicate a moment of non-arising for the faculty of mental joy and so forth like the expressions “at the moment of arising of a consciousness associated with equanimity” or “at the moment of dissolution of all consciousness,” but rather—
"Only illuminating the person. Regarding the distinction of past time:

at the moment of arising of the rebirth-consciousness of those born in the Pure Abodes (suddhāvāsa), both the faculty of mental joy (somanassindriya) and the life-faculty (jīvitindriya) had not arisen for them there. Herein, "at the moment of arising of the rebirth-consciousness" [is the phrase].

Why was it said that, just as in the passage, "For those being reborn in the Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsa) and for non-percipient beings (asaññasatta), neither the faculty of mental joy (somanassindriya) nor the faculty of mind (manindriya) had arisen there," one ought to say "for those being reborn" (*upapajjantānaṃ*) here as well? It should not be so stated.
For, by way of the faculties of mental joy and mind, those persons who are being reborn are possessed of the consciousness of rebirth (*upapatticitta*).
They do not exist in this way by virtue of the mental joy faculty (*somanassindriya*) and the life faculty (*jīvitindriya*).
For it is by virtue of the life faculty that those who are "being reborn" remain so for as long as the first material life faculty persists.
And at that time, from the second moment of consciousness onwards, it cannot be said that "the life faculty has not arisen," because of the immaterial life faculty.
Because it has arisen and then ceased, both [aspects] are indicated by the moment of arising (*uppādakkhaṇa*).
For just as the characteristic "it did not cease" is found in two moments of the rebirth-consciousness (*upapatticitta*), yet is indicated by the very first moment—
the cessation-moment (*bhaṅgakkhaṇa*)— of that rebirth-consciousness, so too should it be understood here.
When the distinction of future time arises, having made a determination, the very fact that another [factor] will arise is what is questioned.
In that regard, just as in the distinction of present time, because only that which is actually arising is grasped through the distinctions of determination and doubt, it is said:
"For whom the eye-faculty and so forth arise, for him who is being reborn, the life-faculty and so forth [arise]."
In the case of those asked about one who is "being reborn" (*upapajjantassa*), their arising is possible only at the very moment of rebirth and not elsewhere;
it is not so here, for regarding those asked about one who is "being reborn"— namely, "for whom the eye-faculty and so forth will arise,
for that person the life-faculty and so forth will arise"— their [arising] is not from anywhere other than rebirth.
Arising does not occur [simultaneously]; therefore it was said: "For whom the eye-faculty will arise, for that person will the joy-faculty arise?
Yes. And having established this, in the section on cessation it was also said:
"For whom the eye-faculty will cease, for that person will the joy-faculty cease? Yes. For indeed, for whom...

The eye-faculty will cease, but the faculty of mental joy will not cease for him—except in the case of one undergoing final existence (*pacchimabhavika*) with a rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) accompanied by equanimity.
For it is not possible that the cessation of the faculty of mental joy occurs prior to death for one who is being reborn.
Herein, in the first sets of questions, the basis for the matter to be asked is intended as a definitive conclusion (*sanniṭṭhāna*).

Just as one who possesses the faculties of both birth and arising—like myself—is a basis for a question even when the matter has already been resolved, so too, in the second questions, [the text] restricts [the meaning] solely to the sense of resolution;
it does not take the arising or cessation as a state of doubt, even though they were grasped in their own form merely by virtue of being future things to be asked about. For this reason...

And thus there is a restriction for the purpose of definitive conclusion; therefore it is said: "For whomsoever the faculty of mental joy (somanassindriya) will arise, will the faculty of the eye (cakkhundriya) arise for him? Yes. This same method applies to the section on cessation as well.
However, in the reverse order, whereas in the forward order the arising and cessation were expressed as "will arise" and "will cease" regarding the future, [here they are treated differently].
Because they are stated by way of their own form and are not stated in this manner, the arising and cessation of the faculty included under the term "doubt" in that context—
which were applied to those rooted in the eye-faculty and so forth even during its active occurrence— should not be applied here in the same way.
For while it is possible to apply arising and cessation as occurring after having transcended or before having reached [the state of] arising and cessation, it is not so [here].
Because non-arising and cessation do not arise by transcending or reaching non-arising and cessation—
since their occurrence does not come about by transcending or reaching what has not yet become and what is non-existent—

and because the absence of arising and cessation of what has not yet become was asked about in reverse order, therefore, for that non-existent state which lacks any specific distinction, there is the arising of present phenomena.

Because there is no connection with another time, just as in the case of the eye-faculty and so forth—wherein, due to the absence of arising and cessation, the basis for what is to be asked has been determined by way of a definitive conclusion—the non-arising and non-cessation of birth, death, arising, and cessation for those very same [faculties], as well as for life and so forth which have that as their basis, are asked by means of the term "doubt" (saṃsaya). Thus: "For whom the eye-faculty..."
It has been stated: "If it will not arise for someone, will the faculty of mental joy (somanassindriya) not arise for them?"—"Yes.
And: "If the eye-faculty (cakkhundriya) will not cease for someone, will the faculty of mental joy not cease for them?"—"Yes.

However, no answer has been given—unlike the case with the life-faculty (jīvitindriya), the equanimity-faculty (upekkhindriya), and so forth—such as: "For those who, having been reborn in the formless realm (arūpa), will attain final Nibbāna," and so on.
Regarding the statement, "For those who, having been reborn in the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), will attain final nibbāna, the nose-faculty (ghānindriya) will not arise,

but it is not the case that the mental-pleasure faculty (somanassindriya) will not arise for them," those here who will have a rebirth-linking accompanied by equanimity (upekkhā-paṭisandhika) are included by the latter portion of the statement:
"and those who, having been reborn in the immaterial sphere (arūpa), will attain final nibbāna."

They should be understood as having been stated specifically for those who will have a rebirth-linking with mental joy (*somanassa-patisandhika*), as they are included by virtue of having identical characteristics.
In the Commentary, regarding those initial manuscripts where it says, "In the section on the past and future, at the moment of the dissolution of the rebirth-consciousness of the Suddhāvāsa deities,
the mind-faculty (*manindriya*) did not arise," this is according to the method of transcending the moment of arising (*uppādakkhaṇa*), just as in the *Dhammayamaka*.
The statement "without grasping the meaning" is a scribal error. However, in those manuscripts where the reading appears as:
