"In the section on the present and the past, at the moment of the dissolution of the rebirth-consciousness of the Suddhāvāsa deities, the mind-faculty did not arise...
[etc. ...the meaning should be understood by way of its never having arisen previously in that existence," that alone is more excellent.
The commentary on the Section on Occurrence (*Pavattivāra*) is finished.
3. Commentary on the Section on Full Understanding (*Pariññāvāra*). 435–482.

In the Section on Full Understanding, [the factors] are mixed with the mundane and the indeterminate (*abyākata*), as well as those included within the Truth of Suffering (*dukkhasacca*) which are exclusively to be fully understood (*pariññeyya*).

Because they are mixed with mundane indeterminate states (*lokiya-abyākata*), it is stated that, by depending on those [mundane states], the mind-faculty (*manindriya*) and so forth are to be fully understood (*pariññeyya*), just like the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-khandha*) and the others.

If something is to be considered "to be fully understood" simply because it is mixed with what is to be fully understood, then why, in the *Dhammayamaka*, is it stated using the term "indeterminate" (*abyākata*) in such passages as:
"He who develops a wholesome state (*kusala-dhamma*) fully understands an indeterminate state"?

Having applied the pairs, why are they not stated? Just as there is an adherence to cultivation and abandoning regarding the wholesome and unwholesome—thinking, "I cultivate the wholesome, I abandon the unwholesome"—so too there is an adherence to full understanding regarding the aggregates and so forth, such as "the aggregate of feeling is impermanent, the base of mental phenomena is impermanent," and so on.
In that context, the aggregate of feeling and the others are to be fully understood as "impermanent" and so forth.
And these [mental states] should be fully understood by way of their nature as the aggregate of feeling and so forth, not by way of their being indeterminate (abyākata).
But why, in this context of the analysis of the truth of suffering (dukkhasacca), is only the abandonment of mental grief (domanassa) mentioned, and not its full understanding?
Is it not the case that the aggregates of feeling and so forth, which are included within the truth of suffering, exist by way of being either wholesome (kusala) or unwholesome (akusala)?

Are even wholesome and unwholesome states to be fully understood (*pariññeyya*)? True; however, while the status of being the feeling-aggregate (*vedanā-khandha*) and so forth exists even without the status of being either to be developed (*bhāvetabba*) or to be abandoned (*pahātabba*), the status of the faculty of mental grief (*domanassindriya*) does not exist without the status of being abandoned.
To show this distinction, it is only the state of being abandoned that is mentioned here for the faculty of mental grief, not because of an absence of the state of being fully understood.
It should be understood as follows: because the unwholesome (*akusala*) is to be abandoned exclusively, by the phrase "to be abandoned," it is excluded that it is not to be abandoned;

however, it should be understood that this does not exclude its being something to be fully understood (*pariññeyya*). As for the faculty of final knowledge (*aññindriya*), since its goal is to be developed (*bhāvetabba-niṭṭha*) and not a goal to be realized (*sacchikātabba-niṭṭha*), its status as something to be developed alone is what is grasped. The passage beginning with "Two persons" (*dve puggalā*)... [and so forth].
It should be understood that the passage beginning with “one does not fully understand the eye-faculty” was written out of sequence;
for after passing over the section based on the eye-faculty, this was stated under the section based on the grief-faculty:
“Two persons do not abandon the grief-faculty, yet they do not fail to develop the final-knowledge faculty.”
And here, there are nine persons: the worldling (*puthujjana*) and the eight noble ones (*ariya*). Among them, the worldling is twofold—by way of being capable or incapable.

In the passages where he is referred to as "the worldling," such as "six persons did not fully understand the faculty of the eye, nor did they abandon the faculty of mental grief," and so forth, he is understood without making a distinction [between the two types]. "Those worldlings who [have not yet attained] the path..."

In passages such as "they will obtain" and "five persons will fully understand the faculty of the eye and will abandon the faculty of mental grief," it is understood by taking [the possibility] after having analyzed it as being indeed capable.
In passages such as "and those worldlings who will not obtain the path," it is said that "three persons will not abandon the faculty of mental grief."
And in such passages as "they will not fully understand the eye-faculty," he is indeed incapable [of doing so]. Furthermore, the possessor of the highest fruit (aggaphala-samaṅgī) is twofold:
the one possessing the first fruit and the Arahant. This too is included—without distinction—in those places where the term "Arahant" occurs, such as in the passage:
"Three persons cultivated the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown' and abandoned the faculty of mental distress. [This applies to] whoever possesses the highest fruit...

In passages such as "he realizes," and in contexts like "three types of persons abandoned the faculty of mental grief (domanassindriya) but did not realize the faculty of one-who-has-known (aññātāvindriya)," the possessor of the first fruit is included by distinguishing [the categories].
In passages such as "he who desired to realize the highest fruit," the other [possessors] are included.
Having thus understood the distinction between these types of persons, one should reach a definitive conclusion in each respective case.
Having extracted the persons mentioned, the answer should be applied.
The commentary on the section on full understanding (*pariññāvāra*) is finished.
The commentary on the *Indriya-yamaka* (the Pairs on the Faculties) is finished.
The Root Commentary on the Yamaka-pakaraṇa is completed.
[Now begins] the Root Commentary on the Paṭṭhāna-pakaraṇa:
An Explanation of the Commencement of the Work.
They sport, play, and dally with the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*) and so forth; or they dwell among them.

By means of their capacity for victory, they desire to conquer adversaries. They engage in worldly affairs (*voharanti*), performing acts of honor such as granting and receiving positions of authority, as well as providing instruction on various matters.
They shine with a radiance attained through the power of their association with merit (*puñña*). And they [enjoy] the objects according to their desires.
They are called *devas* because they move without resistance, or because they are capable of accomplishing whatever they desire;

or because they are worthy of being approached (*devanīyā*) as a refuge and final resort by those seeking to overcome various calamities, or because they are worthy of praise. Or, *devas* are so called because they are desirable due to their possession of exceptional splendor.
They are threefold: conventional deities (*sammutideva*), deities by birth (*upapattideva*), and deities by purification (*visuddhideva*). But the Blessed One, by virtue of his unsurpassed...

Through his play with the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*); through the supreme divine, brahma, and noble abidings (*vihāra*); through the accomplishment of the fivefold victory over Māra within his own and others' continuums;

through his preeminent mode of address—consisting of the mastery of mind, the seven treasures, and so forth, as well as right practice, verified confidence, honor, giving, and receiving, which is termed instruction in accordance with the true nature of phenomena (*dhamma*) and the inclinations of individuals;
through the radiance known as the splendor of the body of wisdom (*paññāsarīra*); and through the incomparable movement of the body of knowledge (*ñāṇasarīra*).

Because he is endowed with the unimpeded power to conquer Māra, to attain omniscience, and to accomplish the welfare of others, he is worthy of being gone to for refuge by the world including the devas; because he is to be praised;

and because he is desirable through the quality of devotion—he has surpassed all devas by those qualities, or he is the supreme among devas; thus he is the Devātideva (the God-Beyond-Gods). [He is] beyond all devas.

"Devātidevo" means either "the god who is more worthy of worship than gods," or "the god above gods" because he has attained the state of a purified deity adorned with the qualities of omniscience, and is thus superior to other gods.
"Of the gods" (*devānaṃ*) refers to those gods present there who were recipients of the Dhamma.
He was worshipped by gods such as Sakka and others, and by dānavas such as Pahārāda, the lord of the asuras. [This refers to] the virtue (*sīla*) of restraint in body and speech.
"Pure restraint" (*suddhasaṃyama*) refers to the absolute subsiding of the adversaries of sense-restraint, mental self-control, and concentration.

Regarding "the seventh seer" (*isisattama*): among those who have attained the status of seers (*isi*) through the realization of the Four Noble Truths and are thus reckoned as seers, he is the most excellent and praised;
this is the meaning. And with reference to Vipassī and the others, the Blessed One is called "the seventh."
"Since consciousness turns back, one brings that name-and-form to cessation by means of the cessation of its arising; thus he is the 'Cesser of Name-and-Form.
The connection [of the sentence] is: "He taught the treatise named *Paṭṭhāna*, a teaching adorned with an exceedingly profound method.
The commentary on the introduction to the book is finished.
Regarding the commentary on the Enumeration of Conditions (*paccayuddesavaṇṇanā*):
One need not ask, "What then are those methods (*nayā*), and what is this so-called *Paṭṭhāna*? Why?

Because this matter is already explained in the Introduction (*nidānakathā*) during the summary of the *Paṭṭhāna*, wherein the methods such as the direct order (*anuloma*) and others, as well as the *Paṭṭhāna* itself, have been shown. Thus he clarifies this point.
“Indeed, by the Fully Enlightened One... [as stated]... it is called ‘Paṭṭhāna’”—thus he cited the Pāḷi of the Aṭṭhakathā found therein.
Regarding that, we shall explain the meaning of the verses and the intention of the Aṭṭhakathā later on.
As for the meaning of the name *Paṭṭhāna*, it refers to the meaning of the names *Tika-paṭṭhāna* and so forth; this is the meaning of the name of this treatise.
Furthermore, the convergence of the twenty-four *Paṭṭhānas* should be explained here.
For when the *Paṭṭhāna* is thus known in brief, its detailed exposition becomes easy to understand. And in that regard, the meaning of the name must first be stated;
therefore, having said, "In this context, the meaning of the names for those [factors]... should be understood as follows," [the author explains] first the name *Paṭṭhāna*, which is common to all.

Showing the meaning of this, he said: “In what sense is it ‘Paṭṭhāna’? and so forth. The syllable *pa-* indicates that it is a prefix (*upasagga*). It illustrates a sense of diversity, as in such passages as:
“Among the phenomena that have been analyzed (*pavibhattesu*), that which is best—that they approached. [Objection:
But surely, since “analyzed by means of modes (*pakārehi*)” is *pavibhattā*, the prefix *pa-* illustrates only the sense of mode (*pakāra*).

Is it not for the sake of various modes? No; because those modes themselves possess a state of diversity. For the word "various" (*nānā*) is used here to show the state of diversity that has entered into the meaning itself.

In this context, the conditionality of various modes should be understood both from the fact that even a single phenomenon possesses many conditions, such as cause and so forth, and from the fact that each individual condition consists of many phenomena.

"By way of being analyzed through the condition of cause (hetupaccaya) and so forth"—by this, he shows the reason for the attainment of the name *Paṭṭhāna* (the Foundation) due to its particularly distinguished analysis, as opposed to the analysis of wholesome states and so on taught in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī* and other texts. "Goṭṭha" means a herd.

"Paṭṭhitagāva" means cows that have gone away. "In the place where they came from" refers to the *Mahāsīhanāda Sutta*. Because there is movement occurring therein, the word "therein" (*ettha*) is an ellipsis [to be supplied].

Alternatively, it is called *gamana* because one goes (*gacchati*) therein. Since each individual *paṭṭhāna* is a place of going due to the movement of omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) proceeding without attachment, this is the meaning.

In that context, the phrase "of omniscient knowledge" is stated in order to show that it is a place of movement for one who possesses movement superior to other beings who possess movement. Of that [knowledge], which has great velocity—
By showing that the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī* and other texts are places where one proceeds with attachment— like a precipice for a man—

and that this [work] is a place where one proceeds without attachment— like a great highway— it demonstrates that its status as a place of exceedingly well-connected progression is the reason for its acquisition of the name *Paṭṭhāna*.
“Tikānaṃ” means of the states spoken of by way of triads. “Samantaṃ” means that they have gone (gatāni) in all modes, such as the direct order (anuloma) and so forth; thus there are twenty-four.

Regarding this meaning, although it should be stated as “twenty-four universal foundations” (*samantacatuvīsatipaṭṭhānāni*), it should be understood that the word *samanta* has been placed after [the number] for the sake of euphonic conjunction (*parayoga*). Alternatively, *samantā* [means] six...
"Having become six" means that by this [phrase], he shows the state of being sixfold—starting from the triads and so on—for every section, such as the *anuloma* (conformity) and others.
Consequently, the word *samanta* (all-around) is a qualification of the specific sets of six beginning with the triads, not a qualification of the twenty-four.

Therefore, taking them as "the twenty-four *paṭṭhānas* all-around," they are called the "twenty-four *samantapaṭṭhānas*. Or alternatively, they are so called because they are "all-around" (*samantato*) through various modes such as the *dhammānuloma* (conformity of phenomena), the triads, the dependent sections, the *paccayānuloma* (conformity of conditions), and those rooted in the causes.
The *paṭṭhānas* are "all-round" (*samanta*) because they proceed by means of no fewer than [twenty-four] methods; this is what is meant.
There are twenty-four of them. For this very reason it was said: "by way of the compendium of these twenty-four all-round *paṭṭhānas*, which are designated as the 'Minor Paṭṭhāna'."
With the statement "it is both a cause (hetu) and a condition (paccaya)," there might be the apprehension of a cause that has also become a predominance-condition (adhipati-paccaya) and so forth;
preventing that, he says: "having been a cause, it is a condition. Since this too would result in the same fault, he says again:
"what is meant is that it is a condition by way of its state as a cause. Therefore, in this context, the word "cause" does not denote the [abstract] phenomenon itself.

This shows that a specific distinction regarding the nature of *dhamma* has been grasped. For, with reference to the grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇatā*) of the terms "cause" (*hetu*) and "condition" (*paccaya*), it is stated:

"It is both a cause and a condition," and "being a cause, it is a condition. And having done so, later in the text, by means of various ways of assisting such as the state of being a cause, etc., it is said: "Causes associated with causes... [etc. ...are a condition by way of the cause-condition (*hetupaccaya*)," and so forth.
The fact that each respective state (dhamma) is beneficial to another has been stated. However, in the Aṭṭhakathā, by means of a description emphasizing the state itself— such as,

“Whatever state remains or arises without rejecting another state, that is its condition,” and “A state that is beneficial in the sense of being a root is the root-condition (hetu-paccaya)” and so forth—
it is shown that there is a causal power of states distinct from the states themselves.
It should be understood that by saying "there is no [separate] name," the capacity of phenomena (dhamma-satti) is demonstrated by means of phenomena themselves.
Or, here too, in the phrase "it is both a cause and a condition," he shows the capacity of phenomena by means of phenomena alone.

For the enumeration beginning with "cause-condition" (hetu-paccaya) is not primarily concerned with the phenomena themselves—unlike the enumeration of the wholesome (kusala) and so forth—but rather it is primarily concerned with the assistance rendered by those phenomena. It goes (eti), thus...
“The meaning ‘occurs’ (vattati) applies,” and this is a term common to both arising and persistence. For this very reason it is said:
“it either persists or arises. For some condition pertains only to persistence, such as the postnascent condition; some only to arising, such as the immediately preceding condition and so forth;
and some to both, such as the root-cause condition and so forth.

And it should be understood that the phrase "characterized by assistance" (*upakārakalakkhaṇa*) shows the assistance rendered by a phenomenon (*dhamma*) through its own functional power (*dhammasatti*).

It is a "cause" (*hetu*) because things "go to" (*hinoti*) or are "established" (*patiṭṭhāti*) therein. Since verbal roots have multiple meanings, the word *hi* should be understood as having the sense of "establishing," just like the word *mūla*.
Alternatively, it is a cause because by means of it—acting as the source of the action and bringing up nourishment from below—the root establishes [the plant].
Just as a tree goes toward, proceeds toward, and attains growth, increase, and development by means of its conditions, so it is called a "cause" (hetu).
"From the teachers" refers to the Elder Revata.
"Monks, for one who attends wisely, unarisen wholesome states arise, and arisen..."
By such passages as, "And wholesome states increase," it is established that the state of wholesomeness is dependent upon wise attention (*yoniso-manasikāra*);
thus he says, "The state of wholesomeness is dependent upon wise attention.

By this very [statement], it is shown that the states of unwholesomeness and the indeterminate (*abyākata*), unlike the state of wholesomeness, are not dependent upon causes. However, some might think: "The causeless..."

"If the state of being wholesome and so forth belongs to other factors associated with it because they are dependent on the cause, just as the state of being unwholesome belongs to the causes of the unwholesome by their very nature," then he spoke the passage beginning with "And if" to provide the following reply:

"Alobha (non-greed) may be either wholesome or indeterminate. If non-greed were wholesome by its very nature, then because of that wholesomeness, it could not be indeterminate. If, on the other hand, it is indeterminate,"
Because it would possess that [specific] nature, it would not be wholesome, just as there is an absence of non-hatred in that which has non-greed as its nature.

However, since it exists in both ways, you should seek the state of being wholesome and so forth—which is bound by causes—among the associated factors such as contact when they exist in both ways, rather than [seeking it] from their intrinsic nature;
in the same way, the wholesomeness and so forth of the roots should be sought as dependent on something else.
"Not by way of intrinsic nature" (na sabhāvato): That which was stated—"the state of being wholesome and so forth exists by way of intrinsic nature alone among the associated causes"—is not tenable.
However, when that [wholesome state] is investigated, it is found to be dependent upon wise attention (yoniso-manasikāra) and other such factors.

Thus, the intention is that just as with the causes, the state of being wholesome and so forth among the associated states is also dependent upon wise attention and other factors; it is established that it is not dependent on the causes [alone].
Regarding the phrase "even having taken as object" (*ārabhitvāpi*): here, by the word "even" (*pi*), he shows this meaning—

that since it was stated without restriction that "having taken whatever phenomenon as object," and because the state of being an object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*) for all bases of form (*rūpāyatana*) up to the base of phenomena (*dhammāyatana*) was taught without limiting it to any single one among them,
there is no phenomenon that does not exist [as an object].
In a consciousness that arises having obtained the support of previous volitional formations (purimābhisaṅkhārūpanissaya), such as the phrase "What indeed does not succeed for one who has zeal?",
zeal and the other factors function as the primary and preeminent elements, accomplishing their associated states themselves;
and those associated states proceed under their control, because they follow along with them in their inferior or other qualities.

Therefore, they are "predominant conditions" (*adhipatipaccaya*). Even an object worthy of esteem becomes a condition for the reviewing, enjoyment, path, and fruition states—which are inclined, bent, and leaning toward it—just as if it were bringing them under its own control.
Thus, this state of being helpful by way of acting as the master over those things dependent on it should be understood as the "predominant condition."
Regarding the phrase "the mind-consciousness element," etc., which refers to the determination of consciousness:

here, by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), one includes the determining consciousness (*voṭṭhabbana*) immediately following the investigating consciousness (*santīraṇa*), and rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) immediately following the death-moment (*cuti*). Thus, for whichever consciousness arises immediately after another, there is a fixed rule of immediate succession;
this belongs specifically to each preceding consciousness as distinguished by its respective cooperative conditions.
He shows that [the result] succeeds by means of this. Regarding the phrase "because it has been warded off by the power of meditation":

just as when a fence is placed around a tree, it does not flower even though it is capable of flowering, yet once the fence of poison has been removed, it flowers precisely because of that same capacity;
so too here, because it has been warded off by the power of meditation, [it does not arise] even though it is capable of being aroused.
The intention is that there is no arousing [of the defilement], and when it has departed, there is an arousing by that very same capacity.
Here, the difference should be understood as being merely in the phrasing (*byañjana*), not in the meaning (*attha*);

the intention is that the difference is merely in the verbal meaning (*saddatthamatta*), like the case of synonyms for "accumulation" (*upacaya*) and "continuity" (*santati*), and not in the sense of what is to be expressed (*vacanīyattha*). For that very reason, the distinction in the verbal meaning...

To demonstrate this, he said, beginning with “How? In this context, the state of being an immediate condition (*anantara-paccaya*) consists in the capacity for uninterrupted production, due to the absence of any interval between the cessation of the preceding [dharma] and the arising of the succeeding one.

Because mental states lack the configuration found in material phenomena (*rūpa-dhamma*), and because the condition and the conditioned do not exist simultaneously, there is no spatial distinction such as “this is below, above, or across from that. Thus, they appear as if identical with themselves.
Having brought [the preceding state] close, the capacity to produce [the succeeding state] by way of immediate succession is "immediate conditionality" (*samanantara-paccayatā*).

Regarding this "capacity to produce," since phenomena (*dhammā*) are devoid of agency, it should be understood that when a particular mode has ceased, or while it is present, other phenomena come to possess specific qualities; it is that very mode which is called the [condition]. Of phenomena...

Furthermore, the expression "time" is used only with reference to the process of occurrence (*pavatti*). Therefore, it should be understood that for one emerging from cessation, for those entering the attainment of the fruit of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and for a non-percipient being passing away—the time-interval between the preceding death-consciousness and the subsequent rebirth-linking does not exist, because there is no interval between their cessation and arising.
Indeed, there is no occurrence of immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhamma*) in the interval between them.
That on account of which a difference in time might be spoken of does not exist;

for the occurrence of material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*) does not create an interval between the occurrence of immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhamma*), because they belong to different continua (*santāna*).

Indeed, the two continua of material and immaterial phenomena, though existing in a state of mutual assistance due to their distinct intrinsic natures (*visadisa-sabhāva*), remain separate from one another. And within a single continuum, regarding the preceding and succeeding moments—
That which occurs in the middle acts as an interval-maker by virtue of being included within that same continuity (*santati*).

However, there is no such thing whatsoever between the fruition attainment (*phalasamāpatti*) of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*); and non-existence itself cannot act as an interval-maker precisely because it is non-existent.

Therefore, there is no interruption—indeed, a complete lack of interruption—just as there is none between one impulsion (*javana*) and the next, or between one life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) and the next.

The phrase "it happens" (*hoti*) should likewise be understood as the capacity for arising even in the case of deaths from the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*).

Furthermore, since the state of being a condition for rebirth is evident here through conditions such as the immediate condition (*anantarapaccaya*), it is described simply as "the capacity for arising.
However, regarding present phenomena that are delimited by their prior and subsequent limits and do not receive the verbal designation "it arises," [the term "happens" is used].

Since the state of being a condition such as "proximity" (*anantara-paccaya*) is stated in passages such as "a past phenomenon is a condition for a present phenomenon by way of proximity-condition," it is understood that this [conditioning] does not occur only at the moment of arising.

For the mention of the "present" is not indeterminate like the mention of "wholesome" (*kusala*) and so forth, whereby the mention would apply only to those possessing the mere act of arising; and for that very reason, in the "Triplet on the Past" (*atīta-ttika*),...
"The sections on dependence and so forth do not exist.

In the phrase "arising itself by way of simultaneous arising," it should be understood that while the state of being a condition for arising is manifest, he thereby demonstrates the state of being a condition for stability as well;
however, the assistance rendered to the dependently arisen states is by way of their being co-nascent.
Regarding "condition by way of co-nascence":

the state of being an assistance to that which assists oneself is "condition by way of mutuality" (*aññamañña-paccayatā*). And this state of being an assistance should be understood solely through the aspect of mutual dependence, not by way of co-nascence and so forth.
For even while being a condition such as co-nascence, something may indeed be a condition by way of mutuality.
It does not exist; nor do the basis-aggregates (vatthu-khandhā), which are beneficial by way of being pre-existent or post-existent, act as mutual conditions for one another.

Just as the earth element is the support for the remaining elements in the manner of a foundation—as in the case of trees and so forth—and as the eye and other faculties are beneficial to eye-consciousness and the rest, the aggregates and so forth are beneficial to the mind and its karma in the manner of a physical support, like cloth and other materials.
"Of those respective bases," such as the aggregates (khandha) and so forth.

Because it exists in dependence upon them, it is "supported by its own fruit"; thus, he states that any cause whatsoever is a "support" (nissaya). Among these, that which is predominant is determined to be the "decisive support" (upanissaya).
Regarding the term "natural" (pakata), the prefix *pa-* is an intensifier; it signifies the state of being well-perfected through its capacity to produce its own fruit.
It illuminates. And since what has been done in that way becomes performed within one's own continuum, he says "in one's own continuum.
To show that performing [an action] is twofold—namely, production and cultivation—he says "either produced," and so forth.

Therein, by the phrase "or cultivated," he indicates both the cultivation of enjoyment through the act of clinging to the body, and the cultivation of the object through the acts of cognizing and so on.

"It shows" (dasseti) is how it should be understood. By this, it is stated that even for future [qualities] such as the perfection of the eye (*cakkhusampadā*), there exists the nature of natural decisive support (*pakatūpanissaya*) through the cultivation of their objects, just as they were cultivated previously.

Just as those phenomena which, in the absence of a posterior-born [condition], would not attain the state of being a cause for the non-interruption of the continuum (*santānāviccheda*) in the manner of a posterior-born [condition]—
The state of being an assistant to those [mental states], distinguished by its mode of dissociation and so forth, is the conditionality of post-nascence (*pacchājāta-paccayatā*).

Likewise, the state of being an assistant to the bases (*vatthu*) and objects (*ārammaṇa*), which do not become assistants except through their prior existence and which are distinguished by their modes of support (*nissaya*), object (*ārammaṇa*), and so forth, is the conditionality of pre-nascence (*purejāta-paccayatā*) by way of their prior existence. Thus it is in all cases regarding conditions.
The state of being a benefactor, distinguished by its specific mode of conditionality, should be applied [here].

By the phrase "like the volition of desire for food in the bodies of vulture chicks," he shows that the material body is sustained by immaterial phenomena occurring through the nutriment of mental volition (*manosañcetanāhāra*). For this very reason, he does not say "like the desire for food" alone.
He takes up volition (*cetanā*).
The meaning of "repetition" (*āsevana*) is the repeated performance or occurrence of an action to be done through an application that resembles oneself in its wholesome nature and so forth;
or it is "perfuming" (*vāsanā*), which is the production of a state of being similar in essence to oneself. In the *Ganthādi* [commentary], it refers to the prior application of previous efforts.
"Passes away" refers to the passing away of each preceding instance of repetition;
this is the intended meaning. "Application of mind" (*cittappayoga*) means mental activity (*cittakiriyā*), the sense being "exertion" (*āyūhana*).

For just as bodily and vocal application constitute intimation (*viññatti*), so too does mental application constitute volition (*cetanā*). When that [volition] arises within a continuum distinguished by the occurrence of such activity, upon the convergence of the remaining conditions...
It is also an aid to the materiality of fruition and kamma-resultant (katatta-rūpa) that is currently occurring, by virtue of that very same state of being functionally active (*kiriyabhāva*).
For their occurrence takes place because that state of being functionally active occurs, and not otherwise. But what need is there to say that it is an aid to co-nascent states by that [state]?

By the phrase "by way of its effortless and tranquil nature," [it is contrasted] with wholesome and unwholesome states that possess resultants and are characterized by effort, which have the quality of having an object (*sārammaṇa*) and so forth.

This demonstrates the state of having an equal result. For, because results cannot be accomplished by means of effort—whether through effort or otherwise—and because they are established solely by the "having-been-done" (kaṭatta) nature of karma once the remaining conditions have been fulfilled, their state is effortless and tranquil;

it is not a state of tranquility consisting in the subsiding of defilements (*kilesa*). Precisely because its intrinsic nature is thus tranquil, the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) and other such states are difficult to discern. This is also the case in the five doors.
For it is understood that the apprehension of visible forms and so forth occurs through the rapid occurrence [of consciousness];

however, the resultant states consisting merely of adverting, receiving, and investigating are indeed difficult to discern. "For the sake of a state of effortless tranquility" means for the purpose of a state of effortless tranquility.
By this, he shows that even those [mental factors] which are not themselves results possess conditions such that their activity conforms to the nature of a result.

Since mindfulness has the function of supporting even while it possesses the quality of generating, it is said that "by way of supporting both the material and the immaterial" the function of nutriment is primary.
For this supporting quality exists in the case of immaterial nutriments and in the case of the physical nutriment that originates the matter born of nutriment;
however, it does not exist in the case of the physical nutriment that supports the matter originated by the [other] four causes. But if the supporting quality were absent...

Since nutriment does not possess the quality of being a producer, its primary function is that of supporting. For even when producing [the body], nutriment produces it only by way of supporting it through non-interruption;
thus, the state of supporting is itself the state of being nutriment. Regarding the phrase "in the sense of predominance":
here, it does not mean having overcome those things that obstruct its occurrence, as is the case with the factors of the predominance-condition (*adhipatipaccaya*).
The meaning of predominance (*adhipati-ṭṭha*) is the state of being weighty by way of occurrence;

moreover, it is [the state of being weighty] through those factors co-arising with faith and so forth, such as eye-consciousness and the rest in the functions of seeing and so on, through the states of being happy and so on while living by means of the life-faculties, through resolve, exertion, establishment, non-distraction, and knowing in the stages of "I shall know the unknown" (*anaññātaññassāmīti*), in the act of knowing, and in the state of one who has known (*aññātāvī*). Thus...
It is the state of the eye and other faculties being subject to the influence of their respective conditions (paccaya) in their various functions.
For in those respective functions, the sovereignty belongs to the eye and the rest, and the conditions for them operate therein by following that sovereignty.

As for the female and male faculties, although there is a state of being subject to influence through the physical marks (liṅga) and so forth, this is not due to their status as conditions. Just as in the case of vitality (jīvita) and nutriment (āhāra)...
Those things which serve as conditions are the protectors and supporters of those [characteristics], and they exist as non-disappearance conditions;
however, the states of female and male do not assist the gender-traits (liṅga) and so forth in any way whatsoever.
Rather, it is simply that the gender-traits and so forth, as they proceed by their own respective conditions, possess the status of being conditions for the apprehension of "female" and so on.

Because they do not occur in a continuum associated with that [state] in any other mode than that, their being subject to conformity through gender and so forth, as well as their status as faculties (*indriyatā*), is stated;

therefore, their status as faculty-conditions (*indriya-paccaya*) is not mentioned. Regarding the statement "the eye and so forth [are conditions] for immaterial phenomena alone," it should be understood that the faculties of pleasure and pain are also included by the mention of the eye and so forth.

The meaning of "contemplating" (*upanijjhāyana*) is the approaching of the object through the functions of initial application (*vitakka*) and so forth—which constitute the contemplation of the characteristic as an object—and the subsequent contemplation, observation, or reflection; this is the common activity of initial application and the other factors.
The intention is that one should set aside the pair of feelings of pleasure and pain, meaning one should exclude both the faculty of pleasure (*sukhindriya*) and the faculty of pain (*dukkhindriya*).
Having said "all of them," it should be understood that by the statement "seven jhāna-factors," the exclusion of the non-jhāna-factors—equanimity and one-pointedness of mind—is effected.
If this is so, why was it stated, "excluding the pair of pleasant and painful feelings," when the phrase "seven jhāna-factors" alone would suffice?
[It is because] among the five divisions of feeling, the pair of pleasure and pain...
It is for the purpose of showing that they are exclusively not factors of jhāna, since they are indicated in the place of jhāna-factors.
Or, even though the term "jhāna-factor" is applied to them, it is for the purpose of showing that the two types of feeling are absolutely lacking the status of being conditions for jhāna.
As for equanimity and one-pointedness of mind, although there is an absence of their being conditions for jhāna, there is no absence of their being factors of jhāna; thus, "all [of these]..."

In this context, the inclusion [of the factors] is made by the phrase "seven jhāna-factors. Therein, the expression "all of them" should be understood as intended to include all the various divisions such as the wholesome (kusala) and so forth, but not as intended to include those present in every single arising of consciousness.
"From whatever [source]" means either rightly or wrongly. Furthermore, both of these [factors] serve as conditions for the jhānas and the paths within rootless (ahetuka) states of consciousness.

Regarding the phrase "they are not obtained": this is stated for the purpose of showing that [these factors] are not absent from minds with roots—that is, they *are* present in minds with roots—but not for the purpose of showing that they are absent from rootless minds.
If the meaning were taken in this way, one would understand only that the obtaining of anything by anything in any rootless mind has not been precluded.

It was composed for the purpose of showing that there is no absence of the jhāna-condition specifically in the cases of consciousness with initial application (*savitakka*) that is rootless (*ahetuka*).

Alternatively, if this statement were intended to show the absence of its acquisition in all rootless consciousnesses, it would follow that the jhāna-condition is not acquired even in those consciousnesses with initial application that are rootless;
therefore, by way of that non-acquisition, [it is excluded] from the sections on the inclusion and emptiness of the mind-element (*manodhātu*) and so forth in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*.

Jhāna has not been mentioned here; this should be understood as referring to its non-occurrence, for it is stated that even the condition of jhāna is absent in rootless consciousnesses (*ahetukacitta*).

For just as in the case of consciousnesses with roots (*sahetuka*), the function of close contemplation (*upanijjhāyana*)—which gathers together initial application (*vitakka*) and the other factors through co-nascence (*sahajāta*) and brings them to a state of unity—is powerful, it is not so in the case of rootless consciousnesses. However, in this treatise...
Even if there is only a slight degree of sustained contemplation (*upanijjhāyana*), it is nevertheless helpful;

therefore, the jhāna condition is indeed stated even in the cases of thought-concomitant-free, root-causeless consciousnesses accompanied by initial application (*savitakka*). Consequently, for those who read as follows:
"But these two [conditions]—jhāna and path—are not found respectively in the two types of fivefold sense-consciousness and in root-causeless consciousness," their reading is the more excellent one.
This is the commentary on the meaning of this treatise (*pakaraṇa*), not on the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*.
Being helpful through association with various modes—as if attaining a state of unity—is "associated conditionality" (*sampayutta-paccayatā*).
Being helpful through a state of dissociation, even while remaining conjoined, by attaining a state of diversity, is "dissociated conditionality" (*vippayutta-paccayatā*).

For there is no state of dissociation-condition for dissociated states such as material phenomena and the like, which—though not conjoined by way of being co-nascent or post-nascent with respect to their basis—are nevertheless helpful as objects and so forth.
However, although material phenomena are inseparable from other material phenomena, they are not dissociated [from themselves];
thus, there is no state of dissociation-condition between them. For it has been said: "Conjunction occurs with four [aggregates], and dissociation occurs with four."
"By the characteristic of the present" means by way of its present intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).

By this, it excludes the state of existence (*atthibhāva*) characterized as being produced and currently obtainable, as stated in such passages as "I have committed an evil deed" and "There is a certain person practicing for his own benefit.
Even though they possess the quality of being producers, [the other formations] are helpful through their state of existence by way of providing support and predominance.

He said: "By way of being a support. And this quality of being a support should be understood as the state of assisting through mere presence, which is common to the physical basis (vatthu), the object (ārammaṇa), and the co-nascent factors (sahajāta), etc.
Since there is no simultaneous existence of the many factors such as contact (phassa) and so forth—which function by way of touching the object and so on—in a single [moment],...
When the aggregate of contact and so forth exists, a second [consciousness] does not arise; when it is absent, however, it does arise.

Thus, the state of being helpful by way of its absence is "absence-conditionality" (*natthipaccayatā*). Even though preceding moments of consciousness are in a state of absence, they do not assist by means of that state of absence;

rather, for those [subsequent states] which, immediately following, would otherwise find no occasion for occurrence due to their own presence, it is by their [preceding ones'] state of absence that the occasion for occurrence is provided.
Because it is helpful as if it were actually giving, he said: "The state of being helpful by providing a locus for occurrence is the conditionality of non-existence (*natthipaccayatā*).

Herein, the state of being helpful by means of mere non-existence is the conditionality of non-existence; the state of being helpful to those things that do not occur due to the non-departure of their own-nature, by means of the departure of their own-nature, is the conditionality of disappearance (*vigatapaccayatā*).
And non-existence is emptiness immediately following cessation, while disappearance is [emptiness] following [the passing away of] what has ceased.

The attainment of cessation (*nirodhappattatā*) is the distinction between these two; likewise, the state of being a presence-condition (*atthipaccayatā*) is the quality of being helpful by virtue of existing with its own intrinsic nature (*sasabhāvato*), while the state of being a non-disappearance-condition (*avigatapaccayatā*) is the quality of being helpful by not having reached cessation due to the non-departure of its own intrinsic nature.

Thus, even though there is no difference in the phenomena (*dhamma*) themselves, the specific difference in their status as conditions (*paccayabhāvaviseso*) should be understood. For [the Buddha] has fully awakened to all the specific potencies of phenomena exactly as they are.

Since the Tathāgata has spoken of twenty-four specific conditions, one should generate the knowledge consisting of what is heard (*sutamaya-ñāṇa*) through faith in the Blessed One, thinking, "These phenomena possess such specific qualities.
Then, for the sake of the direct realization (*abhisamaya*) of those [conditions], one should apply oneself to the practice consisting of reflection (*cintāmaya*) and cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*).

Because there is no inclusion even of a single one among the four aggregates, subsequent states (*anantara*) and the others do not constitute a portion of the phenomena of the name-aggregate (*nāma-dhamma*).

Having stated, "Or they are name-dhammas," he says, "Because Nibbāna is not included," and so forth, to show that it is not only the four aggregates—which partake of the state of condition and conditioned—that are name, but rather that Nibbāna is also indeed name.
In the phrase, "The pre-arising condition is one part of matter," the term "one part" excludes matter from what is other than matter; [that is,] matter itself.
However, in the *Kusalattika*, even that which is yet to come (the future) is indeed included elsewhere as having the nature of a pre-arising condition (*purejātapaccaya*). For it is said:

"A non-manifesting and non-reactive state is a condition for a non-manifesting and non-reactive state by way of pre-arising condition—namely, object-pre-arising (*ārammaṇapurejāta*) and base-pre-arising (*vatthupurejāta*).
Object-pre-arising: the physical base, the female faculty, the male faculty, the water element, and edible food..."
“Food as impermanent... [and so on] ...grief arises.
The commentary on the enumeration of conditions is finished.
The Exposition of Conditions.
1. Commentary on the Exposition of the Root Condition (Hetupaccaya) Regarding the statement, "That which was enumerated as the root condition (hetupaccaya) should be understood thus":

by this, it is shown that the state of being a condition—by way of the root condition—for both the condition-factor known as the root itself (the cause), and for the conditioned factors known as the associated states and the matter produced by them, is established.

"The root-cause condition (hetupaccaya) has been listed" means: it should be understood that the conditioning state which, by way of being a root cause as previously described, acts as a condition for those states arisen through conditions as previously described, is what is indicated as "the root-cause condition.
Thus, it is shown that the root-cause condition is listed as the quality of assisting by way of being a root cause. This same method applies to the remaining conditions as well.
However, the state of being an assistant (*upakārakatā*) is simply the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of a phenomenon; it does not exist as something other than the phenomenon itself.
For the Blessed One, by showing that this or that phenomenon assists in such and such a way, demonstrates that respective state of being an assistant.

In the phrase "roots [are conditions] for those associated with roots," the first word "root" (*hetu*) indicates the specific factor (*paccatta*) and is thus a designation of the condition (*paccayaniddesa*).

By this, he shows that its state of being a condition through its status as a cause is "root-conditionality" (*hetupaccayatā*). The second [term] is a qualification of the conditioned phenomenon (*paccayuppanna*).
By this, he shows that it is not a condition for just any associated states by way of being a root-condition, but rather only for those states associated with the root.
But is it not the case that because the word "associated" (*sampayutta*) is dependent [on another], there is a need for a second word "root" (*hetu*)?

Is it not the case that, even though there is nothing else to be referred to, because no other [referent] is specified, this meaning—that [it] is a condition for its own associated states by way of the root-condition—is understood? This is not certain.

For when the word *hetu* (root) is understood as being specified in its own right—as in the very expression "condition by way of the root-condition"—then it does not serve as a qualification of the associated states; thus, the associated states...
Thinking that "whatever [factors] are included would be undistinguished," he said, "Furthermore...

such might be the meaning," with reference to the fact that when the word *sampayutta* (associated) is occupied solely with the self, there would be a grasping of any associated factors whatsoever in the absence of the qualifying word *hetu* (cause).
Is it not the case that, as in the expression, "the immaterial nutriments of the associated states"?

And when it is said, "the formless faculties [include] those associated with them," even without the second mention of "nutriments" and "faculties," only those associated with nutriment and faculty are included;

might it not be the same here? No, because there is no state that is dissociated from nutriment and faculty. For since there is nothing to be excluded there, even though the second mention of "nutriments" and "faculties" is absent, only those associated with them are taken.
"It is not done because [the term] 'taken' was used; however, since there is something here that must be excluded, it should be stated that this is a second mention of the 'cause' (hetu).

Even so, in the phrase "causes are related to those associated with causes," because no qualification has been made—such as "those associated with causes are related to that very same associated cause"—any cause whatsoever may serve as the causal condition for any other thing associated with a cause.

Does it follow that [the word] *paccaya* (condition) implies *āpajjati* (it follows)? It does not follow, because the cause (*hetu*) already indicated in its own right is stated again by way of being a specific qualification of the associated state (*sampayutta*).
And for this very purpose, although the status of being associated with a cause is established even without a second word *hetu*, its inclusion was made.
Alternatively, in the absence of a second word *hetu*, [it would refer to] those associated with a cause by way of the causal condition (*hetupaccaya*).

Since there might also be an apprehension that [the root-cause] is a condition but not a root-cause, he stated "that" (*so*) in order to preclude that; by this, it is shown that for all those things which possess the state of being associated with a root-cause, as well as for others, it is a condition by way of the root-condition (*hetu-paccaya*).
However, because the root-causes, knowledges, and paths are independent in their status as mere foundations and so forth, [they do not require further support].
The nutriment and the faculty are not dependent [on another] in that way; therefore, for these two alone, a second mention of "cause" and so forth was made.
However, the nutriment and the faculty are indeed dependent on what is to be nourished and what is to be sought;

therefore, even without a second mention of "nutriment" and "faculty," they themselves delimit other associated states that have become the nutriment and the faculty, as well as those things to be nourished and sought.

That [qualification] was not made there; however, here, because the second mention of "root" (hetu) delimits the roots associated with those things arisen from conditions by means of the root that serves as their very condition, there is no further need for qualification.
Thus, it should be understood that in the section on questions, in such passages as "wholesome roots [are related] to the associated aggregates," the second mention of "root" was not made.
"Because that which is to be demonstrated is not manifest": the word *taṃ* (that) depends on a preceding statement; it functions as a demonstrative (*niddesa*) for exactly what has been mentioned.

In such instances as "the visible-form base is [the object] for the eye-consciousness element and its associated states," the word *taṃ* occurs only when that which is to be demonstrated by the preceding statement has become manifest.
And here, the word *hetu* (cause), being demonstrated individually, [is used] in the phrase "it is a condition by way of the cause-condition."

The meaning is that, just as [the word] *byāvaṭo* (engaged) does not require the word *sampayutta* (associated), it likewise does not require the word *taṃ* (that); furthermore, no other term expressive of the object to be demonstrated has been stated.
Therefore, the intention is that the phrase "of those associated with that" (*taṃsampayuttakānaṃ*) was not mentioned.

However, by the phrase "of those associated with the cause" (*hetusampayuttakānaṃ*), which is an incomplete expression for "arising from conditions" (*paccayuppanna*) that depends on another expression for "arising from conditions," [the full sense is implied].

It has been made manifest as that which is to be demonstrated by the word *taṃ* (that) mentioned previously; therefore, the inclusion of the word *taṃ* was made here in the phrase “of those originating from that” (*taṃsamuṭṭhānānaṃ*).

But what is it that has become manifest as that which is to be demonstrated by the word *taṃ* in that expression “associated with causes” (*hetusampayuttaka*)? It is those very causes with which [the states] are associated—those which were called “associated with causes”—and these are both the causes themselves and the qualifiers of the associated states.
And those associated with the cause are qualified by that [cause]. Therefore he said, "They are both causes," and so forth.

Otherwise, if there were a connection with the word *hetu* (cause) as indicated in the singular in the phrase "they are both causes," then just as they are clearly indicated here by that very pronoun *taṃ*, they ought to have been so even previously;
thus, because what was to be indicated was not clear [in the previous context]—

The statement “it would not be appropriate [to say] ‘of those associated with that’” is incorrect. Alternatively, having removed both types of mention of the cause (*hetu*), one objects to the referential nature of the word *taṃ* (that) and then resolves it.
Furthermore, the phrase “arisen from that” (*taṃsamuṭṭhānānaṃ*) is properly understood as “arisen from the cause” (*hetusamuṭṭhānānaṃ*), for causes are indeed conditions (*paccaya*).
“Even though not producing mind-born materiality”—by the word *api* (even), it is implied that it [does] produce it as well.

If it were argued that because the *kaṭattā-rūpa* (materiality produced by past karma) at the moment of rebirth-linking is not included by the expression “of those originated by mind,” it was therefore not mentioned [here], then the state of being a condition for that *kaṭattā-rūpa* by mind and mental factors would not have been stated in the analysis of the co-nascence condition (*sahajāta-paccaya-vibhaṅga*). And if, in that [analysis]:

By way of being a condition for those [material phenomena] that possess characteristics identical to it through their status as conditions for mind-originated [phenomena], the fact that they are also conditions for *kaṭattā-rūpa* (kamma-born matter) is demonstrated;

so too must it be understood here. Furthermore, instead of saying "of mind-originated [phenomena]," the expression "of those originated by it" is used in order to show that mind-originated [phenomena] are originated by all consciousnesses and mental factors. In this manner...
By the expression "originated by that," the expressions for origins mentioned in various places are specified.

[Objection: Is it not the case that by the statement, "Mental states and mental factors are originated by mind," the fact that things originated by mind are also originated by mental factors is stated?
[Reply: It is not so stated. For in that context, only the state of being a condition for mental states and mental factors is stated.
“By being bound to the mind” (cittapaṭibaddhavuttitāya): by this very phrase, he also demonstrates its dependence on causes and so forth.
“Monks, whatever one intends, whatever one plans, and whatever one underlies with latent tendencies—this becomes the objective support for the persistence of consciousness.
When there is an objective support, there is a foundation for consciousness; when consciousness is established and has grown, there is the descent of name-and-form.”
In this sutta as well—“With name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise”—the fact that the rebirth-linking name-and-form has consciousness as its condition is stated;
thus he says, “When that is established,” and so forth.
Just as a seed rests upon earth already established beforehand, [so too does name-and-form rest] upon karma already established beforehand, which produces it.
The establishment of the seed of consciousness means that there is an arising due to the performance of kamma; thus it is said: "Kamma is the field, consciousness is the seed.
But for what is that the field and the seed? For the sprout of name-and-form. And this meaning is as follows:
the state of the material phenomena born of kamma being dependent on mind at the moment of rebirth-linking. "By way of the locus alone" means...
"By way of the scope (*okāsa*) of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) alone; for that is the scope for that state.

When one says "even the mere physical basis (*vatthurūpa*)," one shows that the conditionality of the immaterial states (*arūpadhamma*) toward the remaining material phenomena—which support that physical basis—is precisely through their state of being its supporters, or merely by their coexistence.
In that regard, [this applies] to certain groups (*kalāpa*) such as the body-existence (*kāyabhāva*), etc.
Because of its non-existence anywhere—that is, because of the absence of existence—it is said: “even without a mere physical basis (vatthurūpa).
Regarding the phrase “with an owner,” the term “together with the king” is stated for the purpose of qualifying that very same [term]. Why was it stated:
“because of the exclusion of the state of being a condition for kamma-produced matter (kaṭattārūpa) and so forth during the course of existence”? Is it not [the case that they are conditions]?
There is no possibility of their being conditions [for one another], because of the statement: "Roots are co-nascent [conditions] for those [phenomena].

For those for which roots are not the co-nascence condition cannot be called "co-nascent with roots. If they were so, such statements as "An indeterminate phenomenon arises co-nascent with a wholesome phenomenon, but not by way of the root-condition" would be possible; however, this is not the case. Therefore, they are not [such].

"Are they co-nascent with their causes? "This is true. However, it should be understood that this was said so as to address the possibility that someone, by taking up the mere fact of simultaneous arising with the causes, might imagine a state of being "co-nascent with causes.
The Blessed One does not take into account the relative lightness or heaviness of words;
rather, he does not violate the intrinsic nature of phenomena (dhammasabhāva) in accordance with the inclinations of those to be enlightened.
"In such and such a way he determines the teaching"—thus, one should not raise any objection regarding the abundance or scarcity of syllables anywhere.
The commentary on the exposition of the root-cause condition (*hetu-paccaya*) is finished.
2. Commentary on the Exposition of the Object Condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*).
2. Regarding the phrase "at the very moment of arising" (*uppajjanakkhaṇeyeva*): by this, it should be understood that the entire present moment is included through a portion of the present moment.
For it is not only at the moment of arising that visible forms and so forth are the object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*) for eye-consciousness and the rest;

rather, they are so throughout the entire present moment. Therefore, even while visible forms and so forth are being taken as objects, there is the state of being present for the eye-consciousness and the rest.
This shows that even when they exist subsequently, there is an absence of the state of being an object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*); how much more so for those not being taken as objects?
"They do not exist together" means that all visible forms, such as blue and so forth, do not exist simultaneously, and the same applies to sounds and the rest.
For the expression "whatever [it may be]" distinguishes between visible form and the other [bases]. In this context, by the word "arise" (*uppajjanti*) in its primary sense—
It is shown that the phrase beginning with "whatever phenomenon" was stated for the purpose of illustrating the characteristic of being an object-condition (ārammaṇapaccaya);
and by the subsequent expression "whatever," it is for the purpose of illustrating the distinctions such as form (rūpa) and so forth.
Alternatively, the meaning here should also be understood according to all the objects and so on demonstrated in the commentary on the passage "or whatever [state] one takes as a basis."

"Thus it was said": just as the flowing and the standing of rivers and mountains are described by the present-tense verbs "they flow" and "they stand" because their occurrence is continuous and uninterrupted, so too, because the phrase "whatever phenomena" includes all things—past, future, and present—by way of a collective totality, their arising and occurrence are continuous; thus it is said, "they arise."
The intention is that the present tense has been used.
However, none of these conditions—beginning with *hetu*—apply to both the past and the future. For there is no such thing as a past and a future [dhamma] for which these could serve as conditions.

And this being so, in the "Triplet on the Past" (*atītattika*), no condition whatsoever is stated for the past and the future; therefore, here too, by the expression "arising" (*uppajjanti*), those [dhammas]...

It should be understood that visible forms and other objective phenomena (*ārammaṇa-dhammā*) function as object-conditions (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*), and it is these that are shown here as being exclusively present.
For when those [present phenomena] are shown, the meaning conveyed regarding the past and future is that they "were" or "will be" such-and-such conditions;
however, it does not show their state of actually possessing those respective conditions. This is because only present phenomena possess conditions.

And here, having made the singular designation “whatever state (dhamma) with reference to,” the subsequent plural designation “those states” is for the purpose of showing that there is also a plurality of the objective states (ārammaṇadhamma) spoken of as “whatever.
For the four aggregates together serve as the object-condition (ārammaṇapaccaya), and even though [the consciousness] arises with reference to all of them, [they are designated thus].
It is not that what arises with reference to each one of them does not exist;

therefore, the phrase "whatever" (*yaṃ yaṃ*) is used to show that even each individual factor among feeling and so forth, as well as contact and so forth, possesses the status of an object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*).

The phrase "those those" (*te te*) is used to show that all [factors] included within a single arising of consciousness possess the status of an object-condition. In that context, by the word "whatever" (*yaṃyaṃ*), even a single [factor] such as form is indicated.
It should be understood that by saying "those various," all those numerous factors such as contact and so forth— which were mentioned individually using the word "whatever" (yaṃ-yaṃ)—
are included. Alternatively, it is said "whatever" (yaṃ yaṃ) in order to show that at whatever time they arise by way of an object,
they arise by depending on only one [object] at a time, whether among objects such as blue or within the arising of states of consciousness.

It was said; however, those various phenomena being taken as objects—both those with form as their object and likewise those with sound and so forth as their objects—are expressed by the phrase "those various" (*te te*) for the purpose of showing that they are manifold.

Because it is not included [within the mundane], the wholesome [consciousness] of the sense-sphere and fine-material sphere has Nibbāna as its object, as does the wholesome-resultant and the functional [consciousness] of the sense-sphere and fine-material sphere.

The statement that "these six aggregates are the object-condition (ārammaṇapaccaya) for these [six] groups" is said with the intention that even Nibbāna is the object of fine-material-sphere wholesome and functional states at the time of recollecting the aggregates connected with past lives by means of the knowledge of recollection of past lives (*pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa*).
This being so, just as it is said: "The immeasurable aggregates are the object of the knowledge of recollection of past lives..."
Since it is stated that [it] is "a condition by way of object-condition," it might likewise be said that "[it is] Nibbāna," yet that has not been stated.

For Nibbāna was not previously experienced, owing to its unconditioned nature; nor is there any purpose in knowing Nibbāna through the knowledge of recollecting past lives once the immeasurable aggregates of those previously lived have been known.
For just as the knowledge of penetration of minds (cetopariyañāṇa) is a condition for the sense-sphere consciousness that knows the object of mind precisely by way of discerning that mind itself,
so too this [knowledge] is a condition for the sense-sphere consciousness that knows those aggregates as its object precisely by way of discerning the immeasurable aggregates.
And it is one who has already seen Nibbāna who recollects the immeasurable aggregates previously experienced.
Therefore, it should be understood that Nibbāna is the object of those aggregates exactly as it was seen by him;

however, the manifestation of that object should not be performed by means of the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa*), for that [knowledge] has already made it manifest to him. In the same way, this should be applied appropriately to the knowledge of future states (*anāgataṃsañāṇa*).
Consequently, Nibbāna is not the object of anyone belonging to the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*); thus, [the text says] "of the four..."
It is appropriate to say, "of those residing [in the mind].
The commentary on the exposition of the object-condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya) is finished.
3. Commentary on the Exposition of the Dominant Condition (adhipati-paccaya).
3. *Dhuranti* means that which bears the burden; *dhuraggāhan* means the grasper of the burden. *Jeṭṭhakan* means the eldest or the best.

Regarding the phrase *chandādhipati chandasampayuttakānaṃ*: here, by the word *chanda* itself—which is indicated immediately after the preceding *chanda* as having a similar form and is connected to it—the status of being a qualifier of the associated [states] for the *chanda* that functions as the condition is shown. Thus, "the predominance of desire (*chandādhipati*)"...
It should be understood that instead of saying "of the associated [states]," it is said "of those associated with desire" (chandasampayuttakānaṃ). This same method applies to the others as well.
By the phrase "by way of respect and esteem," he shows the occurrence of wholesome and indeterminate states.

That which has not been obtained is to be obtained; that which has been obtained is not to be abandoned. Alternatively, that without which one cannot exist is what is to be obtained; its meaning is precisely "not to be abandoned."
“Not despised” (*anavaññātaṃ*): even though they are despised, because one perceives no fault in them and takes pleasure in them, they are made “not despised.

Because those [states] fixed in falsehood (*micchattaniyata*)—which are like the destruction of absorption and possess great power—do not arise without a dominant factor (*adhipati*), he said “exclusively” (*ekanteneva*).
And those which consist of the obscurations of karma and defilements are both obstructions to heaven and obstructions to the Path for those who have directly experienced heaven.
They are not even capable of being reborn among the gods of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), let alone those of the fine-material or immaterial realms.

Furthermore, when divided according to the sense-sphere and so forth, the functional object-predominance (kiriya-ārammaṇādhipati) is a condition of object-predominance (ārammaṇādhipati-paccaya) only for unwholesome states accompanied by greed.
Thus, regarding objective phenomena belonging to another's continuum that possess an object, [it is said]: "An internal-objective phenomenon is [a condition] for an external-objective phenomenon..."

Since the statement "a state is a condition for a state by way of predominance-condition" (*dhammassa adhipatipaccayena paccayo*) is absent [in that context], and because the predominance-condition of the object (*ārammaṇādhipati*) is not mentioned in the passage "an external object is [a condition] for an external object," it might be understood that there is no predominance-conditionality;

nevertheless, based on such statements as "one esteems and relishes the external aggregates," the functional states (*kriyādhamma*) of an Arahant— [...are established. (Note: The sentence is incomplete in the source text.)
It should be understood that this was stated with the intention that [beings] take pleasure [in it] by honoring it as something weighty, such as ordinary worldlings (puthujjana) and others do.
It has already been examined that, as in the case of expressions such as "the aggregates (khandha) that are visible and impinging," the word *khandha* ought to refer specifically to form (rūpa).

Alternatively, this was stated with reference to the relishing of future functional phenomena (kiriyadhamma) at the time of being an ordinary worldling and so forth. [This refers to] "phenomena that are neither resultant nor subject to result."

Because of such statements as, "Having made the aggregates heavy (an object of esteem), one relishes and delights in them," functional states (*kiriyadhammā*) indeed serve as predominance conditions (*adhipatipaccaya*) for lust and views.

Furthermore, because of statements such as, "One relishes and delights in future aggregates by making past objects heavy," even future states belonging to the three planes (*tebhūmaka*) can be predominance conditions.
However, this point must also be investigated due to the presence of functional turning-over consciousness (*āvajjanakiriyā*).
The commentary on the exposition of the predominance condition (*adhipatipaccaya*) is finished.
4. Commentary on the exposition of the proximity condition (*anantarapaccaya*):

The conditions "absence" (*natthi*) and "disappearance" (*vigata*) are stated by way of their specific quality of making room [for other states], but the conditions "proximity" (*anantara*) and "immediacy" (*samanantara*) are not so.
These, however, have been stated by way of their specific nature as causes for the determination of consciousness;

therefore, demonstrating that specific nature of being causes for the determination of consciousness, he provides an exposition by way of the elements (*dhātu*) and by way of the wholesome (*kusala*) and so forth, beginning with "the eye-consciousness element.

In this context, when it is said, "the mind-consciousness element [is the cause] of the mind-consciousness element," the distinction between the condition and the conditioned arising from that condition would not be understood.
One should have said, “each preceding one [is the condition] for each succeeding one.

If that were the case, the demonstration of specific types of consciousness by means of specific elements, which he had begun to undertake, would be interrupted. Furthermore, it is not possible to say, “the mind-consciousness element [is the condition] for the mind element,” because there is no fixed rule;
nor likewise can one say, “the mind element [is the condition] for the eye-consciousness element.”
It is not possible. For there is no fixed rule that the mind-element is the immediate condition for the eye-consciousness-element alone;

therefore, having first shown the method by way of illustration starting from the five manifest consciousness-elements up until the point where the specific determination of the elements exists, he spoke the words "preceding, preceding wholesome [states]" and so forth in order to show them without exception. [The phrase] "of similar wholesome [states]"...
The meaning is: "similar wholesome states" or "concordant wholesome states" with respect to feeling or its causes.

By this, it is stated that even those belonging to different planes (bhūmi) can function as conditions. It should be understood that by the inclusion of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), death-moments rooted in wholesome and unwholesome roots are also included;
likewise, by the inclusion of the rootless, registration-moments (tadārammaṇa) are also included.

Regarding the phrase "of the sense-sphere functional adverting consciousness" (*kāmāvacara-kiriyā-āvajjanassa*): it should be understood that by including the term "adverting" (*āvajjana*), the sense-sphere functional consciousness is thereby specified.
The meaning here is this: sense-sphere resultant consciousness is the immediate condition (*anantara-paccaya*) for the entire class of sense-sphere functional consciousness;

and since it [the resultant] serves as such a condition, it applies specifically to the adverting consciousness. Furthermore, by the inclusion of the term "adverting" itself, the determining consciousness (*voṭṭhapana*) is also included here.
It should be understood as "taken.
The commentary on the exposition of the proximity condition (anantarapaccaya) is finished.
6. Commentary on the Exposition of the Co-nascent Condition (sahajātapaccaya).

6. “‘Of one another’ (aññamaññassa) means ‘of one [to] another’ (añño aññassa)”; this is the ancient reading. However, in the canonical text, the meaning must be stated for the word “mutually” (aññamaññaṃ) as it occurs in the phrase “is a condition by way of mutual co-nascence condition” (aññamaññaṃ sahajātapaccayena paccayo), not for the word “of one another” (aññamaññassa) which is not so stated there.
Furthermore, when the meaning of one word has been stated, the meaning of another word—even if they have the same meaning—has not thereby been stated.
Therefore, they read: "Mutually means one [is the cause] for another. "Descent" refers specifically to rebirth-linking in the five-aggregate existence (*pañcavokāra-bhava*) and not to others;
with this intention, he says, "at the moment of rebirth-linking in the five-aggregate existence.
As for the statement "material phenomena [are the condition] for immaterial phenomena," although it was previously stated that "at the moment of descent there is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*),"...
Nevertheless, since it was not thereby excluded that material phenomena (*rūpīnaṃ*) serve as conditions at another moment, this was stated for the purpose of excluding that [possibility].

"At some time" means "some [phenomena] at some time," or alternatively, "some [phenomena] at any time. By this, it is meant that certain material phenomena, having become the basis (*vatthu*), at the time of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), previously served as the conascent condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*) for other material phenomena and for the immaterial [phenomena] of the basis at another time.

It prevents what should not be prevented. And having done so, although one should have said "at some time" (*kañci kālaṃ*) or "at any time" (*kismiñci kāle*), a transposition of case endings (*vibhattivipallāsa*) has been made.

For thus, "kañci" is the singular accusative, which—by its connection with "material phenomena" (*rūpino dhammā*)—is a substitute for the nominative plural; and by its connection with "time" (*kāle*), it is a substitute for the locative singular.

It is understood as follows. By the previous statement, "One aggregate and the [heart-]base are [the conditions] for the three aggregates," etc., it was established that the base, when accompanied by name, must be called a "condition for name";

by this [present statement], it is shown that the base alone may likewise be so called. Furthermore, although there are instances where the three [aggregates] function as mutual and conascent conditions for one another, by this specific statement—[that they are not so related to the base]—it is indicated that the base is not a condition for name in those ways.

It should be understood that this was stated because it is not included [in the previous categories]. Regarding the matter-form (rūpa) originated by kamma, which constitutes a portion of the matter originated by the four [causes], the genitive case should be understood as expressing either a part of a whole (*samudāya-ekadesa*) or as a selection (*niddhāraṇa*).
The commentary on the exposition of the co-nascent condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*) is finished.

8. Explanation of the Description of the Dependence Condition (Nissaya-paccaya-niddesa) In the description of the dependence condition, the phrase “material phenomena [are related] to immaterial phenomena at any time” is not applicable.
However, regarding that which *is* applicable there—namely, “certain material phenomena”—in order to point out those very phenomena:

The passage beginning with “the eye-base” and so forth has been stated. If it is argued that, because it was stated that “basis-matter exists in the five-aggregate existence,” the phrase “excluding the fruition of the formless realm” should not have been said—[we reply: No.
Since it was stated “of the fruition of the three planes,” one who does not know what must be excluded—that which does not arise in the five-aggregate existence—must be informed of it.
The commentary on the exposition of the dependence condition (*nissayapaccaya*) is finished.
9. Commentary on the exposition of the decisive support condition (*upanissayapaccaya*).
