Regarding the phrase "those three groups," he says that in the case of the decisive support condition there are three groups because they comprise many [factors]. In this...
However, in the exposition of the decisive support (upanissaya), those preceding states which serve as the proximity-decisive support for succeeding states are, for all of them, exclusively so;
they do not exist for some at any time. Therefore, since the proximity-decisive support is included within those specific instances, it is impossible to say "for some," and thus that was not stated.
But as for those preceding states which [serve as] for succeeding states...
The object-predominance conditions (ārammaṇa-pakatūpanissaya) exist; however, they do not exist for all [mental states] without exception.

They do not exist for those for whom strong obstructive conditions for their arising are present, but they do exist for others. Therefore, in those instances where the proximity-predominance condition (anantara-upanissaya) is not obtained, it is stated:
"for some" (kesañci). For those established conditions, by which [conditions] and with respect to which produced phenomena...

The meaning here is that they must be unwholesome and so forth, and that "of some of them" refers specifically to those [unwholesome states] which ought to function as decisive support conditions (*upanissaya-paccaya*), rather than referring indiscriminately to "some among the unwholesome and so forth.
It should be understood that "the preceding wholesome... or indeterminate states" refers to those indeterminate states for which the subsequent ones must serve as decisive support conditions;
for a material indeterminate state does not receive a decisive support condition.

How so? First, it does not receive [the condition] of object-proximity or decisive support because matter is non-objective and because it does not occur according to the fixed sequence of prior and posterior;
nor does it receive natural decisive support because there is no "natural" state in a material continuity that is devoid of consciousness.
For just as faith and other qualities are produced by a mental continuity, or as weather and food are utilized, it is not so with matter.

By means of the continuity of form (*rūpasantāna*). And when form proceeds given the presence of conditions such as the season and seeds, or karma and so forth, it is not produced by those [conditions].
For "production" (*pakaraṇa*) is the fashioning (*pakappana*) of volition (*cetanā*) by way of its arising, supporting, application, and so on, in one who possesses consciousness;
and form is devoid of consciousness. And just as in the case of certain phenomena that are effortless and dependent upon conditions...
There is the nature of having an object for some [consciousnesses], but not for others; in this way, the nature of having accessories and the nature of being without accessories should be understood.
Furthermore, seasonal conditions, seeds, and so forth, are conditions for sprouts and the like simply because those [sprouts] do not exist in their absence;

they are not, however, conditions by way of being a decisive support (upanissaya) and so on. In this context, the status of decisive support (upanissaya-paccaya) belongs only to the preceding factors, by way of general prevalence.

And this has been stated by way of what is manifest. However, because of such statements as, "One gives a gift aspiring for future aggregates," even future states can be decisive support conditions (*upanissaya-paccaya*).

It should be understood that these are included here because they share the same characteristics as the previously mentioned object-decisive support (*ārammaṇa-upanissaya*) and natural-decisive support (*pakatūpanissaya*).
The phrase "both a person and a lodging" indicates those phenomena that partake in the state of being a decisive support (*upanissaya*) by way of grasping both the person and the lodging.

By the word "and" (*pi*), all other phenomena that partake in the state of being a decisive support by way of grasping robes, forest, trees, mountains, and so forth, are included. This is as seen in such passages as:
"An indeterminate phenomenon is a condition for an indeterminate phenomenon by way of the decisive-support condition."
Indeed, by stating "the lodging is for bodily happiness" and so forth,

and by showing that those phenomena which partake in the state of being a decisive support (upanissaya) through the taking of a lodging are conditions by way of the decisive-support condition (upanissaya-paccaya),

this same method is shown to apply to persons and other such entities as well. Furthermore, even present objects and natural decisive supports (pakatūpanissaya) possess the characteristic of being similar to a lodging in their state of being present.

These [factors] should be understood as being included right here. For he will later state, by way of such passages as "one produces jhāna depending on present temperature, food, and lodging," that just as lodging has the status of a present [condition], so too present temperature and the rest have the status of natural decisive supports (*pakatūpanissaya*);
and [he will state], "present eye... [and] the present base [as a support] for the present aggregates."
By the passage beginning, “making it heavy and relishing it,” the state of the eye and so forth as object-predominance conditions (*ārammaṇūpanissaya*) is shown.
Furthermore, even for present [states] of that same kind, their status as natural-predominance conditions (*pakatūpanissaya*) should be understood because they were previously natural [states].
With the intention that kasiṇa-objects and the like are merely objects (*ārammaṇa*) and not predominance conditions, he said, “of some.”

Wholesome consciousness of the formless realm (*arūpāvacara-kusala*) is also a decisive support (*upanissaya*) for the arising of a jhāna that has not yet arisen in relation to a particular kasiṇa or other object, for the attainment of all jhānas already arisen, and for the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) such as the various modes of psychic power (*iddhividha*).
It is with reference to this meaning that it was said: "Wholesome consciousness of the three planes is [a support] for wholesome consciousness of all four planes. And this has also been stated:

“Dependent upon faith belonging to the formless realm (arūpāvacara), one arouses jhāna, insight (vipassanā), the path (magga), direct knowledge (abhiññā), and attainment (samāpatti) belonging to the fine-material realm (rūpāvacara).

Sensuous-sphere wholesome kamma (kāmāvacarakusala) serves as a decisive support (upanissaya) for the resultant states of the fine-material and formless realms by way of being their productive support;
it also serves as a support for the wholesome states that produce them, by way of the determining rebirth-linking consciousness and the preceding impulsion (javana) prior to the death-consciousness.

Fine-material-sphere wholesome [kamma] is a condition for fine-immaterial-sphere resultant [consciousness], and fine-immaterial-sphere wholesome [kamma] is a condition for fine-material-sphere resultant [consciousness], by way of being a decisive support (upanissaya) for the wholesome that produces them.

Thus, the conditional relationship of each of the wholesome states belonging to the three planes to the resultants of the four planes and to the functional states of the three planes should be understood according to their respective application. For in the Pāḷi, the natural decisive support (pakatūpanissaya) is indeed mentioned.
"He has answered in the sections of questions by means of the method and vision alone.
By this "method," however, the meaning is: by way of the slight trace of the arising of affection based upon the production of the supramundane.
But since supramundane states do not act as conditions for unwholesome states by any kind of condition, this [point] is not to be taken seriously.

The intended meaning is that it "should be seen. The life-continuum (bhavaṅga) of the sense-sphere and so forth, accompanied by roots, as well as bodily pleasure and so forth, are the decisive support (upanissaya) for wholesome states of the fine-material sphere and so forth.

The resultant consciousness of the immaterial sphere is the decisive support for the wholesome state of the fine-material sphere when one, aspiring for that [resultant], generates a wholesome state to produce it;

and it is also the support for the functional consciousness of the fine-material sphere when, for the purpose of knowing the immaterial-sphere resultants during the prior stages such as the preliminary (nivuṭṭha), one generates that [functional] state.

For an Arahant who is producing the jhānas and direct knowledges (abhiññā), each respective resultant consciousness of the four planes is a decisive support (upanissaya) by way of being the wholesome decisive support that produces it. Therefore he said: "Likewise, the resultant of the three planes.

Even though a Non-returner produces the jhānas and insight for the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship, he has never before seen that [fruit] with those [jhānas], as is the case with worldlings and others.
Like the fruits of stream-entry and so forth, therefore, like those [fruits], the fruition of the highest path (aggaphala) is not a decisive support (upanissaya) for those jhānas and so on.
For only that which has been previously acquired is a decisive support for what is yet to come. Hence he said:
"It is also [a support] for subsequent wholesomeness."

When one performs wholesome deeds such as giving while aspiring even for the analytical knowledge of the meaning of action (*kiriya-attha-paṭisambhidā*) and so forth, the functional states (*kiriyā*) of the three planes also serve as a decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*) for the wholesome states of all four planes. Regarding wise attention (*yoniso-manasikāra*), there is no need for further elaboration;
by depending upon it, unwholesome states arise through the production of lust and so forth, and by way of being a decisive support for both wholesome and unwholesome states.
[This applies] to the fruition of the four planes. In the same way, it should also be applied to functional (kiriya) states. Therefore he said:
"The natural strong-dependence, even when classified as functional, certainly exists for the wholesome and other aggregates of the four planes.

However, in the case of those states that are neither fruition nor subject to fruition, the demonstration of the status of natural strong-dependence for only the three groups—climate, food, and lodging—is merely an illustration of the method.
"By the method set forth in this great treatise, the *Paṭṭhāna*" refers to what was stated with reference to the negation of the decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*)—
such as "a neutral state arises dependent on a wholesome state," and "mind-produced matter arises dependent on the wholesome aggregates"—
and to its non-occurrence in the positive sequence (*anuloma*). "By the method of the Suttanta" means...
“Name-and-form has consciousness as its proximate cause, and the six sense bases have name-and-form as their proximate cause,” and so forth;
and: “Just as upon a rocky mountain in the wilderness, a vast forest, trees grow by depending on it as their supporting condition—those forest lords.”
And with the first [section].
The commentary on the exposition of the decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*) is finished.
10. Commentary on the Exposition of the Pre-existence Condition (*purejāta-paccaya*).
10. By way of method and vision, those [consciousnesses] such as eye-consciousness that do not function without a prenascent object are shown by the demonstration of the prenascent object for them;

likewise, in the mind-door, whatever functions with a prenascent object is also shown—by implication—to have its entire objective base as a prenascent object, even though it has not been explicitly stated in its own form.

He said, "The teaching was given by way of what remains. It should be understood that for one who transforms the body by means of consciousness, and for the supernormal power of transformation (*iddhividhā-abhiññā*), any of the eighteen [bases] may serve as a pre-arisen object (*purejāta-ārammaṇa*).

Regarding the phrase "those which have that as their object," here, because the basis (*vatthu*) that arises at rebirth-linking lacks the status of a pre-arisen [condition], the other [the mind-base] is likewise absent.

There is no inclusion [of the bhavaṅga]. However, the inclusion of that which exists as the bhavaṅga should either be made or not made, because its object is indistinct—just like the rebirth-linking consciousness—due to being merely an object;
and this also applies to the mind-consciousness element existing as the investigating consciousness mentioned in the phrase "and of the mind-elements."
The commentary on the exposition of the pre-arisen condition (*purejāta-paccaya-niddesa*) is finished.
11. Commentary on the Exposition of the Post-Arisen Condition (*pacchājāta-paccaya-niddesa*):

The phrase "of that very [consciousness]" is stated by way of showing the pre-arisen conditions for the resultant states of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) and fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) without exception; however, the resultant consciousness of the fine-material sphere does not arise from nutriment-produced matter (*āhāra-samuṭṭhāna*).
The commentary on the exposition of the postnascent condition is finished.
12. Commentary on the Exposition of the Repetition Condition:
By the phrase "distinguished by being more proficient and more powerful," this [condition] is distinguished from the resultant-inefficient (vipākābyākata).
The commentary on the exposition of the condition of repetition (*āsevanapaccaya*) is finished. 13.

Commentary on the exposition of the condition of kamma (*kammapaccaya*): Since kamma associated with volition (*cetanā*), such as covetousness and so forth, does not constitute the condition of kamma, it is stated that "it is only volitional kamma."
He said: "For even though they possess the quality of being subject to fruition (*vipākadhammadhamma*), they do not have such a nature [as volition].
By the phrase 'capable of producing its own fruit,' it should be understood that the capacity of the kamma—that is, its status as a kamma-condition—is what is being stated.
By saying "only in the fivefold plane (*pañcavokāra*), not elsewhere," he shows that sense-sphere volition (*kāmāvacaracetanā*) does not produce even form in the one-fold plane (*ekavokāra*).
The commentary on the exposition of the kamma-condition is finished.
14. Commentary on the exposition of the result-condition:

In the exposition of the result-condition, the demonstration of the method is made by way of those [factors] for which the result is exclusively a result-condition; for in the formless realm, the result of two planes does not become a condition for matter.
The commentary on the exposition of the resultant condition is finished. 15.

Commentary on the Exposition of the Nutriment Condition “Having made into morsels and swallowed” means having swallowed together with the bases such as what is eaten, drunk, and so forth. For even things that are to be sipped or licked are indeed morsels by virtue of their own nature.

Regarding the phrase "acting merely as a protector of that which is produced by the continuity of consciousness," the status of mind-produced [nutriment] as a nutriment-condition (*āhāra-paccaya*) must be understood after careful consideration.

For it is not said that edible food (*kabaḷīkāra-āhāra*) is exclusively mind-produced, nor that it is non-mind-produced, nor that both together are the nutriment-condition for the body produced by mind;
rather, all three types of nutriment are stated to be the nutriment-condition for the body that is not produced by mind.
The commentary on the exposition of the nutriment condition is finished.
16. Commentary on the Exposition of the Faculty Condition:
Since the immaterial life-faculty is also included, the intention is that because it is mixed [with other factors], the life-faculty should not be excluded in its entirety.

Regarding the phrase "of inseparable phenomena" (*avinibbhuttadhammānaṃ*), this is the intended meaning: there is no conventional expression of mutual inseparability between the material and the immaterial.

Therefore, even though the eye and other [faculties]—which serve as faculty-conditions for immaterial states and depend upon other conditions—do not exercise their function as faculty-conditions for those inseparable phenomena at the very moment they themselves exist, they would still be faculty-conditions. However, whoever...

The faculty-condition (indriya-paccaya) is independent [of time] for those phenomena that are inseparable; there is no moment when it does not exercise its function as a faculty-condition for them while it itself exists.

Furthermore, if the female-faculty and male-faculty were a faculty-condition for sexual characteristics and so forth, they would also be such a condition for those [characteristics] with which they are inseparable. For matter is not a condition for matter, nor is non-matter a condition for non-matter.

[If you argue that] there is a faculty-condition (indriya-paccaya) for what is dissociated [from the body], then because they would be undissociated from the female and male faculties, the sexual characteristics and so forth would exist even during the stages of the embryo (kalala) and so on—at which times those [characteristics] do not exercise their function as faculty-conditions.
Therefore, they are not undissociated from those [faculties]; and because of the absence of such non-dissociation, they cannot have the status of a faculty-condition.
They do not pervade. However, they do not pervade others because those [others] are not the seeds for them [the faculties], which are co-nascent with them;

therefore, because they do not pervade those signs and so forth that have attained a state of dissociation, nor other factors belonging to the same group (*kalāpa*) that are undissociated, these [faculties] do not function as faculty-conditions (*indriya-paccaya*). For those for whom the female and male faculties are the seeds...

Some say that these genders and so forth lack ultimate reality; however, they maintain that even during the embryonic stage of the *kalala* and subsequent phases, there exists a corresponding presence of those genders.

Regarding the classifications stated according to type (*jāti*) and plane (*bhūmi*), within the category of the wholesome (*kusala*), only the wholesome of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara-kusala*) is to be excluded from the immaterial sphere; thus it is said:
"Excluding the wholesome of the fine-material sphere, the remainder are both wholesome and unwholesome. [This refers to] the first supramundane [path].
However, because there is no single birth or plane that is associated with both [joy] and mental grief (*domanassa*), even though it is not found in the formless realm (*ārūpa*), it was not excluded.
This same principle should be applied to the causes (*hetu*) and so forth, as in such passages as: "Likewise, the unconditioned wholesome cause; likewise, the unwholesome causes.

Regarding the phrase "at the moment of persistence," this was stated with reference to the fact that the material life-faculty (*rūpajīvitindriya*) lacks the status of a co-nascent condition (*sahajātapaccaya*).
Furthermore, its status as a faculty-condition (*indriya-paccaya*) at the moment of arising cannot be denied. For it will be said:
"Dependent on an indeterminate state... [and so on] ...dependent on one great primary of non-percipient beings... [and so on] ...the faculty-condition is similar to the kamma-condition.
Indeed, for the matter of non-percipient beings that arises with a faculty-condition, there is no other [condition] than the physical life-faculty (*rūpa-jīvitindriya*).
The faculty condition exists in the fivefold plane during the course of existence for both the mind-produced matter (*kaṭattārūpa*) and the functional matter.

Furthermore, the six sections beginning with the "Dependent" section proceed by taking only the moment of arising; and this being so, the postnascence condition does not apply to these [sections] in the forward order.
The commentary on the exposition of the faculty condition is concluded.
17. Explanation of the Exposition of the Condition of Jhāna (Jhānapaccayaniddesa).
Regarding the phrase "consisting of applied thought, sustained thought, rapture, joy, grief, equanimity, and one-pointedness of mind":
although there are no jhāna-factors here consisting of joy and grief, those consisting of pleasure and pain are indeed of the nature of joy and grief.
The inclusion of "mental joy" (somanassa) and "mental grief" (domanassa) is made for the purpose of showing that the factors of jhāna are not of the nature of bodily pleasure and pain.

But is it not the case that by the very statement "excluding the two sets of fivefold consciousness," bodily pleasure and pain are already excluded, so that only the mention of "pleasure" (sukha) and "pain" (dukkha) should have been made?
No; because the pleasure and pain that are factors of jhāna must be distinguished from those that are not factors of jhāna.
For when it is said, "In the states excluding the two sets of fivefold consciousness, [the factors] consisting of pleasure, pain, equanimity,
and one-pointedness [are present]," it is understood only that bodily pleasure and pain are excluded along with equanimity and one-pointedness in the two sets of fivefold consciousness;
however, it is not understood that there is a state of pleasure or a state of pain which constitutes a factor of jhāna among those pleasures and pains that are indeed jhāna-factors.
And since it is qualified [by feeling], he employs the terms "joy" (somanassa) and "grief" (domanassa) for the purpose of showing that the very states of pleasure (sukha) and pain (dukkha)—
as distinguished by the presence of joy and grief— are the factors of absorption (jhānaṅga) for pleasure and pain. By this,

through the statement "excepting the two sets of fivefold sense-cognitions," it is shown that even though pleasure and pain are excluded from those [fivefold cognitions], they lack the status of being factors of absorption because they lack the nature of joy and grief.
This has been shown. But why were pleasure, pain, equanimity, and one-pointedness excluded when they were excluded [from the definition]?
Because the factors of jhāna (*jhānaṅga*) are extracted in the section on the arising of consciousness (*cittuppādakaṇḍa*), and those [factors] are not extracted there as jhāna-factors.
To show why they were not extracted, he said: "But of the five groups of consciousness," and so forth.
“By the mere occurrence” (*abhinipātamattattā*): by this, he shows the absence of the activity of thinking even at the stage of mere adverting and receiving.
Regarding the phrase “equanimity, pleasure, and pain existing among them,” this is the reading of the ancients (*porāṇapāṭho*).
Therein, it is shown that equanimity, pleasure, and pain—along with one-pointedness of mind which shares their same characteristics—are not mentioned for the very reason already stated.
It should be seen. Previously, however, when the seven factors were shown, four factors were excluded;
thus, in order to show the reason for their exclusion, it should not be shown by means of a "les" (similarity) based on identical characteristics. For this is the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).
And if it were to be shown by means of a "les," then only one [of the three] among those three already mentioned would need to be stated; yet, by stating all three...

Consequently, it would follow that [equanimity] is not included as a factor of jhāna, either because it has been excluded for the reasons already stated, or because it is not excluded for some other reason.
Therefore, in order to avoid this fault, they recite: "equanimity, one-pointedness of mind, pleasure, and pain.
As for those who hold that pleasure and pain are not manifest due to their being obscured by joy (*somanassa*) and the other factors that constitute the jhāna-factors...

They say: "The reason why pleasure (*sukha*) and the other [factors], though they are similar in being associated with the functions of the faculties (*indriyakicca*), are not mentioned as jhāna-factors (*jhānaṅga*) must be stated, and it is not because of one-pointedness of mind (*cittekaggatā*);
therefore, that [one-pointedness] is not included here. For them, this is merely a matter of personal preference.
If a reason must indeed be stated for why those factors similar to the jhāna-factors are not mentioned as jhāna-factors, then [the reason] regarding one-pointedness of mind—

And here, since it is identical to the one-pointedness of mind (citt’ekaggatā) found in the mental element associated with doubt—which is itself a factor of jhāna—the reason for its not being extracted must indeed be stated.

The intention [of the author] is that even in the remaining rootless (ahetuka) states, the factor of jhāna is indeed extracted; this is what is meant by the phrase "in the section on the arising of consciousness" (cittuppādakaṇḍa), which is the place where such extraction occurs.
The commentary on the exposition of the jhāna-condition is finished.
18. Commentary on the Exposition of the Path-Condition:
Wisdom, applied thought, right speech, right action, right livelihood, energy, mindfulness, concentration, wrong view, wrong speech, wrong action, and wrong livelihood.

Regarding the phrase "these twelve factors," here both types of intention (*saṅkappa*), energy (*vīriya*), and concentration (*samādhi*) are included within the terms "thought" (*vitakka*), "energy," and "concentration. This is established by such Sutta passages as:
"Indeed, friends, this eightfold wrong path is the way that is not the holy life. That is to say: wrong view...
[and so on] ...wrong concentration," which likewise includes wrong speech, action, and livelihood.

Because they are established by way of the conventional designation "path-factors" (maggaṅga), the twelve factors—both those obtained and those not obtained here—are spoken of by grouping them together under the common term "path-factor.

For in this way, the conventional usage of the Suttas is also demonstrated; and by demonstrating it thus, [the author] has extracted [the term] as "path-factors" in the "Exposition of Path-Conditions," referring to that which occurs in the text.
These twelve factors should not be presented as having the status of being path-factors (*maggaṅga*).
For the meaning of the term "path-factor" in the Canon cannot be stated as "wrong speech, wrong action, and wrong livelihood.

Rather, those volitional states which are the opposites of right speech and so forth are called "factors of the wrong path" in the Sutta precisely because they are the antitheses of those [right factors], and not because they serve as conditions for the path.
In this text, the path factors that serve as conditions for the path are called "path factors" (*maggaṅgāni*);
one should not extract a different term and explain the meaning of something else.

However, for one who wishes to demonstrate both the figurative and non-figurative sense of "path factor," another word resembling the term *maggaṅga* found in the text must be extracted, which possesses the meanings of both words, as follows:

“‘Legal issue’ (adhikaraṇa) means the four legal issues. However, here in the exposition of the conditions for the Path, only the term *maggaṅga* as it occurs in the actual text (*pāḷi*) has been extracted;
the intended meaning has not been determined by first presenting the general sense of the word.

Therefore, lest the term *maggaṅga* in the text be taken to mean wrong speech and so forth, [the author] specifies: “right view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness, concentration, wrong view, intention, effort, and concentration.”

They recite: "These are the twelve factors. But surely, in that case, one should not say "excluding rootless thought-arising," for in those [rootless states], the aforementioned right view and so forth do not exist such that they would need to be excluded? No;

because it serves the purpose of determining the locus of their arising. These [factors] arise only in those [states] excluding rootless thought-arising, and not in rootless thought-arisings themselves. Those that have arisen therein...
"Twelve factors"—this is the meaning here.
The commentary on the exposition of the path-condition is finished.
20. Commentary on the Exposition of the Dissociation Condition.

20. "Because there is no suspicion of association" (sampayogāsankāya abhāvato): by this, it is shown that the state of being a benefactor, which serves as the basis for the suspicion of association, constitutes the condition of dissociation (vippayuttapaccaya).
The commentary on the exposition of the condition of dissociation is finished.
21. Commentary on the Exposition of the Condition of Presence (atthipaccaya)
21. The presence condition (*atthipaccaya*) is said to be fivefold by way of the wholesome and so forth, but *nibbāna* is not.
For that which, having been non-beneficial through the absence of its own existence, becomes beneficial upon obtaining existence, is a presence condition.

And *nibbāna*, in relation to those things that take *nibbāna* as their object, does not become beneficial by first being non-beneficial through the absence of its own existence and then becoming beneficial by obtaining existence.

It is an assistance. Since the state of being an assistance—which is the opposite of the state of being an assistance through non-existence for those things associated with arising and so forth—is the condition of presence (*atthipaccaya*), Nibbāna is not a condition of presence.
Furthermore, since those things for which it is a condition must arise either simultaneously with them, or earlier, or later, it lacks the status of being a co-nascent or other such conditions.

He said: "Nutriment and faculty do not obtain the distinctions such as 'co-nascent' (sahajāta) and so forth. And their absence should be understood by way of the intrinsic nature (dhammasabhāva) of these phenomena.
The commentary on the exposition of the presence condition (atthipaccaya) is finished.
22–23–24. Commentary on the exposition of the absence (natthi), disappearance (vigata), and non-disappearance (avigata) conditions.
22–23. "In this context, the difference is only in the characteristic of the condition" (paccayalakkhaṇa).

By this it is understood that in the conditions of absence (natthi) and disappearance (vigata), as well as in the conditions of presence (atthi) and non-disappearance (avigata), there is a difference only in the phrasing (byañjana), not in the meaning (attha). This means that regarding that which is the condition, there is no difference;
rather, the difference lies only in the characteristic of the condition as included within the phrasing. It is stated with reference to this meaning.
The commentary on the exposition of the non-existence, disappearance, and non-disappearance conditions is finished.
The commentary on the exposition of the conditions is finished.
The commentary on the discussion of miscellaneous determinations in the exposition of the conditions.
“Greed, hatred, and delusion are not conditions by way of the ripening condition; they are conditions by way of the remaining seventeen conditions”—this is the initial reading.

And here, the status of greed, hatred, and delusion as conditions has been stated individually through each of the seventeen conditions, for the purpose of showing that a single phenomenon can have multiple conditions without taking all the roots together.
Since non-delusion (*amoha*) and the others have been mentioned separately, it would follow that hatred (*dosa*) also possesses seventeen conditions;

and if that were so, the honoring of hatred would also have to be stated in the Canon. Furthermore, regarding the passage, "The unwholesome object-predominance (*ārammaṇādhipati*) is said to be an arising of consciousness accompanied by greed (*lobha*)," one should have said here, "an arising of consciousness accompanied by greed and hatred (*lobha-dosa*)."
It might be so, but since it was not stated [there], the status of hatred as a predominance condition (*adhipatipaccaya*) must also be excluded.

Nor is the predominance condition excluded by the expression "the remainder" (*sesānaṃ*); rather, it is included because it is a remainder among those previously mentioned, such as the prenascence condition (*purejāta-paccaya*).

Therefore, for the purpose of excluding that [predominance condition], one should not take hatred together with greed and delusion, nor should one take it separately; thus: "Hatred is also a predominance condition..."
They recite: "It does not exist [as such], but it exists as a condition by way of the remaining conditions.

By this method, he demonstrates the state of the tangible base (*phoṭṭhabbāyatana*) as a co-nascent and other types of conditions, and the state of all phenomena as causes and other conditions as appropriate. For this is not merely a demonstration that a single condition can function as multiple conditions;
rather, it shows the status of visible forms and so forth as natural decisive supports (*pakatūpanissaya*).
And it should be understood that this is shown by this [passage].
Without touching upon the differentiation of the four aggregates as the eye-consciousness-element and so forth, but taking them as they are, he said, "in the four aggregates.
[This refers to] wrong speech, wrong action, and wrong livelihood, together with those same kamma-nutriment conditions.
It is not possible to say that there are nineteen nutriments (dhātu) in this way.

For wrong speech and the rest do not serve as path-conditions for volition in the same manner as wrong view does, because they lack the status of being path-conditions for volition. If they were indeed [path-conditions], it would have to be stated in the *Pañhāvāra* section: "Three [factors] are path-conditions for the path through the condition of kamma.
Therefore, the status of wrong speech and the rest as path-conditions cannot be asserted.

This is the commentary on the *Paṭṭhāna*. Since the fact that volition (*cetanā*) possesses the nature of the remaining conditions has already been stated by the mention of its manifold conditional states, this [specific enumeration] need not be recited;
thus, they do not recite it. The original reading begins with “Lack of moral shame (*ahirika*)... pe... torpor (*middha*), restlessness (*uddhacca*), and doubt (*vicikicchā*)”;

however, since doubt is not a dominant condition (*adhipati-paccaya*), it is not included there, and instead [the text reads]: “Doubt, envy (*issā*), avarice (*macchariya*), and worry (*kukkucca*)...”
Then, having removed the predominance condition (*adhipatipaccaya*), they recite it here thus:
"The four great elements (*mahābhūtāni*) are conditions in ten ways by way of object (*ārammaṇa*)... [etc.

...by way of prenascence, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance; likewise again, the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*). However, in the earlier reading, the great elements are [treated as] dissociation conditions (*vippayuttapaccaya*).
Regarding the statement "they do not exist," they recite: "Conditions are ninefold by way of prenascence, presence, and non-disappearance;

by adding the dissociation condition, the basis is tenfold. The meaning of "only this much is new here" is that, within this prenascence condition, only the bases of visible form, sound, odor, taste, and the tangible—exclusive of the co-nascent and support conditions—are new. As for the objects:
These [factors] have been stated as being among the many conditions for those phenomena that serve as object-conditions (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*);
thus, with respect to all other conditions, there is no novelty in them. As for the faculties (*indriya*) and so forth, there is no novelty;

thinking that even the material life-faculty (*rūpa-jīvitindriya*) lacks the status of a condition that is not already present in the immaterial life-faculty (*arūpa-jīvitindriya*), its novelty has not been mentioned. However, because it does possess the status of a prenascence-condition (*purejāta-paccaya*), [it is included].
“Unprecedentedness” (apubbatā). The sevenfold mode of conditionality for edible food, together with the relation of pre-existence (purejāta), should be applied.

“Aspect” (ākāra) refers to the aspect of the roots and so forth. “Meaning” (attha) is the state of being helpful by way of that aspect. Alternatively, “by whatever meaning” (yenatthena) is a synonym for “by whatever aspect” (yenākārena).

The phrase “is found only in the case of resultant and root-conditions” (vipākahetūsu eva labbhati) refers here to the state of predominance (adhipatipaccaya) belonging to the non-delusion root-condition (amoha-vipākahetu).
And it is obtained only as supramundane resultant. Thus, in all instances, one should observe what is obtainable and what is not obtainable.
Instead of reading "dissociated," the earlier recension reads "in six ways"; however, having read that, they recite it as "in seven ways.
For here, the maximum limit is being stated; and that which is an object is not [necessarily] a support.
"It is not dissociated.

It should be understood that whatever is a kamma-condition among the immediate (anantara) and contiguous (samanantara) conditions is not a repetition-condition (āsevana-paccaya), and whatever is a repetition-condition is not a kamma-condition.
It is stated: "The natural decisive support (pakatūpanissaya) is indeed the natural decisive support."
Furthermore, it is also a kamma condition; therefore, they recite: "and it is a kamma condition. This is the meaning here:
while natural strong-dependence is for the most part exclusively a natural strong-dependence, some among them are also kamma conditions.
It has been stated: "In this context, however, regarding object-prenascence, the state of being a condition dissociated from the faculties is not found."

In this context, regarding "object-prenascence" (*ārammaṇapurejāta*): if it is stated that some object which is prenascence is intended, then since the state of being a dissociated condition (*vippayuttapaccayatā*) is obtainable for an object that is a physical basis (*vatthu*), one cannot say that it is not obtainable.

However, if, on the other hand, what is called "object-prenascence" refers to an object devoid of the status of a physical basis—distinct from "basis-prenascence" (*vatthupurejāta*)—then [the aforementioned objection does not apply].
Since its status as a support-condition (nissaya-paccaya) is not obtained, it should be stated that "its status as a support-faculty-dissociated condition is not obtained.
Regarding the phrase "from this onwards" (ito uttari): the meaning is "from after the pre-arisen [condition]" (purejātato parato).

Alternatively, from this point—either from the dissociation from faculties or from the dissociation from both support and faculties—one should understand that the object-predominance (ārammaṇādhipati) and so forth are to be understood as being either obtained or not obtained.

The meaning must be stated. However, since one would not speak of what is obtainable or unobtainable among the [twenty-four] conditions such as kamma, it is the former meaning alone that is intended here.
The original reading was "edible food is a nutriment-condition," but it is also a presence-condition and a non-disappearance-condition;
therefore, "edible food, while not relinquishing its status as a nutriment-condition, by way of presence and non-disappearance, [acts] through others as well..."
They recite: "It becomes a condition for many [factors] in two ways. The first reading is:
"By way of these ten—namely, the causes and predominants mentioned as conditions for jhāna according to their respective suitability.
The second is: "By way of these nine—namely, the causes, predominants, and jhānas (excluding the Path) mentioned as conditions for jhāna according to their respective suitability."
The final reading is “by way of these”; having examined them, that which is appropriate should be adopted.

“Similarity of conditionality” (paccayasabhāgatā) refers to the state of being a condition through the state of being an object (ārammaṇa-bhāva) and by way of immediate cessation; “dissimilarity of conditionality” (paccayavisabhāgatā) refers to the state of being a contradictory condition.
From the statement “by this means,” [it follows that] the co-nascent factors such as the root-cause (hetu) and so forth—

Homogeneity (*sabhāgatā*) exists through the state of being co-nascent; heterogeneity (*visabhāgatā*) exists through the mutual dissimilarity of co-nascent and non-co-nascent factors such as causes (*hetu*), objects (*ārammaṇa*), and so forth.
By means of such methods, homogeneity and heterogeneity are to be applied.

Conditions function only as producers, not as non-producers; thus, they serve as conditions primarily by virtue of their status as producers, and not primarily by virtue of their status as supporters.
The meaning should be understood as follows: those for whom conditions such as the "root-cause" (hetu) and so forth exist do not arise nor proceed without them;

thus, their dual predominance has been stated. For these [conditions] do not bring about proceeding merely by way of generating, as is the case with the "immediately preceding" (anantara) and other such conditions.
"All-bases" (sabbaṭṭhānika) means that the state of being a cause is the basis for all; since they possess this, they are called "all-basing. [This refers to] the decisive support (upanissaya).
When breaking [the classification], those three types of decisive support (*upanissaya*) must be mentioned; or else, one should simply include the decisive support without breaking it down.
In that context, "breaking" is for the purpose of showing that material phenomena do not function as conditions for the natural decisive support (*pakatūpanissaya*);

however, since the object-decisive support (*ārammaṇūpanissaya*) and the proximity-decisive support (*anantarūpanissaya*) were already included by the previous mention of the object-predominance (*ārammaṇādhipati*) and proximity (*anantara*), they are here included under the single category of proximity-decisive support.

It should be understood that this also shows the other [condition]. Even though the prenascence and postnascence conditions do not apply to all bases, they function as conditions for the immaterial and material [factors] respectively;

here, the prenascence condition should be discussed under "immediate" (anantara) and so forth, because it follows the same course as those, and the fact that they form a pair is not the reason for mentioning them together with postnascence, since the purpose is merely to show that they do not apply to all bases.

"Because it is intended": having recited that [passage] there, they read, "Even though it is 'subsequently arisen,' it does not have all things as its object, because it is a condition for material phenomena alone.
The commentary on the miscellaneous analysis of the exposition of conditions is finished.
The section on questions.
1. Explanation of the Positive Order of Conditions (Paccayānulomavaṇṇanā) "Each triad and dyad" means each triad and each dyad; it does not mean "a triad-dyad.
"And those which are conditions" refers to those wholesome and other phenomena mentioned as "dependent upon"; these, pervading the sense of dependence, are the wholesome and other conditions.
The meaning is "they are. For this very reason, he said: "And these, moreover, are co-nascent.
However, those conditions such as the root-condition (hetu-paccaya) by which arising is stated may be either co-nascent or not co-nascent.

Here, by the Blessed One—who, through the latter section, clarifies the identical meaning of the former section by means of the designations "dependent" and "co-nascent," which possess the same meaning as the sections on "dependent" and "co-nascent"—the first section [is explained].

It should be understood that the latter section is the "Awakening" (bodhi) in relation to the former section. This same method applies to the sections on conditions (paccaya), support (nissaya), conjoined (saṃsaṭṭha), and associated (sampayutta);
and in this way, skill in etymological analysis (niruttikosalla) is produced.
Having extracted those various questions, it is further written: "The skilled [teacher] [should explain] the states that are causes and the states associated with causes."
The reading “the wholesome roots are [conditions] for the associated aggregates” is a section of the *Pañhāvāra*;

they recite it exactly as it appears in the Pāḷi, considering it to be a scribal error. In the preceding sections, having determined wholesome and other states by way of their status as conascent, support, and associated conditions, and having asked about the arising of those wholesome and other states through the root-conditions and so forth within that determination, the answer is given.
It has been stated that in those [cases], it is not understood that "these indeed are those phenomena existing as conditions such as the root-cause (hetu)," and therefore,

because there is no determination of the root-cause and other conditions among the conditioned phenomena (paccayuppanna) within the root-cause and other conditions— since the state of pervading the meaning of "dependent" (paṭicca) and so forth is subsumed under such formulations as "a wholesome phenomenon might arise dependent on a wholesome phenomenon by way of the root-cause condition"— [the definition does not apply].
Having rendered the questions free from tangles and thicket-like obscurities, they were not analyzed there;

however, here, by means of such formulations as "Could a wholesome state be a condition for a wholesome state by way of the root-condition (hetu-paccaya)?", the wholesome states and so forth that function as conditions—such as the root-condition—and their corresponding conditionally arisen results are definitively determined.
Thus he said: "There is no meaning whatsoever included within the questions that remains undetermined."
“All those questions have been analyzed, having been made free from tangles and free from knots.
However, it should be understood that the state of being "free from tangles" was not stated with reference to the fact that the answer is the same everywhere once the question has been extracted;

rather, the meaning is that they were established and proclaimed by their very arising—that is, they were set forth by the mere act of posing the question—or that they were made known in various ways.
25–34. A hypothetical question (*parikappapucchā*) is a question regarding a possibility (*vidhipucchā*). "Could it be? (*kiṃ siyā*) means: is this possibility existent?
Or, he says that a hypothetical question is a questioning as to whether something might be or might not be. What is this so-called "questioning" (*sampucchana*)?
It is a question posed after due consideration, such as: "Should one master the Suttanta, or rather the Abhidhamma?"—this is by way of another [explanation].

The meaning is "together with the determination. When there is the sense that "whatever wholesome dhamma might arise by way of the root-condition (hetu-paccaya) would do so in dependence upon a wholesome dhamma," then because all questions proceed even regarding the postnascent condition (pacchājāta-paccaya) and the resultant condition (vipāka-paccaya), [it is asked]:
"Whatever wholesome dhamma might arise by way of the postnascent condition and the resultant condition, would that [arise] in dependence upon a wholesome dhamma..."

If this meaning were understood as “it may [arise] dependent [on them],” then, in that case, having singled out that which arises through the condition of post-nascence (*pacchājātapaccaya*) as the condition of fruition (*vipākapaccaya*),
because one asks about the existence [of it] dependent on a wholesome state (*kusala dhamma*),
it would follow that the arising of wholesome states through those conditions is admitted; yet, for wholesome states and so forth that arise from their respective conditions...
In this context, it was the existence of becoming dependent on wholesome and other states that was questioned; however, what is actually addressed is their arising.
Since, by doing so, the answer—“Dependent on a wholesome state, a wholesome state arises”—addresses precisely their arising, this meaning [of the question] is flawed.
Therefore, the phrase “or else” (*atha vā*) was stated as an alternative explanation.

In this context, having admitted the arising with the words "a wholesome state might arise," it is not appropriate to ask whether its existence occurs by way of a root-condition (*hetupaccaya*) with the phrase "might this exist by way of a root-condition?";

nor is it appropriate, having admitted the arising by way of a root-condition with the words "it might arise by way of a root-condition," to then ask about its existence with the phrase "might this exist? For what has been admitted is indeed already determined.

Therefore, it should be understood that by not granting [the premise], he asks: "Could there be such an arising as has been described—namely, 'dependent on a wholesome state, a wholesome state arises by way of the root-condition'?
Alternatively, the phrase "it might arise" (*uppajjeyya*) is also a form of inquiry: "Dependent on a wholesome state, could a wholesome state arise by way of the root-condition?"
The meaning is as follows. *Siyā* asks about the possibility of the very arising that was inquired about: "Could such an arising occur? Might it be possible?
This is the method when the word *siyā* is construed later [in the sentence]. However, when it remains in its original position, this *siyā* is a general inquiry;
yet by means of that inquiry, it is not understood what specific thing is being asked.
In order to qualify that very same question, he asks: "Dependent on a wholesome state, might a wholesome state arise by way of the root condition?
Thus, because they stand in the relationship of the qualified and the qualifier, both questions should be understood as constituting a single question.
The phrase "the expression of an action following upon another" means an expression that refers to a subsequent action having the same agent as the preceding one.
Even though there is no temporal sequence of priority and posteriority between the acts of "returning" (*paṭigamana*) and "arising" (*uppatti*),
the apprehension of even co-nascent conditions and their effects as being "condition" and "conditioned" occurs precisely by way of priority and posteriority; thus,

it is by virtue of the mode of the process of apprehension that the acts of returning and arising— which consist in dependence on conditions and the acquisition of selfhood— are likewise [distinguished].

It should be understood that this is a conventional expression for prior and posterior time. Or, "arising" (*uppatti*) is the same as "going" (*gamana*); thus, for one who is going, there is a "counter-going," and for what is arising, there is a "counter-arising" (*paṭi-uppajjana*), which is a corresponding action. For the prefix *pati-* has the sense of "counteracting" (*paṭikaraṇa*).

Therefore, with respect to the condition indicated in the accusative case as "a wholesome state" (*kusalaṃ dhammaṃ*), [the result arises] depending upon that which is arising, its own arising being dependent upon that [condition].
"Having gone toward" (paṭigantvā) is the meaning here; by that, it is said "having depended" (paṭicca), which means "having made a co-nascent condition" (sahajātapaccaya).
For "going toward" (paṭigamana) is the act of approaching toward that which is about to arise while already arising;
having performed that is the meaning of the word *paṭicca*.
35–38. It is stated that only two [methods] are shown in the text (*pāḷi*) because two questions are presented within the "Duality of Causes and Objects" (*hetu-ārammaṇa-duka*).
Here, it should be understood that the state of having a single root and so forth is stated for the questions;

however, by way of the conditions (*paccaya*), the very first is the "Pure Method" (*suddhika-naya*) because it is unmixed with other conditions, while the second [is so called] because each one among the objects and so forth [is considered individually].

Because the cause alone is the single root, it is called the "method of the single root" (*ekamūlakanaya*). In this way, because the predominance and other [conditions] serve as roots for the pairs beginning with the cause and the object, the methods of the "root-pair" (*dukamūlaka*) and so forth should be understood.
And because there is no further root beyond that, the method of the twenty-three roots is called "the root of all" (*sabbamūlaka*) in the Pāḷi;
therein, by means of the neuter designation, it is referred to as "the single... [root]... the root of all."

It is understood that "going by way of conditions" (paccayagamana) means "going by way of the text" (pāḷigamana); or it is a term for "not being confused regarding the method based on a single [condition], and so forth, up to the method based on all roots.
And here, because it is stated that "based on all roots" refers specifically to the twenty-three-root method, he will say in the reverse order:

"Just as in the direct order (anuloma), for each individual term there is a method based on one root... up to the method based on twenty-three roots, so too should it be expanded in the reverse order (paccanīya)."

39–40. It is said: "From 'conditioned by object' to 'conditioned by root'—to this extent, the method based on a single root is shown, beginning with the condition of object and ending with the condition of root.
This being so, the course of the text follows the manner of binding the spokes as in the Vinaya, rather than the manner of the lower purifications.
And it is by way of the lower purifications that the text proceeds here in the Abhidhamma.

Having proceeded thus, and having cleared up the lower section in the answer, the text proceeds as follows: "With object-condition, three with root; with predominance-condition, three; with predominance-condition, nine with root; with object, three," and so forth.

And that which is called here the "method based on a single root" is simply the pure method (*suddhikanaya*). And because there is no distinction [in its nature], it applies to those methods based on the object-root and the rest.

It is not obtained. For even if each respective beginning among the object and so forth is established, no specific meaning distinct from the "pure" (suddhika) stated at the beginning is obtained due to the absence of a connection with other conditions.
For that very reason, even in the answer, the pure method is not shown among those beginning with the object-root (ārammaṇamūlaka), etc.;
therefore: "With the object condition, the root condition, the object condition, the predominance condition... [etc.]..."

"By way of object condition... by way of non-disappearance condition"—this should be understood as the "Single Rooted Method" (ekamūlakanaya) stated by applying [the remaining conditions] such as root condition and so forth to a single object condition according to the lower method of purification.

Alternatively, in the Single Rooted methods, having shown the object as the root of the immediately preceding condition (anantarapaccaya) in the sequence "by way of object condition... by way of non-disappearance condition," the Single Rooted methods and so forth are abbreviated.
It should be understood that [the exposition] is concluded by means of the non-disappearance condition (*avigata-paccaya*) following the "all-root" (*sabbamūlaka*).

In the passage beginning with "dominant condition," "proximity condition," "contiguity condition," "co-nascence condition," and "mutuality condition," one should see this as a contraction of the "single-root" (*ekamūlaka*) and other categories after having shown only the root itself; it is neither a presentation of the pure [conditions] nor the "all-root."
This is the demonstration of a few conditions. 41.

Then, having condensed the roots such as the support (nissaya) and so forth, the section beginning with “non-disappearance condition, root condition” is commenced in order to demonstrate the method of the non-disappearance root.
And since the pure [condition] is not shown here, [the conditions] beginning with the object-root (ārammaṇa-mūlaka) are treated separately.
It is made known that the pure method (*suddhikanaya*) is not found separately. For the beginning is nowhere included within a summary (*saṃkhepa*).
Indeed, a summary consists in showing the middle by means of the beginning and the end, or in showing the course after having stated a few [terms] from the beginning onwards.
Having stated the second tetrad, the word "conditioned by disappearance" (*vigatapaccayā*) was extracted and set aside. By that, the final tetrad...
[The text] demonstrates this. From the third tetrad onwards, having condensed the pentads from their bases, it concludes with the final [tetrad] of all bases.

And herein, in the cases of the dyad-bases and so forth, just as the remaining conditions were combined with the dyad of cause and object, and the remaining ones with the triads of cause, object, and predominance, and so on;
likewise, [they are combined] with the dyads of cause and predominance, and the triads of cause, predominance, and proximity, and so forth.

And the remaining [factors] should be combined with the remaining [conditions]. Furthermore, since all conditions have been combined by way of their root-status (*mūlabhāva*), there is no distinction between the dyads beginning with "root" (*hetu*)—such as the "root-predominance" (*hetu-adhipati*) dyad—and those beginning with "predominance" (*adhipati*) within the "predominance-root" (*adhipati-hetu*) dyads;

for those very same conditions are merely stated in reverse order. Nevertheless, regarding the dyads beginning with "object" (*ārammaṇa*), such as the "object-predominance" (*ārammaṇa-adhipati*) dyad...

There is a distinction in the application of the remaining [factors] to the remaining [conditions], such as applying the remaining factors of the "root-of-cause" section to the remaining conditions like cause,
predominance, proximity, contiguity, and so forth. However, since even when applied in this way, they are not easily grasped,

and because it is not possible for a wise person to discern all those applications through the aforementioned method of arrangement, one should therefore not apply them in that manner, but rather in successive order.
The method of arrangement (*yojanā*) should be understood as follows: for in the manner of teaching the Dhamma, the Blessed One alone is the authority.
Regarding the enumerative verses (*gaṇanāgāthā*) at the beginning of the recitation, some appear contradictory; therefore, they should be accepted after careful counting.
It is stated: "Having combined each one of the twenty-two triads (*tika*) with a hundred and a hundred dyads (*duka*)."

That [method] was stated according to certain books in the *Duka-Tika-Paṭṭhāna*. However, in some [versions], each *duka* (pair) is joined with twenty-two *tikas* (triads), and that method of proceeding is appropriate.
For in those cases, there is no joining of a *tika* [to a *duka*];
rather, each single term of a *tika* is joined with a *duka*. Therein, among the sixty-six terms of the *tikas*, by means of each single...
By combining them, there are sixty-six dyads based on roots (*hetuduka*), as well as dyads based on roots and so forth; thus, there are six thousand six hundred dyads.

Within each of these, the seven sections beginning with the "Dependent" section (*paṭiccavāra*)—the methods and questions—are all identical to those in the dyad-analysis of the *Paṭṭhāna* concerning the dyad of roots.
It is stated: “Having combined each of the two hundred dyads with the twenty-two triads. This was said according to certain manuscripts of the *Tikadukapaṭṭhāna*.
However, according to the method actually taught, each triad among those that follow the proper sequence is combined with the one hundred dyads.
Among these, by inserting the term “root” (*hetu*), one “wholesome triad” (*kusalattika*) is formed; likewise, by inserting the term “non-root” (*nahetu*), and so forth...
Regarding the "araṇa" (non-conflict) category, there are two hundred [formulas] for the triads of the wholesome;

likewise for the triads of feeling and so forth, making four thousand four hundred in total for all of them. Within each of these, the method of the sequence of questions is the same as that of the wholesome triad in the *Paṭṭhāna*.
Furthermore, by the statement, “Six methods in the *anuloma* are very profound,” this is what is shown:

because it is stated without distinction as “in the *anuloma*” and “the six methods beginning with the triads,” the phrase “six in the *anuloma*” includes all seven types of *anuloma*, such as the section on conditions (*paṭiccasamuppādavāra*), etc.;
thus, the fourfold *Paṭṭhāna* beginning with the *anuloma*—namely, the triads, dyads, tetrads, and pentads—is intended.
Having taken [the section] together as "The Excellent Tikapaṭṭhāna," and likewise having taken the fourfold Duka-paṭṭhāna and so forth together,
it was stated as "The Supreme Dukapaṭṭhāna" and so on, ending with "The Six Very Profound Methods. Taking this meaning,
in this forward order of conditions (*paccayānuloma*), these six types of paṭṭhānas— which are sevenfold— are the fourfold methods of paṭṭhāna.
"They should be extracted by way of questions. For in this way, the entire positive order of conditions (*paccayānuloma*) is shown throughout the entire *Paṭṭhāna*.
The same method applies to the negative verses (*paccanīya-gāthā*) and so forth.

And here, in the *Duka-Tika-Paṭṭhāna* and others, the *Paṭṭhāna* [classified] by the triplets (*tika*) that serve as qualifiers is the "Triplet-System" (*Tika-Paṭṭhāna*). The Triplet-System of the dyads (*duka*) is the "Dyad-Triplet-System" (*Duka-Tika-Paṭṭhāna*). [It is so called because it is] qualified by dyads.
The meaning of the term should be understood according to this method: "the *paṭṭhāna* of the *dukatikas* [is] *dukatikapaṭṭhāna*.
Furthermore, in this context, the status of being a "duka," etc., should be seen as applying to the terms "tika," etc., when they are qualified by "duka," etc.
For indeed, it is the *dukapada-paṭṭhāna* itself that occurs through its connection with the terms "tika" and its connection with the terms "duka" that is the *dukatikapaṭṭhāna*.
There is the *dukaduka-paṭṭhāna*, as well as the *tikapaṭṭhāna* itself, the *tikaduka-paṭṭhāna* which occurs by way of the combination of dyads and the combination of triads,
and the *tikatika-paṭṭhāna*. The commentary on the positive order of conditions (*paccayānuloma*) is concluded.
2. Commentary on the Negative Conditions (Paccayapaccanīyavaṇṇanā) 42–44.
Regarding the phrase "having twenty-three as its root" (*tevīsatimūlaka*): this is stated here with reference specifically to the "two-rooted" (*dumūlaka*) section.
Since twenty-three dyads (*duka*) serve as the roots for the questions within that two-rooted section, it is given the name "having twenty-three as its root."
To whatever extent there is a division, to that same extent the twenty-third root has been expanded according to the direct order (*anuloma*).

It may have been stated with this intention: "In the reverse order (*paccanīya*) as well, it should be expanded; thus, by means of the pair-rooted (*dukamūlaka*), the method for the triple-rooted (*tikamūlaka*) and so forth is shown.
However, if the meaning is: "Just as it was expanded up to the twenty-third root..."
It is intended that there should be the reading "up to the twenty-third root" (*yāva tevīsatimaṃ mūlaṃ*).
For the meaning "the twenty-third root" does not apply to the expression "twenty-three-rooted" (*tevīsatimūlakaṃ*).

Just as in the direct order (*anuloma*), beginning with "of each single word" (*ekekapadassā*) and so forth, everything from the single-rooted up to the all-rooted was shown therein by way of demonstrating the method (*naya*). Of each individual word...

Regarding the phrase "it shows the detailed exposition," it should be understood that here the term "rooted in twenty-three" (*tevīsatimūlaka*) is stated because it is rooted in all [the remaining] roots.
For it is called "rooted in twenty-three" because it is the root for the remaining conditions among the twenty-three conditions,
and it is called "rooted in all" because there is no other root beyond that.
The commentary on the Negative Enumeration of Conditions (*paccayapaccanīyavaṇṇanā*) is finished.
3. Commentary on the Positive-Negative Enumeration (*anulomapaccanīyavaṇṇanā*). 45–48.

Regarding the phrase "having omitted each single term" among all those stated in the Positive Enumeration, such as the "single-rooted" (*ekamūlaka*) and so forth: therein, in the case of the single-rooted...
There are twenty-four conditional terms (*paccayapada*); here, in the single-rooted combinations, there are twenty-three.

However, because one condition stands as the root itself and lacks the quality of being "new" (i.e., it is not a subordinate factor), it is not included in the count. Among those, in the two-rooted combinations, twenty-three conditional terms are included in the count;
thus, the meaning is that they are excluded here from the two-rooted combinations, leaving twenty-two.

The phrase "of the obtainable terms" is stated with reference to the non-obtainability of the pure conditions (suddhika-paccaya) that are not found when one proceeds from the positive order (anuloma) to the negative order (paccanīya).
For otherwise, there would be no condition whatsoever that could be called "unobtainable" by way of a question.
Alternatively, it is stated "of the obtainable terms" with reference to the teaching of the positive-negative method (anuloma-paccanīya-desanā) as it occurs by way of the answer itself.
The commentary on the Positive-Negative (Anuloma-Paccanīya) section is concluded.
The commentary on the Section of Questions (Pucchāvāra) is concluded. 1.
The Triplet of the Wholesome (Kusalattika).
1. Commentary on the Section on Dependent Arising (Paṭiccavāra-vaṇṇanā) 1. Positive Order of Conditions (Paccayānuloma) (1) Section on Analysis (Vibhaṅgavāra)

53. Regarding the statement "those [factors] which obtain [in the] triad of the wholesome (kusalattika), they do not [obtain] by those very same [factors] in the triads of feeling (vedanāttika) and so forth":

this is said with reference to their similarity in terms of the roots and the conclusion, apart from the mere difference in the wording of the triads. It is not only in other triads that this applies;

for even within the triad of the wholesome, those factors which obtain in the section on dependence (paṭiccavāra) do not necessarily obtain in the section on conditions (paccayavāra) and so forth—this is the summary of all the questions.

This is precisely what must be done here. Furthermore, in the *Dhammānuloma-paccanīya* section of the *Tika-paṭṭhāna*, within the exposition of the "Tenfold Thought" (*vitakkattika*) and the "Threefold Rapture" (*pītittika*), all of these receive an exposition;
therefore, the inclusion of the "Threefold Rapture" (*pītittika*) should not be made here [in this context].
For it is not the case that forty-nine questions receive an exposition there.
“Together with that” means it should be understood as “together with that which serves as its co-nascence condition.

By the statements, “It passes beyond [the world] up to the attainment of cessation” and “Or it reaches the arising and so forth,” it is as if it were admitted that what possesses the three moments arises;
however, it should be understood that only that which possesses the moment of arising is spoken of in this way.

However, since the statement "one aggregate [arises] in dependence on one," and so forth, was spoken here with reference to the aggregates included under the term "wholesome" (*kusala*), it must be considered together with the fact that in the "Triads of Feeling" (*vedanāttika*) and elsewhere, it is stated that two [aggregates] arise in dependence on one aggregate, and even one arises in dependence on two;

and furthermore, in the "Dyads of Roots" (*hetuduka*) and so forth, it is stated that even a portion of the aggregate of formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*) arises in dependence on a portion of the aggregate of formations. Thus, [the rule] is stated together with these exceptions.
While being a condition for all phenomena as they arise, it is indeed called a condition for each individual [phenomenon], including those classified into dyads, triads, and so forth;
likewise for those classified into dyads and the rest.
It was stated that "the immaterial-sphere resultant (āruppa-vipāka) should not be included because it does not arise together with material form (rūpa)," but that is not [correct].
All of this statement should be understood; however, it applies only to the phrase "matter originated by mind" (*cittasamuṭṭhānaṃ rūpaṃ*).

Furthermore, not only the immaterial-sphere resultant (*āruppavipāka*) is included here, but also the supramundane resultant, functional, and indeterminate states arising in the immaterial sphere should not be taken as included.
As it is said: "Dependent on one aggregate that is indeterminate as resultant or indeterminate as functional, there arise three aggregates."
In this context, however, there is no resultant, functional, or indeterminate state that arises with or without material form which is not included as being "with root-cause" (sahetuka).
Among these, in order to show the specific conditionally arisen nature of that which arises together with material form, it is stated:
"and matter originated by consciousness."

When it would have been sufficient simply to say, "The aggregates depend on the physical basis" (*vatthuṃ paṭicca khandhā*), the phrase "the physical basis depends on the aggregates" (*khandhe paṭicca vatthu*) was stated in order to prevent the possibility that the physical basis—which serves as the condition—might not be included within the general term "matter produced by karma" (*kaṭattā ca rūpaṃ*) because it is not grasped there as something arisen from conditions.
Thus, it is said: "The physical basis depends on the aggregates; the aggregates depend on the physical basis. This refers to the mutual dependence of the physical basis and the aggregates.
The two statements regarding mutual dependence are spoken for the purpose of showing the specific nature of the conditionality of those things that function as mutual conditions;
thus, even though they are included under the general category, they are mentioned separately.

This is also for the purpose of showing that [matter] arises dependent upon the great primary elements (*mahābhūta*), namely, mind-produced matter (*cittasamuṭṭhānarūpa*) and kamma-born matter (*kaṭattārūpa*).
Derived matter (*upādārūpa*) was stated [in the previous section] as "arising in dependence on the aggregates" without mentioning its dependence on derived matter;
the meaning is that this is for the purpose of showing that it also arises in dependence on the great primary elements (*mahābhūta*).

However, in this present exposition, all derived matter—both that which is accompanied by the aggregate-conditions and that which is not—is included among the subsequent conditions such as the conascence-condition (*sahajātapaccaya*); it is with reference to this point [that the following is said].
The particle *pi* (also) should be understood as being stated [in the phrase] “*kaṭattārūpaṃ paṭisandhiyampi*” (kamma-produced matter also in rebirth-linking).

By the method stated as “dependent on the great primaries, derived matter,” he said this with reference to the fact that this method has been stated here in terms of meaning as: “Dependent on the great primaries, mind-originated matter, kamma-produced matter, and derived matter.

54. “Leaving aside those mixed with matter”: the intention is that one should leave aside those questions in which the conditionally arisen cannot be found without matter, but is found only as mixed with matter.

57. Because of the statement, “The descent into the womb occurs through the conjunction of three factors,” it is established that all rebirth-linking in the five-aggregate plane—which possesses the same characteristics as the rebirth-linking of one lying in the womb due to the presence of the five aggregates—is called “descent.
Since there is an answer regarding complete phenomena here, it is termed “complete answer.”

And here, by the passage beginning “Dependent on one great primary element, three... [and so on]... dependent on the great primary elements, mind-originated matter, kamma-born matter, and derived matter,” all matter originated by mind and kamma in the fivefold plane (pañcavokāra) has been shown.
However, in order to show the remainder, the words “external,” and so forth, were stated. Therein, by the term “external,” matter not bound to the sense faculties (anindriyabaddha-rūpa) is indicated.

It shows that, furthermore, by the terms "nutriment-originated" and "temperature-originated," all matter bound to the faculties (*indriya*)—namely, nutriment-originated and temperature-originated matter—is indicated.

In this context, it should be understood that by the statement beginning with "one [kind] is temperature-originated," the temperature-originated matter of non-percipient beings (*asaññasatta*) is also already included;
for there is no reason for excluding it from that category. However, at the beginning [of the text], the phrase "dependent on one great primary element" (*ekaṃ mahābhūtaṃ paṭicca*) and so forth...

The term "indeterminate" (aviśeṣa) is stated so as to include both the co-nascent non-material condition—which receives many other conditions such as the root-cause (hetu) and so forth—and the pair of mind-originated and kamma-born material phenomena, taking them together. And having done so, at the conclusion of that [section] it is said:
"Dependent on the great elements, there are mind-originated matter, kamma-born matter, and derived matter. Therefore...

In this context, the "matter produced by past action" (*kaṭattārūpa*) that is connected with mind-originated matter and shares its same destiny is understood as being only that which exists in the five-aggregate realm (*pañcavokāra*).

Therefore, in order to show the "matter produced by past action" that was not included [in that definition], it is said: "dependent on one great primary element (*mahābhūta*) of non-percipient beings," and so forth.
Consequently, derived matter (*upādārūpa*) here also—just as in the analysis of the kamma-condition (*kammapaccaya*)—is "matter produced by past action dependent on the great primaries."
"Derived matter" (upādārūpa) should be understood as referring to derived matter distinguished by its state of being "kamma-born" (kaṭattārūpa).
For there is no purpose in stating again what has already been mentioned regarding that which is temperature-born (utusamuṭṭhāna).
But why, when it says in the case of external [matter] and so forth, "derived matter dependent on the great elements," does it not specify [the type of matter]?
It has been stated; however, instead of saying "mind-produced derived matter" (*cittakammaja-upādārūpa*),

[the texts] speak of "matter originated by mind" (*cittasamuṭṭhāna-rūpa*) and "kamma-produced derived matter" (*kaṭattā-rūpa*) together with "derived matter" under the conditions of cause (*hetu-paccaya*) and so forth,

while under the conditions of predominance (*adhipati-paccaya*) and so forth, they speak of them separately as "matter originated by mind" and "kamma-produced derived matter" by way of their respective states of being produced by mind and being kamma-produced.

Are they stated as being specifically distinguished? No; because here, unlike in the case of the mention of "external" and so forth, the great elements (*mahābhūta*) are not distinguished by anything.

Furthermore, for desirable and undesirable external bases such as visible forms produced by supernormal power (*iddhi*) or by kamma, neither consciousness nor kamma is any of the conditions—such as the root condition (*hetu-paccaya*)—among them.
However, for those things produced by nutriment (*āhāra*) and temperature (*utu*), consciousness [is a condition] by way of being posterior-born (*pacchājāta*).
It is merely supportive, not generative; however, the great primary elements (mahābhūtas) themselves are the generators of those [derived forms] by way of being co-nascent and so forth.

Therefore, although they would be non-existent without mind and kamma, the derived forms that arise from the immaterial factors serving as causes and other conditions—namely, the materiality originated by mind (cittasamuṭṭhāna-rūpa), the materiality of kamma-result (kaṭattā-rūpa), and the primary elements—are exclusively derived matter (upādārūpa) and nothing else. This is the distinction.
To demonstrate this, a qualification is applied specifically to those derived material phenomena (*upādārūpa*) born of mental craftsmanship (*cittakamma*).
Alternatively, other [derived matter] that arises from matter of a similar class possesses its own manifest distinction and thus does not require a qualification;

however, these [mental derivatives] arise from immaterial states (*arūpa*) of a dissimilar class and therefore do require a qualification. Thus they should be understood as being qualified. Or, just as with works of mental craftsmanship...

They serve as conditions specifically by way of being the conditions for those things originated by mind through their status as co-nascent and other types of conditions, and because they function as the primary cause;
temperature and nutriment do not act thus toward those things originated by them. Therefore, only those born of mind deserve a separate qualification.
The others, however, were qualified by way of the distinction among the great primaries (*mahābhūta*), whereas here they are qualified by way of the distinction among derived matter (*upādārūpa*).
Like the great primary elements (*mahābhūtāni*). For it is not the case that a qualifier of one [member] cannot be a qualifier of both. 58.

In the context of the mutuality condition (*aññamaññapaccaya*), by showing that "depending on the aggregates there is the basis, and depending on the basis there are the aggregates," the mutual conditionality of the aggregates and the basis is demonstrated;
thus, the aggregates—which were previously shown to have separate conditions—are here presented together.
With the intention of showing the state of being a condition, he said: "It was stated in order to show the mutual conditionality of the four aggregates together with the physical basis.
