However, the phrase "the physical bases in dependence upon the aggregates" is for the purpose of showing that the meaning of *paṭicca* (dependence) extends to all four aggregates taken together, while the phrase "the aggregates in dependence upon the physical basis" refers to the physical basis alone.
And this same method applies not only to the aggregates here, but also to the root-conditions and so forth.

In that context, after showing how all the aggregates individually pervade the meaning of "dependent," and then again showing the basis by means of the phrase "the aggregates dependent on the basis," there is the section concerning both the aggregates and the basis, beginning with:
"dependent on one aggregate and the basis, three aggregates [arise]," and so forth.
It should be understood that it is indeed already shown.
But why is it not stated here in such terms as, “Dependent on a wholesome state, an indeterminate state arises by way of mutuality condition;
dependent on wholesome aggregates, mind-originated great elements [arise]”? Is it not the case that...?
It exercises its influence by way of a condition, yet it need not necessarily be a *aññamañña-paccaya* (mutuality condition) in that same sense as the *hetu-paccaya* (root condition) and others.
For those [factors] described as "dependent on one, three, or two aggregates" are not necessarily only those that function as root conditions.

This same principle applies to the object condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*) and the others as well. Furthermore, in the section on conditions, it says: "Conditioned by an indeterminate state, a wholesome..."
It is said: “A state arises by way of mutual condition. However, the physical basis (*vatthu*) is not a mutual condition for wholesome states;
nevertheless, it has indeed been stated that the aggregates arise from that basis by way of mutual condition.
Even though wholesome aggregates are not mutual conditions for the great primary elements (*mahābhūta*), nevertheless, those elements arise in dependence upon them.

Should it be said [that they are related]? It should not be said, because there is no state of being a condition between the great elements co-nascent with the aggregates and the aggregates themselves.
For the term "mutually" (*aññamañña*) is neither independent like the term "cause" (*hetu*), nor does it depend on one of two [factors] like the term "co-nascent" (*sahajāta*);
rather, it depends on each other as previously described. And here, the aggregates and the great elements are both conditions and conditionally arisen phenomena.
If they were as previously described, then among them the great elements would not be any condition for the aggregates.
And that which arises from its own condition— whether by way of a mutuality-condition (*aññamañña-paccaya*) with that [condition] or dependent upon it—
is fit to be called "arising through a mutuality-condition," such as aggregates conditioned by aggregates, or aggregates conditioned by the [material] base (*vatthu*).

Therefore, because their own condition lacks the status of being a condition for itself, and because the term "mutuality" (aññamañña) implies mutual dependence, it is not stated that the great elements arise with one another as a mutuality-condition (aññamañña-paccaya) in dependence upon the aggregates; nor is it stated that they [the aggregates] are a mutuality-condition for them.
However, when the aggregates arise conditioned by the physical basis (vatthu), they constitute a postnascent condition (pacchājāta-paccaya) for that basis.

And by depending on that [basis], they arise through mutual conditionality (*aññamañña-paccaya*). Therefore, it is said that the arising of the aggregates—whether wholesome or otherwise—occurs through mutual conditionality, conditioned by the basis (*vatthu*).
59. "That is not included" means the intention is that it was not stated that [the aggregates] depend on the eye-base (*cakkhāyatana*) and so forth, which serve as their supports (*nissaya*).

However, by way of being a *nissaya* condition (*nissayapaccaya*), the eye-base (*cakkhāyatana*) and so forth are not included, unlike the visible-form base (*rūpāyatana*) and so forth which are included as object conditions (*ārammaṇapaccaya*).
Regarding the two kinds of *upanissaya*, there is nothing further to be said;

however, it is stated that they are "similar to the object condition" by way of those [beings] who do obtain even the *ārammaṇūpanissaya*. To show this, he said: "In this regard, although... and so on.
In this context, the original reading was: “Not all unwholesome and indeterminate states obtain objective decisive support.
However, since sublime wholesome states never obtain it, and sense-sphere wholesome states sometimes do not, they read: “Not all wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate states [obtain it]. 61.
Regarding the prenascence condition (*purejāta-paccaya*), one should not proceed by giving the teaching without first specifying the condition, as has been done elsewhere. Thus, having not done so—
Why is it said that "the basis is a pre-arising condition" (*purejāta-paccaya*)? Because of the existence of a specific restriction (*niyama*).

For there is no such restriction among the causes (*hetu*) and so forth; for there is no fixed rule that among the states arising from them—such as non-greed (*alobha*), the wholesome (*kusala*), or material form (*rūpa*)—this alone is the condition.
However, in this case, the basis is [a condition] for those states arising through the pre-arising condition among the mental states of the basis.
This was stated in order to show the point that, as a rule, the sixfold basis (*vatthu*) is a pre-arising condition (*purejāta-paccaya*).

For even an object-pre-arising condition (*ārammaṇa-purejāta*) is not obtained when a basis-pre-arising condition is absent; and having established this, it is said that the arising of rebirth-resultant consciousness occurs only through pre-arising conditions, since even for its present object, there is a pre-arising condition.

It is not excluded. Because even the statement, “Dependent on a state that is neither resultant nor of the nature to produce a resultant, a resultant state arises by way of prenascence condition,” is not obtained there, it is said in that context:
“In the case of prenascence, three.
Likewise, at the moment of rebirth-linking, [the dependence] of the great primaries is due solely to the kamma-condition of both simultaneous and asynchronous types.

It should also be understood that [the text] speaks of the material phenomena derived from that [kamma]. Regarding "material phenomena produced by kamma" (*kaṭattārūpa*), the intended meaning is "material phenomena produced by kamma during the course of existence" (*pavatti*).
64. "According to what is obtained": this refers to whichever sense-faculties (*indriyarūpa*) are obtained at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*); it is according to each of those. 69.
Even for certain [phenomena] arising through the condition of dissociation (*vippayuttapaccaya*), the physical basis (*vatthu*) is invariably a condition of dissociation.
In some cases, aggregates do not arise solely in dependence on wholesome states and so forth by way of the condition of being a common dissociation-condition;
rather, they also arise by way of the condition of being a diverse dissociation-condition. Therefore, in order to show that distinction, it is stated here and there:
"by way of the base as a dissociation-condition" and "by way of the aggregates as a dissociation-condition. In that context, because [the state] exists in dependence upon those [aggregates],...
The accusative case should be understood here according to the sense that "the conditionally arisen [dhamma] makes the condition its condition.
The meaning here is: "by making the basis (vatthu) a dissociation-condition for the aggregates. However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, the meaning is:
"dependent on the basis, [there are] dissociation-conditions; by means of the basis, accomplishing the state of being a dissociation-condition."
In that context, since there is no arising of wholesome aggregates dependent upon a physical basis (*vatthu*),
it would not be possible to say "dependent on a basis. However, instead of connecting this with the word *paṭicca*,

it is connected as "they arise dependent [on the basis] by way of dissociation-condition (*vippayutta-paccaya*)," the meaning of which is "by means of establishing the state of being a dissociation-condition for the basis."
It should be understood as "is said. But with reference to what? It refers to that which is stated in the Pāḷi as "dependent on one aggregate," and so forth.

Making that very meaning clear, they recite: "The basis is a dissociation condition; aggregates [arise] dependent on aggregates, establishing the state of being a dissociation condition by means of the basis. This is because it is immediately followed by what is clear.

To ensure that there is no inclusion of only that which is originated by an indeterminate (abyākata) state of consciousness, he said: "both that originated by an indeterminate state of consciousness and that originated by wholesome or unwholesome states of consciousness. This means it is stated that "all," whether near or far, is included.
71–72. It is stated: "This was said by way of those twenty conditions shown in brief. In this regard:

If even a single teaching were merely concise, then why was the beginning—consisting of three conditions, including the dissociation condition (*vippayuttapaccaya*)—expounded in detail without omitting even a single word?

In that case, excluding the post-nascence condition (*pacchājātapaccaya*), one might have said, "These are nineteen conditions," for only so many were shown in summary. However, those [conditions] which were expanded upon in the Pāḷi...
They say that everything has been stated by summarizing what was not expanded upon; for them, the reading should be:

"These are the twenty-three conditions. However, having excluded the three conditions expanded upon at the beginning, from the point where the summary begins—that is, from the fourth condition onwards—the concise and the expanded [explanations] are taken together as "these are the twenty-three."
It should be understood that this is what was stated [in the phrase] “conditions.
The commentary on the section on the analysis (vibhaṅgavāra) is finished.
(2) The section on enumeration (saṅkhyāvāra).

73. "Likewise, regarding the pre-arisen condition (*purejāta-paccaya*)," means that just as there is a distinction in the *Aññamañña-paccaya* (mutuality condition) in the Vibhaṅga, so too is there one in the *Purejāta-paccaya*.
For in that context, the distinction is stated as: "The [material] base is a pre-arisen condition," and "the absence of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*)";
by this, it is shown that neither resultant consciousnesses nor process-consciousnesses are obtained. Thus, [it refers to] a single functional-indeterminate (*kiriya-abyākata*) aggregate.

In the *Vibhaṅga* beginning with “dependent on,” it shows the distinction between the absence of the indeterminate resultant (*vipākābyākata*) and the fact that the non-prompting (*ajavana*) is not obtained at all within the indeterminate functional (*kiriyābyākata*). 74.
Regarding the phrase “taking only the count available in the teaching shown in the Single Root [Chapter],” this refers to this [section] of the Positive Order (*anuloma*).
This was stated with reference to the absence of any other [method] in the methods following that one, based on the enumeration shown in the Suddhika method.
Furthermore, the fact that what is joined by a non-abundant enumeration has an enumeration identical to it should be understood as occurring only in this *anuloma* (direct order);
however, in the *paccanīya* (inverse order), he will state, "With the non-root condition, there is one [result] in the non-object [condition]," and so forth.
76–79. Regarding the statement, "But these, when condensed, are shown here as having twenty-three roots":

since the subsequent-born (pacchājāta) and resultant (vipāka) [roots] have been excluded here, it would have to be called "having twenty-two roots" with respect to those accompanied by repetition (sāsevana) and resultants (savipāka).
However, taking both types of "twenty-two-rooted" [states] together, because both are present within that which is thus included, it is said to be "having twenty-three roots."

It should be understood as "includes. Alternatively, since there is no contradiction between the repetition (āsevana) and the fruition (vipāka), it ought to be based on twenty-three roots according to the method shown in the inquiry;
and having applied its name to the section based on twenty-two roots, it is called "based on twenty-three roots"—this is the conventional usage here.

By the phrase "only in the section on the object," he excludes other sections in the single-rooted [treatise], for in the single-rooted [treatise] there are no [factors] such as the cause and so forth.

This is also the intended meaning of those two [passages]. However, since the Pure Method (suddhikanaya) is not found among the "rooted in the object" (ārammaṇamūlaka) and so forth, it is stated—"in every case, there are only three questions by one who stands upon the object"—in order to show the absence of that additional count of "nine" in the section on the root of the object.
Here, the words "to be made" (*kātabba*) are to be supplied as an ellipsis. Furthermore, the phrase "only three" precludes any calculation beyond that.
It does not exclude the lower [realms]. Therefore, it should be understood that the enumeration as "one in the result" is not precluded.
And because one is included within the three, it is stated as "only three. By the words beginning with "thus," he strengthens his own position with the statement, "in all cases, only three."
80–85. Regarding the phrase "ye... pe... taṃ dassetuṃ" (in order to show those...), this is the intended meaning:

although the number obtained when correlating with a lower count is already shown by stating "three [results] for the root-condition from the object-condition" immediately after [the section on] non-disappearance, nevertheless, in the correlation with both lower counts and equal counts, the lower ones [are further specified].
And it is "the same" (samānā), yet it is not shown by way of explicit manifestation (*āvikaraṇa*); rather, it is shown thus by way of a connection with a perversion (*vipallāsa*).
For the manifestation of a specific meaning occurs either through a statement or through a grammatical gender/sign (*liṅga*).

Therefore, even in the phrase "it manifests this," the intended meaning (*adhippāya*) should be applied in exactly the same way. Furthermore, in the case of the counter-conditions (*paccanīya*) and so forth, [it is said]: "Not from object-condition, not in non-root... [and so on].

In such passages as "One... [etc. ... by way of non-disappearance condition, there is one by way of non-root condition," the application is made by placing the root term at the very beginning; yet this characteristic is not found there. Therefore, the sequence is simply the application of the root term at the beginning, and not a binding of the wheel.
Thus, "By way of object condition, three by way of root" and so forth are applied, and it is not understood otherwise.
There is a purpose for both the statement and the indicative mark.
The commentary on the *paccayānuloma* (conformity of conditions) is finished. The section on "dependent" (*paṭicca*) is concluded.
Commentary on the Negative Enumeration of Conditions (Paccayapaccanīyavaṇṇanā) 86–87:

Regarding the statement, “‘Rootless and resultant-indeterminate’ is to be understood only in terms of the production of material form,” it is not impossible to apply this [definition] in a comprehensive sense as well.
93: “Co-nascence and prenascence conditions are included”—here, both the co-nascent conditions, such as the roots, and the prenascence conditions [are meant].
The meaning should be understood as follows: the conditions, beginning with the object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*), are included [in this classification].

For it is not the case that those things arising by way of the postnascent condition (*pacchājāta-paccaya*) arise solely through the two conditions of co-nascence (*sahajāta*) and pre-existence (*purejāta*); rather, they arise through all [conditions] except for the postnascent condition itself. 94–97.

Regarding the nutriment condition (*āhāra-paccaya*), only a certain kind of material form (*rūpa*) is both the condition and the conditioned; that which arises depending upon it [is the nutriment-conditioned].

This was stated by taking the condition to be material form alone. However, that which arises from conditions may also be immaterial, just as kamma is for the matter produced by kamma (*kaṭattā-rūpa*).
99–102. Although all categories of matter, such as mind-produced matter and the rest, are obtainable in the case of the path-condition (*maggapaccaya*), nevertheless...
Because that which is obtained through the path-condition has been abandoned, it is stated that "some material phenomena are conditionally arisen.
In the same way, however, the state of being conditionally arisen for some material phenomena should also be understood in the case of the non-root-condition and so forth. 107–130.
Regarding the statement that the answers for the non-nutriment, non-faculty, non-jhāna, and non-path conditions are identical in all instances, this refers to these [conditions].
This was stated with reference to their equality in number while they remain as root-factors.

For here, the exposition of the roots is by way of number alone, not by way of showing their specific individual forms. The tetrad beginning with "not co-nascent" (*nasahajāta*) is likewise omitted here;
thus the meaning is that it is omitted even in the case of the roots, just as it is in the Pure Method (*suddhikanaya*).
The commentary on the Negative Conditions (Paccayapaccanīya) is finished.
Commentary on the Positive-Negative Conditions (Paccayānulomapaccanīya), §§131–189:
When the conditions of root (hetu), predominance (adhipati), and path (magga) are established in the positive order... [etc. ... eight [conditions] are not obtained in the negative order.
This is stated by way of including all those [conditions] that are not obtained through the opposition of the three common conditions;

therefore, in the case of the path condition (*maggapaccaya*), only the seven [conditions] common with the others should be applied. As for the root condition (*hetupaccaya*), although it stands in the positive sequence (*anuloma*) within the predominance condition (*adhipatipaccaya*), it is not obtained through the negative sequence (*paccanīya*); however, because it is not common to the path, it was not mentioned here.
It should be understood as follows: those conditions without which the immaterial (arūpa) does not arise are stated here as "the bases of the immaterial" because they are absolute;
therefore, the pre-nascence and nutriment conditions are excluded, since the immaterial can arise even without them.
The mutuality condition, the food condition, and the faculty condition are included, because the immaterial does not arise without them. Thus it should be understood.

"By way of the lower counts alone" means: if the numbers from one up to twenty-two established in direct order (*anuloma*) are the lower counts, then by way of those, the respective counts for that [method] joined in reverse order (*paccanīya*) should be understood.
Alternatively, if the one joined in reverse order is a lower count, then by way of that, the count for what is established in direct order should also be understood.
This is the meaning. However, because of such statements as “Due to mutual conditionality, there is one [condition] that is not an object-condition,” this characteristic is not absolute.
The commentary on the Positive-Negative (Anuloma-Paccanīya) of conditions is finished.
Now begins the commentary on the Negative-Positive (Paccanīya-Anuloma) of conditions.
190. "In all cases" means not only when the cause is present, but rather when all conditions are standing in opposition;
this is the meaning. Showing an example of something that does not receive either pre-nascence or repetition, he said, "But the rebirth-linking result," and so forth.
"When pre-nascence, post-nascence, repetition, result, and dissociation are standing in opposition, with one [condition] set aside, the remainder..."

The statement, "They are obtained in the direct order (anuloma)," is said with reference to the mere acquisition of the remaining [factors]. It should not be understood as meaning that all the remaining ones are obtained.

For although there is no possibility of a posterior-arising (pacchājāta) relation because an exception has been made stating, "In all cases, they are not obtained in the direct order," the prior-arising (purejāta) relation does indeed exist in the case of dissociation (vippayutta), standing as an opposing factor in the direct order.
The phrase "it is obtained" would also apply here if the meaning were taken as "all the remaining [factors].

Furthermore, as for what some say—that this was stated in order to make known the possibility of an object-prenascence even in the formless realm (ārūpa), which lacks the dissociation condition (vippayuttapaccaya)—that too is merely their own personal preference.
For it is not the case that where base-prenascence (vatthupurejāta) is not found, there can be object-prenascence (ārammaṇapurejāta).
"This method has been shown by way of demonstrating what is beneficial. Regarding the phrase "by way of what is applicable":
it is stated because that which stands as an opponent must be set aside; the meaning is "by way of the conditions and the arisen states that are applicable.

As for the reading "When the path condition stands as an opponent, the root condition is not obtained in the direct order," it should be understood that the predominance condition is likewise not obtained.

They recite: “From the root condition and the predominance condition, nine [factors] are not obtained in the forward order. Regarding the predominance condition, when it is established in the reverse order, there is no other [factor] besides the post-nascence condition that is not obtained in the forward order;
thus, this was not investigated. When the mutuality condition is established in the reverse order, it is stated:
“Only for the immaterial [states],” and thus nine [factors] are not obtained in the forward order. That too [is from the reverse order].
Because it is easy to understand due to its similarity with the "fixed" conditions such as the object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*), it will not be examined here.
From [sections] 191–195, up to the repetition condition (*āsevana*), everything is similar;

this was stated with reference to the subsequent roots, because the root that is combined with the others has already been explained in detail. For among those, both the conditions to be applied in forward order (*anuloma*) and the questions (*pañha*) are all similar.

The phrase “In this negative-positive [method]” (imasmiṃ paccanīyānulome) is connected with the statement: “Here, the section on enumeration should be understood through non-confusion by way of these miscellaneous [factors] as well.
In that context, “here” (ettha) should be understood to mean “in these conditions” (etesu paccayesu).
Alternatively, it should be construed as: “In this negative-positive [method], and also in the phenomena produced by conditions (paccayuppannadhammesu) that are being obtained. In that regard:

By the word "pi" (also/even), he illustrates this meaning: not only among the conditions themselves, but when something stands as an opponent to any [condition], some [factors] are not obtained in accordance;
furthermore, even among the phenomena that have arisen from conditions, someone who obtains one particular condition does not obtain another condition.
In that regard, one who obtains the kamma-condition generally...

It receives the faculty-condition (indriya-paccaya). When receiving the path-condition (magga-paccaya), it mostly receives the root-condition (hetu-paccaya); likewise, when receiving the jhāna-condition, it receives the path-condition.

Thus, the acquisition and non-acquisition of these very conditions have been examined. "Where" refers to the occurrence within the fivefold plane (pañcavokāra) and among the non-percipient beings (asañña).
"Material phenomena" (rūpa-dhamma) refers specifically to the aforementioned kamma-produced matter (kaṭattā-rūpa). For [such matter] does not exist in the occurrence within the fivefold plane.

"All material phenomena (rūpadhammā) do not receive [the conditions] beginning with root (hetu). The original reading was, “They do not receive the conditions of root, predominance, fruition, faculty, and path”;
however, since they also do not receive them in the case of jhāna and the path, they read it as, “They do not receive the conditions of root, predominance, fruition, faculty, jhāna, and path.
Among those which are conditions for material phenomena, excluding those that have the immaterial as their basis...

The intended meaning is that they do not obtain these very [conditions]. For even in the case of the condition of dissociation from postnascent nutriment, the *kaṭattā-rūpa* (matter produced by kamma) obtains [it] during the course of existence (*pavatta*).
This is merely a demonstration of which conditions are obtained and which are not; it is not a demonstration of whether their arising or non-arising occurs through those conditions.

Thus, the non-obtainment of the faculty-condition may have been stated with reference to the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*). For, among the factors mentioned as above, [this applies] by way of the phenomena themselves.

There is no *kaṭattā-rūpa* (matter produced by past karma) that does not receive the three [material phenomena] born after it; what need is there to mention those karmas that have all bases (*sabbaṭṭhānika*)?
However, there is that which does not receive a faculty (*indriya*). What is it? It is the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*).

If this is so, then with respect to derived matter (*upādārūpa*), one should say they do not even receive the mutuality-condition (*aññamañña-paccaya*); however, because that is obvious, it was not stated. [This refers to] the non-reception of immaterial faculties.
Or, it should be understood that the non-attainment of the faculty-condition (*indriya-paccaya*) was stated with this intention.
196–197. Regarding the dyads and so forth rooted in the object (*ārammaṇa*), it says "five by way of root" (*hetuyā pañca*).

Although this phrase "five by way of root" does not occur in the triads and so forth, nevertheless, wishing to state what is not [explicitly] mentioned in all the dyads and so forth, he uses the expression "in the dyads and so forth" (*dukādīsū*) as a comprehensive inclusion of all.
Having stated that, he determines what was said there in the first dyad: “Five by way of root-cause. However, some read the text as: “Five by way of root-cause in the section on non-object-root.
Regarding the phrase “One by way of mutuality,” the former reading states that this was said with reference to material phenomena that are primary elements (*bhūtarūpa*) alone;
yet, since the physical basis (*vatthu*) is also applicable, it is said [in the latter version] that this was said with reference to both the primary elements and the physical basis.
They recite [the following]. Regarding "timūlaka" (three-rooted): here too, they say that what is "dumūlaka" (two-rooted) is also "timūlaka.

203–233. In the *Nakammamūlaka* section, concerning the phrases "three by way of cause," etc., it should be understood that this was stated with reference to those cases—such as "three by way of cause"—which include mere volition (*cetanā*) as the conditionally arisen. For the word "etc. (*ādi*) has the sense of "manner" or "type."
"It occurs. However, in the cases of co-nascence, mutuality, support, nutriment, presence, and non-disappearance conditions, material form is also obtained.
The commentary on the positive and negative analysis of conditions is finished.
The commentary on the "Dependent" section is finished.
2. Explanation of the Section on Co-nascence (Sahajātavāra) 234–242.

In such passages as "co-nascent with a wholesome state" (*kusalaṃ dhammaṃ sahajāto*) or "co-nascent with one wholesome aggregate" (*kusalaṃ ekaṃ khandhaṃ sahajāto*), by the term "co-nascent" (*sahajāta*) is meant either the performing of the condition of co-nascence (*sahajātapaccaya-karaṇa*) or the attaining of a state of dependence upon what is co-nascent (*sahajātāyattabhāvagamana*). Of these two—performing and attaining—...

Or rather, it should be understood that the instrumental case is used because wholesome states and so forth function as the *kamma* (action). This same method applies to the section on conditions (*paccaya-vāra*) and others as well.
For there too, by the word "condition" (*paccaya*), either the act of being a support-condition (*nissaya-paccaya*) or the state of coming to depend upon a support is expressed;

and by the word "conjoined" (*saṃsaṭṭha*), either the act of being an association-condition (*sampayutta-paccaya*) or the state of coming to depend upon an association is expressed—thus, because of that status as *kamma*.

The statement regarding "application" (*upayoga*) has been made in relation to the wholesome and so forth. Furthermore, even though it is co-nascent, derived form (*upādārūpa*) is not a condition for primary form (*bhūtarūpa*);
thus, the meaning is that it is not a condition as indicated by the word "dependent upon" (*paṭicca*).
And the phrase "derived form [is not a condition] for primary form" is stated by way of illustration; for indeed, derived form is also [not a condition] for derived form, as previously stated.
The condition does not exist; and as for the material phenomena excluding the bases and the immaterial [phenomena].
The commentary on the Section on Co-nascence (Sahajātavāra) is finished.
3. Commentary on the Section on Conditions (Paccayavāra).
243. Regarding the term *paccaya*: here, *pati* means "support" (*aya*) and *paccaya*. The word *pati* indicates the sense of "establishment," while the word *aya* indicates "going.

Thus, it is said that a support which serves as an establishment and a destination is a condition (*nissaya-paccaya*). Therefore, the meaning is: "from conditions" (*tato paccayā*), or "by way of making a condition" (*paccaya-karaṇato*), or "by way of coming to depend upon that" (*tad-āyatta-bhāva-gamanato*).
The statement, “Derived matter arises conditioned by the great primary elements,” is spoken by including both the primary elements and the derived matter together.
However, in the Commentary, it should be understood that, regarding derived matter arising from the great primary elements themselves— which act as its support—

the example is given by means of the derived matter arising in dependence on those supports, even though [the primary elements] are not themselves the support for that specific instance of derived matter.

255. Regarding "non-percipient beings... pe ... kamma-produced matter (kaṭattārūpa) and derived matter (upādārūpa)": here, the meaning stated in the section on dependence (paṭicca-vāra) by way of co-nascence (sahajāta), namely, that kamma-born [matter] arises from kamma and kamma-conditions (kamma-utuja), and that [matter] produced by kamma (kammaja) arises from kamma either invariably or non-invariably—that is not what is intended here. This is because, by the term "kamma-produced matter," all matter originated by kamma is included;
therefore, setting aside that [previous distinction], it refers to the kamma-produced matter as it has been taken [in this context].
By way of qualification, the meaning “kamma-produced matter (kaṭattārūpa) reckoned as derived matter (upādārūpa)” is expressed.

However, since the arising of derived matter dependent upon and conditioned by the great primary elements (mahābhūta) cannot be denied, the mention of “derived matter” does not exclude the inclusion of kamma-produced matter;
rather, because there exists a category of derived matter that must be excluded, the mention of “derived matter” is [understood] precisely through the mention of “kamma-produced matter.”
The qualification should be understood. 269–276.

Where it should have been stated as “by the indeterminate, the indeterminate; the wholesome; the unwholesome,” it is instead stated as “by the indeterminate, the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the indeterminate.
And where it should have been stated as “dependent on a wholesome phenomenon, wholesome and unwholesome phenomena [arise] for the sake of the wholesome,” [it is stated otherwise].
In the earlier reading, "without having named" (*anāmasitvā*), a scribal error due to negligence should be understood.
Regarding the statement, "Under the conditions of not-root and not-prenascence, there are two," the *Aṭṭhakathā* explains:

"But in the case of the formless realm (*ārūpa*), 'two' is stated by way of rootless delusion and rootless functional consciousness; 'two under the condition of not-dissociation' refers to the case of rootless unwholesome functional consciousness in the formless realm."
What was stated [previously] should be understood as having been stated by way of illustration based on a portion of those factors that are actually obtainable.

However, regarding the statement "two in the case of dissociation," it should be understood that in the formless realm (ārūpa), two are stated by way of rootless delusion (ahetuka-moha), rootless functional consciousness (ahetuka-kiriya), rootless rebirth-linking (ahetuka-patisandhi), and certain types of matter (rūpa).
Thus, the phrase "two in the case of dissociation" is said with reference to rootless unwholesome functional consciousness and certain types of matter in the formless realm.
It is said: “‘In all that has not yet arisen and has not yet ceased, one’ is by way of all materiality.
However, because this method (naya) is rooted in a cause, it cannot obtain a root-cause condition; therefore, it should be stated as “by way of some materiality.
But since everything is obtained by way of phenomena such as the eye, or by way of the categories beginning with mind-originated [materiality], it might be stated as “of all materiality.”
289–296. "Past and future" is stated by way of questions; "present and absent" refers to the present questions by way of the phenomena that are present or absent therein.
The commentary on the section on conditions (*paccayavāra*) is finished.
4. Commentary on the section on dependence (*nissayavāra*).

329–337. Regarding the section on conditions (*paccayavāra*): "The state of being a support-condition" means that the state of being a support-condition as explained in the section on support (*nissayavāra*) is here determined.
The commentary on the section on support is finished.
5. Commentary on the Section on Conjoined Conditions (*saṃsaṭṭhavāra*)

351–368. In the Negative Section of the Conjoined Chapter, the statement “there is no rebirth-linking in non-dissociation” is said because rebirth-linking devoid of a physical basis (vatthu) is not separately extracted.
For in the Dependent Chapter and others, rebirth-linking with a physical basis is extracted for the purpose of showing the conditionality of co-nascent states;
that same [rebirth-linking] is included here as well under predominance, prenascence, repetition, and non-kamma, non-resultant, non-jhāna, and non-dissociation conditions.

It is not obtained; however, it is extracted for the purpose of showing this distinction—that while it is not obtained [in those cases], it is obtained among other conditions that occur both in conformity and in opposition.
Regarding the statement "the remaining thirteen are not obtained," it should actually be "the remaining fourteen.

The phrase "not one in jhāna" is stated for the purpose of merely showing that the five sense-consciousnesses (pañcaviññāṇa) lack the root-condition (hetu-paccaya), by way of the rootless fivefold sense-consciousness.

It should be understood that "the inclusion of the rootless" is stated; for it was said, "In the path, one [consciousness] by way of rootless functional [consciousness]," but it ought to be "by way of rootless resultant and functional [consciousness].
369–391. "By the same method as stated above" means by the method stated in the positive-negative section of the Dependent Chapter. Regarding "those arisen with the non-root condition":

It is said: "Only rootless delusion receives the condition of jhāna and the path; the others do not. However, among the remaining factors—excluding the fivefold sense-consciousness—the rootless aggregates and the phenomena arisen from them receive the condition of jhāna.
There is no combination with the positive order (anuloma) of two conditions in the negative-positive order (paccanīyānuloma); thus, [it refers to] the condition of jhāna and the path.
Nor can it be said that it "obtains [the path] together with [it]"; therefore, it must be stated that "only rootless delusion obtains the condition of the path.
The commentary on the Section on Conjoined (Saṃsaṭṭhavāra) is finished.
6. Commentary on the Section on Associated (Sampayuttavāra).

392–400. Regarding the statements "concordant," "associated," "conjoined," and "intermingled": since "conjoined" does not [apply] to that which is merely associated, both terms—being stated in mutual dependence upon one another—are restrictive of each other.
The commentary on the section on association is finished.
7. Commentary on the Analysis of the Section on Questions (*Pañhāvāra-vibhaṅga*).

401–403. To show those conditions by which the wholesome is a condition for the wholesome, the meaning is that they are shown in their proper sequence—that is, in the sequence of how they have arisen. "The wholesome [is a condition] for the wholesome" is merely an illustration;

by this it is meant that the wholesome is a condition for the wholesome and so forth, the unwholesome for the unwholesome and so forth, the indeterminate for the indeterminate and so forth, and the wholesome-indeterminate...
Regarding the phrase "of the wholesome, etc.," the entire classification beginning with that has been demonstrated; thus, taking all that has been demonstrated, he says:
"to show those conditions in their proper order.
Regarding the word *datvā* (having given), considering that the root *dā* here also carries the sense of purification (*sodhana*), he says: "having made it pure."

The intention is that the phrase "for them, that is the mind" refers to that *gotrabhū* consciousness which is capable of being called "for them," as it precedes the path of the once-returner and so forth.
However, the skill in insight is exclusively of the sense-sphere; thus, he defines the conditionally arisen state according to its plane.
"By that alone" means by way of the phenomena themselves, because it is a vision [of the truth], the intention being that it is a different teaching.
405. Relishing (*assādana*) is the function of lustful joy and of lust accompanied by joy; thus he said, "he both experiences and is lustful.
Delighting (*abhinandana*) is the function of craving (*taṇhā*) together with the function of rapture (*pīti*); thus he said, "by way of craving accompanied by rapture.
Delighting in views (*diṭṭhābhinandanā*) is simply [wrong] view itself. Here, however, taking only the latter sense, [the text says]: "of one who delights..."

It is said: "The view arises by way of [the notions] 'self' and 'belonging to self,' and so forth... However, it cannot be maintained that delight is exclusively delight in views, because of the statement:
"A state to be abandoned by cultivation is the object of a state to be abandoned by cultivation...
[and so forth]... one relishes and delights in lust to be abandoned by cultivation. Therefore, the former meaning [also holds].
It should be understood as "stated. Furthermore, regarding the two types of consciousness accompanied by joy (*somanassa-sahagata-citta*), it is also possible to construe the passage as follows:

for one who relishes those very states through the aforementioned joy and lust, and for one who delights in them through craving accompanied by rapture (*sappītika-taṇhā*) and through delighting in views among the four [types of clinging], view arises.
"By way of birth" means by way of the commonality of having well-practiced the life of a recluse (*sāmañña*).
406. "By way of having that as its object" (*tadārammaṇatā*) means by way of the state of having that as its object (*tadārammaṇabhāvena*). Here, the case ending has been elided.

Alternatively, since there is no state (*bhāva*) other than that which possesses a state, it qualifies the result (*vipāka*) by means of the state itself; the meaning is that the result has become the state of having that as its object.
This is not the case for sense-sphere results (*kāmāvacara-vipāka*), as it is with the results of the base of infinite consciousness and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Although it is established as a rule that "this is the action and this is the object," even though it exists, it was not mentioned.

However, because they share the same characteristic by virtue of having wholesome states as their objects, it should be understood that rebirth-linking and so forth, which have action as their object, are also shown by the mention of those [consciousnesses] that have that as their object.
Or, for one who says "in reverse order" or "by skipping one," [it implies] that in entering [the attainments] in direct order, for the most part...

It should be understood that the state of being an object for a proximate attainment has been shown. However, just as for one who enters attainment in reverse order or by skipping intervals, even a non-proximate attainment becomes an object, so too it might be for one entering in direct order.
Having stated, "The phrases beginning with 'of the knowledge of others' minds' (cetopariyañāṇa) should be connected later with advertence (āvajjanā)," [the text continues]: "Which..."
The meaning stated is "the adverting [consciousness] of these [wholesome aggregates], and of that [adverting consciousness].

If this were the case, it should also have been said "[of the knowledge of supernormal powers (iddhividhañāṇa)]. However, because wholesome aggregates do not become objects for the indeterminate knowledge of supernormal powers, that was not mentioned;

whereas they do become objects for the knowledge of others' minds (cetopariyañāṇa) and so forth, those were mentioned. Therefore, [this applies] to functional [states] such as the knowledge of others' minds and the rest.

The meaning should be understood as follows: by whatever advertence (āvajjanā) there may be, the wholesome aggregates are related to a wholesome object by way of the object-condition (ārammaṇapaccaya). 407–409.

Regarding the phrase "or by way of remorse (vippaṭisāra), etc.," the word "etc. includes the mere state of being undesirable in its own nature through the vision of danger (ādīnava), or it includes the various forms of intolerance (akkhanti).

410. By the passage beginning "The visible-object base [is related] to eye-consciousness," etc., it demonstrates that the indeterminate (abyākata) state serves as an object-condition for indeterminate states through the groups of consciousness which have fixed objects.
For since it is impossible to state everything, he provides an illustration by means of a single portion of phenomena within one continuity (santāna).

413–416. Wholesome consciousness belonging to the four planes is shown here by way of being the object-predominance condition (*ārammaṇādhipati-paccaya*), whereas that which arises conditioned by it belongs only to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*).

417. Emergence from a previously non-existent stream of consciousness is simply the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*); this consists of the life-continuum known as the "root-visitor" (*mūlāgantuka-bhavaṅga*) and the "object-attaining" (*tadārammaṇa*) life-continuum, as well as the natural life-continuum (*pakati-bhavaṅga*).
Regarding the phrase "conformity for the attainment of fruition by one in training" (*anulomaṃ sekkhāya phalasamāpattiyā*), in some instances—

Because it is not to be omitted from the attainment of the fruit of training (sekha-phala-samāpatti), there is nothing further to be said; thus, having extracted this specific fruit-attainment—namely, the wholesome state of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana-kusala) as "fruit-attainment"—he says:

"As 'fruit-attainment,' [it refers] to the attainment of the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala-samāpatti). Regarding the phrase "sense-sphere functional states (kāmāvacara-kiriya) for both types of emergence," here, immediately after the functional state...
Whatever is to be said regarding the emergence with that as its object has already been stated in the *Cittuppādakaṇḍa*.
Both of these... [omission] ...are twelve; this is stated by way of the mind-consciousness element accompanied by joy (*somanassasahagata-manoviññāṇadhātu*).
However, as for the functional consciousness of determining (*voṭṭhabbana-kiriya*) accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhāsahagata*), it pertains to the ten aforementioned consciousness elements.
It should be understood that there are twelve [types of consciousness] for one who performs a mental-constituent (manodhātu) functional (kiriyā) action.
423. The connection is: "having penetrated all forms of success which depend upon meritorious actions such as giving.
However, this should not be taken as an absolute rule; that is to say, the restriction that "only strong volition is obtained, not weak volition" should not be accepted as an absolute certainty.

The intention is that it should not be grasped as being firm. Why? Because [the condition] matures by warding off obstacles for either a strong or a weak [kamma] for which an opportunity has been made;
and because it cannot be said that "if it produces any kind of result, it is not a decisive support" (upanissaya).

Showing this, he says: "For when an opportunity has been made," and so forth. However, in the section on the analysis of questions (*pañhāvāra*) within the *Vipākattika* (Triplet on Resultant), in the negative portion:

Because the kamma-condition is mentioned separately [in the text]—as in the passage: “A state subject to ripening is a condition for a state that is a result by way of object-condition, by way of decisive-support-condition, and by way of kamma-condition”—and because it is stated in the negative section of the question-set regarding the triad of feeling:
“With the absence of root-cause, object, and decisive-support conditions, there are eight [answers].”
It can be said that "even some kamma that produces a result (vipāka) is not a decisive support condition (upanissaya-paccaya).
Or, in that context, "contrary" (viruddha) means contrary to that [result]; or alternatively, "viruddha" is the reading. "Humiliation" (omāna) is the humiliation occurring in another person.
"Lust" (rāga) is the craving of sensual lust (kāmarāga-taṇhā) that occurs by way of coloring; [as it is said]: "May my eye be thus in the future time..."
"Thus, 'form' [refers to] the craving and aspiration that consists in the fixing of the mind toward the acquisition of what has not yet been acquired; this is the distinction between these [terms].
Regarding the phrase "among them, another as well": the meaning is that one kills some other living being besides those previously mentioned.

Or, by way of repeatedly commanding, they say that even the volition of the command that occurred previously receives the designation "matricide" because it is similar to the act of killing a mother. This same method applies here in the case of "by two blows" as well.

For just as... [etc. ...it is said that "one arouses faith by means of giving based on lust"; this is stated with the underlying intention (*adhippāya*) that one gives a gift depending upon lust, and thereby arouses faith through the act of giving based on lust.

Just as there is the statement "one gives a gift depending upon lust" and so forth, so too is it the case that lust and the other [defilements] serve as the decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*) for faith and the other [wholesome qualities]. This is what is meant.

It shows this. By showing bodily pleasure and so forth together as one, it should be understood that what is demonstrated is that these do not function as conditions individually, but rather even when combined.
"Precisely because they are conditions by way of being supportive" (upatthambhakattena) means that by this he shows: unlike in the previous sections, [they are not conditions] in that manner.
In this context, "arising by way of condition" is spoken of; however, it refers to the state of being a condition for those various phenomena that have arisen from those respective conditions.

Furthermore, it is not the case that postnascent aggregates do not act as conditions by way of providing support; therefore, this postnascent condition is included here in accordance with the forward order (anuloma).
427. "Volition is a condition even for the physical basis" means that it is a kamma-condition even for that which has become its own support; this is the intended meaning.

But why, in this section on conditions, are the questions ending with the "pair based on two roots"—namely, those concerning dependence, presence, and non-disappearance—not extracted as they are in the previous section on conditions?
Because they are not obtainable. For in that [previous] case, the teaching was primarily concerned with the produced (the effect). And [here], the skillful...
Since it is possible for indeterminate states and wholesome states arising together to have both wholesome and indeterminate conditions, it is said:
"With a wholesome and an indeterminate state as condition, wholesome and indeterminate states arise.
For what is intended there is merely the arising of the conditioned state from whichever of those two conditions may be present.

There is no state of being a condition for both [the wholesome and the indeterminate] simultaneously. However, because this teaching is primarily concerned with conditions, it is not stated that "wholesome and indeterminate states are a condition, by way of support, for both wholesome and indeterminate states," since such supports and so forth are not found to exist for both together.
Thus, it says: "Wholesome and indeterminate states are a condition, by way of support, for a wholesome state and for an indeterminate state. And so on.
The commentary on the analysis of the section of questions (*pañhāvāravibhaṅgavaṇṇanā*) is finished.
Regarding the forward calculation for the arrangement of the section of questions: 439.

It was stated, “But here, even that which is pre-arisen (*purejāta*) is obtained”; if this is so, why was it stated as “likewise” (*tathā*)? It is because of the commonality of the mere number “three.”
440. “With the exception of investigation, the remaining predominance conditions are dissimilar,” this initial reading should be understood by way of illustration.

However, since [the author], instead of giving an illustration with a single dissimilar object for the root condition, mentions the immediately preceding condition and so forth, thereby showing all [of them] to be dissimilar, therefore the faculty and path conditions are also dissimilar.
"They should be shown" means that they recite: "With the exception of wisdom (paññā), the remaining states are dissimilar [to it] with respect to the conditions of predominance, faculty, and path.
Likewise, this is because of their presence or absence as root-conditions (hetupaccaya) and their presence or absence as co-nascent and other types of conditions. [Objection:

Is it not the case that, just as the conditions of predominance, faculty, and path do not exist for the roots excluding non-delusion (amoha) when they function as root-conditions, so too [they do not exist] for those excluding wisdom?

Is it not the case that because the dominant condition (*adhipatipaccaya*) and others are dissimilar, and likewise because wholesome and other roots possess the state of being a root-condition but lack the state of being a fruition-condition (*vipākapaccaya*), there must be a dissimilarity among fruitions that exclude the root-condition?

It need not be so; for within the aggregate of mind and mental factors accompanied by both types of conditions, while they possess the state of being a root-condition, they lack the state of being a fruition-condition. This is just as in an aggregate accompanied by the root and co-nascent (*sahajāta*) conditions.

Even though there is the presence of factors excluded from being roots (*hetuvajja*), there is no absence of the state of being a conascence-condition (*sahajātapaccaya*) for those roots in their capacity as root-conditions;

thus, it was not stated that roots have a dissimilarity (*visabhāgatā*) with conascent factors excluded from being roots. It is the same here as well. This same method applies to the dissociation-condition (*vippayuttapaccaya*) too.

Furthermore, since conditions are spoken of only in relation to that which has arisen by way of a condition, [the distinction is made] by way of the existence or non-existence of such a state at the moment of arising through a condition.
When "homogeneity" (sabhāgatā) is being discussed, its "heterogeneity" (visabhāgatā) by way of different moments cannot be predicated of that very same thing.

Regarding the phrase "wholesome investigation" (kusalā vīmaṃsā), this should be stated as "having wholesome investigation as its dominant influence" (kusalā vīmaṃsādhipatī). For an investigation that has not become a dominant factor does not constitute a dominant condition (adhipatipaccaya).
441–443. "But if the dissociation condition (vippayuttapaccaya) enters, the other two are obtained"—this is the original reading.
Regarding the statement, “A wholesome state [is the cause] of both the wholesome and the indeterminate,” this is not possible;

therefore, they recite it as: “The wholesome [is the cause] of the indeterminate, and the indeterminate [is the cause] of the indeterminate—thus two [cases] are obtained. Regarding “in cases where the count is fewer”:

the meaning is, “in those cases where, when certain items are included, the count becomes smaller. This refers to cases where the count is fewer, such as three, two, or one, or in the case of mutual relations (*aññamañña*) and so forth.
The meaning is that, by way of those [factors] entering [the classification], even what is deficient from a triad receives the designation "one" according to how it is obtained.
"Without fruition" (*avipākāni*) means that their fruition has not been seized (*anāmaṭṭhavipākāni*); it does not mean they are devoid of a cause for fruition (*vipākahetu*).
In that context, "all of them are indeed co-nascent fruitions" (*sahajātavipākā cevā*) means that all those which were stated to be co-nascent, arisen through conditions, are likewise [fruitions].
The meaning is: "both the resultant [matter] and the matter co-nascent with the resultant.

Regarding the phrase "and the matter originated by that," it should be understood that even the *kaṭattā-rūpa* (matter produced by past karma) during rebirth-linking is included by the term "originated by that.
They also read: "resultant matter, matter originated by that, and *kaṭattā-rūpa* are found. In the fourth [case], "only matter originated by resultant consciousness," here too, it is the same.
This is the method. Furthermore, they also read:
"And [it includes] matter produced by kamma. "In this way too" means according to the method stated in the passage beginning with: "Among these combinations, however, the very first ones...

Now, among those combinations, whichever condition stands as the primary factor, that [condition] is presented according to the sequence of obtaining [the result] in its entirety, less entirely, less than that, and least of all.
"Occurrence" (ghaṭanā) is said [to refer] to the complete acquisition of those things arisen from conditions through the sequence of their complete acquisition;
likewise, this sequence should be understood for cases of partial acquisition and so forth.
The section based on the cause is finished.

445. "He will speak of it as having a support by way of the object" means that this is not a formulation by way of an object that is actually present; with this intention, he says, "or else, by way of the object alone. 446.
However, co-nascence together with object-predominance, and object-predominance together with co-nascence, are not found.
This is because, just as co-nascence and prenascence are both a single supporting condition (*nissaya-paccaya*) and a presence condition (*atthi-paccaya*), [so too are these two].
Thus it is said because there is no single instance where both the co-nascent (sahajāta) and the object (ārammaṇa) conditions function as the dominant condition (adhipatipaccaya).

For while the state of being a support (nissayabhāva) and the state of being non-disappeared (atthi-avigatabhāva) are common to the co-nascent, the prenascence-support (purejāta-nissaya), and so forth, the state of being a co-nascent object-dominant (sahajāta-ārammaṇādhipati) is not so common.
For a co-nascent factor becomes a dominant factor by way of its own simultaneous occurrence, without having entered into the state of being an object.
The one [the co-nascent] is an assistance by virtue of its very existence, while the other [the object] acts by inclining the mind toward itself by way of being an object.
Furthermore, the co-nascent is an assistance through its mere presence, whereas the other is so even when past or future solely by way of being an object.

Therefore, since the co-nascent and objective conditions possess distinct intrinsic natures—just like the co-nascent and objective predominance conditions—they do not both share the status of a predominance condition in the same way.

For that very reason, it is not stated in the *Pañhāvāravibhaṅga* [of the Paṭṭhāna] that "wholesome and indeterminate states are a condition for a wholesome state by way of the predominance condition," and so forth.
447–452. Prior to the combinations of those with nutriment, there are those without nutriment belonging to the path, by way of the commonality of energy, consciousness, and investigation.

The combinations involving the faculty condition (*indriya-paccaya*) should be stated as follows: seven [combinations] consisting of predominance, conascence, support, faculty, presence, and non-disappearance;

three consisting of predominance, conascence, mutuality, support, faculty, association, presence, and non-disappearance; three consisting of predominance, conascence, support, faculty, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance;

one consisting of predominance, conascence, support, result, faculty, presence, and non-disappearance; and one consisting of predominance, conascence, mutuality, support, result, faculty, association, and non-disappearance.
"One: predominance, conascent, support, resultant, faculty, dissociated, presence, non-disappearance—this is one.
Why are those [other conditions] not mentioned? Because there is no other predominance that has become a faculty apart from nutriment and the path.
For mental predominance is nutriment, and energy and investigation are the path; there is no other predominance existing as a faculty for which [the other conditions would apply].
By way of this [classification], there would have to be combinations of the faculties that are both without nutriment and without a path;

therefore, without stating those, these [combinations] are stated only as being with nutriment and with a path, for the purpose of showing that mental dominance and the others are exclusively with nutriment and with a path.
And among those "with a path" (samaggaka) combinations, two conditions are found, whereas among those "with nutriment" (sāhāraka), only one is found; thus they are called "with a path."

These would have been mentioned earlier. However, those accompanied by faculties (*saindriyaka*), which are to be distinguished by the paths of nutriment, were stated later according to their sequence.

In the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), however, "on account of similarity" means on account of having a common agent (*samaggakatta*) or, alternatively, because they are immediately preceding material phenomena (*anantararūpa*).

457–460. “The wholesome and the indeterminate [are conditions] for the indeterminate: four”—this is stated by bringing in even the two-rooted [formula] under the wholesome roots themselves, in order to show that the wholesome serves as a condition for that which is accompanied by the indeterminate.
Regarding the phrase “in the indeterminate, the physical basis (vatthu-rūpa) also,” this should have been stated as “the matter produced by karma (kaṭattā-rūpa) also.
The original reading was: “In the second combination, in the response concerning the indeterminate, only the physical basis is obtained among material phenomena.”
Since material form consisting of the primary elements (*bhūtarūpa*) is also obtainable, they read: "The physical basis (*vatthu*) and material form consisting of the primary elements are obtained.

It was stated [in the previous section] that "in the fourth [consciousness], there is only mind-originated matter (*cittasamuṭṭhānarūpa*)," but it should rather be said: "mind-originated matter and matter produced by kamma (*kaṭattārūpa*) at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhikkhaṇe*).
Regarding the first of those [types of consciousness] accompanied by resultants (*savipāka*), [it is said]: "both the resultant itself and matter originated by resultant-consciousness. Here...
In the fourth [case], it is only that which is originated by resultant consciousness (*vipākacitta-samuṭṭhāna*);

here, it should be understood that even "kamma-produced matter" (*kaṭattā-rūpa*) is included under the term "originated by resultant consciousness. However, some read it as "and kamma-produced matter" (*kaṭattā-rūpañca*).

In this context, among the combinations based on the roots of co-nascence, mutuality, support, result, association, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance, the combinations involving cause, kamma, jhāna, and path have not been applied; [this applies] to those [factors] already mentioned.

[The conditions are] with the exception of nutriment among the presence, non-disappearance, and root conditions; and with the exception of dependence, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance among the predominance and faculty conditions.

Why is this? For when those [conditions] are applied, only immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhamma*)—such as the roots and so forth—which constitute a portion of each respective arising of consciousness, are obtained as conditions.
Therefore, the combinations formed by them in the "root-based" and other groups are exactly like those described [previously], because they lack any admixture of material phenomena (*rūpa*).

They are not stated as being "easy to understand. However, when nutriment is joined with the "not-disappeared" (atthi-avigata) conditions, and the support and other conditions are joined with the predominance and faculty conditions, these become mixed with materiality (*rūpa*).

Therefore, it should be understood that although the combinations are similar to those stated under the roots of predominance, nutriment, and faculties, they have been specifically joined here under the roots of "not-disappeared," "support," and so forth, for the purpose of making them clearly evident through the inclusion of nutriment, predominance, and the faculties.

462–464. Regarding the section based on dependence (*nissaya*), the original reading for the sixth [pair] states, “three, namely the wholesome and so forth, are those originated by consciousness. However, since the eye-base and so forth are obtained as conditions for eye-consciousness and so forth, they read: “and the indeterminate eye-base and so forth. 466.

Regarding the section based on decisive support (*upanissaya*), concerning the two types mentioned by way of natural decisive support (*pakatūpanissaya*), it is stated regarding the first: “worldly wholesome and unwholesome volitions are to be understood as conditions. However, supramundane volitions are likewise certainly to be included.

473–477. Regarding the phrase "the joy of the physical basis (vatthupīti) in rebirth-linking rooted in kamma": the intention here is that the aggregates alone should not be understood as the state of being produced by conditions in the same way as they are in the course of existence (pavatta).
Among the four [cases] stated by way of what is common to both resultant and non-resultant [matter], it is said in the first:
"mind-produced matter is obtained together with the immaterial (arūpa)"; however, matter consisting of past action (kaṭattārūpa) is also certainly obtained there.

But in this context based on action (*kammamūlaka*), why is it not stated: "With action as condition, there are two [conditions] for the object (*ārammaṇa*)"? And in the context based on the object (*ārammaṇamūlaka*), why is it not stated: "With the object as condition, there are two [conditions] for action"? Is it not the case that wholesome and unwholesome volition (*cetanā*), which is the object of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) and so forth, serves as both the action-condition (*kammapaccaya*) and the object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*) for those states?
And just as the physical basis (*vatthu*), being the object, functions by way of the object-condition and the support-condition (*nissayapaccaya*)...
Is it then to be said that karma also should be described as a condition by way of being an object-condition (*ālambana-paccaya*)? No, because the two types of conditionality are mutually exclusive.

For it is appropriate to say that a present base (*vatthu*), without relinquishing its status as a support (*nissaya-bhāva*), is a support-condition both by virtue of being supported by that [consciousness] and by virtue of being the object of that which is supported by it. But as for karma—
However, when that [kamma] has been performed, it becomes a kamma-condition for the processes occurring [thereafter] by virtue of its having been performed and accumulated;

it does not do so by way of being an object (ārammaṇa). And it becomes an object-condition merely by virtue of being a sense-object, not by way of the mode of a kamma-condition—which is defined as the production of a fruit by creating a distinction within the mental continuum.
Therefore, the state of being a kamma-condition precludes the state of being an object-condition, and the state of being an object-condition...

And regarding the state of being a kamma-condition: it cannot be said that "having been a kamma-condition, it becomes an object-condition," nor can it be said that "having been an object-condition, it becomes a kamma-condition"; therefore, this was not stated.

And this is the nature of those bases, such as the eye, which are present and antecedent to the object, and which [function] together with the status of being an object-condition along with conditions such as the support-condition (nissaya-paccaya).

It should be said that they "exist," for this is the nature of past karma: that it cannot be said to exist simultaneously with the condition of the object (ārammaṇa-paccaya) as the condition of karma (kamma-paccaya).

Just as it is the nature of conascent (sahajāta), prenascence (purejāta), and support (nissaya) conditions that they can be spoken of as existing simultaneously with the condition of support, whereas it is not so for conascent, objective (ārammaṇa), and predominance (adhipati) conditions that they can be spoken of as existing simultaneously with the condition of predominance, so it is here as well.
478–483. “By way of the nutriment of consciousness that lacks a dominant influence” (nirādhipativiññāṇāhāravasena):
the intention is that this refers to the nutriment of consciousness for which there is no grasped state of dominance. “The physical basis declines” (vatthu parihāyati):
by way of the physical basis that still receives mutual support, this shows the decline of all kamma-born matter (kaṭattārūpa).

484–495. It was stated [in the previous section] that “in the third [jhāna], there are no immaterial faculties (arūpindriyāni) among the material ones. However, the eye and so forth are obtained in relation to eye-consciousness and the rest.

Therefore, regarding the phrase “six [factors] associated with the Path by way of energy (vīriya),” although investigation (vīmaṃsā) is also present there, it is said “by way of energy” because investigation is included as having the same course as energy by virtue of energy.

511–514. In the section based on dissociation (*vippayuttamūlaka*), it is stated regarding the tenth [condition] that "the wholesome and so forth are conditions for mind-originated matter" (*cittasamuṭṭhānānaṃ*); however, in the case of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), this also applies:
"The aggregates are conditions for the matter produced by kamma (*kaṭattārūpa*), and the physical basis (*vatthu*) is a condition for the aggregates.

Regarding the eleventh [condition], it is stated that "in rebirth-linking, the physical basis is a condition for the aggregates"; this is because the resultant condition (*vipākapaccaya*) has not been included therein. For whom...
The connection was made by way of the basis (*vatthu*); it is stated by way of its observation. Furthermore, the phrase “the aggregates and the basis” is indeed obtainable here as well.
In the original text, it read: “In the twelfth [case], during rebirth-linking, the aggregates [are the cause] of the kamma-produced material phenomena (*kaṭattārūpa*).

However, since mind-originated material phenomena (*cittasamuṭṭhāna-rūpa*) should not be excluded, it is stated: “In the twelfth [case], during the course of existence (*pavatta*), the aggregates [are the cause] of the mind-originated material phenomena.”
"...and of the kamma-produced material phenomena at rebirth-linking," they recite.
In the first combination of the section on the presence condition (atthipaccaya), it is stated:

"Conascence, prenascence, and postnascence conditions are obtained by way of the immaterial [states], bases, objects, great primaries, faculties, and nutriment. [It continues: "Nutriment and faculty conditions..."
And it should also be stated: "For sahajāta and the other [types of conditions] are not obtained by way of the faculties (indriya) and nutriment (āhāra).

Although it was said, "In the second [case], the postnascent (pacchājāta), kamma-produced (kaṭattā), and physical nutriment (kabaḷīkāra-āhāra) are not obtained," they recite, "The postnascent, kamma-produced, and physical nutriments, as well as the material life-faculty (rūpa-jīvitindriya), matter, and so forth, as objects (ārammaṇa) are also not obtained," in order to show that all of these are unobtainable.

The sixth [case] is stated by way of all the faculties (*indriya*). In the seventh, "from that, only the material life-faculty (*rūpa-jīvitindriya*) remains"—thus should their distinction be explained.
Regarding the phrase "Then, the eleventh," here "from that" means "from the ninth.
Regarding the phrase "In the thirteenth, the bases and objects (*vatthu-ārammaṇa*)," here the mention of "bases" includes the bases such as the eye and so forth; likewise in the fourteenth.
Regarding the phrase “vatthumevā” (only the basis), here too: the original reading was, “In the seventeenth [case], that same [basis] acts as a predominance by way of object;
in the eighteenth, that same [basis] acts by way of decisive support as an object.

However, this [term] “by way of decisive support as an object” is not a distinction from the seventeenth [case]; rather, in both the seventeenth and eighteenth [cases], it is simply the basis (*vatthu*) of the object.
Regarding the distinction of being a condition, they recite: "In the seventeenth [chapter], however, the eye and so forth are [treated] by way of the predominance of the object (ārammaṇādhipati);
in the eighteenth, by way of the decisive support of the object (ārammaṇūpanissaya) specifically for the physical bases. 519.
Because they are not restricted by any single co-nascent (sahajāta) condition in the same way as those that are co-nascent, they are called miscellaneous (pakiṇṇaka).

Regarding the phrase "have been stated": here, the prenascence, postnascence, nutriment, and faculty conditions have been stated in a scattered manner according to their non-commonality with the conascence and mutuality conditions.
In the section on the root of the object (*ārammaṇamūlaka*), the decisive support condition (*upanissaya*) should also be recited.
To show those [conditions] by which they are clearly perceived, he said, "of the root-of-cause and so forth," and so on, according to their respective names such as non-greed (*alobha*) and the rest.

However, since the states that serve as conditions—namely, root, object, predominance, nutriment, faculty, jhāna, and path—might not be recognized despite being so evident, he says, "There are only twelve roots," and so forth, in order to show them by way of their delimitation.

By this, he demonstrates that having determined, "The conditions are only this many," even that which is not currently manifest should be sought for within those very factors themselves. In this regard:
By the phrase "six objects," the predominance of the object (*ārammaṇādhipati*) is included because it consists in the state of having visible forms and so forth as its object;
therefore, excluding that, it is stated as "four predominances. The phrase "exclusively wholesome results" is applicable by way of the *aññindriya* among the faculties.
However, the phrase "exclusively unwholesome results" cannot be found, for even among the jhāna factors, there is suffering (*dukkha*).
Because the unwholesome itself is not a factor of fruition, the stability of consciousness (*cittatthiti*) is also a functional state of unwholesome fruition.
However, if the meaning were taken as "the fruitions of the unwholesome are 'unwholesome fruitions,'" then [this term] would apply to the faculty of pain (*dukkhindriya*) among the faculties;
yet, since there is no application of conditions based on the distinction between wholesome fruition and unwholesome fruition, it can be said that this is the intended meaning.
The forward counting in the arrangement of the Questions is finished.
527. Regarding the "explanation of the extraction of the reverse order":
"By one characteristic" refers to [the statement]: "A wholesome state is a condition for a wholesome state by way of the non-root condition."

The meaning is: "conditioned by a condition other than the root-condition. By including conditions other than the root-condition through the method of "inclusion by exclusion," there are eight [conditions].
Among them, a wholesome [state] is a condition for a wholesome [state] by way of three conditions, and for an unwholesome [state] by way of two.
Thus, when each respective condition has been established by way of its opposite, the remaining conditions are included within these very eight, beginning with the object-condition (ārammaṇa).
It should be understood that this is the characteristic to be known here: that [the conditions] are to be applied to the [twenty-four] conditions as appropriate.
Furthermore, among these eight conditions, those mentioned later are included within those not already subsumed by the preceding ones;

thus, *upanissaya* is mentioned by way of two others than the object-condition (*ārammaṇa*), *purejāta* by way of the basis-prenascence (*vatthupurejāta*), and [the rest] by way of co-nascence (*sahajāta*).
It should be understood that [the classification] is stated by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*) for karma; by way of another volition (*cetanā*) for action;

by way of co-nascence (*sahajāta*) for another type of physical nutriment (*kabaḷīkārāhāra*) for nutriment; and by way of both co-nascence and pre-existence (*purejāta*) for another material life-faculty (*rūpajīvitindriya*) for faculty.
And having done so, [it is said]: "A wholesome state is a condition for a wholesome state by way of object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*)."

It is stated simply as, "it is a condition by way of the co-nascence-strong-dependence condition," and because there is no other [condition], it is not stated that "it is a condition by way of the kamma-nutriment-faculty condition.
Therefore, it should be said: "Object-predominance is included within the object-condition.
However, regarding the question in the section on opposites (*paccanīya*) in the *Parittattika*: "An immeasurable state..."
In the statement, “It is a condition for an immeasurable state by way of the co-nascence-strong-dependence condition,” the object (ārammaṇa) is not mentioned;

this is because there is no exclusion of what has been included among those [conditions] stated as not being subsumed under the preceding ones, and because there is no object other than that which is the strong-dependence.
It is not, however, because the object of the object-strong-dependence (ārammaṇūpanissaya) is not included within the category of objects.

Although the presence (atthi) and absence (avigata) conditions are fivefold by way of conascence, prenascence, postnascence, nutriment, and faculty, the state of being a presence and absence condition applies simultaneously to conascent and prenascence factors, as well as to postnascent nutriments and postnascent faculties;
it does not occur separately, as is the case with the three dissociated conditions. Thus, "with respect to each one of the presence and absence conditions... [is said].
The phrase "established in six ways" is stated by including each one within the characteristics of the presence and non-disappearance conditions.

As for the statement, "The material faculty condition, moreover, is twofold according to the division of internal and external," it should rather have been stated as "according to the division of internal and external.
The phrase "for all twenty-four" means not only for sixteen, nor even for eight, but indeed for all twenty-four.

Meaning: Since there is an inclusion within the object condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya) of those conditions that have become objects—namely, the predominance (adhipati), decisive support (upanissaya), dependence (nissaya), prenascence (purejāta), dissociation (vippayutta), presence (atthi), and non-disappearance (avigata)—as well as within the prenascence condition itself, [the author], wishing to state the inclusion of a portion of the object condition and of those [other] conditions such as the decisive support within the object condition, says:
"In the object condition, the object condition itself is included..."
