“It goes, but not the remaining twenty-three,” he said. Regarding the fourth [condition], the *purejāta-paccaya* (pre-arising condition):

here, just as it was stated that “in the case of the *upanissaya-paccaya*, the object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*) acts as the dominant factor (*adhipati*”), so too could it be stated that “the object-condition acts as the pre-arising factor.
However, it may not have been stated because it can be understood by applying the same method explained there. Now...
However, it was not stated that "that which is other than the object is included by the inclusion of the prenascence condition.

If this were so, then since there would also have to be an inclusion of what is other than the object by the inclusion of the decisive support condition (*upanissaya*), one could not say: "The objective condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*) that functions as a predominance condition is included within the decisive support condition.
Thus, it would be improper to state that.
Regarding the questions on "Yesu pañhesu" ... [and so on] ... up to "only one condition has come": here, the word *eva* (only) should be brought forward and connected as "has indeed come.
By this, it is shown that in the twelfth and fourteenth questions, among the co-nascent (*sahajāta*) and prenascence (*purejāta*) conditions, not even one condition is absent;
rather, they have all come. Thus, it is demonstrated that by negating any one of those [conditions], those questions would also fail.
However, in the second and sixth questions where it is asked "in which," it is expressed in the singular by taking them one by one.
"Thus" means by way of object-predominance (*ārammaṇa-upanissaya*).

By this, it excludes the twelfth and fourteenth [questions], for although two conditions are mentioned in those as well, they are not by way of object-predominance. "By way of the remainder" refers to the remainder.

"It should be understood as being according to those [factors] that are obtainable. For in the cases of the thirteenth and fifteenth questions, even though the post-nascence condition is excluded, those questions are not obtained by way of nutriment and faculty; rather, they are obtained only by way of conascence.
And this alone is the defining characteristic here: the inclusion of all conditions within the eight conditions, in the sense of the most prominent (ukkaṭṭha).
It should be understood that this was stated with reference to all of the following: the section on questions; the section on the exposition of conditions shown by grouping those various conditions;
and whether or not each respective question is resolved when its corresponding condition is excluded.
For this very reason, it is said: "by this characteristic."

"In that context" refers to the various classifications and the [twenty] omissions. The statement "nineteen conditions are shown by means of three conditions" is said with reference to the conditions available in the case of "not-root-condition" (*na-hetu-paccaya*).

However, this presentation of conditions is stated by way of the common characteristic of all negative conditions (*paccanīya*), and not merely for the purpose of showing the conditions available specifically in the case of "not-root-condition."
And having done so, in the section on the analysis of questions regarding the root-duad (*hetudukapañhāvāra*) under the negative aspect, it is stated:

"A state that is a root is a condition for a state that is a root by way of object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*), by way of conascence-condition (*sahajātapaccaya*), and by way of decisive support-condition (*upanissayapaccaya*).
Otherwise, in the demonstration of the conditions available here under the heading "not-root-condition" (*nahetupaccayā*), [the phrase] "by way of conascence-condition" would not have been included.

It might be said [that this is redundant]; therefore, it should be understood that here too, because the extraction of conditions (*paccayuddhāra*) is stated by way of including all conditions that can be obtained, twenty conditions are shown by means of three [other] conditions.

Regarding what was stated, "In this regard, here is the detailed exposition" (*vitthārakathā*): having spoken the detailed exposition regarding the classification therein, he shows the deficiency [of the previous summary] by saying, "In that... (*tasmiṃ*).
"But regarding the conditions... [etc.]... we shall explain those later," he said. 528.

Likewise, in the four questions concerning the unwholesome (*akusala*) and so forth, it should be understood that this was stated with reference to the absence of anything other than those very conditions already shown among the wholesome (*kusala*) and so forth, because those respective conditions were demonstrated by those respective conditions. For it is not the case that "the unwholesome... [is absent].
In the passage, “Dhamma is a condition for wholesome dhamma,” three conditions are shown by means of two conditions;
however, there are only two, because even for the indeterminate, the unwholesome is not an object-predominance condition (*ārammaṇādhipati-paccaya*).

As for the conascent conditions (*sahajāta-paccaya*), they do not exist here because the physical basis (*vatthu*) is mixed in; thus, it is by way of the non-conascent physical basis condition (*asahajāta-vatthu-paccaya*).
Because they have been included by way of being co-nascence conditions (*sahajātapaccaya*), he shows that [the bases] do not function as co-nascence conditions along with them;
however, he does not preclude the status of pure co-nascence conditions for those [mental factors] themselves.

But showing that the term "co-nascent" (*sahajāta*) was stated specifically to distinguish that very support (*nissaya*) and so forth by which they become conditions along with the physical basis (*vatthu*), he said, "Therefore, of those... and so on.
But why has this exposition of conditions not been made by way of those four—namely, the object, decisive support, kamma, and presence conditions—which include all conditions within them?

Because it would be difficult to discern the classification of the presence condition when mixed with unmixed [conditions]. For if it were stated simply as "it is a condition by way of the undifferentiated presence condition," it would not be possible to know: "What..."
"Either by way of a pure co-nascent presence condition (*sahajāta-atthipaccaya*), or by way of a presence condition consisting of the pre-nascent, post-nascent, nutriment, or faculty;
or else by way of a mixed [condition] consisting of co-nascent and pre-nascent, or mixed with post-nascent and nutriment, or mixed with post-nascent and faculty.

Furthermore, when the specific types of presence conditions—beginning with the co-nascent—are being stated according to their own nature, [one should consider] where there are pure co-nascent and so forth...

Regarding the state of being a condition (*paccayabhāva*): where the conditionality of pure factors is shown, it is done so by such phrases as "is a condition by way of co-nascence" (*sahajātapaccayena paccayo*);
and where the conditionality of mixed factors is shown, it is made easy to understand by including them through such phrases as "co-nascent and prenascent" (*sahajātaṃ purejātaṃ*).
Therefore, co-nascence and the others are included for the purpose of demonstrating the specific distinctions within the presence-condition (*atthipaccaya*), and by that [means], all conditions—
The inclusion [of all conditions] is shown within the four conditions.
But why is *nissaya* not mentioned alongside *sahajāta* and *purejāta*, or *vippayutta* not mentioned alongside *purejāta* and *pacchājāta*, by way of being specific types of the *atthi*-condition?
Because they cannot be so stated; for instance, *nissaya* cannot be stated as being identical to *sahajāta* and *purejāta*.
Because pure and mixed states must be distinguished on account of their status as support-conditions (*nissaya-paccaya*), they are not differentiated from the presence-condition (*atthi-paccaya*);

furthermore, since the dissociation-condition (*vippayutta-paccaya*)—like the presence-condition—is characterized by co-nascence, pre-existence, and post-existence, it should be distinguished [from the presence-condition], and thus it should not be treated as identical to it.
Moreover, while co-nascent and pre-existent states may be mixed, they possess the status of a presence-condition; however, [the dissociation-condition does not].
It is the state of dissociation. Likewise, there is the state of being a presence condition (*atthipaccaya*) for both conascent and postnascent mixed [factors].

For it will be said: "A state that is not acquired by clinging and is not subject to clinging is a condition, by way of presence condition, for a state that is acquired by clinging and is subject to clinging, and for a state that is not acquired by clinging and is not subject to clinging—[namely] through conascence and postnascence"; however, it is not a dissociation condition (*vippayuttapaccaya*).
Therefore, since mixed states are not included in the category of dissociation (vippayutta), it is not appropriate for that [dissociation] to be a specific type of presence-condition (atthipaccaya);
thus, one should not say even more than this.

But surely, the co-nascent condition (sahajātapaccaya) must also be distinguished by its causes (hetu) and so forth; therefore, like the support (nissaya) and dissociation conditions, it too [should be considered] as a specific type of presence-condition.
Is it not to be said [that they are not simultaneous]? No, because they cannot be distinguished from conditions that are contradictory [to their own arising].

For while the presence-condition (*atthipaccaya*), being dissociated from its support (*nissaya-vippayutta*), must be distinguished by conditions contradictory to the time of its arising, the co-nascent factors are not so. This is because causes (*hetu*) and the like are indeed co-nascent;
they are not contradictory to the time of arising.
The commentary on the Negative Extraction is finished.
The commentary on the Negative Enumeration.
The commentary on the Root of "Not-Root" (na-hetu).
532. Regarding the statement, "The pure object-condition (ārammaṇapaccaya) ceases," there is no purpose in including the word "pure" (suddha).
For when the object stands as an adverse condition, the object-condition—which serves as the dominant condition (adhipatipaccaya) and so forth—necessarily ceases.
Alternatively, the term "pure" indicates that among the eight conditions, it is exclusively the object-condition that ceases, and not the others.

"Of eleven" means by way of eleven [factors] among the fifteen that are included under "conascent" (sahajāta), excluding mutual condition (aññamañña), resultant (vipāka), associated (sampayutta), and dissociated (vippayutta).
"Those" indicates that those factors included within "conascent" do not receive an answer in any other mode once that [conascent condition] is excluded;
however, those not included therein—such as object (ārammaṇa), predominance (adhipati), prenascence (purejāta), and support (nissaya)—do.

"They obtain [them] by way of the mode of object (ārammaṇa), etc."—although these alternatives would not be possible if that [conascent condition] were excluded because there is no such thing as a conascent condition (sahajāta-paccaya), nevertheless, the intention is that these may still be obtained by way of the conditions of dependence (nissaya), presence (atthi), and non-disappearance (avigata). This is shown by the passage beginning with "But since... and so forth.
Even if the co-nascence condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*) does not exist, he shows that those [other] modes are also not applicable because these [conditions],

such as support (*nissaya*), do not exist apart from the states that possess the co-nascence condition; and because those which are excluded when co-nascence is excluded are here excluded by the exclusion of co-nascence itself, those other modes are likewise not obtained.
"Excluding the co-nascence condition (sahajātapaccaya)"—by this it should be understood that the co-nascence condition which serves as a support-condition (nissayapaccaya) and so forth is excluded.

With reference to the meaning that among the wholesome and indeterminate states occurring from a wholesome state, the wholesome is a mutuality condition (aññamaññapaccaya) for the wholesome, he said: "Because of the existence of occurrence by way of states that are mutuality conditions."
"Those phenomena which have entered into the inclusion of mutual conditionality" means that those phenomena, when being designated as conditions for their respective conditionally arisen states,
have entered into the inclusion of mutual conditionality (*aññamañña-paccaya*) by way of being the mutual condition for those phenomena being designated as their own conditionally arisen states.
Having established that "the wholesome is a mutual condition for the wholesome," [it follows that] wholesome and indeterminate phenomena enter into the inclusion of mutual conditionality.
The intended meaning here is that a condition exists by means of states that constitute a whole through those that constitute its parts.

Furthermore, regarding the wholesome [state], it is only by means of wholesome states acting as mutual conditions for wholesome and indeterminate states—through such relations as co-nascence (*sahajāta*) and so forth—and not otherwise;
thus, when mutual conditionality (*aññamañña-paccaya*) is excluded, that category must be said to be lost.

"It is a portion of four aggregates" is said with reference to co-nascence (*sahajāta*). For food and faculties that are not co-nascent are only portions of the aggregate of material form (*rūpakkhandha*). "Those" refers to those states that are dissociated conditions (*vippayuttapaccaya-dhamma*). 533.

It was written, "in order to show the enumeration of conditions by way of the 'Two Rooted' and so forth," but it should rather have been stated, "in order to show the enumeration of the negative (counter) relations. For the enumeration of the negative section has already been shown.

It is stated: “But here, fruition (vipāka) is not obtained because it is combined with the non-decisive-support condition (naupanissaya-paccaya). However, even for fruition, karma serves as a condition—though not as a decisive support—as a kamma-condition;
this is what has been shown in the triad on fruition. The commentary on the root of non-root (nahetu-mūlaka) is finished. 534.

Regarding the phrase “seven, five, three, two, one,” these are delimited enumerations; thus he says that the answers showing delimited enumerations by way of the limits of seven and so forth have been presented in the root of root (hetu-mūlaka).

538. Regarding the phrase "three [factors] in the absence of dependence condition (nanissaya-paccaya) and absence of strong-dependence condition (naupanissaya-paccaya), but not in the absence of postnascence condition (napacchājāte)," this extracts the enumeration stated as "three in the absence of postnascence" from the ten-rooted scheme by condensing the root-sets.

It is stated that "among those, kamma-produced matter (kaṭattārūpa) and nutriment-produced matter (āhārasamuṭṭhāna) are the conditionally arisen"; however, in two cases it is the resultant (vipāka), while in the third case, the body produced from those [nutriments] is indeed the conditionally arisen.

545. Regarding the phrase "the indeterminate is a co-nascent condition for the indeterminate": this was stated with reference to these two cases—namely, that the immaterial-indeterminate is a condition for the immaterial-indeterminate, and the material-indeterminate is a condition for the material-indeterminate.

However, when the material-indeterminate acts as a co-nascent condition for the immaterial-indeterminate, and the immaterial-indeterminate acts as a co-nascent condition for the material-indeterminate, it is indeed a dissociation condition (vippayuttapaccaya).
“‘The indeterminate [state] is [conditioned] by the indeterminate through co-nascence, nutriment, and faculty; thus there are five’—this is what should be stated.

Regarding the phrase “In the absence-condition, with the exclusion of the root-cause condition, there are nine,” it is said that “from the single-root basis up to the end of the one-root basis, they are obtained by way of proximity, natural (pakata), and decisive support conditions.
However, when the presence-condition is excluded, among the remaining eight conditions, there are co-nascence, prenascence, postnascence, nutriment, and faculty.
It should be stated that these [three] are obtained by way of those three which remain, namely, the object (ārammaṇa), the decisive support (upanissaya), and kamma (kamma).
For in all cases, among the eight conditions, whichever have been excluded are set aside, and whichever remain, it is by way of those that the respective sections are obtained;
this is the characteristic here. "As far as even the support (nissaya)..."

The meaning is that not only by remaining on the object alone, but even by remaining as far as the support (nissaya), two conditions should not be made in the non-predominant (naupanissaya). For indeed, among the preceding nine, all nine are obtained;

however, in the case of the non-predominant, seven conditions are excluded by way of the exclusion of the presence-object-predominant (atthi-ārammaṇa-upanissaya) during the course of existence (pavatta). Of what remains...
By way of karma, there are only two.
The commentary on the reverse-order enumeration is finished.
The commentary on the forward-and-reverse order.

550. *Sadisa-vārā* means "corresponding sections. For among the eleven [conditions] obtained through mutual relation (*aññamañña*), namely "the wholesome for the wholesome" and "the unwholesome for the unwholesome," these two are identical to those seven obtained through the root-condition (*hetu*);

however, because of the absence of their respective objects (*attha*), they are not corresponding. Alternatively, according to the expression and the meaning, as appropriate from the enumeration (*uddesa*).
And by saying "from the exposition," he means "similar sections" with reference to their complete identity in every respect. 551.

"With reference to rebirth-linking mind-and-matter": this refers to the causal mental state (hetu-nāma-paccaya) at the moment of rebirth-linking and the physical basis (vatthu-rūpa) as the conditionally arisen (paccayuppanna).
Regarding the phrase "the three, beginning with the wholesome, [are conditions] for mind-originated matter," here [the term] "indeterminate" (*abyākata*)...
And "of the kamma-produced materiality" should also be stated here. 556.

In the section based on predominance (*adhipati*), "ten in the absence of root-cause" (*na-hetu*) is stated by way of both types of predominance; "seven in the absence of object" (*nārammaṇe*) refers to co-nascent predominance (*sahajātādhipati*);
and "seven in the absence of conascence" (*nasahajāte*) refers to objective predominance (*ārammaṇādhipati*). Thus it is in all instances.

When each respective condition has been rejected and each respective condition has been applied during the combinations, one should carefully observe which phenomena decline and which remain when the condition stands as the root.
Then, by way of those phenomena that remain and serve as conditions for others, the enumeration should be extracted. This applies to the combinations stated in the forward order (*anuloma*).
For, having set aside those [conditions] joined as the root-conditions, the remaining conditions are joined by way of their opposites;
thus, it is possible to understand here that the conditions established by way of their opposites are either equal to or fewer than [the root conditions].
The commentary on the Positive-Negative (Anuloma-Paccanīya) is finished.
Commentary on the Negative-Positive (Paccanīyānuloma) [631]:

Regarding the phrase "having excluded the counting of even the excessive count along with the deficient count," this means that one excludes the counting of the excessive count— which stands in the negative order— along with the condition being joined in the positive order.
This is the intended meaning. Furthermore, the equality with a lower number in the calculation of diminution is not absolute.

For when the calculation of the "not-root" and "not-object" dyads is joined with the dominant condition, although it is diminished by the lower number, it is not equal to the number obtained for the dominant condition; rather, it is even lower than that.
He said: "But this does not apply to all combinations.

Since the presence of the root (hetu) and other factors is evident when they stand in opposition to the support (nissaya) condition and do not abide in the positive sequence of co-nascence (sahajāta), he shows that it is indeed not evident when they do not abide in the co-nascent state, saying:
"The object-prenascence (vatthupurejāta) does not abide in the positive sequence."

He said: By the phrase "in nutriment" and so forth, he shows this: while the [mental] states associated with jhāna and the Path do not abide in a state of conformity when standing in opposition to co-nascence, they do abide when nutriment or the faculties stand in opposition; thus the root-conditions and so forth also abide.

However, among all jhānas and Paths, those that consist of four aggregates abide together with those that consist of one part of the four aggregates, and those that consist of the four aggregates abide together with those associated with them.
It should be understood that this shows the position [of the factors] in accordance with all of them; for the others, there is simply nothing further to be said.
Regarding "predominance and decisive support," it shows the position in accordance with those that include the object-condition as well.
As for the statement, "In the case of the faculties, 'one' refers to the material life-faculty," this means that among the eye-faculty and so forth, the material life-faculty...

Furthermore, it should be stated: "and by way of nutriment. As for the phrase "having proceeded in order, three [are] dissociated," this has been extracted in some manuscripts as "three [are] dissociated among the nine roots, etc.," for the purpose of making it clear.
And regarding the statement "these two are by way of the posterior-nascent faculty," it should rather be stated: "And these two are by way of the posterior-nascent nutriment and faculty."
The commentary on the rootless [states] is finished. 636.

Regarding the statement, "Under the condition of not-mutuality, there are three under the condition of root," namely the wholesome and so forth that originate consciousness—here it should also be stated, "and the materiality produced by past karma at rebirth-linking.
He speaks thus with reference to the commonality of the number [of instances], meaning "the three" as stated under the condition of root.

Likewise, regarding "three in kamma," these are stated as being exactly as they were under the root-cause (hetu). However, in all cases among the conditions (paccaya), the specific distinction must be observed.

Regarding "three in predominance" (adhipati): the mutual-cause (aññamañña-hetu) and the object-condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya) are not included; thus, "three in predominance" refers to those same three already mentioned above under the root-cause. 644.

And just as "as below"—that is, just as in the section based on the non-root-cause (nahetu-mūlaka), one proceeds up to "not-resultant" (navipāka) and then only one each is taken for nutriment and faculties—so too here, in the sections based on the non-object (nārammaṇa-mūlaka) and so forth, only one each is taken; this is the intended meaning.
648. Regarding the phrase "Wholesome and unwholesome volitions of various moments [are conditions] for matter originated by kamma":

here, it should also be stated that they are conditions "for results" (*vipākānaṃ*). Among the nutriments and faculties, three are similar to co-nascence because they are conditions for matter as well;

among the jhāna factors and path factors, etc., three are similar to roots because they are conditions for the immaterial [factors] alone—this is how the intended meaning should be understood. By the word "etc. (*ādi*),...
And it includes such passages as: “With non-dissociation, not-root, and object conditions, there are three [results] through the predominance condition,” and so forth.

As for the phrase “but that which...”: the meaning is that even if a certain condition is obtained in its own place from the perspective of direct order (anuloma), if it is not taken there but is instead taken later from the perspective of reverse order (paccanīya), that condition subsequently receives its application from the direct order alone. For example:

However, among the [combinations] beginning with those rooted in non-cause (nahetumūlaka), when nutriment (āhāra) is combined with the faculties (indriya), there is the attainment of the fivefold [knowledge] by way of the faculties;

and when the faculties are combined with nutriment, there is the attainment of the fivefold [knowledge] by way of nutriment. Therefore, having not applied any one of these in the reverse order, they are applied in the direct (anuloma) order.

Likewise, among those rooted in non-arising (noatthi) and non-disappearance (novigata), when decisive support (upanissaya) is combined with kamma, there is the attainment of the fivefold [knowledge] by way of kamma; and when kamma is combined with decisive support, there is the attainment of the fivefold [knowledge] by way of decisive support.
Among these, it should be understood that one [of the conditions] has been applied in the positive (anuloma) order rather than being applied in the negative (paccanīya) order.
Thus, in this negative-positive scheme, all roots are divided into two ways, excluding nutriment, faculties, decisive support, and kamma.
The commentary on the negative-positive order is concluded.
The commentary on the triad of the wholesome is finished.
2. Commentary on the triad of feeling:

Feeling, material form, and Nibbāna, however, are treated as independent triads [not included in the previous categories], along with the rules regarding "dependent upon" (paṭicca) and so forth, and the terminology for the conditioned phenomena that arise.

They are not obtained [there]. However, in the six sections beginning with the "Dependent" (paṭicca) section, since the arising of triplets of phenomena from causes such as the root-cause (hetu-paccaya) has been stated, it should be understood that they are obtained there by way of being conditions such as the object-condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya), according to their respective suitability. 10.
By the statement, "But the co-nascent and other conditions are the graspers of all material phenomena," that which was omitted even in the "Wholesome Triplet" (kusalattika) is [now] included.

It should be understood that by placing "co-nascent" (*sahajāta*) at the beginning because it encompasses both material and immaterial phenomena, and by using the word "beginning" (*ādi*) as a term encompassing all immaterial phenomena,
he demonstrates the deficiency of the objects and other factors that encompass all immaterial phenomena by way of their being conditionally arisen. By this,

one should see the deficiency of the four universal [mental states] among the "all-encompassing" categories (*sabbatthika*), such as the "all-encompassing triads" (*sabbatika*), which are deficient in the threefold wholesome [roots].

It has been shown. By the phrase "and arising even without the postnascence condition," he demonstrates the deficiency in the direct order (anuloma) of the postnascence condition and its presence in the inverse order (paccanīya).

Alternatively, by the term "co-nascent, etc.," it is stated that conditions do not exist without co-nascent states—those rooted in co-nascence and bound by co-nascence—which pervade [the relationship] through the "dependent" (paṭicca) and other such relations.

Why, however, is it that only those [factors] which are conascent conditions and which grasp all material phenomena are excluded, and not that which is postnascent—being neither a conascent condition nor a grasper of all material phenomena?
Stating the reason for this, he says: "Because they do not arise without the conascent conditions and so forth, and because [the postnascent condition] exists even without the postnascent condition."

He said, "Because it does not arise without its co-nascent [factors], etc. Therein, "without its co-nascent [factors], etc. means without those factors bound by co-nascence that encompass all material phenomena.

Alternatively, he states the reason right here for why there is a deficiency only in the case of those bound by co-nascence, and not in the case of the post-nascent factor which is bound by co-nascence:
"Because it does not arise without its co-nascent [factors], etc., and also because it does not arise without the post-nascent condition."
He said, “From arising. This, however, is shown to mean that even those [factors] bound by co-nascence which encompass all material phenomena are excluded. 17.
The same method applies to non-resultant [states] as well; this is merely an illustration of the method, not a demonstration of the general characteristics of the condition and the conditioned.
For, in dependence on states associated with pleasant or neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, [there arise] states associated with those feelings.
Rootless functional states and the delusion co-arising with doubt and restlessness—this is the method here.

Regarding the statement "one in non-disassociation," which was stated in reference to the formless realm by way of adverting, it should be understood as being stated by way of adverting and rootless delusion.
25–37. In the positive-negative method, the wholesome triad should be counted in the same manner as the methods beginning with the root-rooted.
This was stated with reference to the commonality of being graspable by way of having one root, two roots, and so forth, and not with reference to a commonality of numerical count.

This same method applies to similar cases hereafter. However, the passage beginning with "of a mind-moment arising without a root cause" (ahetukassa pana cittuppādassa) was stated with reference to the "rootless" (nahetu) section;
rather, "of a mind-moment arising without a root cause and of delusion" (ahetukassa pana cittuppādassa mohassa ca) should have been said here.

Furthermore, because delusion (*moha*) that lacks a root-cause has no status as a predominance-condition (*adhipati*), there is no possibility for a positive concomitance (*anuloma*) from the perspective of a predominance-condition based on a non-root-cause.

"Even by reversing" means that even though the object (*ārammaṇa*) and so forth are situated in front [in the sequence], one should join them with what follows—namely, "from the non-root condition and the non-predominance condition, there are three in relation to the object. This is the meaning.
39. In the section on questions (*pañhāvāra*), the phrase "grief arises" indicates that which is associated with it.
In the *Upanissaya-vibhaṅga*, the statement "one arouses conceit and adopts views regarding the five factors beginning with faith;

this should be stated for those [factors], but not for the remainder" is said for the purpose of showing the course of the text, and not because conceit and views do not arise through greed and the other [defilements]. This is also the case in the *Kusalattika*.
For regarding lust and the other [defilements], the text does not state, "it arouses conceit" or "it grasps a view.

However, in the passage, "Lust, hatred, delusion, conceit, views, and longing are conditions for lust, hatred, delusion, conceit, views, and longing by way of decisive support condition (upanissaya-paccaya)," it is stated that conceit and views serve as decisive supports for lust and the others.
It should be understood that the same applies here as well.

"But one commits a raid on a village or a raid on a town with a consciousness associated with pleasant feeling" refers to the plundering of villages and towns by means of a consciousness accompanied by joy and conjoined with greed. 62.
"Of the pure [factors]" indicates the non-difference between the conditions and the conditionally arisen factors. These include the prenascence and postnascence [relations].
They do not exist here [in this context]. For it is not the case that pre-arisen or post-arisen immaterial phenomena serve as conditions for other immaterial phenomena;

thus, the intention here is that those very immaterial phenomena associated with pleasant feeling and so forth—which are the subject under discussion in this triplet—are not conditions for immaterial phenomena by way of being pre-arisen, because they lack the state of being pre-arisen. Likewise...
Because they do not exist as posterior-born, or because, having been posterior-born, they do not [so] remain.
63–64. "By way of delusion accompanied by predominance" means: by way of delusion together with the state of predominance.
83–87. "Under the condition of non-root... pe ... under the condition of non-strong-dependence, there are eight": under the conditions of non-root, non-object, and non-strong-dependence.
"Eight": thus he extracts [the number] by way of abbreviation.

"Should be understood by way of asynchronous kamma-condition" (nānākkhaṇika-kamma-paccaya-vasena) is said with reference to the possibility of the asynchronous kamma-condition in all the remaining eight [cases], excluding this one: "associated with a painful feeling, [conditioned by] that associated with a pleasant feeling. For it is not a co-nascent condition (sahajāta-paccaya).
It is found in all eight [types of consciousness], yet it occurs only in three.
The commentary on the triad of feeling is finished.
3. Commentary on the Triad of Resultant States.

1–23. Regarding "dependent on a state that is resultant" (*vipākadhammaṃ paṭicca*) in the Triplet of Resultants (*Vipākattika*): it means dependent on a state that is a result (*vipāka*). For even in a compound, this very same meaning is expressed; thus, it is written in the text as a compound. 24–52. Regarding the analysis (*vibhaṅga*) of the statement:
"Dependent on a state that is neither-resultant-nor-a-state-that-is-resultant, a state that is neither-resultant-nor-a-state-that-is-resultant arises by way of non-resultant condition":
"Dependent on the great elements (*mahābhūta*), mind-originated derived matter (*upādārūpa*) [arises]."
Only this much was stated; it was not stated that it is "kamma-produced matter" (*kaṭattārūpa*).
That was not stated because the purpose was to show the arising [of mind-produced matter] dependent on the great elements (*mahābhūta*), which arises dependent on the aggregates (*khandha*).

For there is no arising of kamma-produced matter here dependent on the aggregates such that its arising dependent on the great elements would need to be mentioned. [This applies] during the course of existence (*pavatti*).

However, the "matter produced by kamma" (*kaṭattārūpa*) of non-percipient beings is already shown by this very statement: "derived matter produced by kamma dependent on the great primary elements (*mahābhūta*) of non-percipient beings.

And having established it thus, because the matter of non-percipient beings shares the same destiny (*samānagatika*), "matter produced by kamma" was not separately mentioned under the nutriment condition (*āhārapaccaya*) during the course of existence (*pavatti*). For even that [matter] lacks the nutriment condition at the moment of its arising (*uppādakkhaṇa*).
"Arises" means it "should be extracted.
The commentary on the Triplet of Resultant [States] is finished.
4. Commentary on the Triplet of Clung-to [States].

15. In the "Triplet of Clung-to" (Upādinnattika), regarding the statement: "Dependent on a state that is not clung-to and not subject to clinging, a state that is not clung-to and not subject to clinging arises, but not by way of the predominance condition" (*adhipatipaccaya*), this indicates that it should not be said that even in the case of objective-predominances (*ārammaṇādhipati*) which are themselves not devoid of being a predominance, [the result] arises by way of both types of predominance conditions; for this is its specific nature.

72. Regarding the statement, “Edible food, which is both clung-to and subject to clinging, is a condition for the body, which is both clung-to and subject to clinging, by way of the nutriment-condition”:

herein, the nutritive essence (*ojā*) contained within the material phenomena born of kamma is a condition for those very same kamma-born material phenomena by way of sustaining and supporting them—just as the material life-faculty (*rūpa-jīvitindriya*) is for the kamma-born body—but not by way of generating them. This is the meaning.

This is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*. However, given this meaning, when it is said that "states that are both acquired and subject to clinging, as well as those that are neither acquired nor subject to clinging, are conditions by way of presence for a state that is acquired and subject to clinging—namely, the postnascent faculties"—one should also say "nutriment" (*āhāra*) here.
This is provided that the nutritive essence born of karma (*kammaja-ojā*) is the nutriment-condition for all subsequent material phenomena.

If that were so, it would not be right to say: "Edible food, which is both appropriated and subject to appropriation, is a condition for the body, which is unappropriated but subject to appropriation, by way of nutriment-condition.

Yet this has been said; and that was said with reference to the nutriment-condition for the unappropriated but subject-to-appropriation body of the nutritive essence (*ojā*) that is itself appropriated and exists within one's own continuum, even though it has not yet been swallowed. And this being the case, [the statement] "that which is both appropriated and subject to appropriation..."

And the statement, “States that are not acquired by clinging and not conducive to clinging are a condition, by way of presence-condition, for a state that is not acquired by clinging but conducive to clinging,” this question too should be raised by way of postnascent nutriment;
therefore, because the acquired nutriment that has been swallowed is absent at the supramundane moment, the word “nutriment” is not mentioned in the first question among the two-rooted [questions].
And the second question was not raised because there is no absence of the possibility of the other, the acquired nutriment, occurring in the sense-sphere existence (kāmabhava);
rather, it was stated with reference specifically to the acquired nutriment existing in the bodies of frogs and so forth that has been swallowed:
"Acquired-and-to-be-acquired edible nutriment is a condition, by way of nutriment-condition, for the body that is both acquired-and-to-be-acquired and not-acquired-but-to-be-acquired."
Among those who speak, the argument of the stronger is more persuasive. For it is not the case that frogs and other creatures do not cause the expansion of the belly merely by being swallowed;
nor is it the case that strength does not arise [thereby], nor that a specific difference in form is not perceived. [The formula:
"A state that is not acquired and not subject to clinging is related to a state that is both acquired and subject to clinging, and to a state that is not acquired and not subject to clinging..."

Just as in the answers to the questions beginning with "A state is related to a state by way of presence-condition (atthipaccaya) through co-nascence (sahajāta) and post-nascence (pacchājāta)," which are stated here in groups of one root ending in groups of two and three, [it is said] here, as at the end of the second group, starting with: "A wholesome state is related to a wholesome and indeterminate state by way of presence-condition through co-nascence. Etc.
It is understood that an answer is obtained. However, for the sake of easy comprehension, the answer there was given solely by way of co-nascence (*sahajāta*).

In the negative (paccanīya), because [a factor] is obtained when there is no negation of co-nascence itself, and not obtained when there is negation, the [answers] were extracted there starting from the condition of co-nascence and ending with the single-rooted dyads; but here, by means of these...
In the exposition, it is shown that among the specific types of presence conditions—such as co-nascence and others—a single phenomenon may serve as a single presence condition for many phenomena.
For indeed, a single phenomenon is a presence condition for a single phenomenon by means of only one specific type of presence condition;
it may also be a presence condition for many phenomena by means of either one or many types. Likewise, many phenomena may be a presence condition for a single phenomenon, or many for many.

Regarding the conditionality of phenomena that have arisen together (*paccayuppannadhammā*), among the five specific types of presence-condition (*atthipaccaya*), the presence-condition exists together with both the co-nascent (*sahajāta*) and the pre-nascent (*purejāta*). It exists with the post-nascent (*pacchājāta*) when there is no difference in the nature of the phenomena, but not when there is a difference in their nature.

If it were otherwise, [it would follow that] "phenomena that are both acquired by clinging and subject to clinging (*upādinnupādāniya*), and those that are neither acquired by clinging nor subject to clinging (*anupādinnānupādāniya*), [would be conditions] for that which is acquired by clinging and subject to clinging..."
Regarding the statement, "The faculty is a condition for the mental state by way of presence-condition through post-nascence," it might also be said that it is "by way of co-nascence.
For there is no single state of being a presence-condition for both co-nascent and post-nascent elements born of kamma— even when supramundane states are obtained in the same moment—
because co-nascent and post-nascent phenomena possess distinct and mutually incompatible natures.
It should be understood that this was not stated [in the original]. And having done so, it is said in the reverse order: "In non-faculties, twenty-two.
For otherwise, even when excluding the faculties, since that question would still obtain [answers] by way of conascence and post-nascence, one would have to say "twenty-three.
Co-nascence is a presence condition only together with conascence, and not with the others; that too...
The object-condition (vatthu-purejāta) is only that which is co-existent with the physical basis (vatthu-sahita), not the other kind. For in the Question Section of the *Kusalattika*, it is stated:

"In the case of the non-dissociated condition, there are five [conditions] by way of presence"; however, in the *Sanidassanattika*, it is stated: "In the case of the dissociated [condition], there are twenty-two.

Furthermore, that which is extracted there in the analysis of presence (*atthi-vibhaṅga*) and in the enumeration of conditions (*paccayuddhāra*), ending with the triple-root and single-root sections, refers to the object-prenascence (ārammaṇa-purejāta) that is co-existent with the physical basis.
"By way of co-nascence" means "by way of being a condition together";

thus, the postnascent [condition] occurs only with nutriment and faculties, and not with other states or by way of co-nascence; nutriment occurs only with postnascent faculties, and faculty occurs only with postnascent nutriment.

Having thus observed this classification of the presence-condition (*atthipaccaya*), the questions that obtain in the positive order (*anuloma*) as well as in the negative order (*paccanīya*) and so forth should be extracted.
The commentary on the Triplet of the Clung-to (Upādinnattika) is finished.
6. Commentary on the Triplet of Applied Thought (Vitakkattika). 22.

In the positive section of the "Dependent" (paṭicca) chapter of the Triplet of Applied Thought, there are twenty-three [answers] for each of the seven root-questions in relation to predominance (adhipati), in their respective order.
Seven, five, three, one; three, three, one—thus twenty-three. In the case of mutuality (aññamañña), eight, seven, five, five, three, four, three, one—thus [twenty-five].
In the case of prenascence (purejāta), eleven; three, four, two;
in the second and third root-duads, one, one—thus [sixteen]. Likewise for repetition (āsevana). The other reckonings are similar to those for root-cause (hetu) and object (ārammaṇa).

31. Regarding the absence of the predominance condition (*adhipati-paccaya*) in the first question of the reverse order (*paccanīya*), after stating, "In dependence on aggregates that are without applied thought but with sustained thought (*avitakka-vicāramatta*), there is a predominance [condition] that is without applied thought but with sustained thought," the answer is then given by way of specific instances, such as, "In dependence on one resultant aggregate that is without applied thought but with sustained thought," and so forth, rather than without distinction. Why? Because [the answer refers specifically to] those aggregates without applied thought but with sustained thought, excluding the resultants (*vipāka*).
Because they possess predominance exclusively. However, as for the resultants, only those that are supramundane possess predominance, not the others;
therefore, they have been stated separately. And here, the inclusion of the predominance of the supramundane resultant should be understood as occurring within the first category itself. 38.

Regarding the section rooted in non-repetition (*nāsevanāmūlaka*), the phrase "together with the resultant that is without applied thought but with sustained thought" refers to this root by means of the terms "without applied thought but with sustained thought" and "without applied thought and sustained thought."

It is stated that when one joins [the factors] together with those that are without applied thought (*avitakka*), the method of following the text (*pāḷigamana*) should not be treated as if it were identical.

Here, both similarity and, for the most part, dissimilarity should be observed. For in that [previous section on the formless realm], one should join "in the formless realm, [there is] only sustained thought without applied thought" with "here, [there is] resultant [consciousness] only with sustained thought without applied thought," and so forth;
this is the distinction here. And this [section] follows immediately after the analysis of non-repetition (*nāsevanavibhaṅga*).
It should be written; it is not [to be written] immediately after the section on *jhāna*, though it is written in some manuscripts.

Regarding the first combination in the section on conditions (*paccayavāra*), in the *Dumūlaka* [text], it is stated for all seven questions in the first [section]: "having combined occurrence (*pavatti*) and rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). 49.

In the negative formulation (*paccanīya*), seven instances of delusion (*moha*) are to be extracted from the root-terms (*mūlapada*) as follows: in the terms such as "with initial application and sustained application" (*savitakka-savicāra*), etc.

The meaning is that, in those seven questions to which the very first term is applied as the final member, seven instances of delusion (*moha*) are to be extracted. In the negative section of the Questions Chapter (*Pañhāvāra-paccanīya*):

"A state without applied thought but with sustained thought (*avitakkavicāramatta*) [is related] to a state without applied thought but with sustained thought by way of object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*), co-nascence-condition (*sahajātapaccaya*), decisive-support-condition (*upanissayapaccaya*), and kamma-condition (*kammapaccaya*)."

The reading “condition” (paccayo) is seen in some manuscripts; however, because it is already included under the decisive support condition (upanissaya-paccaya), it cannot be said that it is a “kamma-condition.
For in the negative section of the *Upādinnattika* chapter, it is stated:

“A state that is not acquired by clinging and is not subject to clinging is a condition for a state that is not acquired by clinging and is not subject to clinging by way of the co-nascent decisive support condition (sahajāta-upanissaya-paccaya).”

Only this much was stated. And in the section on the negative analysis of the *paritta-ttika* (the triad of limited states), it is also stated only as follows: "A sublime state is a condition for a sublime state by way of object, conascence, and decisive support conditions.
Furthermore, it is precisely because of these [factors] that karma which is without applied thought but with sustained thought (*avitakkavicāramatta*), immeasurable, and sublime, is not weak.
"It is known by means of words.
The commentary on the Triplet on Applied Thought is finished.
8. Commentary on the Triplet on What is to be Abandoned by Seeing.

Regarding the triad of states to be abandoned by vision (*dassanena-pahātabba-ttika*), the statement that "a state to be abandoned by vision is not a condition for a state to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāya-pahātabba*) even by way of a single condition" should be investigated according to the method analyzed in the *Paṭiccasamuppādavibhaṅga*.
The commentary on the triad of states to be abandoned by vision is concluded.
[The following are] the verses for counting the questions.
The triads of the wholesome and so forth are to be understood by their beginning, middle, and end;
likewise, the dyads by their beginning and middle, and the triads by each of their three parts.
Taking each of these as a root, there are seven sets of seven questions for each.
Just as there are forty-nine [answers] for the single condition,
there are one thousand one hundred and seventy-six questions for the simple conditions.
This method applies to the direct order (*anuloma*) and the inverse order (*paccanīya*), and not otherwise.
Half of the heap multiplied by the heap is the total of that heap;
or half of the heap plus one, multiplied again by the heap.
Thus, there are two hundred and seventy-six [combinations] beginning with the dyads and triads rooted in the cause.
In this [work], there are twenty-four questions and three thousand five hundred [sub-questions].
Since their method is based on the pure (suddhika) formula rather than on individual conditions,
this enumeration is for those multiplied by twenty-four together with the pure formulas.
The three characteristics amount to twenty-two thousand seven hundred and fifty-two;
these are the questions combined in the direct order (anuloma).
The method of calculation for the reverse order (paccanīya) is the same as that for the direct order.
But having set aside the remainder, one obtains two pure methods (naya).
There are fifty-six questions, along with one hundred and thirteen lakhs [of sub-questions],
calculated within the four sections on Dependent Origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) among the methods of questioning.
Multiplied by seven, in the wholesome triad there are two hundred and ninety-five thousand,
four thousand, and nine hundred and one lakhs.
Multiplied by twenty-two, across all the triads, there are twenty crores.
Three hundred and twenty-four [combinations] are to be understood for the triplets.
This concludes the *Tikapaṭṭhāna*.
As for the single conditions, however, by taking nine times nine, there are one hundred and sixty-two.
In the first section on the *hetu-duka*, there are questions according to the first method (*naya*) in the pure (*suddhika*) category.
In the method based on the *hetu* and other roots, where each is joined with the divisions of *duka* and so forth,
there are two thousand four hundred and eighty-four questions.
When these are multiplied by twenty-four, they become the "pure" figures here in the direct order (*anuloma*):
nine hundred thousand, eight hundred and thirty-two.
Thus, in the reverse order (*paccanīya*), there are two [sets], which, when deprived of the pure figures, result in four [thousand].
Nine million nine hundred and eighty-three thousand two hundred.
When those are multiplied by seven, they become fourteen million two hundred and seventy thousand;
from that, in the "pair of causes," there are one million six hundred and seventy-two thousand.
One hundred times that is one hundred and twenty-seven thousand two hundred;
and then sixty-one million one hundred and sixty thousand questions.
This is the *Duka-paṭṭhāna*.
In the *Dukatikapaṭṭhāna*, there is the insertion of the triads into each individual dyad;
by multiplying that by sixty-six, those become one hundred and sixty-six dyads.
The questions obtained from the dyads of causes, when multiplied by those [triads], result in the very same number of triad-terms.
In the *Dukapaṭṭhāna*, the questions and their enumeration should be known as follows:
nine hundred and fifty-two thousand, ninety-nine million,
six hundred and thirty-three lakhs, and one hundred thousand koṭis.
The *Dukatika-paṭṭhāna*.
In the *Tikaduka-paṭṭhāna*, having divided each of the triplets (*tika*) into two hundred varieties,
it should be known that twenty-two times two hundred varieties are obtained in the wholesome triplet (*kusalattika*).
The *Tikapaṭṭhāna* and *Dukapaṭṭhāna* consist of two hundred and eight questions more than four thousand and twenty million, plus another six million and four thousand million.
In the *Tikapaṭṭhāna*, there are sixty-three triplets, each having its own subdivisions;
when multiplied by those [subdivisions], they constitute the questions for the wholesome triplet, which are the same as the questions themselves.
There are twelve hundred and fifty-four thousand, nine hundred and ninety-nine.
Sixty-one lakhs and twelve hundred koṭis [of combinations] constitute the *Tikapaṭṭhāna*.
Each [term] in the *Dukapaṭṭhāna* has two less than two hundred times the number of those [combinations]; by means of these, [the combinations are calculated].
The questions, derived from the pairs of causes and increased by their various permutations,
amount to fifty-eight thousand six hundred and one hundred and nine, eleven crores,
and further, three billion three hundred million.
The Singlefold Exposition.
When the questions are combined across all six types of the Positive Exposition (anuloma),
they total thirty-six million, eight hundred and seventy thousand.
Six lakhs, forty-nine novem-millions (nine hundred and ten millions), seven hundred and nine koṭis—
these questions, multiplied by four, constitute the Samantapāṭhāna in its fourfold division.
Three hundred and forty-four thousand,
one hundred and thirty-eight million, seven hundred and eighty-seven lakhs,
and eight hundred and thirty-eight thousand— such is the calculation.
The Verse Summary of the Enumeration of Questions for the *Paṭṭhāna*.
The Root Commentary on the *Paṭṭhānapakaraṇa* is completed.
Thus ends the Explanation of the Obscure Terms composed by the Venerable Master Ānanda.
The root commentary on the Abhidhamma is completed.
